Hello, it is wonderful to see you again. Before we start, how are you feeling today compared to where we left off last time? Additionally, have anything specific come up in your life since our last chat that you'd like to bring up, or is there a particular topic you want to focus on today?

Uh, hi. I'm okay, I guess. Still pretty anxious, honestly. There's been a couple more shifts at the cafe since we last talked, and each one feels heavier. I keep replaying every little thing I do wrong in my head. I don't know if there's one big thing to focus on—it just all feels like it's piling up.

Hearing that every shift feels heavier and that the replays are piling up really shows how exhausting it is to carry that weight alone. Since everything seems to be building up, let's see which part of this pile is causing the most distress right now—is it the fear of getting fired, or perhaps the constant self-criticism while you're working?

I think it's the constant self-criticism, honestly. Like, I'll be taking an order and my mind just goes, "You're messing this up, they can tell you're not supposed to be here." Then by the end of the shift, I'm convinced my manager is just waiting for the right moment to let me go. The fear of getting fired is bad, but the voice in my head all day is what really wears me down.

That internal voice sounding like a boss who wants you to quit immediately is incredibly draining, and it makes total sense that you feel worn down carrying that kind of relentless judgment all day. When your mind turns simple tasks into threats of immediate dismissal, it creates a heavy pressure cooker effect that builds up over time. Could we take a closer look at one specific moment today where that voice got particularly loud, and what exactly happened right before it spoke up?

Alright. Um, I guess yesterday there was a moment. A customer asked for a refill on their coffee, but I was already carrying a tray of dirty dishes. I had to tell them I'd be right back, and I saw this little sigh they let out. Right then, that voice went, "See? You're slow. You're annoying them. The manager saw that, too." I just froze for a second and felt my face go red. I don't even remember finishing the rest of my shift clearly after that.

That moment freezing you mid-task and leaving you feeling red-faced is incredibly painful, especially when it's triggered by something as minor as a customer's sigh. It sounds like that sigh became the spark that ignited your entire belief system about being incompetent and unwanted. When you notice your face heating up and realizing you've lost track of the rest of your shift, what do you tell yourself in that split second to try and ground yourself back into the present?

I don't really tell myself anything to ground myself. I just kind of... keep moving, like I'm on autopilot. I try to look busy so nobody talks to me, and I avoid making eye contact with my manager until I feel like I can breathe again. I guess I just hope nobody noticed, but I'm pretty sure they all did.

It takes immense effort to keep moving on autopilot while hoping nobody notices the way you're avoiding your manager; that constant vigilance to hide your vulnerability is incredibly taxing. When you're on high alert scanning for judgment, it naturally drains your energy reserves and makes every interaction feel like a performance you're failing. If we could slow down for just a moment, what is one small piece of evidence from that shift that contradicts the idea that everyone saw you fail and decided you were done?

I mean... the customer did get their refill eventually, and they didn't complain to my manager. And my manager actually told me to take my break on time, which she doesn't always do if she's annoyed with someone. I guess that's... something. It doesn't feel like enough to cancel out the rest, though.

Those are powerful pieces of evidence that stand in direct opposition to the story your brain is telling, and finding even one piece of support is a huge victory. It makes sense that the mountain of fear feels bigger than these individual facts, but let's look at the gap between what happened and what your mind predicted. If your manager was truly waiting for a reason to fire you, would she have given you permission to take your break on schedule, or would she have pulled you aside instead? How does knowing her actions contradict the "you are finished" narrative change the tightness in your chest right now?

Huh. I never really thought about it that way. She definitely would have pulled me aside if she was that angry. She's done it before with other people. I guess that does loosen things a little bit in my chest, yeah. It's just hard to hold onto that thought when I walk in tomorrow and see her face, you know?

It makes perfect sense that logic feels fragile when your body is screaming danger; seeing her face will almost certainly trigger that old alarm bell before you can catch up with the new reality. Our job isn't to eliminate the fear entirely tomorrow, but to create a tiny buffer so you can recognize the lie before it takes control. What if, the moment you walk in, you simply named her expression aloud to yourself—"She's just tired today, not judging me"—and then turned your attention to a task for thirty seconds instead of scanning for threats? Would you feel able to try that small experiment tomorrow?

I... I think I could try that. Just naming what I see and then focusing on a task for half a minute. It feels a little weird, like I'm tricking myself, but I guess it's better than spiraling for the whole shift. I'll give it a shot. What's the worst that could happen, right? I just... I'll try.

It takes real courage to admit that trying feels like a bit of a trick, but that doesn't make it any less valuable for breaking the cycle. Even if it feels unnatural at first, the act of naming her expression and anchoring your attention to a task gives your brain a chance to reset before the worst-case scenario takes over. I am so proud of you for agreeing to this small experiment, and I want you to know that if it feels overwhelming tomorrow, we can adjust the approach together. Does trying to name her fatigue and focus on a task for just thirty seconds sound like a manageable goal for tomorrow morning?

Yeah, it does. Thirty seconds I can handle. I'll just pick something simple, like wiping down the counter or checking the sugar caddies. And, uh... thanks. For saying you're proud of me. That's not something I hear very often. I'll let you know how it goes.

I want you to know that acknowledging your own bravery is just as important as anyone else validating you, and I am honored to be the space where you can hear it. Taking that thirty-second window to ground yourself before the shift even begins is a powerful step toward reclaiming your calm. Please remember to reach out anytime you need to unpack how that experiment lands, because we will navigate whatever comes up together.

I'll keep that in mind. It helps knowing I can come back and talk about it, no matter how it goes. Thanks for listening and not just telling me to snap out of it. I feel a little less alone in this, which is more than I felt when I walked in today.

Hearing that you finally feel a little less alone is such a meaningful relief, and I am so grateful you trusted me with that vulnerability. Remember, this space is exactly for bringing up whatever comes up, whether it's progress or setbacks—we will just figure it out together. I look forward to hearing how those thirty seconds went when you get home, and please take good care of yourself tonight.

Hello again, and thank you for being here. To start, could you tell me a bit about how you've been feeling since our last session, and what your mood is like right now? Based on what you shared before, it seems the fear around being seen in public has grown, so would you like to focus entirely on building confidence for going out today, or would you prefer to touch base quickly on calling your sister about the family reunion?

Well, if I'm being honest, I've been dreading coming here today because it means facing all this head-on. My mood has been pretty low, and I've spent most of the week in the house again, avoiding any plans that involve leaving. I think I'd rather focus on trying to build up the confidence to go out, because that's what's really holding me back from everything else, including calling my sister.

It takes real courage to admit how hard it is to face things head-on, and I want you to know that feeling overwhelmed doesn't mean you're doing anything wrong—it just means the fear is loud right now. Since you've chosen to tackle the public visibility fear, we can use that energy to explore exactly what thoughts come up before you decide to stay inside, so we can understand them better.

Thank you for saying that. When I think about going out, the first thing that hits me is this image of people turning to stare, and I just know they're thinking things like "What's she doing here?" or "She must be such a burden." It's like I can feel their eyes before I even leave the driveway.

Those images of judgment are incredibly painful, and it makes complete sense that they would make you want to stay hidden in your car to keep yourself safe. Before we dig deeper into how to challenge those specific words, could you tell me if this feeling of being judged happens every time you think about leaving, or is there a particular situation that makes it stronger?

It definitely happens every time, but I think it's worst when I think about going somewhere new, like a party where I don't know everyone. At the grocery store, I can kind of tell myself I'm just there to get things done and leave, but at a social event, there's no hiding or rushing out. All I can picture is being stuck in one spot while people whisper.

It makes perfect sense that your brain imagines you're trapped at a party with no escape, especially when you feel vulnerable in a wheelchair; that scenario feels much more threatening than a quick stop at the store. Since you mentioned parties are the hardest part, would you be willing to try a small experiment where we identify one specific situation or crowd size that feels slightly less scary than a large party but still triggers those judgments, or shall we start by examining the evidence behind those whispered comments right now?

I think examining the evidence behind those whispered comments might help me more, because that's the part that really eats away at me. I keep saying they're judging me, but when I try to think back, I honestly can't remember a single time someone actually said something cruel to my face. It's just this strong feeling I have, like I know what they're thinking even though nobody's said it out loud.

You are absolutely right to notice that gap between the intense certainty of what you *think* people are saying and the lack of any actual proof from others. It is exhausting carrying the weight of these invisible accusations when no one has ever voiced them, and that exhaustion is likely why the fear feels so absolute right now. Let's take a moment to acknowledge how heavy that mental load feels, and then gently explore whether there is any evidence—past or present—that contradicts the belief that everyone is actively plotting to hurt you.

You know, that's the thing that stops me cold—I can't really find any evidence that anyone's actually been cruel. My husband always tells me that people are probably just curious or maybe even looking out to see if I need help, but I always brush him off. I guess if I really think about it, there have been times when a stranger held a door for me or smiled, and I just assumed they were pitying me instead of being kind.

It is completely understandable why you would dismiss your husband's perspective when the alternative—a world full of cruelty—is so frightening to imagine. Reinterpreting neutral actions like a smile or holding a door as kindness requires stepping back from the immediate pain of the fear, which is exactly why those moments happen so rarely in your memory. Now that we've acknowledged how real that feeling of being judged is, let's shift our focus to gathering some fresh data: would you be willing to try a small exercise tomorrow where you note down three interactions you had, even just glances exchanged, and describe what actually happened versus what your fear told you to expect?

I think I could try that, even though the idea makes my stomach clench a little. Maybe I could start small, like just sitting on my front porch for ten minutes instead of going all the way to a store. I could write down what I expected people to think when they walked by, and then what I actually saw in their faces or heard if they said anything.

That is a wonderful compromise; starting with the safety of your porch allows you to practice noticing the difference between your prediction and reality without the pressure of moving through traffic. To make sure we capture that effectively, would you like to prepare a simple template for your notes beforehand, listing just two columns: "What I Thought They Were Thinking" and "What Actually Happened"?

That sounds like a good plan, having it set up before I go out there so I don't overthink it in the moment. I'll write "What I Thought They Were Thinking" on one side and "What Actually Happened" on the other, and keep the notebook right next to me. I'm still nervous, but at least I'll have something to focus on besides the knot in my chest.

Setting that notebook aside right next to you will give you a tangible anchor to hold onto when the panic tries to grab you. Would you be okay with us scheduling a quick check-in call for tonight or early tomorrow morning, so we can review what you noticed and discuss how the porch went compared to your expectations?

That would actually be really helpful, because I know I'll be second-guessing everything I wrote down by the time tomorrow comes. Let's do a quick call tomorrow morning, right after my husband leaves for work, so I can talk about what I noticed before my brain starts twisting it all around again.

That timing is perfect; catching those details before your brain fills in the gaps will make the evidence much clearer and easier to trust. I am really proud of you for taking this small step toward gathering facts instead of staying stuck in your worries, and I know we will have great results once we look at your notes together. Does that schedule feel comfortable for you, or would you prefer to set the exact time a bit further apart?

Tomorrow morning at around 9:30 works for me, that gives me enough time to settle in after he leaves and write down my thoughts from the porch. I think I'm actually a little curious now to see what I'll find, which is a strange feeling but not a bad one. I'll be ready for that call.

That curiosity is a fantastic sign of hope, and it proves you are ready to test your fears rather than hide from them. I believe tomorrow's call will be very rewarding as you compare your predictions with reality, and I am here to listen carefully to whatever you discover. Please take care today, and I will see you soon!

Thank you, I really appreciate that. I'll try to keep that curiosity alive and not let the fear talk me out of sitting on the porch. I'll talk to you tomorrow morning and share whatever happened, even if it's just me waving at the mailman. Take care.

You are very welcome, and I'm so glad we found that spark of curiosity within you. Remember that even a simple wave at the mailman is valuable data that could change your story. I look forward to hearing your findings tomorrow at 9:30 AM, and until then, please be gentle with yourself as you navigate those thoughts. Drive safely and have a calm day.

But then the thought came back anyway, like "well, that pause doesn't change the fact that I'm still single and will be forever."

That interruption felt strange because your brain is built on autopilot, so having to hit the brakes manually requires a lot of mental energy. Yet, the fact that the thought returned doesn't mean the exercise failed; it just shows that the old story is deeply rooted and needs consistent gentle nudging rather than one big knock-down. Since we have a few minutes left, would you be open to testing one small variation: instead of just pausing, could we try naming the thought aloud to ourselves internally during that ten seconds, like saying "The thought that I'll be alone is just a thought," to see if separating it from *you* feels easier?

That sounds kind of scary, to be honest. Like if I say it's just a thought, I'm pretending the problem isn't real or something. But... I guess that's different from saying the problem doesn't exist, right? I could try it. I mean, the worst that could happen is I feel silly talking to myself in my head.

You are absolutely right; labeling a thought as "just a thought" isn't denying the pain you feel, it's simply stepping back from the story to look at it objectively, much like watching a movie from the theater seat rather than acting the lead role. Many people initially feel silly doing this, but that feeling usually fades once they realize it actually reduces the power the thought holds over them. If you're curious, would you be willing to try silently saying "That's just a thought" for those ten seconds next time, keeping the tone calm rather than defensive?

Okay... I can try that. Calm, not defensive. I think part of me gets defensive because it feels like I'm betraying my own sadness by pushing it away. But I guess if it's just a thought, I'm not pushing away my feelings, just... giving them some space. I'll give it a shot on my walk home tonight.

That insight about "giving them space" rather than "pushing them away" is a powerful shift that honors your feelings while protecting your peace. It sounds like you have a clear plan for tonight: use that calm voice to step back from the story just for a moment. Before we close, does trying to name the thought with a neutral tone feel like something you can trust yourself to do, or does that still feel a little risky?

It still feels a little risky, like I'm tricking myself somehow. But I trust you when you say it helps, and I trust that I can at least try it without losing anything important. I'll give it a real effort tonight and see what happens.

It is completely understandable to feel cautious when changing a deeply held belief; trusting that you won't lose your reality is a sign of wisdom, not weakness. I am confident that even a shaky attempt to name the thought creates a tiny crack in the armor, allowing light to get in where it hasn't before. Let's circle back next time to see how that evening walk feels with this new lens. Does closing with that sense of safety feel right for us to end here?
Yeah, that feels okay. I'm a little nervous but also kind of curious to see what happens. I'll try to notice the thought and name it calmly, and I'll let you know how it goes. Thanks for today.

That mix of nervous curiosity is a perfect sign that you are ready to grow, and I appreciate your willingness to take that step forward. Please remember that if you find the calm tone feels forced, you can always drop back to just observing without naming it—the goal is consistency, not perfection. We will chat next time about how that evening went, and I look forward to hearing your results. Take care!

Hello again, I'm glad to see you. Last time we worked on separating the panic of the moment from the heavy belief of being a failure, and I noticed you mentioned feeling a bit lighter afterward. How has that been since we wrapped up? Did you get a chance to try the "three reasons" check when you looked at the reports this past week? Now that we are connected, could you help me decide what feels most important for us to focus on today, and let's prioritize it together?

Hey, yeah... I did try that "three reasons" thing a couple of times. It was... weird, honestly. Like, I'd look at a bad number and my brain would immediately just say "your fault," but then I'd force myself to write down three other possible reasons. The market was down, a client pulled out suddenly, stuff like that. It did sort of... quiet the noise for a bit, but by the end of the week, that heavy feeling just crept back in. I think what's bothering me most right now is how I can't seem to shake it for good.

It makes perfect sense that the relief was temporary; listing the other reasons bought you some breathing room, but once the immediate crisis passed, the deep-seated fear that you are solely responsible took the wheel again. That heavy feeling returning suggests the root belief is still driving the behavior, even when you successfully interrupt it temporarily. Since you've tried the "checklist" method and found it helpful yet insufficient on its own, should we spend today investigating why that original belief of "total responsibility" is so resilient when the surface-level distractions are gone?

Yeah... I think that's exactly it. When I'm actually doing the exercise, I can see the logic, but the moment I stop actively fighting it, my brain just goes right back to "you're the one who messed this up." It's like there's this default setting in my head that I can't delete. I guess I never really asked myself why that belief is so stubborn... I just assumed it was true because it felt true.

That "default setting" description perfectly captures what we call a core belief—a deep-seated rule your brain follows automatically, often because it formed early to keep you safe from pain. You are absolutely right that you haven't questioned *why* that rule exists or how much evidence truly supports it, which is why it feels so hard to erase even when you succeed at the surface level. Before we dig into that stubbornness, does the idea that this belief was likely built to protect you from disappointment ever feel familiar or relieving?

Huh... I never really thought of it like that—that it might be there to protect me. I always just saw it as me being honest with myself, you know? Like, if I don't take full blame, I might get lazy or miss something important. But... yeah, I guess it does feel less crushing when you frame it as something my brain cooked up to keep me from being surprised by failure. It's weirdly comforting, actually.

That is such a profound shift in perspective; realizing the belief was a protective mechanism rather than a harsh truth helps remove the shame attached to holding onto it. It reframes the "stubbornness" not as a personal flaw, but as an old safety system that is now reacting to a threat that doesn't quite match the current reality. Given how relieved you felt hearing that, does that protection-focused view feel like a better foundation for building a new, kinder way of thinking about these mistakes?

Yeah... it does feel like a better foundation. When I think of it as an old safety system, it makes me feel less like I'm broken and more like I'm just... running outdated software or something. Like, the program worked when I was a kid trying to avoid getting in trouble, but now it's just making me miserable at a job where nobody is even blaming me the way I blame myself. I think I'd like to work on building that kinder way of thinking, but I'm nervous I'll just fall back into the old habit.

That computer analogy is brilliant because it clearly shows the mismatch between the old program's purpose and your current environment; the code works for avoiding childhood trouble but fails miserably at modern professional risks. It makes total sense to feel nervous about falling back, since deleting a safety system is scary—you don't want to accidentally lose that protection when things go wrong. Let's spend the rest of our time designing a gentle upgrade plan that keeps the safety net while replacing the harsh "you're the sole cause" message with a more balanced one. Does the idea of keeping the protection but changing the warning sound like something you could actually try?

Yeah... I think I could try that. Keeping the protection but changing the warning sounds a lot less scary than just trying to shut the whole thing off. Like, I can still pay attention and care about my work, but maybe the message in my head doesn't have to be so brutal. What would that look like, though? How do I actually change the warning?

To change the warning without losing the protection, we need to swap the blunt command "This is your fault" with a softer, more accurate statement that acknowledges your effort while allowing for outside factors. Instead of erasing the vigilance that kept you safe, we can teach your brain to speak to itself like a supportive coach rather than a harsh critic. Could you try writing down a new phrase that says "I am caring deeply, but this result isn't entirely on me" and tell me if that strikes the balance you're looking for?

Okay... let me think for a sec. How about something like, "I did what I could with what I had, and the outcome isn't just on me"? That feels... a little less heavy. It still lets me care and take responsibility for my part, but it doesn't dump the whole weight on my shoulders. I think I could actually repeat that to myself next time I see a bad report.

That phrasing is a great compromise because it honors your accountability while removing the catastrophic assumption that you bear full responsibility for everything. By saying "what I had," you subtly remind your brain that circumstances vary, which acts as a buffer against the "default setting" of total blame. Before we lock this in as your new internal script, does repeating that sentence to yourself feel manageable, or would you prefer to try a variation that feels even softer to your voice?

No, I think that one feels right. It's honest but not crushing. I'll try it out this week and see how it sits with me when I'm actually in the moment. If it feels too stiff or fake, I can always tweak it a bit. Thanks for helping me get to this point—it feels like I have something real to work with now.

That is such a strong moment of clarity; having a sentence that balances honesty with kindness gives you a tangible tool to hold onto when the panic tries to rise. It's completely normal for the words to feel a little stiff at first—they are learning to become part of your internal dialogue just like a new muscle. Before we close, how would you like to handle the week ahead? Should we set a specific time to check in on how that new phrase is landing for you, or would you prefer to reach out whenever you feel it slipping back into the old habit?

I think checking in at a set time would be good for me. Knowing there's a specific moment coming up where I have to report back will keep me honest and make me actually try using it. Can we do the same time next week? That way I can give you a full week of trying it out, good or bad.

That is a perfect plan; having a dedicated check-in slot removes the uncertainty of "when" and ensures you get consistent support regardless of whether the experiment goes smoothly. Setting that same time next week gives you a clean window to reflect on the data without interference, which will make it easier to spot patterns in how that new phrase lands for you. Shall we schedule that meeting for the same slot next week, or would you prefer a slightly different day?
Same time next week works for me. I'll put it in my calendar and make sure I'm here, ready to talk about how it went. Thanks again—I actually feel a little hopeful for the first time in a while.

That hopefulness is the most beautiful part of all—it shows that this shift in perspective is finally taking root in your heart, not just your mind. Carrying that feeling into the week ahead is going to be incredibly empowering, and I'm so proud of you for trusting enough to try something new even when the old fears linger. I'll see you next week at the scheduled time, ready to celebrate whatever wins come up along the way.

Hello again, and I'm so glad to connect with you. Last time we worked on creating a supportive script to counter the feeling of selfishness after talking to your mom, and I heard that you found it helpful to visualize holding both perspectives at once. How has that idea been landing for you since we wrapped up, and is there anything else weighing on your mind that we should include on our agenda for today?

Hi, thanks for asking. The script has been... okay, I guess. I do try to hold both perspectives, but it still feels heavy, like I'm just pretending to be okay with it. What's really been on my mind lately is this one phone call where she said she missed seeing me, and I just froze up. I couldn't say anything back, and now I can't stop thinking about it.

It sounds like that frozen feeling creates a huge gap between the "pride" and "sadness" you were working on, leaving you with nothing to anchor yourself to afterward. Since you're bringing up a specific incident where you felt unable to respond, would you like to walk through exactly what went wrong in that moment so we can see if there's a different angle to take?

Yeah, I think that would help. It's like I was just standing in my kitchen, phone pressed to my ear, and my brain went totally blank. All I could hear was her voice saying she missed me, and then this wave of guilt just washed over me. I ended up changing the subject to the weather, which felt so stupid and cowardly afterward.

That freeze-and-skip response makes perfect sense given how much pressure you feel to perform perfectly; your brain likely interpreted her simple compliment as a demand for perfection that you couldn't meet, triggering a defensive shutdown instead. When you look back on that moment and judge yourself for skipping to the weather, does that judgment feel like an accurate description of what happened, or do you think it's an exaggeration born from the panic of that split second?

I think you might be right about the exaggeration part. When I replay it now, I did say something, even if it was just about the rain. But in the moment, it felt like I'd failed completely. Honestly, the judgment feels louder than what actually happened, like I'm punishing myself for not having the perfect, heartfelt response ready.

That insight about the judgment feeling louder than the reality is a crucial clue—it suggests your brain is rewriting the scene based on its expectation of perfection rather than the facts on the floor. You mentioned earlier that you often focus on the "worst possible version" of events; in this case, turning a simple weather comment into a total failure seems to fit that pattern perfectly. If we looked at that exact moment without the filter of hindsight, what is the smallest piece of evidence that proves you didn't fail, perhaps even showing that you stayed engaged despite freezing up?

Well, I guess... I didn't hang up. I didn't make an excuse and end the call. I stayed on the line, even though my heart was pounding. And I did say something to keep the conversation going, even if it was small. That's not nothing, right?

You are absolutely right; staying on the line and offering a small comment is a significant act of connection, not a failure, especially when your heart was racing. That tells us your brain is lying to you by framing a brave, albeit imperfect, attempt as a total collapse. Let's test that narrative further: if you imagined your mother reacting to you saying "the rain is pretty" instead of waiting for a grand speech, how do you think she would describe your effort? Would she see it as a defeat, or as you finally finding your footing?

She'd probably say I was just being me, a little awkward but trying. She's never been one to demand big speeches from me. Honestly, she'd probably just be glad I didn't change the subject to something like traffic or work. She'd see it as me still being there, even if I stumbled. That actually makes me feel a bit lighter, thinking of it that way.

That shift in perspective is powerful because it separates your internal panic from her actual experience of you, which directly challenges the "failure" story. Since you've already noticed that reframing brings some lightness, would you like to try weaving that specific image of her accepting your stumble into your daily mental routine when the guilt creeps back in, or would you prefer to discuss how to handle the physical sensation of freezing up the next time you pick up the phone?

I think the physical freezing is what scares me the most, honestly. The guilt I can talk myself through, but that moment where I just can't say anything feels like I'm losing control. If I could figure out how to handle that, maybe the guilt wouldn't have such a strong hold on me. Can we work on that?

That is a brilliant insight—shifting from fixing the guilt to addressing the physical sensation of freezing shows you truly understand the source of your distress. Since you want to tackle that moment of silence before it turns into guilt, we can practice a simple grounding technique right now: when you feel your throat tightening, name three things you can see in the room and one sound you can hear, which will remind your body that you are still present and safe. Would you like to try that visualization together, or would you prefer to write down a reminder for yourself on your sticky note to use right before calling her?

Let's try the visualization. If I can get that down, it might feel more real than a sticky note. So, when I feel that tightness in my throat, I should just look around and name what I see, like the coffee mug, the window, the clock... and then one sound, like the hum of the refrigerator. That sounds doable, actually. Can we walk through it slowly once?

Yes, let's walk through it together right now so it feels familiar before you try it alone. Imagine you are sitting there, suddenly feeling that tightness rise in your throat; instead of panicking, you gently turn your attention outward and silently name three things you see—the blue mug, the green plant, the clock ticking—and then listen closely to one steady sound, like the hum of the refrigerator. Notice how your breathing slows just a tiny bit as you shift your focus from the scary feeling to these neutral, safe details. Does that slow rhythm feel manageable as we do it together?

Yeah, it does. I'm actually taking a breath now just thinking about it. The hum of the fridge is always there, isn't it? It's steady and boring, but it's real. I think if I can anchor onto that sound, it might keep me from spiraling into that blank panic. I can picture myself doing that while she's talking, and it feels like I have a little more room to think before I respond.

That is a wonderful realization; anchoring on a steady, boring sound like the fridge hum gives your brain a secure place to stand instead of floating in panic. Since you now have a physical tool to ground yourself and a revised narrative to soften the guilt, let's quickly confirm our final plan: will you carry both the "three things + one sound" exercise and the updated mental script with your mom's acceptance into your next call?

Yes, I will. I'll have the grounding technique ready in my head, and I'll try to remember that she's not waiting for some perfect answer from me. It feels a bit more manageable now, like I have a real plan instead of just hoping I don't mess up. Thank you for helping me see that.

You are very welcome, and I want to acknowledge how much strength it took to move from hoping you wouldn't mess up to having a concrete plan that works for *you*. Remember, the goal isn't to speak flawlessly every time, but to use that grounding sound and the knowledge that your mother sees you as she is, even when you stumble. Take care of yourself tonight, and thank you for trusting me with this process.

Hello, I'm really glad we can meet again. Before we dive in, could you briefly share how you've been feeling emotionally over the past week and what you were hoping we'd tackle first today?

Hi, thanks for having me. Honestly, this past week has been a bit of a rollercoaster. I've been feeling really tense and anxious, especially after that night I couldn't read my book. I guess I'm hoping we can talk about that feeling of panic when I can't do the things I love, because it's starting to scare me.

Thank you for being so open about how much that tension has been weighing on you. Since we worked on creating those "anchor facts" last time, let's briefly review: do you feel like you successfully used those three specific successes to ground yourself when you noticed the spiral starting? Also, given that feeling of panic is still surfacing, shall we spend the rest of our time exploring exactly what happens in your mind right when that tightness begins?

I did try using those anchor facts, like reminding myself that I finished my last big project on time and that my husband and I had a good conversation recently. But honestly, when that panic hit about the book, it felt like none of that mattered in the moment. I think it would help to really dig into what goes through my head right when that tightness starts, because it all happens so fast.

It makes complete sense that those helpful reminders can feel drowned out by the sheer speed of the panic attack itself. When the body feels so tight, logic often takes a backseat, which explains why your brain might skip straight to the scary story before you even have a chance to recall your recent successes. Let's slow down and trace exactly what pops up in your thoughts the second you notice that initial tightening—is it usually a sudden feeling of doom, or maybe a specific image of failing everything again?

It's more like a sudden feeling of doom, like everything is about to fall apart. I'll be looking at my book, and then it's like my mind jumps straight to "what if I can never focus on reading again?" and then it's like a domino effect—I start thinking about failing at work, letting my husband down, not being able to be there for the kids. It all just floods in at once.

That domino effect sounds incredibly frightening, like one small crack leads to the entire foundation crumbling. It seems like your mind is jumping from that one blocked moment to imagining every area of your life falling apart simultaneously, which creates that overwhelming sense of doom. Before we explore how to interrupt that chain reaction, does finding yourself in that middle spot—the moment you realize you're sliding into "everything will go wrong"—feel manageable, or does it already feel impossible to step away from?

It feels almost impossible, to be honest. By the time I realize I'm in that middle spot, I'm already halfway down the slope, and it's like I'm just holding on, waiting for the crash. I don't feel like I have any control to step away or change direction once that train of thought starts moving.

That sense of powerlessness once the momentum starts is truly heartbreaking, and it explains why you feel so trapped in those moments. It sounds like your brain has learned to accelerate the process so quickly that you barely have time to intervene before you're deep in the tunnel. Let's treat this like we're learning to drive a car that suddenly accelerates faster than expected; even if you can't stop it instantly, can we figure out a safe place to pull over or steer slightly differently while it's still moving? What would happen if we tried to identify the very first flicker of doubt before the full flood of "everything will fail" kicks in?

I think the very first flicker is when I feel that resistance—like I'm trying to read but my eyes just glaze over the words. That's when the thought creeps in: "Why can't I just do this simple thing?" And then it's like a switch flips, and I'm already thinking about all the other things I'll fail at. Maybe if I could catch that moment right when I notice the glazing over, I could try something different instead of letting it snowball.

That observation is brilliant because catching that "glazing over" moment is essentially spotting the engine revving before the car speeds up. Instead of waiting until the whole avalanche is rolling, we could try to pause the sequence the instant you notice your eyes drifting. Does it feel doable to just gently say to yourself, "Okay, my eyes are getting heavy," and then deliberately pick up the pen or turn the page, treating it as a small victory before the panic even gets a chance to start?

That actually sounds manageable—like I'm not trying to fight the whole avalanche, just redirecting that tiny moment before it gains momentum. I think I could try that. Just noticing the glazing over and doing one small thing, like shifting in my seat or taking a sip of water, to break the pattern before my brain runs wild. It feels less overwhelming than trying to argue with the panic once it's already there.

That is a wonderful strategy because it shifts your goal from stopping a hurricane to planting a garden seed—much smaller and more achievable. Since you identified that specific "glazing over" moment as the trigger, would you be willing to try practicing this "micro-interruption" tomorrow morning right as you sit down with your book, perhaps pairing it with a conscious breath before you even try to read? How does that sound as a first experiment?

Yes, I think I can do that. Tomorrow morning, I'll sit down with my book, and the moment I feel that glaze, I'll take one conscious breath and maybe just look out the window for a few seconds before trying again. It feels like a small enough step that I won't get intimidated by it. Thank you—that actually gives me a bit of hope that I can handle this better.

That is such a smart approach—breaking the cycle into tiny, manageable pieces often removes the intimidation factor completely. To make sure we get the most out of this, I'd love to check in with you: how does the idea of pausing for thirty seconds and looking out the window feel practical for your morning routine, or do you foresee any distractions that might make it hard to find that quiet moment?

I think it's pretty practical, actually. My mornings are usually quiet before the kids wake up, so that window of time is usually mine. I can't think of many distractions—maybe just my phone buzzing or my mind wandering to work, but I think I can handle that. The key is just committing to that one breath and pause before I let anything else in.

That clarity is exactly what we need to build confidence in. Before we close, could you walk me through how you imagine doing this tomorrow: Will you write down the "three good night facts" you created earlier on a sticky note nearby, or is your mind sharp enough to just call upon them from memory when the panic starts rising?

I think I'll write them down on a sticky note and place it inside my book cover. That way, when I feel that glaze coming on, I can glance down and see those three facts before I even take my breath. It feels more concrete than trying to remember them in the heat of the moment. I'll do that tonight so it's ready for tomorrow morning.

That is a brilliant plan; placing the evidence right next to the trigger turns abstract thoughts into a physical tool you can reach for instantly. You have now built a clear roadmap: spot the glazing, use the micro-pause, and rely on your sticky-note anchors to steady you before the panic takes over. I'm really encouraged by your willingness to put this into action this morning. Is there anything else you'd like to discuss before we finish our time together today?

No, I think you've given me a lot to work with today. I feel like I have something concrete to try, which is more than I felt walking in. Thank you for helping me break it down into something that doesn't feel so overwhelming. I'll let you know how tomorrow goes.

You're so welcome, and I'm truly pleased to hear that you feel more empowered and have something tangible to hold onto. Remember that even if tomorrow isn't perfect, simply noticing that first moment of "glazing over" is a brave win in itself. Take care of yourself, and I look forward to hearing how your little experiment went.

Hi, yeah... thanks for having me back. I guess not much has changed since last time, honestly. I mean, I've still been surfing most days, but that knot you mentioned? Yeah, it's still there. We said we'd focus on that fear of getting stuck under the waves, and maybe figuring out why my brain goes straight to drowning even when the conditions are perfect.

It takes courage to stick with the plan when the knot hasn't loosened yet, especially after putting so much effort into the grounding exercise. Since we haven't found a permanent fix for that sudden drop into the drowning image, let's explore specifically what tells your brain that the ocean is dangerous right now. When you see that perfect condition with calm waters, what thought is the first one to pop up before the fear kicks in?

Usually, it's like, "This looks easy now, but you never know what's underneath." That thought just slides in, you know? Like even if it's glassy and calm, I'll catch myself thinking about that one wave that could come out of nowhere and hold me down too long. It's almost like my brain won't let me just enjoy the moment.

It makes total sense that your brain defaults to that "what if" story because it's trying to protect you from a memory of powerlessness, even though the current looks different. That protective instinct feels helpful in theory, but it's probably doing more harm than good by locking you out of enjoying the calm surface right now. Have you noticed if that "never know" thought tends to appear more often when you're alone versus when you're with other surfers or friends?

Yeah, actually... it's way worse when I'm alone. When I'm with my buddy Jake, I can kind of brush it off and laugh about it. But if I'm paddling out solo, that thought just echoes in my head louder. I guess being alone makes me feel like there's no one to help if the worst happens, even though rationally I know I'm a strong swimmer and I've never even come close to getting in trouble.

That distinction between being alone and with a friend highlights a core belief—that you need external reassurance to feel safe—but it also shows how your brain magnifies risk when support isn't physically present. It seems like when you're by yourself, that old script about being vulnerable takes over faster than when Jake is there to bridge the gap. If you imagined a scenario where Jake wasn't there, what part of his usual presence helps counteract that feeling of isolation?

That's a good question... I think it's his voice, honestly. He's always shouting stuff like, "You got this, Sam!" or making jokes when I wipe out. Just that presence, someone seeing me and knowing I'm okay. When it's just me, there's no one to tell me I'm fine after I take a breath. I just sit there waiting for that panic to pass on my own.

Hearing that his voice acts as an external anchor makes sense; it gives you proof that you aren't alone in the struggle, which lowers the stakes. It sounds like when he's there, his words interrupt the cycle of panic before it can fully take root, whereas without him, you're left to wait for the feeling to fade on its own. What happens in your mind if you imagine saying one of those encouraging phrases aloud to yourself before you even hit the water?

I think I'd feel a little silly at first, honestly. Like, talking to myself out loud? But... maybe it wouldn't be so different from having him there. Like, if I just say, "You're fine, you've done this a hundred times," before I even paddle out, maybe that would shut down the panic before it starts. I never really thought about trying that before.

That is such a creative insight—treating your own encouragement as a substitute for his presence is a brilliant way to simulate safety without needing anyone else. It shifts the dynamic from waiting for rescue to proactively signaling to your nervous system that you are capable. Would you be open to testing this idea tomorrow before you even reach the water?

Yeah, I think I could try that. I mean, what's the worst that could happen, right? I look a little crazy talking to myself on the beach. But if it helps me actually enjoy the session instead of dreading it, I guess it's worth a shot. I'll give it a go tomorrow morning.

That is a fantastic mindset—focusing on the benefit of enjoyment rather than avoiding embarrassment removes the barrier to trying it. Even if it feels slightly odd at first, the fact that you're willing to prioritize your peace over how others might perceive you speaks volumes about your growth. Let's commit to that one sentence for tomorrow, and whenever you're ready, we can discuss how that small shift lands for you once you've had the chance to use it.

Thanks. I'll let you know how it goes. It's weird, just talking about it here makes it feel a little more manageable, you know? Like the fear isn't this giant wall anymore—maybe just a hurdle I can step over. I'll report back on Wednesday with the results.

That shift from seeing the fear as a giant wall to a hurdle you can step over is a beautiful perspective change, and it sounds like you have a clear path forward. Please remember to report back on Wednesday regardless of how the trial went—even small steps count as progress. I look forward to hearing your update and celebrating whatever tiny victory comes your way.

I will, I promise. Even if I just stand on the beach and say it to myself and paddle out for five minutes, that's still something, right? Thanks for helping me see it that way. I'll see you Wednesday.

Absolutely, standing on the beach and paddling out for just five minutes is a huge win in itself, regardless of whether you used the phrase or felt perfectly brave. It honors the journey, not just the destination. I'll be here on Wednesday to celebrate whatever result comes your way, big or small. Until then, take care of yourself.

Hello again. Before we dive into the day ahead, I'd like to check in on how you've been feeling since we last spoke and then set a quick agenda for our time together. Could you share how your energy and mood compare to last session, and what would be most helpful for us to focus on today?

Hi. I guess my mood has been up and down this week. Some days I feel okay, especially when I'm busy with photo shoots, but other days I get stuck thinking about my friends and that whole bar situation. I think it would help to talk more about why I feel like they only like me when I'm drinking, because it's been on my mind a lot.

That’s a clear summary of where things stand, and focusing on that core belief—that your friends only like you when you’re drinking—is definitely a great place to start. So, if we were to map out our agenda, should we spend some time unpacking those thoughts behind the belief, and then decide on a small experiment to test it out?

Yeah, that sounds good. I'm willing to try an experiment, even if it feels a little scary. Sometimes I worry that if I push too hard to hang out without alcohol, they'll just stop inviting me altogether.

That fear of losing their friendship entirely is completely understandable given how much you value their approval. Before we jump straight into a big social event, I wonder if we could try a smaller, lower-stakes experiment first, like spending one afternoon with them without mentioning drinks at all, just to see what actually happens? Would you feel comfortable starting with something like that, or does it still feel too risky?

I think I could try that, maybe just a quick coffee or a walk in the park with one friend instead of the whole group. That feels a little less overwhelming. But I still get nervous that she'll seem bored or distracted without a drink in her hand.

That specific worry about her seeming bored is a very common pattern where we assume others' reactions based on how we feel inside ourselves. Let's take a moment to slow down and check in: As you imagine the scenario of meeting her without a drink, do you notice that tight chest sensation returning, or is it mostly just that mental image of her looking bored?

It's more like a mental image, I think. Like, I can picture her checking her phone a lot or looking around the room like she wants to leave. My chest does feel a little tight when I think about it too much, but mostly it's just that picture in my head that keeps repeating.

That distinction between the physical tightness and the vivid mental movie of her checking her phone is really helpful—it shows the thought is driving the anxiety right now. Since we've agreed to talk about *why* that belief feels so sticky and then run a small test, does exploring the origins of that fear feel like the right order, or would you prefer to sketch out the details of the low-stakes meeting first?

I think I'd rather sketch out the details first, actually. That way I can picture it in my mind as something real and doable, instead of just a scary idea. Maybe if I plan it out, the thought won't feel so powerful.

That is a brilliant insight; turning a vague fear into a concrete plan often makes it feel much less threatening. Let's build that picture together: You mentioned a quick coffee or a walk with one friend. Who is that person, and what does the perfect version of this meet-up look like—from how you greet her to how long you stay?

I think I'd ask my friend Mia. She's usually pretty easygoing and doesn't seem to judge me much. The perfect version would be us meeting at that little coffee shop near the park around noon, grabbing our drinks, and then walking along the trail for maybe thirty or forty minutes. I'd want it to feel natural, like we're just catching up without any pressure.

That sounds like a lovely, realistic setup, and choosing Mia who is known to be easygoing is a smart strategic move. With that scenario clearly defined, does it feel slightly less intimidating to visualize walking into that coffee shop and starting the conversation as planned, or does the "natural" part still feel like a high-pressure requirement?

It does feel a little less intimidating now that I've got a clear picture. But the "natural" part still makes me nervous, because I feel like I have to perform or be interesting enough for her to want to stay. I guess I'm scared there will be awkward silences and she'll think it's because I'm boring without a drink.

That fear of awkward silence acting as proof you're "boring" is a classic example of assuming others' interpretations, which is exactly why we're running this experiment—to gather real data instead of relying on that internal script. Let's do a quick mental rehearsal: Imagine sitting across from Mia, realizing a few seconds of silence happen, and instead of panicking or rushing to fill it, you simply take a sip of your coffee and smile. How does that scenario feel right now, or does your body still tense up imagining that silence?

I actually feel a little bit of relief imagining that, like I could just let the silence happen without it being the end of the world. My shoulders just dropped a little bit, so I think that's a good sign. But I still wonder in the back of my mind if she's secretly wishing she was somewhere else.

It makes complete sense that your mind jumps to the worst-case scenario—the idea that she's mentally checking out—even though you just visualized staying calm. That "secret wishing" thought is likely just your brain's old safety alarm going off, trying to protect you from potential rejection. Before we finalize our plan, does treating the silence as a normal pause feel like a manageable way to handle the meeting, or does the fear of her disapproval still feel like a heavy blanket you can't shake?

Honestly, it still feels a little heavy, but maybe that's because I've never tried letting the silence just be there before. I think treating it as a normal pause is something I can try, even if it feels weird at first. I guess I won't know until I actually do it.

That is a very honest and realistic assessment; trusting the outcome requires a leap of faith, which is completely normal. Since you've outlined the plan and acknowledged that the "heavy" feeling is just resistance to change rather than proof of failure, would you be comfortable saying yes to moving forward with this specific experiment this week?
Yeah, I can say yes to that. I'll text Mia later today and see if she's free this weekend for coffee and a walk. I'll try to keep our plan in mind and not let my head take over too much.

That is a fantastic commitment, and breaking it down into texting her today followed by the weekend activity makes it feel very achievable. Before we wrap up, does scheduling this specific time slot for Saturday morning feel doable for your current routine, or does the idea of coordinating it still feel a bit slippery?
Saturday morning sounds good to me. I usually don't have shoots on weekends, so it fits my schedule. I'll ask Mia if she's free then, and if she says yes, I'll just go with the plan we talked about.

That sounds like a solid plan, and knowing you have flexibility in your schedule adds confidence to the process. One final check before we close: On a scale of 1 to 10, how confident do you feel you can stick to this plan once you receive her confirmation, and is there anything else weighing on your mind about Saturday?

I'd say maybe a 7 out of 10. I'm still a little nervous that she might cancel or seem hesitant, but I think I can handle it. I guess the only thing weighing on me is the worry that even if this goes well, it won't change how I feel about the whole group. But I'm willing to start with Mia and see what happens.

That is such a mature realization—acknowledging that one successful interaction with Mia might be just enough evidence to slowly chip away at your bigger worry about the whole group. A score of 7 shows you're grounded in reality while recognizing the challenge ahead. Since we've covered the goal, the detailed plan, and your readiness level, does taking this next step feel like a natural progression for us to conclude today?
Yeah, I think that's a good place to stop for today. I feel like I have something concrete to work on, and that's better than just worrying about it all week. Thanks for helping me get there.

You're absolutely welcome, and I'm so proud of you for moving from worry to a concrete plan—that shift alone is a major victory. Remember, even if the result isn't perfect, the act of facing the situation without spiraling into your usual fears is what matters most. I'll be here next time to hear how the experiment unfolds with Mia, and we can adjust our approach together if anything comes up. Take care, and trust in your ability to navigate this!

Since you mentioned wanting to focus on the concert worry, let's take a moment to see if bringing up that specific feeling helps clarify exactly what you're experiencing right now. Yeah, it's like a knot in my stomach, right when the first few notes play. I get this immediate thought like, "There it is again, that reminder that you're never going to see them live." And then I just feel kind of heavy and quiet for a while, like I've already lost something.

That physical knot in your stomach really captures how urgent and immediate that fear feels to you. It seems like hearing the music triggers a belief that this is your absolute final chance, so missing it means losing everything forever. When you sit with that thought and feel so heavy, does it seem like your mind is protecting you from disappointment by assuming the worst-case scenario, even though you know touring continues?

I guess... I never really thought of it that way. It does feel like the end of the world when I think about missing this one show. But you're right, they do keep touring, and there could be other chances. It's just that in the moment, it feels so certain that this is my only shot, and if I lose it, it's over.

That certainty that "if I miss this, it's over" explains why the knot feels so tight and unmovable right now. It sounds like your brain is locking onto that single possibility to shield you from the pain of failure, even though it leaves you feeling trapped. If we tried to gently push aside that "only shot" idea for just a minute, what comes up as the very next logical step in your life after August 15th passes?

Well, after August 15th, the concert will be over, regardless of whether I'm there or not. I guess life would just... go on. I'd still have my job, I'd still feed Spot every morning, and I'd probably still listen to their music. Maybe I'd even watch some fan recordings online, even if it stings a bit.

Noticing that life goes on—that you'd still have your job, care for Spot, and find ways to enjoy their music later—is a powerful glimpse of reality cutting through the panic. It shows that the consequence isn't total loss, just a temporary bump. If we treat the "missing this once" thought as an exaggeration of a normal feeling, does that shift the knot in your stomach slightly less tightly?

Yeah... it does feel a little less heavy when I think of it that way. Like, maybe I'm blowing it up bigger than it actually is. The knot is still there, but it's not as crushing as before—more like a dull ache instead of a tight fist.

That shift from a "tight fist" to a "dull ache" is a massive victory, showing how much power you have to soften that initial panic. It seems like acknowledging that life keeps moving—even with a sad memory attached—has given your brain permission to relax a little bit. Would you be willing to try focusing on that "life goes on" perspective whenever that knot forms again tomorrow?

I think I could try that. It might take some practice, because my first instinct is still to go straight to the worst-case scenario. But if I remind myself that I'll still have my routines and my pet and the music itself, maybe that will help quiet that panic before it takes over.

That is a really smart plan, and I appreciate your honesty about the first instinct being to jump to the worst case. Trying to pause that automatic reaction and consciously reminding yourself of the routine and Spot is a strong way to regain control. Since this involves noticing a pattern, would you be comfortable writing down one specific moment you caught yourself doing this this week, along with the "life goes on" thought you chose to replace it?

Yeah, I can do that. I'll keep a little notebook by my desk or on the kitchen counter, and when I feel that knot forming, I'll jot down what triggered it and then write down the "life goes on" thought instead. It feels like a concrete way to fight back against that automatic panic.

That's a fantastic plan—having a tangible spot to write creates a clear boundary between the panic and your rational thinking. It turns an overwhelming feeling into a simple, manageable task you can control right there in the moment. Before we wrap up, how does it feel to have that specific action ready for when the music plays again?

It actually feels reassuring, like I have a tool instead of just sitting with that heavy feeling. I'm still nervous about whether I can catch myself in time, but having a plan makes it feel less hopeless. Thanks for helping me see a way out of that thought spiral.

It is wonderful to hear that feeling reassured by having a concrete tool in hand, especially when uncertainty creeps in. Your willingness to carry that notebook and practice the pause shows real strength and flexibility in facing this challenge. As we close today, is there anything else you'd like to adjust in our approach, or does this plan feel ready to start immediately?

Hi, thanks for having me. I'd say my energy is maybe a 6 or 7 right now. I'm a bit tired from work, but I'm okay. It's just, when I'm alone on my night shifts, my mind starts going in circles about whether I'm cut out for college, and that really drains me.

Comparing your current silence to Lisa's busy schedule is a very common way our minds try to predict the future, but it often misses how much effort Lisa is actually putting in right now. When that fear of "not keeping up" hits you, what happens physically or emotionally in that moment at the front desk? Do you feel your stomach tighten, or do you feel like you need to rush somewhere?

My chest gets really tight, like someone's sitting on it. And I start tapping my fingers on the desk, just little nervous movements. I feel this cold kind of dread, like I'm already failing at something I haven't even started yet. It's weird, because I'm just sitting there, but my heart starts racing like I'm in danger or something.

That physical sensation of a heavy chest and racing heart is your body reacting to that intense fear, even though logically you know you're just sitting in a quiet office. It sounds like your brain is interpreting your preparation as proof that you aren't "natural," which is why it triggers such a strong survival response. Given how powerful these feelings are, does it feel easier for us to explore the specific stories your mind tells itself about being "not smart enough," or would you prefer to try a small exercise right now to see if those physical sensations calm down on their own?

I think I'd like to try the small exercise. If there's a way to make that tightness in my chest ease up a little, I'd really appreciate it. It gets so overwhelming sometimes that I can't even think straight.

That willingness to pause and breathe through the physical symptoms is a brave step, even when it feels impossible. We can try a simple grounding technique: I'll count to three, and you can slow your breathing in and out deeply until the next number. One... Two... Three. Now, take another slow breath in, hold it gently, and exhale slowly as you imagine that tightness in your chest loosening like fog clearing in the morning light.

(Exhales slowly) Okay... I think that actually helped a little. The tightness isn't gone, but it's like it moved back a bit, you know? Like I'm not stuck inside it as much. That foggy feeling in my head cleared up some too.

Since this was our first meeting, I want to make sure we leave with a clear direction. Would you be open to focusing on understanding *why* those "not smart enough" thoughts appear so strongly, or would you prefer to start practicing tools to handle them when they strike again tomorrow?

I think understanding why they show up would be good. It feels like they just appear out of nowhere, and that makes me feel kind of helpless. If I can figure out where they're coming from, maybe I can feel a bit more in control.

That sense of helplessness is understandable, but discovering the source of those thoughts often turns the feeling of being trapped into a puzzle you can solve. To start looking at where they come from, could you recall a specific time recently when you felt especially doubtful about your intelligence, and what was happening in your life just before that thought popped up?

Last week, I was looking at college application websites on my break at work. I was reading about the requirements for a program I'm interested in, and there was all this talk about prerequisite courses and GPA minimums. And I just thought, "I wasn't the best student in high school, so why would I be any different now?" Suddenly, I felt like I was back in my eleventh-grade math class, struggling with algebra while everyone else seemed to get it.

That connection between past struggles and present fears makes perfect sense; your brain is using old memories as a shortcut to predict what will happen now. It sounds like the core belief driving this is that your worth or ability is fixed and defined by how you performed in the past rather than what you are building now. When you compare your current effort to that memory of struggling in math class, does that specific thought ("I wasn't the best student") feel like it explains everything, or do you think there might be other factors involved?

I guess it does feel like it explains everything, at least in the moment. Like, if I wasn't naturally good at math back then, why would I be good at anything now? But... I mean, I've been working hard, saving money, I even got promoted at the hotel. That takes some kind of skill, right? So maybe it's not just about being naturally smart. I don't know, it's hard to see that when I'm in the middle of it.

Noticing the contradiction between your past struggles and your current promotions is a huge breakthrough—it shows your brain already knows you possess skills that require effort and strategy. Those achievements suggest your capability isn't fixed; it's something you build, just like applying to college is a project requiring research and planning rather than pure innate talent. Since you've identified that belief ("If I struggled before, I can't succeed now"), what happens in your body when you actively remind yourself that your recent promotion proves you *can* learn difficult things?

Huh... when I think about the promotion, I feel a little lighter, like there's a tiny crack in that heavy feeling. It makes me think, "Well, I did figure out that new scheduling system even though it was confusing at first." So maybe I can learn, I just have to give myself time. But then that other voice whispers, "That's different from college, that's just a hotel job." So it's like a tug-of-war in my head.

That tug-of-war is classic—it's your logical brain recognizing your achievement versus your fearful brain trying to isolate the difference. The key insight there is that both the promotion and college involve learning complex systems under pressure; the fact that you succeeded in one doesn't disprove the worry in the other, it just provides evidence that your ability to grow exists. If we tested that thought ("I learned scheduling, therefore I can handle college stress"), what would be the strongest counter-evidence you could gather right now? Perhaps looking at a specific task you completed recently where you had to figure something out on the fly?

Well, last week the computer system at work crashed, and I had to check guests in manually using paper forms and then enter everything later. I was nervous at first, but I figured it out step by step. It wasn't smooth, but I got through it. I guess that's kind of like college, right? Not knowing exactly what to do, but working through it anyway.

That example is powerful because it shows you thrive in uncertainty—you didn't wait for perfect instructions; you adapted and solved the problem. It proves that your ability to handle pressure comes from your willingness to learn, not from having all the answers upfront. If we look closely at that thought, "College is different," does it mean college will be *impossible*, or does it mean it will require a different set of tools you haven't tried yet?

I think... maybe it just means I'll need to learn new tools. Like, I won't have a boss telling me what to do, I'll have professors and deadlines. But I can learn how that works. It's not impossible, it's just different. Saying it out loud like that makes it feel a little less scary.

That shift in perspective—from "it's impossible" to "it's just different"—is a massive step toward reclaiming control. You've moved from seeing your struggle as a permanent flaw to viewing it as a temporary gap in knowledge that you can bridge. Since we've explored the root of those thoughts, what would feel most useful for us to tackle next: refining a plan to challenge these voices during your shifts, or practicing a specific calming technique to use when they strike?

I think practicing a calming technique would be good. If I have something I can actually do when that tightness hits, it might help me get through my shifts without spiraling so much. Those late nights are long, and I need something I can use right there at the front desk.

That is a brilliant choice—having a reliable tool ready for those long, quiet hours gives you a sense of safety. We could try a quick "grounding box" exercise: pick four items in your line of sight (a pen, a coaster, a shadow, etc.), name each one out loud slowly, and notice how your chest feels as you focus on the details. Would you like to try that right now, or would you prefer to write down a verbal cue phrase you can repeat to yourself instead?

Let's try the grounding thing. I can see my coffee mug, the clock on the wall, the keycard scanner, and the little lamp on the desk. (Pauses, looking at each one) The mug has a chip on the rim, and the clock is ticking so quietly I barely notice. The scanner blinks green, and the lamp has a warm yellow glow. My chest feels... not so tight anymore. That's actually pretty helpful.

That is a wonderful result—you successfully redirected your attention from your internal panic to the concrete reality of your surroundings, and your body responded by relaxing. Since we are at the end of our first session, I want to make sure we leave with a clear path forward. For your homework, I suggest you try this grounding box exercise every time you feel that familiar tightness at work, and next time we can check in to see how it held up. Before we finish, is there anything about today's discussion or this technique that feels unclear, or is there one last thing you wanted to share?

No, I think I understand it pretty well. I'll try to use the grounding thing tonight at work when those thoughts start creeping in. Thank you for listening and helping me see that it's not as hopeless as I thought. I feel a little more ready to face my shift now.

You are very welcome, and I am so glad to hear that you left feeling more ready and less hopeless. Remember that hope is a muscle—it grows stronger every time you choose to engage with it, even when it feels uncertain. Please go ahead and try the grounding box tonight, and I look forward to hearing how it went in our next session. Take care of yourself, and I'll see you soon.
