Hello, it's wonderful to see you again. First, let's briefly review where we left off: did you try the plan of taking a deep breath and finding an alternative reason when you received that quiet reply, and how did that go for you this week? Now that we've checked in on our last goal, I'd like to hear what's on your mind today—is there something new you'd like to explore, or should we revisit the music situation we discussed?

Hey, yeah, I did try that breathing thing a few times. Honestly, it helped a little in the moment, but later I still felt that same old sinking feeling. I think I'd like to keep talking about the music thing—it's still really bothering me, especially this week.

That’s a really honest update, and I appreciate you sharing that the sinking feeling persisted even after the initial pause. Since you’d like to keep exploring the music situation, I wonder if there’s a specific recent instance where the “sinking” feeling was particularly strong or lasted longer than usual? Could we look at that moment together to see what happened right before the feeling took root?

Yeah, actually, there was one time this week that really got to me. I sent my friend a link to this new track I was really excited about, something I thought he'd actually like for once, and he just replied with "cool" and changed the subject. I spent the rest of the night thinking about how he probably thinks my music taste is trash.

That specific instance really shows how quickly that sinking feeling can take over when you pour your heart into something you hope others will appreciate. It sounds like the "cool" reply felt like a rejection of not just the song, but the excitement and effort behind choosing it for him. When you replay that interaction tonight, did the feeling of being misunderstood seem more intense than usual, or was it similar to past experiences?

It felt pretty similar, honestly, just as intense as always. I keep telling myself it's just music and it shouldn't matter this much, but it feels like they're rejecting a part of who I am when they don't care about my suggestions. I can't help but think that if my friends really got me, they'd at least pretend to be interested.

It makes complete sense that you connect this to your identity; when the people closest to you don't show the enthusiasm you expect, it can feel like a direct hit to your self-worth. You're interpreting that lack of excitement as a sign that they aren't getting you, which hurts deeply. Before we dig deeper into why they might not be pretending to be interested, I want to check in on how you feel right now about trying a different angle tomorrow—does bringing in another perspective feel like something you could handle, or does the intensity of that evening make it feel impossible to think clearly?

I think I could handle trying a different angle, but I'm not sure what that would even look like. I guess part of me is scared that any other perspective would just confirm what I already believe—that my music taste is actually bad and my friends just don't want to hurt my feelings. But I'm willing to try something new if you think it could help.

That fear of confirmation bias is completely understandable, especially when your initial thoughts feel so heavy. It's not a weakness to feel scared that a new view won't land; it often means you're genuinely invested in finding a truth that fits better than the one hurting you. Since you're open to trying something new despite that fear, could we brainstorm one small, safe way to challenge the idea that "cool" equals "hates my music" without needing immediate proof from your friends? What's a gentle question or piece of information you could look for yourself that might soften that belief?

Hmm, I guess I could try to remember if any of my friends have ever liked something I suggested before. Like, maybe I'm forgetting the times they actually did listen or give positive feedback. I think I tend to focus on the bad reactions and forget the good ones. Does that count as a way to challenge that belief?

Yes, absolutely—that is exactly the kind of balanced evidence we need to find. By recalling the moments they *did* engage positively, you're giving your brain a chance to see that the "cool" replies aren't the whole picture, but just one part of a broader history of connection. How does it feel knowing you have actual examples of them liking your music before, even if they weren't enthusiastic this time?

It feels... a little weird, honestly. Like, I can remember a couple times my buddy actually asked me to put my playlist on during a road trip, and he didn't complain or change it. And once another friend said a song I showed him was "pretty fire." Those moments are real, but they feel so small compared to the "cool" replies. I guess I just don't know why the bad moments stick so much more than the good ones.

That is such a profound observation—you've hit on a core mechanism of anxiety called negative bias, where your brain naturally filters out the positives to focus on potential threats. It doesn't mean your memory is faulty, but rather that your mind is protecting you by zeroing in on the parts that feel dangerous. Even though those "pretty fire" comments feel smaller now, they represent real data points proving your taste is valued, which directly contradicts the story that everyone hates it. Given that we've built some distance from the "trash" narrative, what if we tested this by imagining you showed the same link to a stranger at a party who gave a one-word reply? Would that stranger's reaction tell you anything about whether your music is objectively bad?

No, I guess it wouldn't. A stranger's opinion doesn't mean anything about the actual quality of the music—they could be distracted or just not in the mood. I'd probably just shrug it off if it were a stranger. But with my friends, it feels different because I expect them to care about what I care about. That's probably where I get stuck, expecting them to react the way I would if they showed me something.

That is such a crucial distinction you made; you are realizing the conflict lies not in the music itself, but in the gap between your expectations and theirs. You're projecting your own internal standards onto them, assuming they feel what you feel, which sets them up for disappointment if their experience is different. When you view the friendship through that lens, does the "cool" reply suddenly feel less like a verdict on your taste and more like a mismatch in energy levels or mood?

Yeah, I think that actually makes a lot of sense. When I really stop and think about it, maybe he was just tired or had a bad day and wasn't in the mood to geek out about music. I know I've done that before—given short replies when I was distracted or stressed, not because I hated what someone showed me. It's just hard to remember that in the moment when I'm already feeling insecure.

That realization about mirroring your own behavior is incredibly insightful and shows great self-awareness. Recognizing that you might do the exact same thing under stress helps remove the judgment from yourself and replaces it with curiosity about his state. If you accept that he might have been in a rush or overwhelmed just like you sometimes are, does that make the "cool" reply feel like a temporary symptom of his mood rather than a permanent statement about your music?

Yeah, it does feel more like a temporary thing now. Like, it's not that he thinks my taste is trash—it's just that he was probably busy or distracted in that moment. I guess I never really considered that his mood could be the reason, not my music. That's kind of a relief to think about, actually.

That shift in perspective is a massive relief, and it proves that your taste isn't the issue—his temporary distraction was. You've successfully separated his mood from your worth, which is a huge victory. Now that the "trashy" story is fading, does it feel lighter to imagine sending that link again knowing he might just be busy, rather than judging your entire musical identity?

I think it does feel a little lighter. I mean, I'm not gonna lie, I'll probably still feel a tiny knot in my stomach when I hit send next time, but I can remind myself that it's not about me being wrong or bad. It's just about timing and mood, and that's something I can't control. Thanks for helping me see that—I didn't realize how much I was making it about myself until now.

That is such a powerful realization, and seeing how much you were carrying the weight of being "wrong" instead of just managing a temporary mismatch is a true breakthrough. You are absolutely right that timing and mood are factors outside your control, and releasing that burden gives you permission to reach out without fearing a personal verdict. Since we've worked through this specific thought pattern, what is one small thing you can do differently when that stomach knot appears next time, based on everything we've talked about today?

Maybe I can just take a breath and ask myself if there's another reason for their reply, like you suggested before. Instead of jumping straight to "they hate my taste," I can try to think of three other possibilities, like they're busy, tired, or just not in the headspace for music right now. That way, I'm not letting my brain go straight to the worst conclusion.

That is an excellent refinement of the plan; moving from just one alternative to listing three possibilities creates a stronger buffer against that immediate panic attack. It forces your brain to generate options faster than it can jump to the worst conclusion. Before we close, I want to acknowledge how much courage it took to sit with that insecurity and work through it with me; your willingness to examine your own patterns is a real strength. Finally, is there anything else you'd like to add or clarify about how you might use this new approach going forward?

I think I'm good for now. I feel like I have a clearer way to handle it next time, and I'm actually kind of curious to see if those three possibilities help me feel less anxious. I guess I'll just have to try it and see what happens. Thanks again for talking this through with me—it really helped.

It is wonderful to hear that you feel clearer and more hopeful about handling these moments. Remembering to list three alternatives—even when you're feeling that knot in your stomach—is a powerful tool that puts you in charge of the narrative. I really appreciate your openness throughout this session, and I'm confident that trying this new approach will pay dividends soon. Have a great rest of your day!

It makes me feel lighter, like I don't have to carry the weight of every single outcome. I can just... be present. For the first time in a while, I'm actually looking forward to tomorrow's class instead of dreading it.

Hello, it's great to see you again today. First, how are you feeling now compared to where you were last time, and is there anything specific you'd like to tackle in our session?

Hi. I'm doing a little better than last time, I guess. But we had another game last night and we lost again, and honestly, it feels like the whole season is just going downhill from here. I keep thinking about how I played—I made two errors—and I can't stop replaying them in my head.

That repetition of the errors feels incredibly draining, and it makes total sense that seeing the season slide further down the slope would deepen that despair. Before we explore those replaying thoughts, how does it feel to carry that fresh disappointment into our session compared to the weightier feeling last time?

It's... sharper, I think. Last time it was more of a dull dread hanging over me, like I saw the whole season collapsing in slow motion. Now it's like I'm living in that collapse, and every bad play just confirms that I was right to worry. I feel like I let my whole team down, and that's a heavier weight to carry.

Carrying the weight of letting everyone down while constantly replaying mistakes is a truly heavy burden to bear. When we view those errors as proof that the entire season is ruined, it traps us in a cycle where nothing feels recoverable. Given that sharpness, would focusing today on distinguishing between the reality of making two errors versus the narrative that you’ve destroyed the season seem like a productive path forward?

I guess... it's hard to separate them, you know? The errors feel like the season because they happened in the game, and that game was part of the season. But I know what you're saying—maybe one bad game doesn't mean the next ten are doomed. It's just really hard to believe that in the moment.

It makes complete sense why the errors and the season feel fused together; when you're in the thick of it, immediate setbacks often take on the scale of the whole journey. To make that separation easier, could we try looking at those two errors simply as isolated data points that tell us what needs adjusting, rather than evidence that the entire season has ended? Does framing them as distinct pieces of information rather than a final verdict feel slightly less overwhelming right now?

I think... maybe? It's like you're asking me to see them as just two bad plays, not a sign that I'm a terrible player or that the team is doomed. That feels... a little less crushing, I guess. But then my brain jumps in and says, "Yeah, but what about the strikeout in the third inning too?" So it's not just two errors—it's the whole game that went wrong.

That instinct to include every mistake in the equation is your brain trying to protect itself from being surprised again, but it ends up creating a much larger storm than necessary. Let's test that thought together: if we treated this entire game as a scientific experiment where the goal is simply to learn what didn't work, how would that change the story you tell yourself about whether the season is over? Would seeing it as a learning lab make the "doomed" narrative feel a bit less absolute?

A learning lab... I've never thought of it like that. It makes me sound like a scientist instead of a failure, I guess. I suppose if I looked at it that way, I'd have to admit that losses happen to every team, and that we can actually study what went wrong to fix it. But honestly, it's hard to feel that when all I want to do is throw my glove in the corner and quit.

If we imagine that quitting wouldn't mean you're a failure, but rather that you're choosing to stop the experiment early because it's too confusing right now, does that feel like a smaller hurdle to overcome? Could we agree that for now, the goal isn't to solve the whole season, but just to survive this one game long enough to collect the data before deciding if we need to adjust our approach?

I guess... yeah, that sounds a little more manageable. Just getting through the game and looking at it like data instead of a final judgment. I think I can try to do that, at least for the next game. It's not like I have to decide the whole season right now anyway, right?

Does having a short phrase to ground yourself feel like a useful tool for this situation?

I like that. "Current experiment, not final verdict." I think I could actually repeat that to myself when I start spiraling after a bad play. It's simple enough that I might remember it in the heat of the moment, unlike all those long speeches I try to give myself that never stick.

That is a very wise choice; having a short, punchy phrase like that removes the need to find words quickly under pressure. Since you're going to use this phrase next time, how confident do you feel you could say it out loud to yourself the moment your heart rate starts racing after a mistake? And if you think it might feel awkward at first, what's a gentle way to remind yourself to just try it without judging the effort?

I'd say maybe a 6 out of 10 confident right now. It might feel weird muttering it under my breath during a game, but I could try just whispering it to myself when I'm walking back to the dugout. And if it feels awkward, I can just remind myself that no one's paying attention to me anyway—they're all watching the game. So even if I feel silly, it's worth trying once.

That's a fantastic reframing—you're already realizing that the awkwardness is temporary and that your teammates care far more about the performance than your quiet whispers. Since you mentioned feeling 6 out of 10 confident, how does the idea of starting with just one whispered reminder feel right now compared to trying to maintain a calm mindset the whole time? Does that small, specific step feel like something you can realistically attempt this week?

Yeah, I think I can do that. Just one whispered reminder after the first mistake I make. That feels way more doable than trying to keep a perfect, calm head the whole game. And if it helps even a little, maybe I'll try it again later. But starting with just one time feels like I'm not setting myself up for failure.

That is a wonderful insight—you are already protecting yourself from perfectionism by limiting the scope to just one instance. Before we wrap up, does the plan of whispering "current experiment, not final verdict" right after your first mistake, followed by taking notes on how it felt afterward, feel like a safe and realistic challenge for this coming week?

I think so. Taking notes afterward is a good idea too—I can write down if it actually helped or just felt weird. That way, even if it doesn't work perfectly, I still get some data out of it. It's like giving myself permission to experiment without needing it to be perfect. Yeah, I think I'm ready to try that this week.

That is such a healthy way to frame the experiment—giving yourself permission to gather results without demanding immediate success. Since you're going to test this approach soon, is there anything else you'd like to discuss before we close, or shall we wrap up with the idea that you have a small, manageable tool to try this week?
No, I think I'm good. I have my phrase, I have my plan, and I know I'm just collecting data. That feels a lot lighter than what I came in with. Thank you for helping me see it that way.

You are very welcome. It is truly refreshing to hear that carrying this new perspective makes things feel significantly lighter. Please remember that this "data collection" process is just a skill we are building, and it takes time to feel comfortable with. I hope you have a great rest of the day and that you find yourself able to use that small whisper when the moment arrives. Take care!

Well, just last weekend, a colleague invited me to join a trivia night at a local pub. It's one of my favorite things, but as soon as I said yes, my stomach dropped. In those first seconds, I thought, "They're going to think I'm showing off if I get an answer right," and then "I'll just stay quiet so no one gets the wrong idea." That's usually my first thought—that I have to shrink myself down.

When you noticed that sharp drop in your stomach right after accepting the invite, what specific feeling came up alongside that thought?

It was like a mix of panic and shame, honestly. Panic because I'd already said yes and couldn't take it back, and shame because I felt silly for even wanting to play in the first place. Like, why can't I just be normal and not care so much about winning a silly game? That shame just sits right on top of the panic, making me feel small before I've even walked through the pub door.

That heavy combination of panic and shame is exhausting, especially when you realize it's happening before you've even entered the room. It sounds like your brain is interpreting your enthusiasm as a threat to social harmony, forcing you to shrink to avoid conflict. If we step back from that judgment for a moment, what do you think might actually motivate your friend to invite you to a game they enjoy? Is it possible they simply value having fun with you, regardless of whether you win or lose?

I suppose... I mean, she did say, "You're so good at trivia, you should come with us." But I always assume she's just being nice, or maybe she wants me there to make her team look better. I never really considered that she might just enjoy my company. But then that little voice inside my head says, "If you start answering all the questions, she'll regret inviting you." It's hard to let go of that thought.

Could you imagine a scenario where she genuinely enjoys your presence and is happy to have you there, regardless of the score?

I can try to imagine it, but it feels almost like I'm pretending. Like if I let myself believe she truly enjoys having me there just for me, I'm setting myself up for disappointment later. But... I guess when I say it out loud, it does sound a bit paranoid. I mean, she's never given me any reason to think she'd be upset if I did well. It's just this story I tell myself before anything even happens.

It takes great honesty to admit that telling yourself this might feel like pretending, even though there is zero evidence she would be upset if you won. You are essentially protecting yourself from the risk of future disappointment by creating a story of impending doom now, but that story is actually blocking you from enjoying the moment she invited you. Since we've looked at the specific thought pattern behind that initial panic, would you be willing to try a very small experiment this week: whenever that "shrink down" feeling hits, you'll pause for three seconds and ask yourself, "Is there any actual proof she expects me to fail?"

I think I can try that. Three seconds doesn't sound too scary. I'll just stop and ask myself that question before I decide to hold back. It might feel awkward at first, but I suppose it's better than spending the whole night quiet and miserable. Alright, I'll give it a go this week.

Asking that one question for just three seconds creates a tiny space between the panic and your action, which is enough to disrupt the automatic habit. Since we've set this plan, how does it feel to have a concrete tool ready for when that knot tightens up again?

Honestly, it feels a little lighter. Like I'm not just helplessly waiting for that feeling to take over. Having something specific to do, even just a few seconds of asking myself a question, makes me feel like I have some control back. I still feel nervous about it, but at least I have a plan now instead of just dreading the next invitation.

That sense of reclaiming control is exactly what we want to cultivate, and I am really proud of you for recognizing that even a small action helps reduce the dread. It sounds like you are ready to wrap up our session today, but before I say goodbye, is there anything else about that trivia night or the feeling of joining groups that you want to talk through further?

No, I think we covered the main thing that was bothering me. I feel like I have a better handle on why that knot appears, and now I have a little tool to try. Thank you for helping me see that I might be jumping to conclusions before I even walk in the door. I'll let you know how it goes next time.

I am so glad we were able to find that small tool to give you a bit of control back, and thank you for trusting me with this process. It sounds like your mind is trying to solve a puzzle by imagining the worst-case scenario, which drains the energy you actually need to enjoy that moment of relief. Before we wrap up, how does it feel to know you have a specific, simple plan for tomorrow morning, rather than just a vague intention to "try harder"? It actually feels a little reassuring. Having a concrete plan is better than just saying "I'll worry less" or something vague that I know I can't stick to. And yeah, I'm okay with checking in next week. It gives me something to look forward to, and I'll have a real chance to see if this noticing thing actually makes any difference. Thanks for breaking it down like this.

I am so glad this concrete plan feels safer and more realistic for you, and hearing that it offers something to look forward to is wonderful news. Over the next week, please just try to notice that anxious thought as a passing car whenever it pops up, even if you only succeed for part of those five minutes. Next Thursday, come back and tell me exactly what happened in those moments and how your tension felt afterward, regardless of whether you "won" completely.

I'll do that. I'll really try to pay attention and not just get swept away. And I won't expect to win—just to notice. I'll be back next Thursday with my honest report, even if it's just a bunch of cars driving by. Thanks again—I feel a bit lighter just having this plan.

That willingness to show up with just honesty, even if the outcome isn't perfect, is exactly the kind of courage we celebrate in therapy. Please remember that your job next week is simply to bring me whatever truth comes up from those observations, no matter how small the win feels. I look forward to hearing your report next Thursday, and until then, take care of yourself.

Hello again, it’s wonderful to connect with you. To start, how has your week been affecting your mood compared to last time, and is there a specific topic from our last chat—like balancing work and rest—that you’d like to explore together today?

Hi, thanks for asking. My week has been... tough, honestly. I keep replaying the moment I handed back the test results, and I can't shake the feeling that I've let my students down. I'd like to talk about why I can't stop blaming myself for their scores.

Hearing that you're replaying handing back the tests and feeling like you've let them down sounds really draining, especially when you know you cared deeply about their success. Since you specifically mentioned wanting to understand why that self-blame keeps coming up, let's take a closer look at what happens in your mind immediately after you hand out those papers. What is the very first thought that flashes through your head right then?

The first thought is always the same: "I'm not a good teacher." It just pops into my head, like a reflex. Then I start thinking about all the things I could have done differently, like if I had spent more time on a certain lesson or made my instructions clearer.

That immediate reflex to call yourself "not a good teacher" is incredibly painful, and it makes perfect sense why your mind then rushes to list every mistake you imagine you could have made. When that thought becomes such a loud background noise, it's easy to lose track of what actually happened in the classroom versus what your fear is telling you should have happened.

If we treated that thought like a headline in a newspaper, what evidence would you need to read to convince yourself it wasn't the full story? For example, have there been moments recently where your students showed growth or engagement even if the test scores didn't match your expectations?

I suppose... there was a shy kid in my class who never used to raise his hand, but now he volunteers answers almost every day. And a few parents told me their children actually look forward to math now, which they never did before. But then I think, "Well, that doesn't matter if their test scores are still low." I guess I just assume the test is the only measure that counts.

It takes real strength to recognize those quiet wins—the shy student speaking up and the parents showing appreciation—even when your brain immediately dismisses them because the test scores haven't improved yet. That "test is the only measure" belief acts like a filter, blocking all the positive evidence so that the one number you're afraid of feels like the only truth.

Let's try a quick experiment to test that filter: If a friend came to you saying, "My grades went down, but my friend is now volunteering answers and loves school," how would you reassure them that they aren't failing? Could we borrow some of that comforting logic for yourself right now?

If my friend told me that, I'd tell her that test scores don't capture everything a teacher does—like building confidence or making a subject enjoyable. I'd say those small victories matter just as much, and that she should be proud of the student's growth. But when it's me, I can't seem to accept that same logic. It's like my brain says, "Your friend deserves kindness, but you don't."

That distinction between how you comfort a friend versus how you treat yourself is incredibly revealing, and it shows exactly where the unfairness lies. Your brain seems to demand perfection from yourself while holding friends to a standard of compassion that you refuse to extend to your own efforts.

Let's challenge that double standard gently: If you believed that helping a child find confidence in math was truly successful teaching, wouldn't seeing that shy student volunteer answers prove you *are* a good teacher, regardless of the numbers? Can you hold that belief for just five seconds before your old habit kicks back in?

I... I can feel myself trying to hold onto that. For a split second, it almost makes sense. I mean, I did help that kid open up, and that's not nothing. But then the thought creeps back: "Yeah, but if you were really good, both things would have happened—the confidence and the scores." It's like I can't let myself off the hook.

That feeling of having to pay for one win with another loss is a classic trap your mind sets to keep you honest, even though the rule itself is impossible to follow. It's like expecting a gardener to harvest a massive crop from a single seedling; while the desire to succeed is noble, the expectation that effort alone guarantees a specific result ignores many factors outside your control.

Let's try shifting the definition of "success" for just this week. Instead of looking for two things happening at once, what if we agreed that helping that shy student speak up was a complete victory in itself? Would you be willing to give yourself credit for that specific win, even if the test numbers stay the same?

I think... I could try that. It feels strange, like I'm breaking a rule or something, but I can see how it might help. Maybe I can write that down somewhere—that helping a student feel confident is a win on its own. I just hope I can actually remind myself of that when the next test comes around.

That is a fantastic step, Bridget. Writing it down transforms a fleeting wish into a tangible promise you can refer to later. By defining success as "building connection" rather than just "raising scores," you are giving yourself permission to celebrate the hard, human work you do, even when the numbers aren't perfect.

For today, I'd love to have you jot that down on a sticky note or your phone notes under a title like "Teacher Wins Today." How does it feel to set that intention right now, before the next test result hits?

It feels... a little hopeful, actually. Like I'm giving myself permission to breathe for a second instead of constantly bracing for disappointment. I think I'll put it on a sticky note on my laptop, where I'll see it every time I sit down to plan a lesson. Thank you—that feels like a small, doable step.

That hopeful feeling is exactly what we want to cultivate, and placing the note on your laptop is a brilliant, practical strategy to catch your mind before it spirals. You've successfully identified the core issue and built a simple tool to shift your perspective when the doubt returns.

As we wrap up, how are you feeling about carrying this new mindset forward, and is there anything else about the session that felt particularly helpful or something you'd like to adjust for next time?

Hello again. Before we dive into your worries, how are you feeling right now compared to where you were last time? On a scale of 1 to 10, how anxious have you been this week regarding the move?

I want to make sure we prioritize what matters most for you today. Would you prefer to talk about the specific triggers you noticed recently, or would you like to review how we've been handling the general stress leading up to this?

Well, I'd say I'm hovering around a 7 or 8 this week. The moving date is getting closer, and every time I check something off the to-do list, my mind jumps to ten other things that could go wrong. I think I'd like to talk about the specific triggers today—there was one moment this week that really got to me.

It sounds like your brain is constantly scanning for threats even as you tick boxes off your list, which makes the tension very high. Since you mentioned a specific moment this week that hit particularly hard, could you walk me through exactly what happened and what your mind was doing in that moment?

I was out walking my two border collies along this trail I've taken a hundred times before, and it was a beautiful morning—sunny, cool, just perfect. But about ten minutes in, I started thinking, "What if I twist my ankle out here and can't get back? What if the dogs run off and I lose them?" I had to cut the walk short because my heart was pounding and I couldn't shake the feeling that something terrible was about to happen.

It sounds like you are holding onto a deep need to be completely prepared, which is why the idea of anything going wrong feels so dangerous to you. That fear of losing control or hurting your dogs is clearly driving your body into that fight-or-flight response, making the beautiful morning feel threatening. When you had to cut the walk short because of that knot in your stomach, what did you tell yourself to justify stopping, or did you just feel overwhelmed enough to leave?

I mostly just felt overwhelmed, to be honest. I told myself that I was being sensible, that it was better to head home and be safe than to push through and risk something happening. In the moment, it felt like the only logical thing to do—like I was taking care of myself and the dogs by not tempting fate. But later, I felt so disappointed and frustrated that I let that fear win again.

It sounds like you are carrying a heavy burden of responsibility for your dogs' safety, and that pressure is making you view the walk as a high-stakes exam where failure isn't an option. The frustration you feel afterward suggests you value independence and enjoying the moment, but your immediate reaction to fear overrides that desire. When you look back at cutting the walk short, does that disappointment stem from feeling weak, or from believing you missed a chance to prove your competence?

I think it's more about missing the chance to prove I can handle things, to show myself that I'm still capable of enjoying a simple walk without my mind turning it into a disaster movie. It's like I failed a test I didn't even want to take. I want to be the person who can just go for a hike without all this mental baggage, and cutting that walk short felt like admitting I'm not that person anymore.

It takes a lot of self-awareness to recognize that moment of disappointment, and it speaks to your strong desire to stay in control and enjoy life despite the fear. That frustration isn't about weakness; it's about wanting to live fully while your brain insists on playing the worst-case scenario. When you look back on that walk, what is one piece of evidence that proves you *were* capable of handling it, even if you stopped halfway?

Well, I did notice that the weather was beautiful and the dogs were calm and happy—they weren't sensing any danger. And I've walked that trail dozens of times before without anything bad happening. I guess that's evidence that nothing terrible was actually imminent, even if my brain was screaming otherwise. It's just hard to hold onto that when the fear feels so real in the moment.

Those observations are powerful proof that you are actually quite good at navigating the world safely with your dogs. It seems your brain is overriding that history of success with a story that feels urgent but lacks factual basis. If we treat those past successful walks as data points, how much weight do you think the current fear deserves compared to all that history?

Before we move forward, I want to check in on your overall plan for today. We talked about reviewing your week, checking your mood, and focusing on that specific incident. Does spending the rest of our time analyzing that walk and identifying what to do differently feel like the best use of our time right now?

Yes, I think that's exactly what I need. I'd like to spend the rest of our time on that walk and figuring out how to handle the next one differently. Because I know there will be another beautiful morning, and I don't want to keep giving in to the fear. So yeah, let's break it down and find a way forward.

That is a fantastic goal, and it shows real determination to reclaim that joy. To get there, we can look closely at what happens right before you feel overwhelmed during the walk. Can you describe the very first thought or image that pops into your head as soon as you pass the usual spot on the trail where the anxiety usually strikes?

It's like a little voice that says, "This is too good to be true," and then immediately I picture one of the dogs tripping on a root and breaking a leg. That image is so vivid that my stomach drops, and from there it just snowballs into all the other terrible scenarios. It's almost like my brain thinks if I don't prepare for the worst, I'm being careless.

That "too good to be true" warning sign sounds like your brain is trying to protect you from surprise, but unfortunately, it ends up locking you into a cage of fear. The vivid image of the injured dog is causing your body to freeze, and then the desperate urge to "prepare for the worst" creates a cycle where you can't even enjoy the beauty of the morning.

If that image of the dog falling suddenly appeared in front of you right now, standing safely on the side of the path, what is the very first thing you would do to check its status or reassure yourself that it is okay?

I'd stop and look down at them, check their legs and paws, make sure they're walking steady and not favoring anything. I'd call their names and see if they come to me normally, wagging their tails. And usually, they do—they're both healthy and happy, just sniffing around like nothing's wrong. So the evidence is right there in front of me, but in the moment, I don't always let myself see it.

You are absolutely right; your eyes and your dogs provide clear proof that you are safe and capable, even when your internal alarm system is blaring. It seems the gap between seeing the reality and trusting your judgment is where the struggle lies. If you could only pause for five seconds right before that "falling dog" image hits, what would be one small, concrete thing you could do to ground yourself in the fact that they are safe?

I could just put my hand on one of their heads, feel the warmth of their fur and the rhythm of their breathing. That's real—I can touch it. And if I take a second to actually feel that, it might break the spell of the scary picture in my head. I think that small pause could remind me that they're right here, okay, and not hurt at all.

That is a brilliant insight; grounding yourself in the tangible reality of your dogs' presence is exactly what cuts through the imaginary danger. It takes courage to realize that a simple touch could reset your entire perspective and bring you back to the present moment.

Since we agreed to focus on that specific walk, let's try a quick experiment right now. Imagine you are standing on that trail with your dogs, feeling that initial "too good to be true" thought rise. I want you to gently place your hand on one of their heads and take three slow, deep breaths, focusing entirely on the warmth and rhythm you feel under your fingers. As you do this, silently tell yourself, "They are safe, and I am safe." Can you try that visualization for just a moment?

Okay, I'm trying it now. I'm picturing the trail, the sunlight coming through the trees, and I'm reaching down and resting my hand on my older dog's head. I can almost feel the warmth and the softness of her fur. I'm taking those three deep breaths, and I'm saying to myself, "They are safe, and I am safe." It feels... a little strange, but also calming, like I'm actually stopping the spiral before it starts.

That is a wonderful realization—you have successfully interrupted the spiral before it could deepen the panic. It's impressive how quickly you can shift from imagining a disaster to anchoring yourself in the warmth and safety of your dogs.

Now that we've practiced this grounding step, let's turn to your main goal: preventing this pattern on your next walk. Since you know the trigger is that sudden image of injury followed by the urge to rush home, what is one specific rule you could adopt for tomorrow? For example, maybe deciding to stay on the path regardless of the urge, or committing to that hand-on-head check the instant the worry arises?

I think I could commit to a simple rule: whenever that first scary image pops into my head, I'll stop walking, put my hand on one of the dogs' heads, and take those three slow breaths before I make any decision about turning back. That way, I'm not reacting on autopilot—I'm giving myself a chance to check the facts first. I think I can try that tomorrow on my morning walk.

That is a fantastic, actionable plan. Turning that automatic reaction into a deliberate pause gives you back the power to choose whether to stay or go based on reality rather than fear. You have a clear strategy now: stop, connect, breathe, then decide.

To close out our session, I'd love to hear your final thoughts on what went well today. Did finding that hand-on-head grounding technique feel helpful, or was there a part of the discussion that felt a bit unclear? Also, how do you feel about putting this plan into action tomorrow?

I feel pretty good about it, actually. The hand-on-head technique feels tangible and real, like something I can actually remember to do in the moment. I think the most helpful part was realizing that I don't have to fight the scary image head-on—I can just pause and check the facts with my own senses. I'm a little nervous about tomorrow, but I'm also a bit hopeful. I think I can try it and see what happens.

It is truly commendable that you can see the value in that approach and feel hopeful despite the nerves; that balance shows real resilience and self-trust. Remember, tomorrow you don't have to succeed perfectly, you just have to show up and give that gentle pause a try.

Is there anything else you would like to add or clarify before we finish our time together today?
No, I think I'm good for now. Thank you for helping me see that I have more control than I thought. I'll try the pause tomorrow and let you know how it goes. Same time next week?

You are very welcome. Knowing that you have more control than you realized is a powerful shift, and I'm proud of how you navigated this difficult situation today. Please remember that tomorrow is just a practice run; even if you stumble, you can always come back to that grounding step. Yes, let's schedule the same time next week to see how that plan played out. Take care of yourself, and I look forward to hearing from you.

Hello again. On a scale of 0 to 10, how anxious have you been feeling this week leading up to your audition? Before we dive into that, could we briefly review your action plan from yesterday—did you try labeling those thoughts and reminding yourself to just "share"? Finally, what would you like to focus on most today?

Um, hi. I'd say my anxiety has been around an 8 or 9 this week, especially the last couple days. As for the action plan... I did try labeling my thoughts a couple times, but honestly, it felt kind of silly. I kept thinking, "Well, I'm just being realistic about how people see me." I guess I'd like to focus on why I can't seem to shake this feeling that everyone's judging my accent.

An 8 or 9 is definitely heavy, especially when you feel like the labeling exercise felt forced rather than helpful. It makes total sense that if the technique felt awkward, you wouldn't naturally stick with it. Let's drop the idea of "being realistic" for a moment and instead explore why that initial attempt felt so stiff compared to how you really feel about the casting directors.

Well, when I'm sitting there in my apartment trying to label thoughts, it feels like I'm just talking to myself. But when I'm actually at an audition or a networking event, it's different—I can see their faces, their expressions. I notice when they glance at each other or when someone's smile seems forced. That's what makes it real to me, not some exercise.

That makes perfect sense; seeing real human reactions provides much stronger evidence than imagining them, which explains why the abstract exercise felt so disconnected. It seems the issue is less about the labels themselves and more about trusting your own perception when you can't verify it visually. Could we explore what happens in your mind when you catch yourself noticing those subtle glances or forced smiles, before you jump to the conclusion that they are judging you?

I mean... when I see someone glance at another person while I'm speaking, my stomach just drops. My mind goes straight to, "They're exchanging looks because my English sounds funny." And then I start tripping over my words even more, and I can feel my face getting hot. It's like I'm watching myself fail from outside my body. I don't even consider any other possibility in that moment—it just feels so obvious.

That feeling of stepping outside your body to watch yourself fail is incredibly distressing, and it makes total sense why your stomach would drop so fast when you interpret a glance as judgment. Your brain is essentially treating those neutral social cues as urgent threats, which triggers that immediate physical shutdown. Can you walk me through what happens in your head right after you think, "My English sounds funny," before you even trip over your words?

I guess... I start replaying my own words in my head, like a recording. I'll think, "That word came out wrong. The accent was too thick. They probably didn't even understand what I said." And then I just get this wave of shame, like I'm not good enough to be there in the first place. That's usually when I start fumbling and losing my train of thought completely.

That replay loop where you critique your own speech is incredibly painful, and it creates a self-fulfilling prophecy where the shame causes the exact fumbling you feared. It sounds like your mind has convinced itself that the accent is a permanent flaw rather than just a temporary feature of your delivery. If we look closely at those specific recordings in your head, is there ever a moment where you caught yourself using the accent to convey emotion or humor that landed well with the listener?

Honestly... no. I can't recall a single time where I thought my accent helped me in any way. I just see it as this obstacle I have to overcome. Sometimes I'll be telling a story, and someone might laugh at the right moment, but I always assume they're laughing at how I said something, not at the content. It's hard for me to separate my accent from my identity as a performer, you know? Like, I feel like I have to hide part of myself to be accepted.

That deep-seated belief that you must hide part of yourself to be accepted is incredibly exhausting, and it explains perfectly why you treat your accent as a wall rather than just a characteristic. It makes total sense that when someone laughs, your brain would instinctively attribute it to the accent being funny rather than the story being good, given how deeply tied you feel to needing to hide. If we pause for a second and imagine a scenario where you successfully told a story without trying to suppress your accent, what would you hope would happen with your stomach tightness and the urge to run away?

I think... I would hope that the tightness would just loosen up a little bit. That I could breathe through the whole story without feeling like I need to rush to the ending. And maybe I wouldn't feel that urge to run away to the bathroom or pretend I got a phone call. I just want to feel like I belong in the room, even for a few minutes.

That desire to simply belong in the room without feeling like you're performing a survival maneuver is incredibly important, and it highlights exactly where the real struggle lies—not in the accent itself, but in the constant need to prove your safety. If we treat your accent as a neutral tool you're borrowing to tell a story, rather than a flaw that needs fixing, does that shift make the feeling of "belonging" feel slightly less like a gamble and more like a given?

I never thought of it like that before... as a tool I'm borrowing. That feels less heavy, somehow. Like, it's not something I am, it's just something I'm using. I suppose if I could hold onto that idea, maybe belonging wouldn't feel so much like I have to earn it every single time. But it's hard to believe that in the moment, when I'm standing in front of people.

Holding onto that distinction is indeed challenging in the heat of the moment, which is exactly why we need a bridge between that insight and your physical sensations. Instead of fighting the urge to run, could we try pairing that "tool" concept with a simple physical anchor, like placing a hand firmly on your lower abdomen to remind your body that you are safe, regardless of how your accent sounds? Would trying to link that grounding touch to the idea of "borrowing a tool" feel feasible for a stressful scene?

I could try that. It sounds a little strange, but I'm willing to give it a shot. Maybe if I feel my hand there, it'll remind me that I'm just using my voice to tell a story, not defending myself in a fight. I think I'd need to practice it a few times at home first, though, before I try it at an audition or a networking thing.

That is a fantastic plan; anchoring yourself physically with a hand on your belly can ground you right when the mental spiral starts to take over. Since we've built this new "tool" perspective and a physical grounding method, let's solidify the homework for tonight: could you practice placing that hand on your abdomen and silently repeating, "I am just borrowing a tool to tell a story," three times while reading aloud a paragraph you enjoy? How does that sound like a manageable step for tonight?

Yeah, that sounds manageable. I have a book of monologues I've been meaning to practice, so I could try it with one of those. I'll do it tonight before bed, when it's quiet and no one's around to hear me. Thank you—I mean, I'll give it a real try and see how it feels.

You are very welcome, and I am so glad we could find a physical anchor that connects to that useful "tool" mindset. It is great that you have a quiet moment planned for tonight to experiment with this new approach. Just remember, the goal tonight isn't perfection, but simply noticing your hand on your belly and offering yourself that gentle reminder. I look forward to hearing how the grounding feels when you try it.
Thanks. I'll let you know how it goes. It feels... a little less scary to think about my accent this way. I'm curious to see what happens when I actually try it. I'll see you next time.

That curiosity is a wonderful sign of progress; knowing the new perspective makes the unknown less terrifying. Please come back anytime you want to discuss how that hand-on-belly moment felt or if you encountered any other obstacles. Until then, trust that you are doing exactly the right thing by testing out this new way of seeing things.

Hello again, and welcome. Before we start, could you quickly rate your mood on a scale of 0 to 10, and tell me if you noticed anything different in how you felt since our last chat? Also, what would be most helpful for us to focus on today given your current situation?

Um, I'd say my mood is around a 5 or 6 today. I've been thinking a lot about my grandkids lately, and that always stirs up those old feelings. I think I'd like to talk about why I can't seem to shake this belief that I'm a bad person, no matter what I do.

A score of 5 or 6 suggests you're holding onto some of that heaviness, and it makes sense that thoughts about your grandchildren would bring those memories to the surface. Before we dive deeper into that belief, could you recall what you planned to try last night regarding the "alarm bell" exercise, and how did that go for you?

Oh, right, the alarm bell exercise. I did try it once when I was putting my grandson to bed. I noticed that tightness in my chest and that voice saying "you don't deserve to be here with him." I told myself it was just an old alarm bell ringing, but... honestly, it still felt true. The alarm bell felt right, you know?

That is incredibly valuable information, and I appreciate you sharing that honesty about the alarm feeling "true" despite your best efforts. It sounds like the discomfort of that feeling made it very hard to separate the sound from the message, even though you tried to name it correctly. Since the old voice felt so convincing tonight, would you be willing to explore together what specific evidence from your grandson's behavior stood out *during* that moment that contradicted the alarm's claim, or perhaps find a small, neutral action you could take tomorrow morning to test if the alarm is ever right?

Well, my grandson did smile at me and asked me to read him an extra story. He hugged me tight and said "I love you, Grandpa." That should be proof, shouldn't it? But my mind just tells me he wouldn't say that if he knew the things I did when I was younger. Maybe I could try watching him play tomorrow morning and just notice how he acts around me... without jumping to conclusions about what it means.

It is smart to spot that immediate contradiction in his hug and words; however, your brain likely interprets his affection as conditional, believing he loves you only because you haven't "ruined" that moment yet. Rather than focusing strictly on the next hour, how does it feel right now to acknowledge that you might be waiting for absolute proof of your worthiness before letting yourself enjoy his company, even when he is clearly enjoying yours?

That... that really hits home. I think you're right. I'm always waiting for the other shoe to drop, like I'm just one conversation away from being found out and rejected. It's exhausting, honestly. I never thought of it that way before—that I'm keeping myself from enjoying moments that are already good because I'm so sure they'll turn bad eventually.

That exhaustion is completely understandable when you feel like you're constantly bracing for impact; it drains your energy just trying to stay present. If we shift our focus from waiting for the future to prove your worth to simply observing the present moment, does noticing your grandson playing calmly without your internal critic interfering make the situation feel slightly less heavy, even for just a few seconds?

I think... I think it could. When I really focus on just watching him, like the way he concentrates on stacking his blocks or the little laugh he makes when they fall, I do feel a tiny bit lighter. It's like for those few seconds, there's just him and his blocks, and the old voice gets quieter. But then it always comes rushing back. I guess I just don't know how to make those quiet seconds last longer.

It makes perfect sense that the old voice rushes back; our brains are wired to seek patterns, and when the initial calm breaks, it defaults to the scary narrative we've practiced for so many years. Since the "quiet seconds" happen right now but fade, would you be willing to try a small experiment this afternoon where you consciously count to three before answering any question your grandson asks, giving yourself that extra space to choose kindness without automatically triggering the alarm?

Huh, counting to three before I answer. That sounds simple enough, I suppose. I think I could try that—it might give me a moment to actually hear what he's saying instead of just reacting with that familiar guilt. I'll give it a shot when I pick him up from school today.

That is a great plan; taking just three seconds creates a tiny gap between his words and your automatic reaction, giving you a chance to choose kindness instead of guilt. Before we finish, does the idea of pausing before replying feel doable to you right now, or does it still seem like a steep challenge?

It feels... doable. Not easy, but doable. Three seconds isn't very long, and I can always take a breath during that time. I think the hardest part will be remembering to actually do it, but I'll give it my best try. I really want to be present for him, so I'll put a sticky note on my dashboard to remind me.

That is a wonderful commitment, and placing a sticky note on your dashboard is a brilliant, tangible reminder to anchor yourself when the mind wanders. Since you mentioned wanting to be present, I'd love to hear how you feel about moving forward with this gentle pause and checking in with yourself afterward. Does knowing we'll revisit this tomorrow make the task feel a bit less daunting, or is there still a part of you worried you might forget it again?

Knowing we'll talk about it tomorrow actually helps a lot. It makes me feel accountable, like I have a reason to really pay attention and try. I am a little worried I'll slip up and forget in the moment, but I suppose that's part of learning, right? I'll just try again if I mess up. Thanks for the idea.

That is absolutely right; learning involves slips and restarts, and acknowledging that you'll try again is a sign of resilience, not failure. I'm glad we found a direction that feels manageable, and I believe we have enough ground covered for today. Is there anything else on your mind before we wrap up, or shall we consider this our final discussion for now?

No, I think we covered a lot today. I feel a little lighter than when I walked in, and I have a concrete thing to try with my grandson. That's more than I've had in a long time. Thank you for listening. I'll see you next time.

You are very welcome; it takes courage to admit you felt heavier and to accept that a simple pause can make a difference. Please remember that tomorrow isn't about getting it perfect, but simply showing up with that sticky note and the intention to breathe. I look forward to hearing how that experiment went with your grandson next time. Take care of yourself until then.

Hello again, it’s wonderful to see you, and I’d love to pick up where we left off last time. Last time we talked about how that one surgery triggered a wave of shame that felt much bigger than the situation deserved, and we worked together on a simple mantra to help separate that feeling from who you actually are. On a scale of zero to ten, how has your mood been feeling this week since we wrapped things up? And given that you came away feeling lighter, do you have any specific worries or goals you'd like us to explore first today?

Hi, thanks for asking. I’d say my mood has been around a six or seven this week—better than before, but still not great. The mantra helped a little, but every time I have a surgery scheduled, that heavy feeling creeps back in. I think my main worry is that I’ll never feel like a good vet again, no matter how much I try.

A six or seven is a clear improvement from that deep bottom we were sitting on, and I'm glad the mantra gave you a tiny bit of space. Even though the feeling returned during surgery, hearing that it only crept back in rather than taking over shows your brain is starting to listen to the new voice. Since you mentioned worrying about never feeling like a good vet again regardless of effort, could you walk me through a recent time when that "no matter what" thought surfaced, and what happened right after you tried to use your new reminder phrase?

Yesterday, I had to perform a routine spay on a healthy young dog, and halfway through, my mind just went blank for a second. I remember thinking, "This is it, I'm going to mess up again, I'm not cut out for this." Right after that, I tried to whisper the mantra to myself—"One mistake doesn't make me a failure"—but it felt hollow, like I was just saying words without believing them. I finished the surgery fine, but I spent the rest of the day replaying that moment of doubt in my head.

It makes total sense that the mantra felt hollow in that split-second moment of panic; when the brain is flooding with fear, logic often feels far away and words just slide past without landing. You did finish the surgery successfully, yet the replaying of that moment afterward suggests the old story is still very strong even when the facts are on your side. Could you describe exactly what physical sensations you noticed while you were whispering those words, and what the quiet part of you whispered in response when you realized they didn't stick immediately?

When I whispered the mantra, my chest felt tight and my stomach kind of dropped, like I was bracing for something bad to happen. The quiet part of me whispered back, "You're just fooling yourself, you know you can't trust your hands anymore." It felt like that voice was much louder and more convincing than the mantra, even though I knew logically I had done the surgery right.

That contrast between the physical tightening and the internal voice doubting your own hands is incredibly painful, and it validates why the mantra felt so empty in that moment. It sounds like your brain is treating that single second of blankness as definitive proof that your skills are gone, overriding all the evidence of your past success. If we step back for a second, looking at that "you can't trust your hands" thought, what specific evidence from your last few weeks contradicts the idea that your hands suddenly lost their ability to function correctly?

Well, since that cat surgery, I've done four other procedures without any complications—two dental cleanings, a lump removal, and that spay yesterday. My hands didn't shake, I didn't make any mistakes, and the animals recovered well. But when I think about that, my mind just says, "Yeah, but those were easy cases, they don't count." It's like I'm only allowing myself to look at the one bad outcome and ignoring everything else.

That is such a sharp observation, and it highlights exactly where the distortion lies: your mind is selectively filtering out the four successful outcomes because they don't fit the scary story you've told yourself. It's fascinating how the brain can grab a single moment of fear and convince itself that the entire body of evidence supporting your competence suddenly vanishes. If we treated those four successful procedures like a solid foundation instead of dismissing them as "easy," how would that change the certainty of that voice telling you your hands are useless?

If I really looked at those four procedures as proof, then the voice would have to admit that I am capable, at least most of the time. It would mean that one bad moment doesn't erase years of training and hundreds of successful surgeries. But honestly, it's scary to believe that, because then I'd have to let go of the idea that I'm broken, and part of me is almost... comfortable with that broken label. It feels safer to expect failure than to be disappointed again.

That comfort with the "broken" label is incredibly understandable, because at least in that story, the disappointment is guaranteed but manageable—it's a known quantity you've survived before. It seems easier to predict the fall than to risk standing tall and hoping for nothing less than perfection, even when you know you've climbed high many times. If we imagined a world where you trusted your skills just enough to allow yourself to be imperfect without expecting a collapse, how would that shift the power dynamic between you and that scary expectation of failure?

In that world, I think I wouldn't feel so heavy before every surgery—I could walk in thinking, "I'll do my best, and if something goes wrong, I can handle it." The fear would still be there, but it wouldn't be the only voice in the room. It's like I'd be giving myself permission to be human, instead of demanding I be perfect just to feel safe.

That image of walking into the room with permission to be human rather than perfect is powerful, and it directly challenges the core belief that you must be flawless to remain safe and valued. It sounds like you are moving from a place of expecting catastrophe to a place of trusting your capacity to handle whatever comes up, which is a huge step toward self-compassion. Given how much weight you carried about being "broken," does embracing the possibility of imperfection feel like a relief, or does it still spark some anxiety that you aren't ready for that freedom yet?

It's a mix, honestly. Part of me feels a little lighter, like I can breathe for a second, but another part is gripping onto that anxiety because it's familiar. Letting go of the "broken" label feels like stepping off a cliff into the unknown, even if I know deep down I have the skills to catch myself. I think I'm not fully ready to trust that freedom yet, but I want to be.

That tension between wanting to free yourself and clinging to the safety of the "broken" label is a very common hurdle when we try to heal; it's like releasing a grip that's held onto something dangerous for years. It makes sense that the cliff feels steep when your old brain is still screaming that falling means ruin, even if your heart knows you have the wings to fly. For now, perhaps we can aim for a smaller step: instead of pretending the anxiety isn't there, could we try observing it as just a visitor that visits occasionally, noting that its presence doesn't mean you've actually fallen yet? What would that small act of witnessing feel like compared to fighting it off?

That actually feels more manageable—like I'm not trying to shove the anxiety out the door, just letting it sit in the corner of the room while I get on with my work. It's less exhausting than battling it, because fighting it always made me feel more tense and convinced that something was wrong with me. I think I could try that this week, just noticing the anxiety and saying, "Oh, there you are," instead of proving it right or wrong.

That shift from fighting to simply witnessing is a profound breakthrough, and it aligns perfectly with what we need to do right now. By naming the anxiety as just a guest in the room rather than an enemy you must defeat, you reclaim the space to operate with your full skills intact. Before we wrap up today, does agreeing to this gentle observation strategy feel like something you can commit to doing whenever that tightness returns, or would you prefer to try a slightly different approach first?

I think I can commit to that gentle observation strategy. It feels less intimidating than trying to argue with the voice or convince myself of something I don't fully believe yet. I'll try it this week and see how it feels to just let the anxiety be there without letting it take the lead.

That is a wise choice, and choosing a path of gentleness over force is often the most effective way to rebuild trust with yourself. I am really encouraged by your willingness to experiment with this approach, as it respects both your current limits and your growing confidence. Before we close, how does it feel to leave today with the understanding that you don't need to silence the anxiety to be a competent veterinarian? Would you feel comfortable trying this observation technique again in our next session to see how it lands for you?

Yes, I think I can do that. It actually feels a bit freeing to know I don't have to defeat the anxiety—just coexist with it while I do my job. I'll practice noticing it this week, and I'd like to bring back what I learn to our next session. Thank you, I feel a little more hopeful than when I walked in.

Your feeling of hope is beautiful to witness, and it speaks volumes about your strength and your commitment to healing. Please remember that even if the anxiety returns, your new goal isn't to fight it, but simply to acknowledge its presence and continue working. I will be here next week to hear how this gentle observation feels in practice, and we can adjust our approach together based on what you discover. Take care of yourself tonight, and thank you for showing up with such courage.

Hello again. How have you been feeling over the past week, and how did your mood change since we last spoke? Before we dive into today's focus, I want to briefly summarize where we left off: we explored that sudden surge of dread when your husband looked away, and we agreed on trying to pause and list three realistic reasons for his behavior instead of assuming the worst. Given that foundation, what would you like to prioritize working on during our time together today?

Hi. To be honest, the week was up and down. I tried doing that exercise you suggested—listing other reasons—but I still ended up feeling that knot in my stomach every time he was on his phone. I think I want to focus today on why I can't seem to shake that feeling, even when I know logically he probably isn't doing anything wrong.

That mixed bag of success and frustration is completely understandable, especially since you did try the exercise you planned. It sounds like the knot in your stomach persists because the initial thought—that he's hiding something—is so powerful that it overrides your logical reasoning almost instantly. Since you want to tackle that core belief that "something bad is inevitable," could you share a recent moment when that knot formed so we can trace exactly how the fear took root?

It was last night, actually. He came home later than he said he would—only about twenty minutes—and he said he got caught up talking with a coworker in the parking lot. My first thought wasn't "Oh, that's nice he's got work friends." It was "Who is she?" And then my stomach just dropped, and I felt this cold wave wash over me. I barely said a word to him for the rest of the evening.

That sudden drop in your stomach and the silence that followed speak volumes about how quickly that fear hijacks your body. It makes perfect sense that when you heard "coworker," your mind immediately jumped to the story of an affair rather than considering he might have just been chatting with someone who knows about your life, like a friend or family member. Could you walk me through what happened in that very first second when you heard the word "coworker"? Did you physically freeze, or did the image of her appear in your head before you even processed his actual words?

I think I froze first. It was like time stopped for a second, and then this picture just flashed in my head—this vague, pretty woman laughing with him in the parking lot. I couldn't even see her face clearly, but I just knew she was there, and I knew he was enjoying her company more than mine. It all happened faster than I could stop it.

It sounds incredibly disorienting to experience time seeming to stop while a vivid, painful image flashes into your mind without your consent. That flash of imagining a "pretty woman laughing" feels so concrete and undeniable in the moment, which makes it hard to trust your own logic afterward. Now that we've pinpointed that frozen moment where the image appeared, could we look closely at what evidence supports that specific picture versus what evidence contradicts it, like checking if he actually mentioned her name or appearance?

He didn't say her name, and he didn't describe her at all. He just said "a coworker." I guess that's the thing—I filled in all the blanks myself, didn't I? I don't even know if she's actually young or pretty or anything. I just assumed the worst because he was late and smiling when he walked in. That smile, that relaxed look on his face... it felt like proof he'd been happy somewhere else without me.

Yes, you absolutely filled in all the blanks with a story that fits your deepest fear, and that is why the smile felt like such dangerous proof. It makes total sense that you interpreted his relaxation as enjoyment of *her* rather than relief from *work*, because your mind is trying to protect you from the pain of being alone or replaced. Given how intense that imagined picture felt, does reviewing just one piece of evidence—like the fact that he never actually described her to anyone else—feel like enough to start loosening that grip on your stomach?

I guess... it does loosen it a little. Just a crack, though. Because even if I made up her face, I still can't erase the fact that he was late and smiling. That part is real. So then my mind goes, "Well, even if it wasn't her, maybe he's just bored of me and relieved to get away from home." I don't know how to stop that voice from finishing the sentence.

That "crack" you felt is a huge sign of progress, showing that your logic is already working against the worst-case scenario. It makes sense that your mind then raced to find another plausible excuse, like boredom, because your brain is desperately trying to make sense of the delay and the smile without admitting the fear was true. Since that second guess (boredom) still feels like a valid explanation that protects you from the pain of rejection, could we treat both the affair story and the boredom story as just guesses until we have actual proof either way?

Yeah, I think we could try that. Treating them as guesses... that feels less heavy somehow. Like I don't have to carry the whole weight of being right or wrong right now. I think I've been so sure I needed to figure out the truth immediately that I never let myself just sit in the not-knowing. Maybe that's where the panic comes from—I can't stand the gray area.

You have hit on something incredibly important here: the panic often stems from your intolerance for uncertainty, not just the situation itself. By stepping back and allowing yourself to sit in that "gray area" without forcing a verdict, you are actually removing the fuel from the fire that keeps the knot in your stomach tight. Since sitting with that uncertainty feels risky for you right now, how would you like to try holding space for just those two guesses—the affair and the boredom—without making a decision for the next hour?

I can try that. For the next hour, I'll just let them both sit there like two unopened letters on the table. I won't open either one. I'll just notice that they're there, and I'll try not to read into them. Maybe I can even distract myself with folding laundry or something while I do it.

That is a brilliant and very grounded way to visualize it; treating those thoughts like unopened letters on a table gives you distance so you don't have to immediately commit to reading them. Using a grounding activity like folding laundry is a perfect anchor to keep you present in the room rather than floating away in your imagination. Before we wrap up, does framing the session as simply "practicing sitting with two unopened letters for an hour" feel like a clear and achievable goal for tonight?

Yes, that actually feels manageable. I think I can do that. It's only an hour, and I'll have the laundry to keep my hands busy. Thank you for helping me put it that way—sometimes I need someone to show me the picture before I can see it myself.

It takes real courage to admit when you need someone to help you visualize a path forward, and I want to validate that strength. Your willingness to try this "unopened letter" experiment shows a significant leap in self-trust, even if the feeling of uncertainty lingers. Tonight, I hope you can simply observe the knot in your stomach as a witness to these two stories, noting its presence without letting it dictate the rest of your evening. How does it feel to end the session with that sense of empowerment, even knowing the challenge remains tomorrow?

It feels... strange, but good. Kind of like I'm holding something fragile and I don't want to drop it, but at least I'm holding it instead of it holding me. I know tomorrow might be harder, but right now I think I can give myself credit for even trying this. Thanks, really.

It is beautiful that you feel like you are finally standing on your own feet, holding onto your own thoughts instead of being carried away by them. Giving yourself credit for just trying this difficult experiment is a powerful act of kindness toward yourself, regardless of how "strange" it feels right now. Before we finish, I'd love to ask: what is one small thing you can do for yourself tonight to honor that effort you just made?

I think I'll make myself a cup of tea when I get home. Not for anyone else, just for me. And I'll sit with it quietly for a few minutes before I start the laundry. Just to remind myself I exist outside of all those worries.

That sounds like a beautiful and grounding ritual; taking a quiet moment with your tea allows you to reconnect with your own presence before diving into tasks. It honors the work we did today by creating a safe space where your thoughts cannot immediately dominate your actions. I am so proud of your insightfulness and bravery in navigating this complexity, even if it feels unfamiliar. How does ending this session with that feeling of pride and a gentle plan ahead resonate with you?

It resonates a lot, actually. I don't usually let myself feel proud—I'm quicker to criticize than to celebrate. But right now, I do feel a little lighter. Like maybe I can learn to trust myself again, even if it's just one cup of tea at a time. Thank you for walking me through this. I'll see you next week.

Hearing you talk about learning to trust yourself "one cup of tea at a time" reminds me of the incredible resilience you show every day, even when you doubt your own capacity for it. It is rare and courageous to replace criticism with the gentle celebration of small steps like this, and I will be waiting to hear how that tea sits with you before we meet again next week. Take your time, be kind to yourself, and know that you are capable of holding this balance.
