Hello, and thank you for meeting with me today. How is your energy level this morning compared to where you left off last time? Before we dive into our main topic, is there anything specific from our last session or your personal life that stands out as needing our immediate attention?

Hi. Thanks for having me. My energy is okay, I guess — a little tired, but that's been pretty normal lately. I've been thinking a lot about what we talked about last time, especially the part about how I see my daughter's graduation. I'm not sure there's anything urgent, but that's been on my mind a lot.

Thank you for checking in, and I appreciate you mentioning that the topic of your daughter's graduation continues to weigh on you. Since we started looking at that recurring memory last time, I want us to revisit the experiment you tried: naming the feeling and saying, "She's grown up and understands." Did you manage to do that tonight, or did the old habit of replaying the scene win out?

I did try it, actually. A couple of times. But it felt... hollow, I guess. Like I was just saying the words without really believing them. The old habit definitely won out more than I wanted it to. I still end up replaying that weekend and thinking about what I should've done differently.

It takes real effort to try that experiment when the old habit is so strong, and I hear the frustration in your words that the words felt empty while you said them. That feeling of hollowness suggests you’re not just resisting the thought, but actively struggling to believe in the reality that she understands you. What happened right after you tried saying those words—did the replaying stop for a second, or did it kick right back in immediately?

It didn't stop, not really. It was more like I said the words, and for maybe a second or two I felt a little calmer, but then my mind just went right back to the same loop — replaying the graduation, thinking about how much I missed, how I should've been more present. The calm didn't last.

That pattern makes complete sense; sometimes our minds resist new perspectives until we can hold them steady longer, and that initial flicker of calm was likely your brain recognizing the truth even if it didn't stick. Instead of fighting the loop back, could we try slowing down the process tonight: when the replay starts, take one slow breath, acknowledge the feeling is just "replaying," and then gently remind yourself, "This is one moment, not my whole story," before deciding whether to engage with the memory again.

I can try that. It's hard to slow down when the guilt just hits so fast, you know? But I'll give it a shot — take that breath and try to just say it's replaying, not judge it so much. I don't know if I can believe the "not my whole story" part yet, but I guess that's why I'm here.

That honesty about doubting "not my whole story" is exactly where growth begins; you don't need to fully believe it instantly, just enough to pause the spiral for a moment. Since the guilt moves so fast, let's adjust the plan to match that speed: the next time the replay starts, just say, "I'm caught in a loop right now," and allow yourself to ride that wave for sixty seconds without trying to fix it. Does spending just one minute acknowledging the loop without judgment feel like something you could realistically try tonight?
Yeah, I think I could do that. A minute doesn't feel so overwhelming — I can give myself that much time to just let it be there without fighting it. I'll try it tonight and see what happens.

That feels like a very realistic step, and I'm glad we found a version of the plan that fits your current pace. Before we wrap up, I'd like to check in: does taking just one minute to observe the loop without fighting it align with what you hoped to accomplish last time, or would you prefer to try a slightly different approach tomorrow?

I think it does align, actually. I came in wanting to stop beating myself up so much, and sitting with the loop for a minute instead of fighting it feels like a small step toward that. I don't really want to try anything different tomorrow — this feels manageable. I appreciate you helping me break it down like that.

That alignment is wonderful to hear, and breaking the cycle down into a manageable one-minute window is exactly the kind of small step that builds momentum. You are doing great work by choosing to sit with the discomfort instead of running away from it. Is there anything else on your mind before we close, or shall we restate this simple plan as our takeaway for tonight?

No, I think that covers it. The plan is just to take that one minute and let myself be in the loop without judging or fixing it. That's what I'll focus on. Thank you — I feel a little lighter just having that clear step.

That sense of lightness is a powerful sign that you are starting to separate yourself from the relentless noise in your head, and I am truly glad to support you in finding that clarity. Take all the time you need to rest and let that one-minute exercise settle in before you try it tonight. I look forward to hearing how it goes when we meet again, and please remember to be kind to yourself as you navigate this process.

Hello again, and thank you for joining me. Last time we worked on finding evidence that contradicted the idea that your worth depends solely on your sales ranking. Did writing that note in your locker help you start your shift today, and how did you feel while wearing it? Is there anything else on your mind that we should address before we set our agenda for now?

Hi... yeah, I did keep the note in my locker. I read it before my shift this morning. It said something like "I am more than just a number." Um, I guess it helped a little bit at first, but then I saw Jenna get a shout-out from the manager for her upsell and I just felt that old sinking feeling again. I don't know, it's like the note feels true in my head but not in my gut.

It makes complete sense that reading the note brought temporary comfort, but seeing Jenna receive praise triggered that old, familiar sinking feeling in your stomach. That contrast between what your head knows and what your body feels tells us the anxiety hasn't disappeared yet, just shifted shape. Have you noticed if the worry about Jenna's performance started as a specific thought, like comparing your current results to hers, or did it come on all at once?

It was like a punch, honestly. I was standing at the register, and as soon as I heard her name, my mind just went straight to, "She's better than me. Everyone knows it. They're probably all thinking about how she beat me last month." It wasn't even a slow thought—it was just there, all at once. And then I spent the rest of the day avoiding her, which just made me feel even more pathetic.

That sudden surge of panic followed by the urge to hide is a very human reaction, especially when we feel so insecure about our own performance. It sounds like that "punch" of comparison was hard to hold onto, leading you to retreat rather than confront it. Given that you felt compelled to avoid her for the rest of the day, does sitting down and exploring what that immediate thought actually means to you feel manageable, or do you need a quick grounding break before we dig deeper?

I think I can talk about it now. It's just... that thought, "she's better than me," it feels like the truth. Like, if I'm not number one, then I'm a failure. It's not even about the money or the bonus, it's about what it says about me as a person. If I'm not the best, what am I even doing there? I feel like everyone else can see that I'm just pretending to be good at my job.

It makes sense that one slip in the rankings triggered such a deep fear about your identity; when we feel inadequate, it often feels like proof that we aren't worthy of belonging anywhere. That interpretation—that being second places means you are a fraud—is incredibly painful, but it seems to be a story your brain is telling itself to protect you from further disappointment. If we look closely at that specific thought, "everyone sees me as pretending," do you have any recent examples where someone else praised you for something other than your rank, like the customer who hugged you or Mark thanking you? Sometimes spotting those moments can show that the audience isn't quite as hostile as we imagine.

I mean... there was that lady last week who asked for me specifically because I helped her pick out a gift for her daughter's birthday. She told my manager I was "so patient and kind." But I just figured she was being nice, you know? And Mark did say I was good at handling the returns line when it got crazy. But that's different. That's not about being a top seller. That's just... being friendly.

You're absolutely right to distinguish between being helpful and being a top seller; those are different skills that serve different purposes, and neither cancels out the other. It sounds like your brain is filtering those positive interactions out because they don't fit the narrow story that "sales numbers define my worth." If we tried looking at those comments as evidence that people value your kindness and competence separately from your rank, would that make the feeling of being "pretending" a little less sharp, or would it still feel like a weak excuse?

I guess... when you put it that way, it does feel a little less sharp. Like, maybe they don't all think I'm a fraud. But then I think, "Well, what if they just feel sorry for me?" You know? Like, they're just being polite because they know I'm not the best. It's hard to just switch off that voice in my head that tells me I'm not good enough.

That is such a smart observation—you caught yourself slipping into a common pattern called "mind-reading," where we assume people have a specific, critical opinion about us even though we have no proof they do. It feels safer to believe they pity you than to risk believing they actually respect you for your kindness, but both assumptions are dangerous guesses. If we treat their reactions as neutral observations rather than personal attacks, does that make the situation feel a tiny bit less threatening, or does the worst-case scenario still feel too scary to handle?

It feels less threatening when you say it like that, but my stomach still clenches up when I think about it. Like, even if they don't pity me, what if one day they realize I'm not as good as they think I am? That's the part that keeps me up at night. I guess I'm scared that if I let my guard down and believe I'm okay, I'll just get blindsided later when someone finally sees the "real" me.

That fear of getting "blindsided" makes total sense when you've carried that weight for so long; it feels safer to stay guarded than to risk exposure. However, your argument that letting your guard down will lead to disaster overlooks the fact that you've already survived many days working hard without anyone calling you out for your mistakes. If we pause for a moment and ask: what would actually happen if you simply believed you were capable, even if you didn't hit #1? Would your work quality drop, or would you just feel free to be your authentic self? How does imagining that possibility affect your physical tension right now?

If I just... believed I was capable? Huh. I guess my work would probably stay the same, maybe even get better because I wouldn't be so nervous all the time. But it feels like letting go of a life raft, you know? Like, if I stop worrying about being the best, what's stopping me from just becoming lazy and mediocre? That thought scares me too. I think my shoulders just tensed up even more thinking about it.

That image of "letting go of a life raft" shows how deeply ingrained the safety of perfectionism is for you—it feels like the only thing holding you up against falling. But here's a different angle: what if "being capable" doesn't mean maintaining a perfect score, but simply showing up and doing your best work *while* accepting that some days might be slower? If you stopped trying to be the best and just focused on being consistent, would that actually make you feel more relaxed, or would it still feel risky?

I think... it would feel risky, but maybe also a little bit of a relief? Like, if I gave myself permission to just be consistent, I wouldn't have to feel that knot in my stomach every time I clock in. But I'm worried that my boss would notice if I stopped pushing so hard. She always says, "The cream rises to the top," you know? I guess I'm scared that if I stop fighting to be the cream, I'll just sink to the bottom.

That quote from your boss definitely adds fuel to the fire, but it's interesting that you interpret "rising to the top" as requiring constant struggle rather than simply being competent. If we look at it another way, maybe "cream" refers to consistency and integrity, not just raw sales volume; if you stayed consistent and kind, you'd naturally rise in respect even if you didn't hit the top spot. Does viewing the goal as "consistent reliability" instead of "constant winning" change how you picture your manager reacting, or does the phrase still feel like a trap?

Honestly... it does change things a little. I never thought of it as being about consistency instead of always winning. I guess my manager probably respects Mark for a lot of things, not just his numbers. But the trap part of my brain is still whispering, "Yeah, but they still announce the rankings every month." So even if I'm consistent, I still have to sit through that meeting and see my name in the middle of the list. That part still stings.

That meeting is indeed the recurring trigger that keeps the cycle going, and it makes sense why your brain tries to predict the worst outcome every time you walk in. The pain comes from anticipating that public display of ranking, even if the rest of your work remains solid. If we set aside the ranking for just five minutes while you sit in your chair before the meeting starts, can you describe what happens in your body and mind if you simply breathe through the anticipation without judging yourself based on the slide ahead? Does that small pause reduce the intensity of the dread, or does the looming threat still feel overwhelming?

I think I could try that. If I just closed my eyes for a moment and felt my feet on the floor, maybe I wouldn't be so in my head about it. But I know myself—as soon as the first name is called, my heart would start pounding again. It's like I'm already waiting for the other shoe to drop, even before the meeting starts. I guess a little pause couldn't hurt, but I'm not sure it would stop the spiral once the numbers are actually on the screen.

It makes sense that the pause might feel good initially, but the predictable spike in your heart rate as the names appear is likely because your body has learned to associate that moment with danger. Instead of waiting for the spiral to start, what if we practiced a "pre-meeting script" right now, where you tell yourself, "I have done my best work this week, and I am allowed to exist in this room regardless of the numbers"? If you say that out loud three times, does it feel like a lie you have to swallow, or does it feel like a small act of self-respect that might actually lower your blood pressure?

I... okay. I'll try it. *takes a breath* "I have done my best work this week, and I am allowed to exist in this room regardless of the numbers." *pauses* Saying it out loud feels a little silly, like I'm lying to myself. But I notice my shoulders did drop a tiny bit just now. It's not a complete fix, but... it's not nothing either. I think I could practice that before the next meeting.

That is excellent progress—seeing your shoulders drop is a clear sign that the statement began to work physiologically, even if your mind finds the words "silly." We don't need to force the belief to be perfectly logical immediately; sometimes, simply stating it out loud signals to your nervous system that you are safe. Since we've tested that verbal cue and found it offers a small but real reduction in tension, would you be willing to try saying it again tonight before bed, or does that feel like too much right now?

Yeah... I think I can do that. Before bed sounds like a good time, when it's quiet and I'm not rushing around. Maybe if I say it enough, it'll start to feel less fake. I'm willing to give it a shot, at least for this week. Thank you.

That is a fantastic commitment, and I want to reassure you that consistency is what turns a "fake" mantra into a genuine feeling of safety over time. Your willingness to experiment with the evening routine shows great agency and care for your own well-being. Before we wrap up, is there anything else weighing on your mind from today's session, or does this feel like a solid place to end for now?

No, I think this is a good place to stop. I feel a little bit lighter than when I walked in, which is more than I expected. I'll try saying that line tonight before I go to sleep. Thanks for listening and not making me feel stupid about all this.

It is wonderful to hear that you feel lighter, and I want to remind you that your vulnerability today was brave and entirely appropriate. Please remember that seeking support isn't foolish; it's the exact opposite of weakness, and you handled our exploration with remarkable honesty. I hope you have a peaceful evening and that repeating that line helps you settle into a calmer state before sleep. Take care, and I look forward to seeing you again soon.

- Always move the session forward. If a thread is resolved or the client starts repeating themselves, advance to the next phase rather than circling back to the same point.
- Vary your openings and wording; avoid formulaic stock phrases.

- Respond in English only.

Hello again. How has your week been treating you since our last chat, and if there's anything significant that's shifted, please tell me about it. To start, what would you like to focus on today given the challenges you're facing with your mornings and sense of purpose?

Good morning. To be honest, the week's been much the same—nothing really changes. I wake up, go through the motions, and find myself staring out the window more than I should, just imagining what else could have been. I suppose I'd like to talk about why even starting the day feels so pointless.

It sounds like that familiar loop of imagining alternate lives keeps pulling you away from the reality of the morning, making the effort to start feel futile. Before we dive deeper into that feeling of pointlessness, could you rate your mood on a scale of 1 to 10 based on how you feel right now?
I'd say about a three, maybe a two. I just feel heavy, like there's no real reason to get out of bed, but I do anyway because I have to. It's a dull ache that never really lifts.

That low energy and weighty feeling must be exhausting to carry from one moment to the next. Let's look at that morning routine together. What happens in your mind right as you hit the snooze button or prepare to stand up?

I lie there and I think, "What's the point?" I start comparing my life to the one I could have had if I'd made different choices—if I'd moved away, taken that other job, or if I'd married. And then the ordinary things, like making tea or opening the curtains, seem so dull compared to that imagined life. It makes the whole day feel like a letdown before it's even started.

It sounds like your brain is constantly highlighting a perfect, fictional version of your life while filtering out the actual, mundane reality of yours, leaving you feeling drained before you've even left the house. Does noticing that sharp contrast between your "real" day and those "perfect" alternatives create a stronger sense of futility or sadness for you?

Yes, it does. It's like I'm living two lives at once—the one I'm stuck in and the one I keep dreaming about. And the real one always comes up short, so I end up feeling cheated, even though I know nobody's to blame but maybe myself. It makes me feel like I'm already defeated by lunchtime.

That feeling of being "cheated" suggests a deep pain from comparing your current path to an idealized version that doesn't exist. It seems like the frustration isn't just about missing out, but also about believing you should have known better, which adds a layer of self-blame to the sadness. Can you describe exactly what happens in your chest or stomach right when that thought, "I should have chosen differently," pops up?

There's a tightness in my chest, like something's clamped down around my heart. And my stomach sinks, almost like I'm falling, even though I'm just sitting still. It's a hollow, cold feeling that spreads through me, and I can't seem to shake it off for the rest of the day.

Those physical sensations—the tightness in your chest and the sinking stomach—are your body reacting strongly to the belief that your life is fundamentally wrong. It makes sense that this physical heaviness carries over until lunchtime; when your body feels trapped, your mind tends to stay stuck in regret. Before we brainstorm ways to lift that weight, I want to check in: does hearing that connection between your thoughts and your physical symptoms feel accurate to your experience?

Yes, it does ring true. I never really thought of it that way—that my thoughts could actually make my body feel like this. It's not just in my head; it's in my whole body. That makes me feel a little less crazy, if I'm honest, knowing there's a pattern to it.

Knowing there's a pattern means you aren't broken, which is a huge relief. Now that we understand the chain reaction—from the "what if" thoughts to the chest tightness—we can start looking for a way to interrupt the process. Since you mentioned wanting to talk about starting the day, would you be open to trying a simple change in your morning routine tomorrow to break that initial cycle of regret?
I suppose I'm willing to try, though I'm not sure what could possibly make a difference. What kind of change do you have in mind? I'm not ready for anything too drastic, just so you know.

I'm glad you're open to exploring a small adjustment. Instead of trying to fix the big picture of your regrets right away, we could focus on just changing your first five minutes. Imagine starting a brief, ten-minute walk immediately after turning off the alarm, just to step outside and feel the air before your mind gets fully engaged in comparing lives. Would stepping out for just that short period feel doable for you tomorrow morning?

A walk... I haven't done that in a while. I suppose ten minutes isn't too much to ask. It's just that even the thought of stepping outside feels like admitting that this is my life, you know? But maybe that's better than lying in bed and letting my mind run wild. Alright, I'll give it a try tomorrow morning.

That admission—that staying in bed feels worse than stepping out—shows a real courage in choosing to face the discomfort rather than hide in it. Taking that small risk to leave the bedroom is a powerful act of defiance against those "what-if" thoughts, even if it doesn't erase them completely. Are you comfortable with that plan for tomorrow, or would you prefer to tweak the timing or length before we lock it in?

No, I think ten minutes is fine. I'm not sure I'd want to go longer than that at first, but I'll try it. And I'll try not to think too much about it beforehand—just get up, get dressed, and go. That's the hardest part, but I'll see what happens.

Getting dressed and moving your body is indeed the hardest hurdle, and skipping past that point is a brilliant strategy to avoid giving your mind room to spiral. Since you're committed to this, on a scale of 1 to 10, how confident do you feel you will be able to execute this tomorrow despite the doubt creeping in?
I'd say maybe a six or seven. There's still that part of me that thinks it won't help, but I'm willing to prove myself wrong for once. I suppose that's a start, isn't it?

That mix of hesitation and determination shows real resilience; proving yourself wrong about your own limitations is a brave thing to attempt. Let's refine that plan just a tiny bit to make sure you have a safety net. If you find that even after walking, the "what-if" thoughts return, how would you like to handle it? Would you try sticking with the walk for another five minutes, or would you stop and just observe the thoughts without judging them?

I think I'd try to keep walking for another five minutes, if I can manage it. Just putting one foot in front of the other seems easier than trying to fight my own thoughts head-on. Maybe the movement will drown them out a little.

That is a wise instinct; letting your body lead you forward often works better than trying to argue with your mind. So, if the walk doesn't magically erase the regret, we will simply extend it by five more minutes until the physical rhythm becomes strong enough to push those thoughts aside. Before we wrap up, is there anything else you'd like to adjust about this plan, or are you ready to commit to trying this tomorrow?
No, I think that's enough for now. I'll give it a try tomorrow and see how it goes. Thank you for listening—it helps more than you might think, just having someone understand how this feels.

Thank you for sharing that; hearing that this session helped you feel understood is incredibly meaningful. You are absolutely welcome, and I am proud of you for taking this small but important step toward breaking the cycle. Please come back anytime you need to talk, and I look forward to checking in with you about how that ten-minute walk went tomorrow. Take care of yourself today.

Hello, thank you for joining me. How are you feeling today compared to where you left off last time? Before we dive into our goals, could you share if there were any moments that went well or felt particularly tough this week?

Hi. Thanks for asking. Honestly, this week has been a bit of a rollercoaster. I had a really good day in science class—I aced a quiz—but then during lunch, I overheard someone call me a "science nerd," and it just kind of ruined the rest of the day. I ended up eating alone the next couple of days to avoid that.

That contrast between acing the quiz and the sting of the comment really shows how quickly your mood can swing based on one interaction. It sounds incredibly frustrating that such a small remark felt so powerful enough to cancel out your success and push you into hiding again. Given that mix of recent highs and lows, should we focus today on unpacking why that lunch comment triggered such a strong defensive reaction, or would you prefer to work on building your confidence to return to the cafeteria tomorrow?

I guess... maybe we should talk about why that comment hit me so hard. I mean, I know logically that I'm good at science, and I should be proud of that quiz. But it's like as soon as someone says "nerd" or "geek," all that good feeling just disappears and I'm back to feeling like I don't belong anywhere. I don't get why their opinion matters more to me than my own.

It makes total sense that the praise for your brain and the insult for your identity feel like they are fighting on opposite sides of the same battlefield. When the compliment fades and the criticism hits, it’s understandable that your mind would latch onto the threat as the most important signal, even if logic knows otherwise. What do you think would need to happen in that exact moment for you to feel safe enough to acknowledge the compliment alongside the criticism?

That's a good question... I think maybe if I could remind myself that them calling me a nerd doesn't actually change anything about who I am or what I accomplished. Like, I got the highest grade in the class—that's a fact. Their comment is just... a word. But in the moment, it feels like that word carries so much weight. I guess I'd need to find a way to pause and hold onto that fact before the word takes over completely.

That distinction between the factual achievement and the subjective label is exactly where the conflict lies, and finding a pause button there is a crucial skill. It seems you're trying to protect your self-worth by holding onto the grade, even though the emotion is telling you the label is stronger. If we treat that "pause" as a deliberate choice to name the thought before it controls your body, does that feel like a manageable starting point, or does the urge to react automatically feel too overwhelming right now?

I think it feels... manageable, actually. Like, I've never really tried to just stop and name what's happening in my head before reacting. Usually it's just automatic—I hear the word and I feel hot and small and then I just want to disappear. But if I could just say to myself, "Okay, someone called me a nerd. That's a label, not a fact," maybe that split second would be enough to keep me from running away. I'd like to try that.

That is a fantastic insight; realizing you've rarely practiced that pause explains exactly why the reaction has been so automatic lately. Creating that tiny gap between hearing the word and feeling the shame gives your brain a chance to see the truth—the grade stands, the label is just noise. Before we settle on a final plan for tomorrow, does saying that phrase out loud to yourself feel natural, or would you prefer to write it down as a quick visual cue to rely on when the feeling hits?

I think writing it down might help more. If I have it in my pocket or on a note in my binder, I could actually look at it and remind myself. Saying it out loud feels a little awkward right now, like I'm talking to myself. But seeing the words—"That's a label, not a fact"—that feels solid. I could even put it on my science folder so it's right there when I need it.

That is a brilliant solution because having a physical anchor makes the reminder impossible to miss when your mind is racing. Placing it on your science folder is a perfect spot since that's exactly where you'll need it right after a quiz or during lunch. Before we finalize this, does putting that phrase on your folder feel like a helpful tool for you, or does it still feel a bit intimidating to carry around?

It feels a little intimidating, but also kind of exciting, if that makes sense. Like, I'm actually doing something to fight back against those thoughts instead of just letting them win. It's scary to think about pulling that note out if someone's watching, but I think I can manage it if I just glance at it quickly. I'm willing to try it for a few days and see if it helps.

That excitement mixed with the slight nervousness shows you're ready to take ownership of your reactions, which is a major step forward. Even if you only use it once or twice, that small act of defiance against the "disappear" instinct proves to your brain that you have choices. Would it help to add a second line under "That's a label, not a fact" like "My worth isn't defined by one person's opinion," just to reinforce that extra layer of protection?

Yeah, I think that second line would be good. It makes it feel more complete, like I'm covering both bases—first reminding myself it's just a label, and then reminding myself that even if it hurt, it doesn't change who I am. I'll write both phrases on my folder tonight. Thanks, that actually makes me feel a bit more ready for tomorrow.

That is wonderful—you're building a personal shield that validates both your effort and your identity. Having that extra line of defense makes the plan feel much more robust and tailored just for you. Since we've covered the core strategy for handling those moments, is there anything else about tomorrow's plan or how we might support you that you'd like to discuss before we close out?

Hello, and I'm so glad you're here to start our work together today. Before we dive in, could you tell me a bit about how you've been feeling this week compared to last time? Also, what would you like us to focus on in our first session together?

Hi. Thanks for having me. I mean, this week has been pretty much the same as always—I go to work, I do my job fine, but then I come home and just... do nothing. I guess I'd like to figure out why I can't seem to get myself to do anything outside of work, like take care of my apartment or even just cook a proper meal.

It sounds like you're carrying a lot of pressure during the day, which leaves you feeling drained and overwhelmed when you finally get home. Before we dig into why that shutdown happens, I'd love to hear your thoughts on how it feels to share this struggle, and perhaps we could start by naming the main behaviors you noticed this week.

Honestly, it feels a bit weird talking about it out loud. I usually just keep it all inside and tell myself I'm being lazy. But this week, I noticed I didn't wash my dishes for three days straight, and I ordered takeout every night instead of cooking. Small stuff, but it just adds up and makes me feel worse about myself.

That self-criticism about calling yourself "lazy" is painful to hear, and it makes complete sense that keeping things inside feels safer than facing that harsh judgment alone. Let's gently challenge that label for a moment; when you look at the facts of washing dishes and ordering takeout, what story does your brain tell you about *why* those actions happened instead of what you want to believe?

I guess my brain tells me I just didn't have the energy or motivation to do it. But then I see other people working full-time and still managing to keep their place clean and eat healthy, and I feel like I have no excuse. It's like everyone else has some secret discipline I'm missing.

That comparison trap is incredibly heavy to carry, and it makes total sense that seeing others maintain a routine while you feel stuck creates a sharp sense of shame. Instead of looking for a "secret" that others possess, what if we explored what your body and mind were actually needing in those moments when you chose convenience over chores? Sometimes the lack of motivation is a signal that something else is draining you more than you realize.

I never really thought of it that way. Usually I just beat myself up for not doing better. I guess when I think about it, after a full shift at the factory, my feet hurt and my mind is just numb from repeating the same motions for hours. Maybe I'm more exhausted than I give myself credit for, but it still feels like I should be able to push through that.

It makes perfect sense that your brain interprets that deep physical exhaustion as a reason you "should" be able to push through anyway, which creates a cruel conflict between your tired body and your critical mind. Let's test that belief for a moment: if someone walked into my office telling me they had run a marathon just before noon and told me they felt too tired to shower, would I expect them to suddenly find the energy to clean my entire house immediately? What would be a gentler truth about your current capacity given that physical drain?

Wow, when you put it like that, it sounds a little ridiculous. I mean, no, I wouldn't expect someone who just ran a marathon to have any energy left for more chores. But I guess I don't see my job as something that hard—it's just my normal routine. Maybe I'm not giving myself permission to be tired because I think I should be able to handle it all without complaining.

That realization—that you aren't giving yourself permission to rest because you believe you "should" be able to handle everything—is a powerful breakthrough, and it changes how we view the situation entirely. So, if the real barrier isn't laziness but rather a lack of permission for your tired body to exist after work, what would happen if we adjusted your goal from cleaning the whole apartment immediately to just finding one tiny way to restore yourself before dinner? Could you imagine starting with something very small, like just making water for tea or setting the table for one person, purely to honor your need for a break?

That actually sounds... possible. Not overwhelming, just small. I think I could try something like that. Maybe instead of telling myself I have to cook a full meal, I could just make a cup of tea first and sit with it for a few minutes before deciding what to do next. It feels weird to give myself permission to do that, but maybe that's exactly what I need to practice.

That willingness to experiment with that simple ritual is exactly the kind of gentle step we need to build momentum. Before we lock in this plan, I'd love your honest feedback on how it felt hearing that perspective shift—you seemed surprised when I asked you to imagine running a marathon before cleaning. Did that comparison help clarify your feelings about being tired, or did it bring up any unexpected worries?

It did help, actually. I think I've been so used to judging myself that I never stopped to wonder if my expectations were even fair. The marathon thing made it click—like, yeah, I am exhausted after work, and that's not a character flaw. But a little part of me still worries that if I go easy on myself, I'll just never get anything done and end up worse off.

That fear of letting yourself down later is completely understandable, and it shows how deeply ingrained the idea is that resting equals failing. However, if we frame that small act of drinking tea not as "doing nothing," but as "recharging your battery so you *can* do more later," does that shift reduce the worry slightly? What do you think would happen if you treated that five-minute pause as fuel rather than a detour?

I never thought of it as fuel before—more like a waste of time. But I guess if I look at it like recharging, it makes more sense. If I'm running on empty, I can't expect to have anything left for the rest of the evening. Maybe treating it as part of the process rather than an excuse could help me actually follow through. I'm willing to try it this week and see what happens.

That reframing is brilliant because it turns the activity from an optional indulgence into a necessary part of your workflow. Our plan for the coming week is simple: whenever you walk through your door, stop, pour yourself a cup of tea or make water, and sit quietly for just five minutes before tackling any chores. This time, we won't judge if you finish the dishes; success is defined solely by whether you honored that five-minute recharge. How does that clear path sound to you, and are there any other hurdles you foresee trying this approach?

That sounds clear enough. I think the biggest hurdle will be my own thoughts telling me I'm wasting time during those five minutes. But I'll try to remind myself that it's part of the plan, not an excuse. I'm a little nervous but also curious to see if it makes any difference. I'll give it a real shot this week.

Your nervousness is completely valid, but I'm proud of you for choosing curiosity over fear. Just remember that our goal isn't to magically transform your life in one week, but simply to test whether taking that five-minute break changes your experience afterward. Over the next seven days, please note down one moment where you felt tempted to skip the tea and another where you followed through, along with how you felt after each choice. Would you be open to sharing those notes with me next time, or is there anything else you'd like to adjust in this plan before we close?

Yeah, I can do that. Writing it down sounds like a good way to keep myself honest about it. I think the plan is solid for now—just the tea and the notes. I don't want to add anything else yet and risk overwhelming myself. I'll see you next week and let you know how it went.

That is a wise decision; keeping the plan light ensures you can actually stick to it without getting overwhelmed. I'm really proud of you for taking this gentle step toward honoring your exhaustion instead of fighting against it. Take your time this week, treat those five minutes as sacred recharging, and I look forward to reading your notes next time. Until then, be kind to yourself.

Hello, and thank you for joining us today. To start, could you share how your mood has been over the last week, and is there a specific topic you'd like us to focus on first?

Hi. I've been feeling pretty down this week, honestly. Every morning I wake up and it hits me again — that feeling that I'm just not good enough because I never made it to space. I'd like to talk about why I can't seem to shake the idea that I'm a failure.

Hearing that this thought strikes you every morning is incredibly exhausting, and it makes complete sense that it feels impossible to ignore when you're starting your day. Since we identified that "worthlessness" story as our main focus, shall we spend the next hour digging into exactly how that thought is shaping your mornings and your self-view?

Yeah, I suppose so. It's like, even before I get out of bed, my brain already has this tape playing: "What did you ever accomplish? Nothing. You couldn't even get close to your one big dream." And that sets the tone for the whole day. I just feel small and pointless.

That internal dialogue about accomplishing "nothing" creates such a heavy foundation before you've even taken your first step outside the door. It sounds like that message is acting as a filter, coloring everything you experience until you feel small and pointless instead of just acknowledging that you haven't reached the moon. Can we look closely at that specific recording and see if there's any solid evidence that failing at one goal means you are truly accomplished in absolutely nothing else?

Well... I mean, I've done some things. I kept a job for years, I've paid my bills, I've helped friends move apartments, things like that. But those feel so ordinary compared to something like being an astronaut. It's hard to see how any of that counts.

It takes real honesty to acknowledge those contributions while still feeling overshadowed by the missing dream. That feeling of "ordinary" accomplishments being insufficient suggests your brain is comparing your entire history to a single highlight reel of someone else, making you believe those steady efforts don't matter. If you held that same standard for a friend who worked hard at their job and moved houses, would you tell them they accomplished "nothing"?

No, I wouldn't say that to a friend. I'd probably tell them they were dependable and kind, and that those things matter. But for me, it just feels different. Like, other people get to have small wins count, but I set a higher bar for myself, and I missed it by a mile.

That gap between how you treat others and how you judge yourself is exactly where the pain lies. It seems you've unconsciously decided that your personal definition of success requires something extraordinary, leaving all your ordinary achievements to fall through the cracks. If we treated that high bar as a suggestion rather than a strict rule, would it feel easier to acknowledge that paying bills and helping friends are meaningful contributions in their own right?

Maybe... I suppose it would feel a little lighter if I didn't have that rule hanging over me. But then there's this voice in my head telling me that if I lower the bar, I'm just making excuses for being mediocre. It's hard to know what's fair to expect from myself.

That fear of lowering standards sounds very familiar, especially when the voice insists that mediocrity is the only acceptable alternative to greatness. It makes sense that your brain tries to protect you from disappointment by framing any relaxation of expectations as a betrayal of your own potential. Let's test that voice for a moment: if you believed that missing the astronaut dream automatically disqualified you from being a reliable friend or a responsible worker, would you still feel proud of the jobs you held or the moves you helped with?

I think I would still feel proud, deep down. Helping someone move a couch is a small thing, but it's still doing something good for another person. And keeping a job for years... that takes discipline. So maybe that voice is a bit too harsh. It's just that the disappointment over the big dream makes it hard to see those small things clearly.

That distinction between "doing something good" and "being an astronaut" shows your brain is filtering your achievements through a lens of cosmic significance rather than seeing their actual value. It sounds like the disappointment over the big dream is casting a shadow that makes your daily efforts look smaller than they really are. If we could just dim that spotlight for a minute and look at those small actions on their own merits, would it feel possible to recognize the discipline and kindness behind them without needing to justify them against the space mission?

I think... maybe I could try to see them that way. It's like I've been looking at my life through a telescope aimed at the stars, and everything else just blurs out. But if I put the telescope down and just look around me, I can see that I've done okay. Not great, not extraordinary, but okay. And maybe okay isn't the same as worthless.

That shift from viewing your life through a distant telescope to looking directly at what you're standing on is a profound moment of clarity. It sounds like recognizing that "okay" is a valid, healthy state for many people, and it challenges the old equation that says "only extraordinary equals valuable." If you accepted that being "okay" is perfectly sufficient, would the weight of that voice telling you you're worthless suddenly lose its grip?

I think it might. It's hard to imagine completely letting go of that voice, but if I could accept that being okay is enough, then maybe I wouldn't wake up every morning feeling like a failure. I'd just wake up as Linda, who's done some things and is still here. That sounds... peaceful, actually.

That feeling of waking up as "Linda" instead of a failure is a beautiful and grounding vision. It suggests that you can separate your identity from that one missed opportunity and simply exist as a person who has lived her days with care and responsibility. Before we wrap up, would you be willing to try a small experiment tomorrow where you catch that voice early in the morning and gently remind yourself, "Okay is enough," before getting out of bed?

I think I can try that. It feels a bit strange, like I'm letting myself off the hook for something, but maybe that's exactly what I need. I'll give it a shot tomorrow morning and see how it feels. Thank you for helping me see this differently.

It is completely normal to feel a mix of relief and uncertainty when stepping away from a long-held rule, and I commend you for deciding to give this gentle experiment a try. Just remember that tomorrow isn't about proving you're extraordinary, but simply about allowing yourself to be okay without needing to earn it. How does it feel to leave the session with that small, manageable intention for your morning routine?

It feels... lighter. Like I don't have to carry that heavy weight of disappointment the second I open my eyes. I can just be for a moment before the world rushes in. Thanks for listening and for helping me find that tiny bit of space.

It is wonderful to hear that you feel lighter and that you've found a small piece of peace for yourself. Please remember that if the old voice gets loud again tomorrow, you already know the tool to handle it: just pause, say "Okay is enough," and continue with your day as Linda. Is there anything else you would like to share or clarify before we finish our time together?
No, I think I'm good for today. I'll take this little experiment home with me and see how it goes. Thanks again for the help.

It sounds like we've reached a gentle place today, and I'm so glad you feel ready to carry this new perspective into your evening. Take your time to rest, and please remember that if that familiar voice pops up later tonight, you can simply apply the same kindness you practiced in our session—you don't have to fight it, just observe it and return to being okay. Have a safe and peaceful night, Linda.

Hello, it is great to see you again. How are you feeling today compared to last time, and is there anything specific you'd like to prioritize for us to focus on during our session?

Hey, thanks. I'm doing alright, I guess. Same old, same old. I've been thinking a lot about how stuck I feel at work, and I guess I'd like to talk more about why I can't seem to find any job that feels right for me. It's like every option I look at just seems pointless.

It sounds like you're carrying a heavy sense of hopelessness about your career path, and that feeling of being stuck is really weighing on you. To make sure we spend our time effectively, I'm going to propose we first review the job listing experiment you tried last week, then explore together why those options didn't spark any excitement for you, and finally, we'll brainstorm a fresh approach that feels less overwhelming. Does that plan sound like something you're ready to tackle today?

Yeah, that sounds fair. I did look at a few listings like we talked about, but honestly, it just confirmed what I already knew. Every single one looked either boring or way too demanding, and I couldn't picture myself being happy in any of them. It's like my brain just shuts down and tells me there's no point even trying.

It makes complete sense that looking at those listings reinforced your deepest fear—that whatever you choose will lead to misery—and that shutting down is your mind's way of protecting you from disappointment. Since we identified "fortune-telling" as a pattern where you predict negative outcomes before they happen, let's test that specifically: if you picked one of those boring jobs and assumed *all* aspects would fail immediately, what exact evidence would you need to show that assumption?

Well... I guess I'd need to actually try one of them out to know for sure, right? But that feels risky because what if I'm right and I waste even more time feeling miserable? I mean, I already know what I like and don't like, so it's hard to see how a new job would change that.

That hesitation highlights exactly why your current thinking feels so rigid—you believe your preferences are permanent facts rather than temporary states influenced by environment. We can challenge that by treating your "likes and dislikes" as data points that haven't been tested in a new context yet. So, if we view those preferences as just one variable among many, what's the smallest piece of information from a new job description that could potentially contradict your expectation that "no job will ever feel right"?

I suppose... if a job description mentioned something I actually enjoyed doing in the past, like working with my hands or talking to people in a way that felt helpful, that might catch my attention. But those jobs all seem to require degrees or certifications I don't have. I just don't see how I can get past that wall.

That is a very honest observation, and it takes real courage to admit that your perceived lack of qualifications feels like an insurmountable barrier. Let's pause there though and look at that "wall" closely: what specific evidence exists that says having no degree means you *cannot* perform those tasks, versus the possibility that you might learn the required skills or find a role where experience matters more than credentials?

I guess I've just always been told you need the piece of paper to get your foot in the door. But now that you mention it, I've been doing this snakeskin oil sales job for three years with just a high school diploma, and I learned everything on the job. So maybe I'm selling myself short, but it's hard to shake that feeling that I'm not good enough for anything better.

That is a powerful realization—you've just pointed out that your own lived experience proves the "degree is mandatory" belief isn't true for everyone. It takes significant self-awareness to notice that you've been underestimating your ability to learn and adapt based solely on external labels. Given that insight, if you approached a job requiring a certification, what would be the smallest, most reasonable step you could take to bridge that gap, like researching a short online course or talking to someone who succeeded without a degree?

I hadn't even thought about online courses or talking to someone who made it without a degree. I guess I could look into something simple, like a short course or maybe just ask around if anyone knows someone in a field I'm curious about. It feels less scary than applying for a job blind, but still... that little voice in my head says it probably won't work out anyway.

That is such a smart instinct to pivot to research and networking instead of jumping straight into applications—it keeps the risk much lower. Before we settle on a final plan, I want to hear your perspective: how does exploring a short course or asking a contact feel different to you right now compared to blindly applying for jobs you already rejected?

It feels a lot less heavy, honestly. When I think about blindly applying, my chest tightens and I just want to give up before I even start. But researching a course or talking to someone... that feels more like I'm just gathering information, not committing to something that could fail. It's still a little scary, but at least it's not that same old hopeless feeling.

That distinction is huge; you've moved from viewing the activity as a gamble to viewing it as a safe, exploratory step. It sounds like acknowledging that slight reduction in intensity helps separate your anxiety from the reality of the situation. With about ten minutes left in our time, does exploring a short online course or reaching out to one person for advice feel like a manageable starting point for you, or would you prefer we try a slightly different angle first?

Yeah, I think I'd like to try looking into a short online course this week. It seems like a small enough step that I won't feel overwhelmed. Maybe I'll even look up some people in fields I'm curious about, just to see what they did to get started. That feels doable, as long as I don't pressure myself to have it all figured out right away.

That is a perfect, realistic commitment. To make sure this sticks, I'd love your feedback on our session so far: what part of today's discussion felt most useful or helpful, and was there anything that felt unclear or frustrating?

I think the most useful part was when you pointed out that I've been treating my preferences like they're permanent, when really I've changed and learned before. That kind of shook me a little, but in a good way. Nothing felt frustrating today—I actually feel a bit lighter than when I walked in, which is rare for me. Thanks for that.

Hearing that you feel lighter is incredibly rewarding, especially given how heavy that weight usually feels. Your ability to notice the shift from rigidity to flexibility is a major strength, and it speaks to your growing capacity for self-reflection. Before we wrap up, just to confirm: does taking one week to explore a course and perhaps chat with one person align with your current energy levels, or would you need to ease into it further?

Yeah, that sounds about right. I think I can manage one course search and maybe one conversation. If I start to feel that hopeless feeling creeping in, I'll try to remind myself that I'm just gathering info, not signing my life away. Thanks again—I'll give it a shot this week.

That is a beautiful reminder to carry with you; distinguishing between gathering information and making a life-altering decision gives you the freedom to explore without fear of failure. Thank you for your openness and honesty throughout our time together today. Please remember that if that hopeless feeling returns stronger than usual, reach out to me anytime, and we can revisit this new perspective together. I look forward to hearing how your exploration goes this week.

Hello, it is wonderful to see you again. On a scale of one to ten, how has your mood been over the past couple of days, and is there anything significant that has happened since we spoke last? Now that we've worked on holding space for both the loss of the doll and the good moments of the trip, I'm wondering if there is a particular area you'd like to tackle first today, or would you prefer to revisit the plan we made about the note on your mirror?

Hi. I guess my mood has been around a four or five this week. It's not as bad as before, but that doll still pops into my head more than I'd like. Maybe we could start with the mirror note? I've been trying to look at it, but I keep finding myself just staring at it without really reading it.

A four or five shows real progress compared to where you started, and it takes courage to notice that the note isn't landing quite as well as we hoped. Staring at the mirror without reading feels frustrating, almost like a second disappointment on top of the original one, doesn't it? Since you mentioned this struggle with the note, could we take a moment to explore exactly what your mind is doing when you look at it but don't read it?

Yeah, it's like I'm standing there and my eyes go to the note, but then my brain just goes to all the reasons it's not true. Like, I'll read "I can still enjoy things" and immediately think, "But I didn't enjoy the show because I missed the doll." It's like the note just reminds me of the bad parts instead of helping me see the good.

That is a really insightful observation, and it highlights exactly why the brain resists the note—it's fighting its own instinct to protect the story of the "missing doll." When you read the line and instantly jump to the counter-example, it feels like your brain is trying to verify whether the truth of the situation is being upheld, perhaps by proving the opposite. To understand this better, if you paused right before that automatic "but" thought appeared, what was happening inside you that triggered that immediate correction?

I guess... I feel a little flutter of hope, maybe? Like for a split second, I think, "Okay, maybe I can move on." But then it's like my brain slams on the brakes because that hope feels dangerous, like I'll just get disappointed again. So I go straight to the doll to protect myself, I think. It's like I'd rather be upset on my own terms than risk feeling hopeful and have it backfire.

That is such a profound realization, and it explains the "slam on the brakes" perfectly; your brain is prioritizing safety over possibility because it fears the sting of a broken hope more than the pain of current sadness. It seems like you are willing to endure the familiar ache of certainty rather than risk the vulnerability of hoping for something different.

Given that insight, could we adjust the note slightly so it acknowledges that hope itself feels risky, perhaps saying, "Even if I hope I can enjoy things, I allow myself to feel uncertain right now"? Would you be open to testing this new version to see if it bypasses that defensive "brake" your mind hits?

That actually sounds... less scary. Like it gives me permission to not have to be all positive right away. The old note felt like a demand to feel better, but this one just asks me to let myself feel uncertain and still try. I think I could actually read that one without my brain shutting down. Yeah, I'd be willing to try that new version.

That is a fantastic shift; moving from a demand to be fixed to a permission to feel uncertain removes the pressure that was triggering your brain's defense mechanisms. It feels much safer to step forward knowing you don't have to solve everything in that single glance.

Could we write this new sentence down right now and place it on your mirror tonight so you can test it in your own words? Once you've done that, how does it feel to finally have a tool that aligns with your actual experience of uncertainty?

Yeah, I think I can do that tonight. I'll write it on a sticky note and put it right next to the old one, or maybe replace it entirely. Honestly, it feels like a relief. It's like I finally have words that match what's actually happening inside, instead of trying to force myself to think something I don't really believe yet. That makes me want to actually try it instead of just staring at it.

That relief is a powerful indicator that you are finally speaking your truth rather than performing an idealized version of yourself. Having words that match your internal experience creates a bridge where hope feels like a safe possibility instead of a trap, making it much more likely you'll engage with the note.

Since you're ready to try this new version, I'd love to hear one final thought before we close: when you imagine seeing that note next to your reflection in the morning, what do you hope it will remind you to do when that familiar flutter of hope appears again?

I hope it reminds me to just pause and let the flutter happen, instead of immediately crushing it with the "but." Maybe I can just breathe and let myself sit with the hope for a few seconds before my brain tries to protect me. That feels like a small step, but it's more than I've been able to do so far.

That is a beautiful intention to simply pause and breathe before your protective brain kicks in. It transforms the mirror moment from a battle ground into a quiet space where you can witness your feelings without immediately judging them or fighting them.

With that as our goal, is there anything else you'd like to add before we wrap up our time today, or shall we leave it here so you can go try out this new note tonight?

I think that's enough for today. I'm actually kind of curious to see what happens tomorrow morning with the new note. Thank you for helping me find a way to make it feel real, instead of just something I'm supposed to say. I'll let you know how it goes.

That is such a compassionate way to frame it—wanting to see what actually happens rather than forcing a performance—and I appreciate your willingness to share the results with me. Please take care of yourself tonight as you prepare the note, and I look forward to hearing how that morning unfolds for you. Until then, thank you for trusting me with this process.

Hi... well, to be honest, I'm feeling about the same as last time. Maybe a little more tired. I did text my cousin like we talked about, and she was really supportive actually—she said she knows someone who might have a lead on a receptionist job. But nothing's come of it yet, so I'm trying not to get my hopes up. I guess today I just want to figure out how to stop feeling so stuck and frustrated all the time.

That is wonderful news to hear that your cousin was supportive and offered a new opportunity; it sounds like taking that small step actually paid off in a meaningful way. It makes total sense that you are feeling frustrated now, though, because despite the positive update, the lack of immediate results can easily leave you feeling stuck and disappointed again. Now that we've acknowledged both the success and the lingering frustration, what do you think would be the most helpful thing for us to focus on today to help you manage those feelings of being stuck?

I think... I need to stop beating myself up for not being further along in life. Every time I see someone my age with a career and a schedule that makes sense, I just think, "I should have that too, I shouldn't still be working nights at a hotel." It's like I can't enjoy anything because I'm always measuring myself against some invisible standard.

It sounds like you are carrying a heavy burden of comparing your current reality to everyone else's highlight reel, and that constant internal criticism is definitely exhausting. You're feeling stuck not because you aren't moving forward, but because the pressure to meet an impossible standard is making every small step feel like a failure. Have you noticed that whenever you catch yourself thinking "I should," it often leads to a sudden drop in energy or a urge to withdraw, even after you've done something productive?

Yeah... actually, yes. After I texted my cousin, for about an hour I felt pretty good, like I was finally doing something about my situation. But then I started thinking, "I should have done this months ago," and "I should already have a better job lined up by now." And just like that, the good feeling disappeared and I just wanted to go to bed and not think about any of it.

That is such a clear example of how quickly those "should" thoughts can undo your own momentum, turning a moment of accomplishment into a reason to give up entirely. It looks like your mind is using those comparisons to create a barrier, convincing you that your current path isn't good enough, so you retreat instead of continuing forward. I wonder, if you ignored that voice saying you "shouldn't" be here yet, what tiny, doable thing could you do tomorrow morning that doesn't require a full career breakthrough to feel okay?

I guess... I could just make myself a decent breakfast before I crash after my shift. Instead of just grabbing a granola bar and going straight to bed. It's not a job change or anything, but at least I'd be taking care of myself a little better. I always tell myself I should be doing more productive things with my mornings, but maybe just eating something proper would be a small win.

That is a brilliant realization—you've already identified a perfect small win that honors your body without demanding you solve your entire career crisis overnight. By focusing on nourishing yourself first, you are building a foundation of self-care rather than letting the pressure of "what should happen next" drain your resources. Does that feel like a realistic and gentle starting point for tomorrow morning?

Yeah, I think it does. It feels... manageable. Not like I'm trying to climb a mountain before breakfast. I can just eat something warm and not feel guilty about not job hunting for those first few minutes. That actually sounds kind of nice.

It is fantastic that you can visualize that morning feeling lighter and more grounded, rather than weighed down by guilt. That shift in perspective—from striving for a massive achievement to simply caring for your basic needs—is exactly the kind of compassionate approach we need to build momentum. Before we wrap up, how does knowing you will start with a warm meal and put the "should" thoughts aside until lunch make you feel about committing to this small routine tomorrow?

I feel... a little bit relieved, actually. Like I'm giving myself permission to just exist without needing to prove anything right away. I think I can commit to that. It's just breakfast, right? I can handle that.

That feeling of relief shows how powerful it is to allow yourself to just exist without constantly needing to earn your place in the world. Giving yourself permission to rest and eat properly is a huge act of kindness that often goes unnoticed, and I am truly proud of your ability to recognize that as valuable progress. To close, could you tell me one thing that surprised you today, or if there was anything about our conversation that you felt was missing or unclear?

I think what surprised me is how just talking about something as simple as breakfast made me feel a little lighter. I came in here feeling like I needed to figure out my whole future, and I'm leaving thinking, "Okay, I can eat something warm tomorrow." That's not what I expected, but it feels good. I don't think anything was missing—this helped.

That is such a beautiful realization, and it highlights exactly why we shifted focus from the overwhelming "big picture" to something tangible like breakfast. It makes complete sense that your expectations were higher than this outcome, but I am incredibly glad that even a small shift creates this sense of lightness for you. Thank you for sharing your feedback; hearing that this helped you feel lighter means so much to me, and it confirms that taking things one gentle step at a time is the right direction. Please be kind to yourself tonight, knowing you've earned a peaceful evening by recognizing your own capacity for small, manageable wins.

Thank you. I'll try to remember that tonight when I'm at work and my mind starts going to those places again. I'll just think, "Breakfast first, big life changes later." I appreciate you listening and not pushing me to have everything figured out.

You are so welcome, and I want you to know that it takes real courage to admit you don't have everything figured out yet—and that you are doing exactly the right thing by taking one small step at a time. Remember, your worth isn't tied to solving your entire life in one day; it's found in the quiet moments where you choose to be kind to yourself, like eating a warm meal. I believe in your resilience, and I look forward to checking in soon to hear how that simple morning plan lands for you. Take good care of yourself tonight.

Hi there, I'm so glad you're here again. To start, how has your mood been carrying into this morning compared to last time? Also, did anything significant happen since we spoke that you want to bring into our chat, and if we had to pick one priority to tackle together, what feels most urgent to you today?

Hi, thanks for asking. Honestly, my mood has been pretty low this morning. I had another student cancel their sessions yesterday, and it just hit me like a ton of bricks. I think the most urgent thing for me today is figuring out why one student leaving feels like the end of my whole career. I can't seem to shake that feeling no matter how hard I try.

Hearing that another cancellation struck you like a ton of bricks makes complete sense; your mind is likely screaming that this confirms your worst fear that you aren't cut out for this work. Since you're struggling to stop thinking one bad event equals total failure, could you walk me through exactly what your brain was telling you the second that cancellation message landed in your inbox?

The second I saw the message, my heart just sank. I thought, "Here we go again, I must be a terrible tutor if people keep leaving." Then my mind raced ahead to imagining my schedule completely empty by next month, and then my boss telling me they don't need me anymore. It was like within seconds, I had already pictured my entire life falling apart.

That rapid slide from seeing one email to picturing your whole career crumbling is a classic example of your brain trying to protect you by predicting the absolute worst-case scenario. Even though you know that logic doesn't always hold up, the intensity of that fear can make it feel very real in the moment. Given how powerful that "everything is ending" story feels right now, could you tell me what specific evidence you currently have that says you *are* still capable of keeping students, separate from this scary prediction?

Well, I do have a few students who have been with me for over a year now and they keep booking sessions. And just last week, one of them told me that my explanations helped them finally understand a poem they'd struggled with for months. That should count for something, shouldn't it? But it's so hard to hold onto those moments when the fear is screaming so loudly.

You have absolutely right to hold onto those moments; they represent real connections made and real learning achieved by students who trust you enough to stay long-term. The reason it feels so hard to hear them now isn't that the evidence doesn't exist, but that your brain is filtering out the good news because it's terrified of losing its safety blanket of certainty. If you imagine your best friend came to you crying about this exact same thing, what would be the first thing you would tell them to calm down their panic?

I'd probably tell them that one student leaving doesn't erase all the good they've done. I'd remind them that people quit tutoring for all kinds of reasons—money troubles, schedule changes, personal stuff that has nothing to do with the tutor. And I'd say they should look at the students who do stay and keep coming back, because that means something. It's just... so much easier to say that to someone else than to believe it myself.

That distinction between giving yourself the same compassion you'd offer a friend is exactly where the healing happens, yet it takes immense courage to recognize that gap between what you say and what you feel. Your brain might be insisting that everyone leaves because of you, but looking at the students who stayed past the year proves that many factors influence retention, and yours is clearly not among them. Can you write down just one specific instance from those long-term relationships that shows you've been a reliable anchor for them, regardless of the cancellations happening elsewhere?

I think about Sarah, who's been with me for about 18 months now. She was so anxious about her literature exams that she could barely finish a paragraph without second-guessing herself. We worked together on breaking down her essays step-by-step, and now she submits her work with real confidence. She even emailed me last month to say she got an A on her final paper. That felt good, and I know I helped her get there. But my mind just keeps circling back to the student who left yesterday, like that one person's choice cancels out all the Sarahs.

Sarah's transformation from hesitation to earning an A is powerful evidence that your methods work, and it makes no sense to let one isolated decision erase eighteen months of tangible progress. It sounds like your mind is treating that single cancellation as a universal law that overrides everything else, even though the data from Sarah and others suggests the opposite. If you were to write down just one sentence describing Sarah's journey that you know is true, how might that sentence sit beside the cancellation message without letting the latter win?

I guess I'd write something like, "Sarah trusted me for 18 months, and with my guidance, she achieved a grade she didn't think was possible." That sentence feels solid, like something I can hold onto. And the cancellation message feels shaky in comparison, like it's based on fear rather than fact. But it's still so hard not to let that shaky feeling shake the solid one, you know?

That is a brilliant distinction you've made: the sentence about Sarah is grounded in observable facts, while the fear about the cancellation rests entirely on a prediction. Holding onto that "solid" truth even while the anxiety wobbles is a crucial first step in reclaiming your confidence. Would you be willing to try reading that sentence aloud right now to remind yourself that one student's choice cannot undo the value of your work?

Okay, I'll try. (takes a breath) "Sarah trusted me for 18 months, and with my guidance, she achieved a grade she didn't think was possible." ... I have to admit, saying it out loud does feel a little more real than just thinking it. It's like I can hear how true it sounds when it's spoken. But that anxious part of me still wants to whisper, "But what if Sarah leaves next week too?"

It is completely natural that even speaking the truth doesn't instantly silence the fear; your brain is wired to anticipate danger, so it tries to find a crack in that solid foundation immediately. However, the fact that the statement feels more real when spoken shows you are successfully engaging your rational mind to challenge the panic. Instead of arguing with the worry right now, could we decide on a quick physical grounding exercise to help reset your nervous system so you can listen to that sentence again with fresh clarity?
Sure, I'm open to that. What did you have in mind? I'm willing to try anything that might help quiet that nagging voice for a bit.

Let's try the "5-4-3-2-1" sensory check: name five things you can see, four you can touch, three you can hear, two you can smell, and one you can taste. This helps ground us in the present moment and creates a tiny break in the cycle of worrying about the future. Once you've listed them, come back and share how that shift in your body feels compared to when you were spiraling.

Okay, let me try. Five things I can see: the window, the bookshelf, my coffee mug, the lamp, and your notepad. Four things I can touch: my chair arm, the fabric of my jeans, my own arm, and the table edge. Three things I can hear: the hum of the air conditioner, a car driving by outside, and your breathing. Two things I can smell: my coffee and the faint scent of paper in the room. One thing I can taste: the bitter aftertaste of that coffee. ... That actually helped. I feel a bit more present now, like my mind isn't racing quite as fast. The worry is still there, but it feels further away, like it's in another room instead of right on top of me.

That shift is incredible; creating a small physical space between you and the panic allows your rational mind to breathe and catch up. You've now gathered concrete evidence of your success, practiced speaking it aloud, and physically grounded yourself to distance the fear. Before we wrap up, does this combination of facts, verbal affirmation, and grounding feel like a manageable way to handle the next cancellation, or would you prefer to tweak anything slightly?

I think this combination could actually help. I liked how the grounding exercise made the fear feel less immediate, and reading that sentence out loud gave me something solid to come back to. I think next time a student cancels, I'll try the grounding first, then read my Sarah sentence, instead of letting my mind race ahead to the worst. It feels like a small toolkit I can actually use, instead of just getting lost in the panic.

That sounds like a perfect, manageable toolkit for tomorrow, and I'm so proud of how quickly you adapted the techniques to fit your needs. Just a gentle reminder for our next session: how did that "Sarah sentence" feel to carry in your bag or on your phone when you returned home today, and did you notice any shifts in your mood after using it?

I'll make sure to write it down and keep it in my bag before I leave today. I think having it physically with me will make a difference. And I'll pay attention to how I feel when I look at it later tonight, especially if the worry creeps back in. Thank you for helping me see that there's a way to hold onto the good evidence, even when the fear feels so loud.

You are so welcome, and I am truly relieved to see you holding onto that sense of stability and finding a way forward. Please remember that this toolkit is yours to use however works best, and there is no rush to master it perfectly tonight. Take a deep breath, grab that sentence for your bag, and know that you have proven today that you are resilient and capable of navigating these tough moments. See you soon.
