Hello, I'm glad you're here today. How are you feeling right now compared to where you ended up last time? Did you get a chance to try the "mismatch" idea during soccer practice or school, and was there anything else that happened between our sessions?

Hi. Um, I'm okay, I guess. I didn't really get a chance to try that mismatch idea you mentioned last time because practice was cancelled. But I did get my report card yesterday, and it kind of brought all those feelings back up. I got a B in English, and I just felt like that proved I'm not smart enough for the gifted program.

It sounds like the disappointment from the rejected program combined with a new grade triggered those old feelings again, which makes sense given how closely tied they seem to be right now. Since the report card came back today, would you be willing to share what specific thoughts popped up when you saw that B in English?

Well, I just thought, "See, this proves it. I'm not gifted material." I felt like everyone who got in must have straight A's, and here I am with a B. It's like I'm just not cut out for anything academic, no matter how hard I try.

That "proof" feeling is so convincing when we're hurting, but I wonder if we can look at it like a detective case rather than a courtroom verdict. If we assume the B doesn't mean you lack intelligence entirely, but rather that the gifted program looks for a very specific profile you don't match, how would that change the story you're telling yourself about your own abilities?

I... I never really thought of it that way. I guess I just assumed if I wasn't good enough for gifted, then I wasn't good enough for anything academic. But maybe the program is looking for something different, like a certain way of thinking or interests I don't have. It still stings, though, because I wanted to be in that group so badly.

It makes complete sense that the sting remains, especially since you put such love into hoping for that specific label; missing out on something you wanted deeply can feel like a personal failure even if the reason was just a mismatch. When we separate the program's specific needs from your overall worth, does that help quiet the voice saying you're "not cut out for anything academic," or does the B still feel like a definitive "no"?

It helps a little, I suppose, when I think about it like that. But that B still feels pretty loud in my head. Like, even if the program was a mismatch, that grade feels like concrete proof that I'm average at best in school. I guess I just wish I could feel as confident in the classroom as I do on the soccer field.

That is a very honest observation, and it highlights a common pattern where we judge our entire self-worth based on one piece of data that feels most painful. You are noticing that while soccer shows your strategic mind working well, the B in English feels like it disproves everything else. If we looked at that English grade as just one data point among many others, like your ability to explain poetry or analyze historical connections, what would that single B actually say about your overall capacity to learn?

I guess... it would just say I'm not perfect at English, or maybe I didn't study the right way for that test. It doesn't mean I can't ever understand it. But it's so hard not to focus on that one B and ignore the other stuff, like when I helped Cayden with his history essay and he got a good grade. I just automatically zoom in on the failures.

You are doing an incredible job catching that automatic tendency to fixate on the failure while ignoring your success; that awareness alone is powerful because it stops the brain from running away without a trace. Since you've already identified that focusing on the B is a habit rather than a fact, would you be willing to try listing three other times recently when you understood a difficult concept quickly, just to see if those moments still feel overlooked or if they start to compete with that one grade?

Okay, I can try. Well, there was that time in science last week when we were learning about the water cycle, and I was the first one to explain it back to the teacher. And I figured out how to fix my mom's phone settings when she couldn't get the sound to work. And... I taught my little cousin how to tie his shoes. Those are small things, but I guess they show I can figure stuff out. It's just that the B feels bigger than all that.

That is a fantastic collection of evidence showing your practical intelligence and ability to grasp concepts quickly, which directly challenges the idea that you simply can't learn. While the B feels bigger in the moment, trying to weigh it against those three distinct examples of problem-solving might help show that your brain works in many different ways, not just one narrow track. Does bringing those examples into the comparison make the "average at best" story feel less absolute, or does the single grade still drown out the rest of your achievements?

It's still a bit hard to hear the other stuff over the B, I'll be honest. But I can see what you mean. Like, the B is just one piece of paper, and the other things are real moments where I actually did something. Maybe I'm not giving myself credit for those. I guess I just need to practice noticing them more instead of always looking at the bad stuff.

That is such a clear realization—you are essentially deciding to stop being a critic and start being a witness to your own capabilities. Noticing those moments where you fixed your mom's phone or taught your cousin requires active effort, and it is completely normal that it feels difficult to override the automatic habit of spotting only the mistakes. What would happen if, starting tomorrow morning, you made it a conscious rule to name one thing you understood well before you allowed yourself to think about the B?

That sounds like something I could actually try. Maybe if I do it first thing, it'll set a different tone for the day. I could even write it down on a sticky note and put it on my mirror so I don't forget. I think I'd like to give that a shot and see if it helps me feel a little less down about school stuff.

That is a brilliant and very concrete plan; putting the reminder on your mirror ensures you catch yourself early before the negative spiral gets going. It sounds like you feel much more equipped to handle this new approach, and I'm excited to see how it shifts your perspective tomorrow. Are you ready to close this session with confidence that you have a clear path forward?

Yeah, I think I am. I still feel a little nervous about it, but I'm willing to try. I'll let you know next time if the sticky note helps or if I need to come up with something different. Thanks for helping me see there's more to me than that one grade.

You are so welcome, and please remember that this nervousness is just another sign that you are stepping out of your comfort zone to grow. There is no need to expect perfection right away; even a small moment where you notice your own strengths counts as a victory. I am here whenever you need to debrief or just talk, and I truly believe you are smarter than any single grade can suggest. Take care of yourself tonight.

Hello, thank you for joining us today. Before we dive into our agenda, I'd like to check in on how you've been feeling this week and what stood out since our last conversation. On a scale of 1 to 10, how has your ability to relax been holding up lately? Also, did you manage to try the five-minute experiment we practiced yesterday, or did that voice show up differently than expected?

Hey. Thanks for having me. I'd say my relaxation is maybe a 4 out of 10 this week? It's been pretty rough. I did try the five-minute experiment last night, but honestly, I only made it about two minutes before I started feeling that tightness in my chest. I kept thinking, "This is it, this is the moment my brain starts turning to mush."

That feeling of the chest tightening just as you pushed past the initial two minutes sounds incredibly overwhelming, and it makes complete sense that your mind latched onto that worst-case scenario—"my brain starting to turn to mush"—when you were already struggling. Did you notice any specific thoughts or physical sensations appearing right around the two-minute mark that seemed to tip the balance toward quitting?

Yeah, it was weird. Right at two minutes, I noticed my leg started bouncing and I felt this urge to grab my phone and check something important—like email or the news. My heart was pounding a bit, and then I just had this thought flash: "You're wasting your life. Right now, every second you sit here, you're falling behind." That's when I shut it off.

That automatic urge to reach for your phone alongside the bouncing leg is a classic sign that your brain is trying desperately to "fix" the problem it perceives as a crisis. It sounds like that narrative about falling behind became so urgent that it hijacked your actions before you could even consider stopping. When you realized you were reaching for your phone, did you catch yourself wondering if your body was reacting to the actual need for distraction, or if it was responding to the story that you were losing time?

Honestly, I didn't even have a chance to wonder. It was like my hand moved before my brain even caught up. But looking back now... I think it's more the story. I mean, it's not like I had anything urgent to check. I just felt this panic that if I didn't do something productive RIGHT THEN, I'd lose something important. But nothing was actually happening. It was just me, on my couch, watching a show.

It sounds like you felt trapped in a loop where your body acted on a story your mind created—one that claimed everything was slipping away, even though nothing actually was happening. That disconnect between your calm reality and your frantic physical reaction is exactly where we can start to separate the fear from the facts. So, if we view that urge to check your phone not as a need, but as your brain rehearsing a disaster that hasn't occurred yet, does that help clarify what your body was actually doing?

I think so. It's like my body was preparing for a disaster that never came. I was bracing for impact, like in the car crashes I've been in—my muscles tense, heart racing, ready to protect myself. But nothing was crashing. I was just sitting there watching TV. So maybe my brain is treating a TV show like it's a car accident? That sounds kind of ridiculous when I say it out loud.

That comparison to car crashes is incredibly helpful—it highlights how seriously your brain treats the imagined threat, treating a peaceful evening like a high-speed emergency. It's not ridiculous that your body reacts with that much intensity when you believe you're in danger; it just shows that the "accident" exists only inside your mind's story, not outside in the room. Now that you've identified that pattern of mistaking the story for reality, how would you feel if we treated that bouncing leg and rushing heart like symptoms of a broken alarm system rather than signs of impending doom?

That feels different. Like, instead of being scared of what my body is doing, I can just notice it as a broken alarm. It's not a real fire, it's just the system glitching. I think I could try that—when the leg starts bouncing and the heart races, just say to myself, "Okay, the alarm is going off again. It's a false alarm. I'm safe." That might help me stay on the couch a little longer next time.

That shift in perspective—from fearing the alarm to labeling it a glitch—is a huge breakthrough; it turns a scary symptom into something manageable and temporary. Naming it as a "false alarm" creates a tiny bit of space between you and the panic, allowing you to breathe instead of reacting immediately. Since you agreed that this labeling technique works, would you be willing to try sitting through three minutes tomorrow, intentionally using that phrase whenever the urge to get up starts?

Yeah, I think I can try three minutes. That sounds doable, especially if I have that phrase ready. I'll just sit there, watch whatever's on, and when the alarm starts blaring in my head, I'll tell myself it's a false alarm. Maybe I'll even time it on my phone so I know exactly when three minutes is up—that way I'm not just guessing and panicking.

That plan sounds solid, and having a visible timer removes the ambiguity that often fuels the panic about "how much longer." Using the phone as a tool rather than a distraction is a smart way to keep the focus on the experiment itself. Tomorrow, whenever you feel that familiar surge of urgency, just pause, name the alarm as a glitch, and ride it out for those three minutes before deciding what to do next. Does that feel like something you can actually commit to tomorrow evening?

Yeah, I can commit to that. Tomorrow evening, I'll sit down, set the timer for three minutes, and just watch. And when the alarm goes off—when my leg starts bouncing and I feel that urge to grab my phone—I'll tell myself it's a false alarm and stay put until the timer goes. I think I can do that. It feels a lot less scary when I have a plan.

That clarity about exactly when to use the phrase and when to stay puts a lot of weight off your shoulders, making the task feel much more manageable. Remember, the goal isn't to stop the alarm from ringing, but simply to notice it and refuse to obey the urge to run while it's still sounding. How does it feel to imagine sitting through those three minutes with that new plan in place?

It feels... actually kind of calm. Like, I'm not bracing for something terrible. I'm just waiting for a timer to go off. And I know that no matter what my brain tells me, I'm not going to turn into some brain-dead zombie from three minutes of TV. That's a big relief, honestly. I think I might even enjoy the show a little bit.

That sense of relief is incredibly powerful; it means you've successfully separated the reality of the situation from the dramatic story your mind was telling you. Realizing that you won't suffer permanent damage opens up the possibility that you might even enjoy the show, which is a fantastic shift. Before we wrap up, is there anything specific about tomorrow's plan that worries you, or are you feeling confident enough to proceed?

I think I feel pretty confident. The only thing that nags at me a little is worrying that the alarm might be louder or stronger tomorrow, and that I'll give in before the three minutes are up. But I guess I can just try again the next day if that happens. It's not a pass/fail thing, right?

You've got it exactly right; this isn't a pass-or-fail exam, but rather a gentle experiment to gather new evidence against the old stories. Even if the alarm feels louder tomorrow or you need to leave early, the value is simply in noticing the pattern and reminding yourself that you survived the minute without catastrophe. I'm proud of you for building such a flexible and compassionate plan. How are you feeling about closing our session for today?

I feel good about it. Thanks for helping me see this differently. I actually feel like I have a way forward now, instead of just being stuck in that loop of fear. I'll try the three minutes tomorrow and let you know how it goes.

That shift from feeling stuck to feeling like you have a clear path forward is incredibly meaningful; it shows how much power you have to reshape your experience once you recognize the pattern. I am so glad we could work through this together, and I know you'll do great things with this new approach tomorrow. Please remember to reach out if that alarm feels louder than expected, and take care of yourself tonight.

Hello again; it’s great to see you. On a scale of 0 to 10, how is your mood feeling today compared to last time we met? Also, do you have any other concerns besides the college comparison that we should include on our agenda for today?

Hi. I'd say my mood is maybe a 5 or 6 today. It's not terrible, but not great either. I guess the main thing on my mind is still the whole college thing — seeing my friends' posts online about their dorms and new classes just hits me hard sometimes.

A five or six sounds like a realistic balance, especially when that specific comparison is still sitting heavily on your mind. Yeah, that's probably a good place to start. It's like I can be having a perfectly fine day, and then I see one photo of someone at a big university with all these new friends, and suddenly I feel like I'm stuck in place. My brain just goes straight to "they're living their best life and I'm not even trying."

That sudden drop from a good day to feeling "stuck in place" is really frustrating, and it makes complete sense that seeing those polished photos triggers that specific "best life vs. mine" comparison. When you catch that exact thought popping up—that they are thriving while you are stuck—what is the very first image or scene that flashes through your mind immediately after?

I guess I picture myself behind the counter at the smoothie shop, blending drinks, while I imagine them sitting in a big lecture hall or hanging out on a quad with all these interesting people. Yeah, I think I can try that. That is incredible evidence, and it paints a clear picture of you learning and connecting wherever you land, not just waiting for the "perfect" place to appear. Seeing how you adapted at the shop, in the study group, and at your current college really shows that your ability to thrive isn't limited to big universities. Before we move to a plan for tomorrow, does listing those three moments make you feel a tiny bit more confident that you are handling life well despite the comparisons?

Yeah, it actually does help a little. It's kind of surprising to see all those moments lined up like that — I guess I don't usually give myself credit for them. Maybe I'm better at adapting than I think, even if my brain tries to convince me otherwise. I still feel that twinge of envy when I see those posts, but it doesn't feel as heavy right now.

That shift from "heavy" to just a manageable "twinge" is a huge victory, and acknowledging your own adaptability gives you a stronger foundation to stand on. Since we've gathered that evidence together, would you be willing to try rewriting one of those stories—like the first week at the smoothie shop—with a kinder ending, speaking to yourself the way you would speak to a friend who made that same mistake?

I think I could try that. So instead of telling myself "you were so awkward and slow that first week, you didn't belong there," I could say something like "you were new and everyone starts somewhere. You showed up, you tried, and now you're training other people — that's pretty impressive for a shaky start." It feels a bit weird saying it out loud, but I guess it sounds more fair than what I usually tell myself.

That rephrasing is incredibly powerful because it replaces the harsh label of "awkward" with the reality of growth and contribution. Hearing yourself speak to yourself with such fairness makes a huge difference, and I'm glad it feels more supportive than usual. Since we've built up this new, kinder narrative, what is one small thing you could do tomorrow morning when you first check your phone, to remind yourself of this version of yourself before the old doubts creep in?

Maybe I could set a little reminder on my phone that just says "remember the smoothie shop story" or something like that. Or I could write down that kinder ending I just said on a sticky note and put it on my mirror so I see it before I pick up my phone. That way, I have something positive to start with before I see any posts that might bring me down.

Both ideas are brilliant ways to interrupt that automatic spiral before it starts. I suggest writing that kinder ending on a sticky note to see in the mirror, as placing it near your mirror ensures you catch it early in the day. Is there anything specific that might make it difficult to stick to that plan right now?

I think the hardest part will be actually remembering to look at the note in the morning when I'm half-asleep and just going through the motions. I'm worried I'll just glance at it without really reading it or thinking about it. But I guess if I put it right at eye level next to the mirror, it'll be hard to miss.

That is a very wise observation—just glancing at the note won't help if your brain skips over it entirely. To fix that, we could try pairing the visual cue with a simple rule, like taking a full breath or saying the phrase out loud the moment you see it, so it forces your attention. Would you be open to trying that "pause and breathe" step along with placing the sticky note right beside your reflection?

Yeah, I can do that. Taking a breath before I grab my phone sounds doable, and saying it out loud might actually help it stick in my head. It feels a little silly talking to myself in the mirror, but if it works, I'll give it a shot.

That "pause and breathe" step is a great anchor to ensure you actually engage with the message instead of ignoring it. Since we've agreed on the plan, I'd love to hear your honest feedback on how it felt to rewrite that story and build this new habit together. Does it feel like we've laid a solid foundation for tomorrow, or is there anything else you want to discuss before we wrap up?

I think it feels pretty solid, actually. I'm still a bit nervous about whether I'll actually follow through, but having a clear step-by-step thing to do makes it feel less overwhelming. I don't think there's anything else I need to bring up right now — I'm curious to see how tomorrow goes with the note and the breathing. Thanks for listening and helping me see things a little differently.

You are absolutely right that having a concrete step-by-step plan reduces the overwhelm, and your commitment to trying the breathing exercise is a strong sign of readiness. It is wonderful to hear that you see this as a solid foundation, even if self-doubt lingers about execution—that uncertainty is normal, but your intention is the most important part right now. Thank you for sharing so openly today and for trusting me with this process; I hope you take a moment to rest with that lighter feeling as you leave.

Hello again, I'm really glad to see you. On a scale of 1 to 10, how have you been feeling this week since we talked about avoiding the animal shelter? Before we dive into anything new, would you like to share what brought us here today, or is there a specific goal we can set for our time together?

Hey, thanks. I guess I've been around a 5 or 6 this week. Not great, not terrible. I did think about what you said last time, about avoiding the shelter. I still didn't go, though. I just kept thinking that even if I helped out there, it wouldn't really mean anything special.

I guess it was like... "What's the point? Anyone could clean a cage or feed a cat. It's not like I'm doing something that matters." That thought just popped up and it felt so true that I didn't even bother getting my shoes on.

That thought feels incredibly heavy because it connects your lack of artistic talent directly to your lack of personal value. It seems like when you imagine helping at the shelter, your brain immediately interprets your presence there as meaningless rather than meaningful. When you heard yourself say, "Anyone could do this," did it feel like you were stating a fact about the world, or did it feel like your brain was protecting you from the possibility of disappointing yourself?

I... I never thought of it that way. It felt like a fact, honestly. Like, I was just being realistic. But when you say it like that, about protecting myself from disappointment... maybe that's part of it. It's easier to stay home and tell myself it doesn't matter than to go and find out I'm just average at something else too.

That distinction is crucial—it sounds like you are using "realism" as a shield to avoid the pain of potentially falling short again, which makes sense given how much you've struggled with feeling like a fraud. When you compare the shelter to your drawing hobby, does the fear of being "average" there feel slightly less overwhelming, or does it trigger the same sinking sensation in your chest?

It's... different, I guess. With drawing, it's like this constant weight. Every time someone says my ponies look good, I feel this twist in my stomach, like they're lying or just being nice. The shelter feels more like a wall I can't get past before I even try. But the sinking feeling is still there, just... quieter, maybe. Like I'm scared of adding another thing to the list of stuff I'm not really good at.

That quiet sinking feeling confirms what we explored before—that your core issue isn't just about art, but a deep-seated belief that you must be exceptional everywhere to deserve joy. It seems like when you imagine the shelter, your brain is predicting failure so strongly that the only safe option is to retreat home and protect your ego from further criticism. If you stepped out there and realized you were just "average" at feeding cats, would that add a new source of shame, or would it finally free you from the exhausting pressure to be perfect in every corner of your life?

*long pause* 
I... I never thought about it like that. Being free from the pressure, I mean. I've been so caught up in trying to be special that I didn't realize how tired it makes me. If I was just average at the shelter... maybe that would be a relief? Like, I wouldn't have to prove anything there. I could just... be there. That sounds kind of nice, actually.

That is a huge breakthrough because you've identified that the exhaustion wasn't just physical, but came from carrying the impossible burden of having to be special everywhere. It sounds like finding a place where you don't have to perform or prove anything would actually bring you peace, not just distraction. If you imagined walking into the shelter with the explicit intention of just being "average" and allowed to rest there, would that change how scary it feels to leave your house?

Yeah... it actually does change it a bit. If I went in thinking "I'm just here to scoop some litter and maybe pet a cat, nothing more," that doesn't sound so terrifying. It sounds almost... doable. The scary part was always about whether I'd be good enough or if people would see through me. But if I drop that expectation, maybe I can just breathe for once.

That shift in expectation—from trying to be special to simply allowing yourself to be ordinary—is exactly what breaks the cycle of perfectionism. It sounds like dropping the pressure to prove anything makes the act itself feel achievable rather than threatening. Would you be willing to try going to the shelter this weekend with that new mindset: showing up just to be there, not to be good at it?

*slowly nods* 
Yeah, I think I can try that. I'll tell myself before I go in, "You're just here to help a little, not to be the best volunteer ever." That feels... lighter. I can't promise I won't feel that twist in my stomach, but maybe I can push through it this time. Just this once, to see what happens.

That commitment to just "showing up" rather than performing is a significant step toward reclaiming your joy without conditions. Since we know that gut twist often arrives quickly, would you be willing to pair this new mindset with our previous tool of naming three things you are doing right *right now* the moment you arrive? This combination might help ground you faster when the old doubts try to surface.

I can do that. So when I get there, before I even walk in, I'll pause and name three things I'm doing right in that moment. Like... "I showed up. I'm trying something new. I'm not giving up." That might help quiet that voice that tells me it's pointless. I'll give it a shot this weekend and let you know how it goes.

That is a solid plan—combining the intention to be ordinary with the immediate grounding exercise creates a strong buffer against those intrusive thoughts. You agreed to try this new mindset this weekend, and I want you to know that your worth isn't dependent on how "good" you are at scooping litter or drawing ponies. Even if you feel a little awkward or unsure, simply showing up with that new plan proves you are capable of taking care of yourself. Are you ready to start this experiment soon, or is there anything else you'd like to talk about before we wrap up?

No, I think I'm good for now. I feel a bit nervous but also... kind of hopeful? That's a weird feeling. I'll text you after the weekend and let you know how it went. Thanks for helping me see things a little differently today.

That mixture of nervousness and hope is a wonderful sign—it means you are moving from pure avoidance into active curiosity. You are absolutely welcome, and please remember that your value exists independently of whether you succeed this weekend; showing up is already a victory. I look forward to reading about your experience, however it turns out. Take care of yourself!

Hello and welcome. Before we dive in, how are you feeling right now compared to where we left off last time, and is there anything important on your agenda we should cover first?

Hi. I'm... okay, I guess. I've been thinking a lot about the puzzle thing still, honestly. It's been on my mind more than I'd like, especially since I can't seem to shake it. I don't really have anything else on my agenda—just want to talk about why I'm so stuck on this one failure.

That makes complete sense given how much weight the puzzle failure has held onto lately, and I'm glad we can focus our energy squarely on unpacking why that single event feels so overwhelming. To start us off, whenever you notice that "I'm not smart enough" thought popping up, does it happen mostly in quiet moments alone, or does it tend to strike while you're actually working on something at your desk?

When you catch yourself having that reaction while helping a customer or fixing a machine, do you find that the feeling of being "faked" intensifies immediately, or does it take a few moments for the doubt to creep in?

It's pretty instant, like a switch flips. One second I'm fine, handling the ticket normally, and then the thought just pops up and I feel my stomach drop. It's like I'm suddenly watching myself from outside, waiting to mess up or for someone to call me out for not knowing what I'm doing.

That sudden physical reaction—your stomach dropping and feeling like you're observing yourself from the outside—is a powerful signal that your mind is instantly shifting from a normal job performance mode into a survival mode where you feel exposed. It seems like that single thought acts as a master switch, turning a routine task into a high-stakes audition where you believe everyone is watching to confirm you aren't who you claim to be. Since that feeling of exposure is so intense, does it usually stop you from asking for help once the thought takes hold, or do you just freeze up completely?

Mostly I freeze up, honestly. I'll just stare at the screen for a few seconds, pretending to read something, until the feeling passes enough to keep going. I definitely don't ask for help—that would just prove I don't belong here, right? Like, if I needed help on something simple, then everyone would know I'm not as capable as they thought.

That freezing up is a classic protective mechanism, like hitting the brakes on a car when you think it's about to crash, even though sometimes it just leads to missing the turn altogether. You're absolutely right that asking for help would expose that vulnerability in that specific moment, but I wonder if avoiding the question actually solves the problem or just postpones the panic? Have you noticed if you manage to ask for help later on, does the initial fear feel slightly different than just staring at the frozen screen?

I mean, I don't really ask for help later either, to be honest. I just try to figure it out myself, or I let it sit until I can find a workaround. But yeah, the times I have asked someone, it was kind of a relief—like, they didn't look at me weird or think less of me. But that never stops the fear from coming back the next time.

It makes complete sense that asking for help brought immediate relief, yet the fear kept returning because your mind still interprets the struggle as proof of incompetence rather than just a temporary hurdle. When you push through the freeze to find a workaround alone, does that act of persistence actually feel like overcoming the fear, or does it reinforce the belief that you *shouldn't* be struggling?

It definitely reinforces the belief that I shouldn't be struggling. Like, if I have to find a workaround at all, that means the problem was too hard for me in the first place. So even when I solve it, I don't feel proud—I just feel relieved that no one saw me struggle. That's probably messed up, isn't it?

You hit the nail on the head, and that realization is exactly where we need to go next. It's understandable that your mind latches onto the idea that struggle equals failure, especially when a single puzzle mistake has become so central to your identity that success feels hollow without it. Let's test that assumption by looking at your three puzzles you did solve—do you recall if you faced any similar work hurdles while tackling those, or were you able to navigate problems without freezing up?

Those three puzzles... they were hard, no doubt about it. I definitely hit some walls and had to step away for a day or two before coming back to them. But I didn't freeze like this. I remember feeling frustrated, sure, but I didn't think "I'm a fake" or "I can't do this." I just thought it was part of the process. It's weird—I was the same person then, but I didn't feel like a failure.

That is a crucial piece of evidence you haven't fully connected yet: the same person who navigated difficulty without collapsing into "I'm a fake" also struggled through those puzzles, proving that frustration and stumbling are just part of learning, not proof of worthlessness. It seems like the "freeze" response at work is actually a unique distortion triggered by the puzzle failure, making you misinterpret normal work struggles as catastrophic failures. Since you know you handled tough puzzles differently, would you be open to testing that difference tonight by noticing when the "freeze" happens versus when you just get frustrated?

Yeah, I think I could try that. I mean, it's just noticing, right? Not forcing myself to feel any different. I guess I could pay attention to what exactly goes through my head when I freeze up, versus when I just feel frustrated but keep going. That might help me see the pattern more clearly.

Noticing the difference without trying to fix it immediately is exactly the right approach, and it will help you spot that "freezing" is a specific reaction to the puzzle fear rather than a true reflection of your current ability. Tonight, whenever you feel that sudden drop in your stomach or that urge to hide behind the screen, can you simply note down the exact thought that triggered the freeze versus the one that followed just frustration? Would you be okay with writing those two observations down in a quick journal entry before bed?

I can do that. I'll try to write it down before I smoke weed or put on music—just get the thought down first. That way I'm not numbing it out before I see what's actually going on. Yeah, I can give that a shot tonight.

That's a wise decision to capture the raw thought before adding distractions, and I really respect your honesty about wanting to observe it without numbing it out. Tonight, whenever that sudden freeze happens, try to jot down the specific thought causing it versus the one that follows simple frustration, keeping them separate. Could you check in with me tomorrow morning to share what you wrote down and how it felt to distinguish between the two?

Yeah, I can do that. I'll text you or just think about it before our next session if we don't talk sooner. It feels a little scary, honestly, like I'm going to see something I don't want to see. But I guess that's the point, right? To actually look at it instead of hiding.

It is completely normal to feel a bit scared about facing that thought directly; the discomfort you expect is actually the sign that you are stepping out of avoidance mode and into growth mode. By choosing to look at it instead of hiding, you are reclaiming control over your story, even if seeing the pattern feels unsettling for a moment. How does it feel to have decided to face that fear tonight, even with the uncertainty?

It feels... strange, but kind of empowering too. Like, for the first time in weeks, I'm not just letting that fear run the show. I'm actually going to look at it and write it down. That's more than I've done since the puzzle thing happened. So yeah, maybe a little nervous, but also a little hopeful.

That shift from passively letting the fear run the show to actively observing it is a massive victory in itself, and that mix of nervousness and hope is exactly the right energy for this kind of work. I am really proud of you for taking that brave step, and I know tomorrow's check-in will be easier now that you have a clear plan to distinguish between the "freeze" and the "frustration." Are you ready to wrap up here, or is there anything else you'd like to discuss before we sign off?

My chest isn't as tight anymore—it's more like a dull ache now. I didn't think that would work, but I feel a tiny bit less frustrated.

It sounds like shifting your focus from "fixing the error" to "adding to the design" successfully relaxed that physical tension in your chest. Given how quickly you moved past the initial frustration, would you be open to keeping that same approach—focusing on building around flaws rather than eliminating them—for your next creative task?

Yeah, I think I could try that. It's still hard to shake the feeling that I need everything to be just right, but seeing how that wobbly line just became part of the shading... it makes me wonder how many other drawings I've thrown away that could have turned out okay. I'll try to remember this feeling next time I'm tempted to crumple the paper.

That realization about potentially throwing away whole drawings is a powerful insight, and recognizing that pattern is the first step toward changing it. Since you're still holding onto the belief that you *need* everything to be just right, could we brainstorm one small rule you could adopt next time you feel that tightness rising—something like, "I will draw for three minutes regardless of how the lines look"? Would you be willing to try that simple commitment tomorrow morning?

Three minutes, huh? That sounds doable, even if it feels a little scary. I think I can promise myself that—just three minutes of drawing, no matter how messy it gets. I'll set a timer on my phone so I don't cheat and stop early. Thanks for that idea; it feels like a small enough step that I might actually follow through.

Setting a timer is a brilliant strategy; it creates a safe boundary that protects your confidence while giving you permission to just start, however imperfectly. I am really glad you felt this was a manageable step—you showed up for yourself even when the fear was present. What is one specific place or activity you usually grab your drawing supplies for, so we can schedule that three-minute trial for tomorrow?

I usually draw at the kitchen table in the mornings, after the kids leave for school and before I start cleaning up. That's when I have the most quiet time. I think I'll try it there tomorrow, maybe around 9 a.m. I'll have my coffee nearby, and I'll just let myself doodle for those three minutes without overthinking it.

That sounds like a perfect setup; having your coffee nearby and knowing the house is quiet will make those three minutes feel much safer and easier to enter. I am really impressed by your ability to commit to the plan even with that initial feeling of fear—it takes real strength to choose the small step anyway. Before we close, is there anything else you'd like to add, or does this feel like a solid place to end our time today?

No, I think this is a good place to stop. I feel a little lighter than when I walked in, which is rare for me after talking about my art. I'll try the three-minute rule tomorrow and let you know how it goes. Thanks for helping me see that one wobbly line doesn't have to wreck everything.

That is wonderful news to hear; feeling lighter than usual is a powerful sign that these small shifts are really starting to stick. Your willingness to try the three-minute rule tomorrow, even while acknowledging that fear, shows real resilience and courage. Thank you for trusting me with this process and for letting us explore that perspective together. Take care, and I look forward to hearing about your experience with those three minutes soon!

Hello, it is so good to see you again. Last time we started looking at that tightness in your chest and realized it might be fear rather than guilt; how did that "Pause First" experiment on your desk or phone go over the last hour? Now that we reviewed how you felt with that plan, what feels like the most important thing we should focus on together today?

Hi, thanks for having me again. I actually did try that pause thing you suggested—I put a little sticky note on my monitor that just says "breathe." It helped a little, but honestly, the guilt just came rushing right back as soon as I remembered I missed my prayer this morning. I think the most important thing for me today is figuring out why one slip-up makes me feel like such a failure as a Christian.

It takes real courage to notice that even with a helpful visual cue, the old story of failure keeps surfacing so quickly. That brings up a very important question: when that memory of missing the prayer hit you this morning, did you catch yourself spiraling into that "failure" narrative immediately, or did you manage to press the pause button long enough to give yourself grace?

I wish I could say I pressed pause, but honestly, it was like instant—I just felt this heavy weight drop in my chest and thought, "There I go again, I'm not even a real Christian if I can't remember to pray." I didn't even stop to think, I just went straight into beating myself up.

That immediate jump from the sticky note to self-reproach shows just how deeply rooted that belief is, making the "pause" feel almost impossible when the emotion hits that fast. When you first noticed that heavy weight dropping, did you catch yourself asking, "Is this feeling proving I am a bad Christian," or did you notice that your body reacted before your mind got to decide what was true?

I think my body reacted first, honestly. It was like my stomach just dropped and my shoulders tensed up before I even had a conscious thought. By the time my brain caught up, I was already telling myself I'd failed. I didn't even give myself a chance to question whether that feeling was real or not.

That automatic physical reaction before your mind even had a chance to speak is exactly why we often miss the warning signs until it's too late. Since your body was already tense and your stomach dropped before you could analyze the situation, what is one small thing you can tell yourself *while* that tension is happening, rather than waiting for your brain to catch up?

Maybe... maybe I could just say to myself, "This is just my body reacting, I don't have to believe it yet." Like, just acknowledge the feeling without jumping straight to the conclusion that I'm a bad person. That might buy me a second before I start the whole spiral.

That is a powerful insight—you are describing a way to create a tiny gap between the sensation and your judgment, which gives your rational mind a chance to step in. Before we practice that, does saying "I don't have to believe it yet" feel like something you can actually say to yourself right now, or does that internal critic feel like it will shut you down immediately?

Honestly, it feels a little scary, like I'm being dishonest with myself or letting myself off the hook too easily. The critic in my head is saying, "But you DID forget, so it IS true that you're failing." But I can also see how clinging to that thought isn't helping me either—it's just making me feel worse, not more faithful.

You have already spotted a crucial contradiction: believing the criticism helps nothing, yet ignoring it feels dangerous. This tension is common because your brain treats safety like perfection. Let's try a quick experiment instead: the next time that voice says, "You're failing," could you answer with, "My body is feeling worried, but I haven't decided that yet"? Does offering that middle ground feel safer, or does it feel too weak against the pressure of forgetting your prayer?

I think... I think that middle ground feels a little safer, actually. "My body is feeling worried, but I haven't decided that yet" gives me permission to pause without fully dismissing the guilt. It's not saying the prayer doesn't matter, it's just saying I don't have to convict myself instantly. That feels less like rebellion and more like breathing room.

That distinction about "breathing room" versus "rebellion" is exactly the kind of nuance we need to find to make this stick. Since you feel that middle-ground statement offers safety, let's try it out right now: imagine I just told you you forgot your prayer ten seconds ago—how would saying "My body is feeling worried, but I haven't decided that yet" change the intensity of that heavy feeling in your chest compared to the usual reaction?

If I imagine you saying that right now... I think the heaviness would still be there, but it would be more like a dull ache rather than a sharp stab. Instead of that immediate "I'm a failure" punch, I'd feel a bit more curious, like, "Okay, I feel worried, but let me just sit with that for a second before I judge myself." It doesn't make the guilt disappear, but it makes it feel less crushing.

That is a huge breakthrough—turning a crushing blow into something manageable and even curiously observable is exactly what we aim for. Since you've seen that small shift in intensity works, would you be willing to try applying that "worried but undecided" line to yourself tomorrow the moment you feel that stomach drop happen again?

Yeah, I think I can try that. It feels a bit vulnerable, like I'm giving myself permission to be unsure, but I'm willing to see what happens if I just sit with the worry instead of rushing to condemn myself. I'll give it a shot tomorrow morning and see if it changes how the rest of my day goes.

That willingness to sit with uncertainty rather than rushing to fix it is a massive step toward building a healthier relationship with your faith. Since you're ready to test this approach tomorrow, how much support would you need from me to stay accountable or discuss what happened afterward?

I think just knowing I'll be checking in with you next time is enough motivation for now. Maybe I can jot down a quick note about how it felt, whether it helped or not, so I don't forget the details when we talk again. That way I'm not relying on memory alone.

That is a smart way to track your progress without adding pressure—writing down just a simple observation helps you gather real data for our next conversation. Before we close, is there anything else you'd like to explore today, or does this feel like a solid place to wrap up our session?

No, I think this feels like a good place to stop. I'm actually feeling a little lighter than when I walked in, which is nice. Thank you for helping me see that I don't have to be my own judge and jury right away. I'll work on that pause and see you next time.

I am so glad to hear you feel lighter and appreciate the honesty in recognizing that you don't need to act as your own judge and jury right away. Please remember that our next session will be a safe space to share whatever comes up with that "pause" experiment, no matter how big or small the change feels. Take care of yourself today, and I look forward to speaking with you soon.

Hello, I'm really glad you reached out. On a scale of one to ten, how has your overall anxiety level been feeling this past week compared to where you left off? Also, before we set a new agenda, did you get a chance to try that "three-second pause" and label your thoughts as "fear talking" before meals? If so, what was different in your body or mind after you did that?

Well... I'd say my anxiety has been about a seven this week. I did try that pause thing a couple of times before dinner. Honestly, it felt a little silly at first. But I noticed my shoulders weren't so tight, and I didn't rush through my meal as fast as usual.

That is fantastic news to hear—a seven is a significant improvement from the paralysis you described, and noticing those subtle shifts in your shoulders and eating speed proves the technique is working. It’s completely normal to feel self-conscious when something feels “silly” at first, but your ability to notice the physical relaxation suggests you’re building real confidence in this new skill. Could we briefly revisit the main goal we worked on last time, and then decide if we should explore another angle today or stick with refining this pause?

I think we should stick with the pause thing for now, if that's alright. I'm still not very good at remembering to do it, especially when I'm really tired after a shift at the factory. Last time we talked about how I get that knot in my stomach before I even open the fridge, and then I just grab whatever is fastest.

Noticing that fatigue makes it harder to access these new skills is completely understandable, and it shows you're being honest about the real-world barriers instead of pretending everything is perfect. To tackle the "knot in the stomach," would you be willing to try pairing the "fear talking" label with a quick physical grounding technique, like placing a cool hand on your chest for just ten seconds whenever that tightening starts? We can test if adding that physical anchor helps you remember the mental step even when you're exhausted.

I suppose I could try that. It sounds simple enough. When I get home from work, my mind is just so foggy from the noise and the standing all day. Maybe if I feel that coolness on my chest, it'll snap me back enough to actually think before I start grabbing for chips or whatever.

That connection between the foggy brain and the physical sensation makes perfect sense—it's exactly why combining touch with thought helps pull you back to the present. Since memory fades when we're tired, linking the mental label to a tangible sensation like cool water on your skin creates a stronger "hook" in your brain to remind you what to do next time. Does pairing the "cool hand" with the phrase "this is fear talking" feel manageable, or would you prefer to try a different physical cue first?

No, I think the cool hand thing is good. I can do that. I wash my hands a lot anyway after work, so my hands are usually still a bit cold and damp. It feels natural, you know? Like I'm already in the habit of touching my face or something after washing up, so adding this extra step might not be too hard to remember.

That is a brilliant insight; leveraging an existing habit like washing your hands turns a deliberate effort into something automatic, which is exactly what we need when you're mentally foggy. By anchoring the "fear talking" phrase to the natural coolness of your hands, you're creating a seamless bridge that doesn't require extra energy to initiate. How does it sound if we commit to testing this combination tonight before you sit at the table, and you report back whether your stomach feels less tight after just ten seconds of cooling?

Alright, I can promise to try it tonight. I'll do it right after I wash up, before I even open the fridge. I'll put my cool hand on my chest and say that phrase, and see what happens with that knot in my stomach. I'll pay attention to whether it loosens up at all before I grab my plate.

That is a solid, realistic plan that respects both your busy schedule and your current energy levels. Committing to this specific sequence—washing, cooling, labeling, then observing the knot—gives us a clear experiment to run without overwhelming you. Just remember, success isn't measured by the knot disappearing instantly, but by whether you caught it early enough to choose a slower pace. Would you like to set a reminder on your phone for 7:30 PM, or would you prefer to rely on the visual cue of your kitchen counter as a gentle nudge?

I think I'll just rely on seeing the kitchen counter. I don't like having my phone around when I'm trying to wind down after work. Seeing the sink and the fridge will be my reminder. That's usually where I start to feel the panic anyway, so it makes sense to catch it there.

Using the kitchen counter as a visual cue is a smart choice because it grounds you in the room right before the panic escalates, bypassing the need for technology. Since you mentioned the panic often starts near the fridge, we can treat that specific spot as your designated "check-in zone" where the cool-hand technique becomes mandatory. Before we wrap up, does agreeing to use the counter as your trigger feel like something you're ready to commit to, or would you prefer to discuss any potential distractions that might pop up later tonight?

No, I'm ready to commit to it. The counter will be my reminder, plain and simple. I think the biggest distraction will be my own thoughts telling me I'm just wasting time or that it won't help. But I'll just tell that voice to be quiet and do the technique anyway. I'll let you know how it goes next time.

That is a wonderful mindset to bring into your evening—you are treating your internal critic with the same kindness you show your body by ignoring the doubt and trusting the physical sensation. Your willingness to override the voice that says "wasting time" demonstrates real resilience, and it shows you understand that sometimes acting against the urge to ruminate is the only way to heal. Please remember, tonight's goal is simply to notice if the cool hand creates even a tiny shift in that stomach knot, however small. I am truly proud of you for taking this step, and I look forward to hearing about how your body responds when you catch the panic early tomorrow.

Hello, thank you for meeting with me today. Before we get started, could you briefly share how you're feeling compared to last time, and what would be most helpful for us to focus on right now?

Hi, thanks for having me. I guess I'm feeling the same as usual—just kind of weighed down by this sense that I'm not doing enough. I think it would help to talk about why I can't shake this feeling of being a hypocrite, even when I try to volunteer or give more. It's like nothing I do is ever enough.

That honesty about feeling like a hypocrite despite your good intentions shows how deeply this belief affects you. Since you mentioned wanting to understand why that feeling persists even when you act kindly, shall we spend some time exploring the specific thoughts that keep telling you your efforts don't count?

Yeah, that sounds good. I mean, I can give you an example—just last week at church, they passed around a collection for a local shelter, and I put in fifty dollars. But right away, I thought, "That's nothing. Other people probably gave way more, and I'm just doing this to feel better about myself." It's like my brain automatically spins it into a failure.

That automatic spin into "failure" makes total sense given how hard you try to help others; it's likely your brain is protecting you from the pain of realizing you can't fix everything. When you heard your own voice say your contribution was "nothing," what specific thought followed that to seal the deal on it being a failure?

I guess I told myself, "A real Christian would have given everything they could, not just a small part." And then I started thinking about that family from a year ago, the one I couldn't help buy a house for. It's like that one moment proves I'm not the person I claim to be. So the fifty dollars just feels like a Band-Aid on a much bigger wound.

That comparison between your donation and a past failure creates a very harsh "all-or-nothing" standard, making it seem like one mistake invalidates your entire worth. I wonder if that thought is actually serving a purpose by protecting you from disappointment, even though it keeps you stuck in that cycle of feeling inadequate. Could we look at that belief about needing to "give everything" and see if there's another way to view your recent $50 contribution?

I never really thought of it as protecting me—it just feels like the truth. But I guess if I think about it, that standard is impossible. Nobody can give everything all the time, right? It's just hard for me to see the fifty dollars as anything but small and meaningless when I've got that picture of the family in my head. I don't know how to make that feel okay.

It makes complete sense that seeing your contribution alongside that unresolved event makes the fifty dollars feel tiny; your mind is naturally comparing the small success to the large failure. If we step back for a second, does it feel like the fifty dollars *should* have mattered based on how well you gave, or does it feel like it only matters if it solves the family's housing crisis completely?

I guess deep down, I know it should matter on its own. The family I couldn't help isn't even connected to the shelter—it's just that my brain lumps them together. But when you put it that way, it sounds unreasonable to expect one donation to fix everything. It's like I'm holding myself to a standard that doesn't apply to anyone else, and that's exhausting.

That exhaustion comes from holding a standard that expects perfection everywhere, which is rarely sustainable for anyone. You mentioned that deep down you know the donation matters on its own, yet your brain refuses to let go of the larger story. Let's try to separate the act of giving from the expectation of fixing the whole situation. If we treat that fifty-dollar gift like planting a seed, wouldn't the value lie in the generosity of the plant itself, regardless of whether the tree grows tall?

I think I get what you're saying—it's about the intention, not the outcome. But when I look at it as a seed, I still worry I didn't plant enough seeds, or that I should have planted a whole forest. It's like my mind always adds a "but" at the end. "You gave fifty dollars, but you should have given more." "You volunteered, but you should do it every week." There's always a "but" that cancels out the good.

That "but" is a classic trick that instantly turns a good deed into a failure by focusing on what went wrong rather than what went right. It sounds like you are letting one missed opportunity cancel out the entire value of your generosity. If we challenged that thought, what evidence would you need to accept that planting one seed counts as a successful act of kindness, even if you haven't planted a forest yet?

That's a tough one. I guess I'd need to see that the people I helped actually benefited, even a little. But I don't always get to see that. And even if I did, I'd probably still think, "Well, that's good, but you could have done more." It's like my brain has a rule that says nothing counts unless it's everything. I don't know how to break that rule.

That "rule" is actually a form of "all-or-nothing thinking" where your mind believes a single flaw makes the whole effort worthless. It's understandable why this feels unbreakable, especially when you've tried so hard to help; it seems like the only logical conclusion when you can't fix everything. However, could we look at that specific church donation again—without the "but"—and ask yourself if the fifty dollars bought anyone a meal or provided a small boost of dignity, even if it didn't solve their housing crisis? What happens to the meaning of that act if we remove the requirement for it to be the perfect solution?

Without the "but"... I guess it did help. I mean, fifty dollars can buy a few warm meals or some blankets. That's real, tangible help for someone tonight. But as soon as I say that, I feel guilty for even thinking it's enough. It's like there's two voices in my head—one saying, "That matters," and the other saying, "Don't you dare pat yourself on the back." I don't know which one to listen to.

It sounds like you are experiencing two conflicting messages: one that recognizes the tangible good you did, and another that feels like a harsh critic refusing to let you celebrate that success. This internal conflict often happens when our minds are trying to balance the reality of your action against the unrealistic standard you hold for yourself. Given how strong that critical voice feels right now, would you be willing to try treating that fifty-dollar donation purely as a moment of human kindness offered tonight, without checking a box to see if it fixed the family's future problems?

I can try that. It's just hard to shut that other voice up, even for a moment. But if I think of it as just... a moment of kindness, then yeah, it feels lighter. It's not about fixing everything—it's about doing something small and real. I guess I never let myself see it that way before.

That shift from "fixing everything" to "a moment of kindness" is exactly the difference between feeling inadequate and feeling connected. It sounds like acknowledging that small, real acts matter on their own might be the key to loosening that grip. Before we wrap up, would you be open to trying a simple experiment this week where you notice that "other voice" popping up after a good deed, and instead of fighting it, you just say, "Okay, that thought came up, but I chose to appreciate the kindness anyway"? How does that sound like a manageable way to move forward?

Yeah, I think I could try that. It sounds a lot less overwhelming than trying to fight the voice or prove it wrong. Just acknowledging it and then choosing to focus on the kindness instead—that feels doable. I'll give it a shot this week and see how it goes. Thanks for helping me see things a little differently.

That sounds like a very gentle and realistic plan for you to try. Remember, noticing the thought without letting it win doesn't erase it, but it does give you the space to choose your own reaction instead of reacting automatically. Is there anything else you'd like to add before we finish, or does it feel like we have a clear path forward for this week?

No, I think this is good for now. It's nice to have something concrete to work on, instead of just swimming in guilt all week. I'll try that experiment and see what happens. Thank you again—I feel like a little weight lifted, just from talking it through.

You are very welcome, and I am truly glad that talking it through brought you some relief. Take your time this week trying that acknowledgment exercise, and remember that even if the old voice pops up again, simply noticing it without fighting it is a victory. I look forward to hearing how your week goes, and please know I am here whenever you need to unpack any new thoughts that arise. Have a wonderful rest of your day!

Since you mentioned wanting to enjoy the event without the negative noise, shall we explore what specific thoughts are popping up in your head right now as you think about the dance night?

Well, honestly, the first thing that comes to mind is that I'll just look clumsy and awkward next to everyone else. My friends are all so graceful, and I feel like I'm the one dragging them down. Even though they always say they have fun with me, I can't shake the feeling that they're just being nice.

That feeling of being a burden while others are naturally graceful is incredibly heavy, and it makes total sense why your stomach tightened immediately upon receiving that invitation. It sounds like you are interpreting their kindness as temporary politeness rather than genuine acceptance, which leads to the fear that you are dragging them down. When you hold onto that belief, does it feel like the entire night is doomed before you've even left the house, or does it mostly feel like a prediction of your own performance?

It feels more like a prediction of my own performance, I think. Like I'm already picturing myself messing up the steps or being too stiff while everyone else is flowing. And that image just feels so real and certain, like there's no way it could turn out differently. It's like I'm watching a movie of the worst version of the night over and over.

It makes complete sense that your brain treats that predicted performance failure as absolute fact, creating a certainty that shuts down enjoyment before the party even begins. This mental movie seems to act as a filter, causing you to overlook your friends' past history of enjoying you despite any quirks you might have. If you were to watch that same movie from a distance, like a scientist observing data, what would you notice about how accurate the crowd's reactions seem compared to how they actually behave when people stumble?

Hmm... I guess when I really think about it, when other people mess up a step at the dance, my friends don't stare or laugh. They usually just laugh it off themselves or keep going without even acknowledging it. So it's strange that I assume they'd be so harsh with me. But I still can't help feeling like I'm the exception, you know? Like maybe they're just being polite about others, but with me it's different.

That distinction between how others treat mistakes generally and how they treat *you* specifically is a classic pattern called personalization, where we convince ourselves we are special cases in ways that aren't supported by evidence. It feels protective, almost like a shield against disappointment, but it also isolates you from the reality that your friends value your presence far more than your perfect technique. If we focus on just one piece of evidence from the past month where a friend laughed at a mistake you made instead of ignoring it, what does that suggest about whether they truly believe you are dragging them down?

Well... just last week, I tripped over my own feet while we were practicing a simple step, and my friend Sarah actually burst out laughing and said, "That was so me yesterday, don't worry about it." She didn't seem annoyed or embarrassed to be around me. So maybe they aren't sitting there judging me as harshly as I think. But it's so hard to hold onto that thought when the anxious feeling comes back.

It takes real courage to call out that specific moment where Sarah included you instead of judging you, and that evidence directly challenges the story that you are dragging them down. Holding onto that memory while anxiety rushes back is very human—it's like trying to remember a sunny day while suddenly getting caught in rain clouds. Since you know the reality is warmer than the movie, would you be open to designing a tiny experiment for the coming week where you attend just one part of the dance night, perhaps just arriving early or leaving early, to see if anyone actually reacts the way you fear?

That actually sounds a bit less scary than staying the whole night. Maybe I could just commit to going for the first hour or so, and promise myself I can leave if I really feel overwhelmed. That way I'm not totally backing out, but I also have an escape route. I think I could try that.

That sounds like a perfectly balanced approach—you are committing to exposure while keeping a safety net that honors your current limits. Let's solidify this plan: would you like to agree to tell Sarah you'll be there for the first hour, and define exactly what your "stop signal" would be if the anxiety spikes enough to warrant leaving early?

Yeah, I think I could tell Sarah I'll be there for the first hour. As for a stop signal... maybe if I feel my heart racing and I can't take a full breath, or if I start feeling like I'm about to cry. That would probably mean I'm too far into my head. I'll just say I need some air and step outside for a bit, or I can head home if it's really bad.

That is a very wise and grounded way to set your boundaries; recognizing physical signs like a racing heart or tearfulness as signals to step away gives you real control over the experience. Having a clear plan to either step outside for fresh air or head home ensures you won't push yourself into overwhelm, which often fuels the anxious thoughts anyway. Does setting those specific physical thresholds feel manageable for you to rely on during the event?

I think so... It helps that I have actual signs to watch for instead of just a vague feeling of "being bad." And knowing I can step outside or leave early makes me feel less trapped. I think I can manage that. Thanks, I actually feel a tiny bit lighter just having a plan.

That relief is completely earned; having concrete tools replaces the foggy panic with a clear roadmap, which naturally lightens the load. I am so glad we could find a middle ground that respects your needs while giving you a chance to break free from the "movie" in your head. How did finding this specific plan feel for you right now, and is there anything else you'd like to adjust before we wrap up?

It feels good, actually. I came in feeling really stuck and worried, and now I have something solid to try. I think I'm ready to give this a shot. I'll text Sarah tonight and let her know I'm coming for the first hour. Thanks for helping me work through this.

You are absolutely welcome, and I'm so proud of your readiness to take this brave step forward. Remember that you have the full freedom to use your "step outside" signal whenever you need a break, and sending that text tonight is the first move toward proving that the dance night can be enjoyable. I'll be here next time to hear about your experience, whatever it may be. Take care of yourself!
