Hello Sam, it's wonderful to see you again. To start, could you share how your mood has been feeling since we last spoke? Also, before we dive into the main topic, did you get a chance to mention your plan to ask your wife for a gentle nudge tonight?

Hi. Um, my mood has been kind of up and down, honestly. I had a couple good days where I stuck to my meal plan and felt pretty proud, but then yesterday I slipped up and ate a slice of cake at a friend's birthday, and it just... crashed. I felt like such a failure. And yes, I did mention the nudge to my wife. She said she'd try, but I'm not sure I even know what I want her to say.

It makes total sense that you feel like a failure after celebrating a slice of cake, especially when you're working so hard to stick to your plan. That contrast between your recent wins and the slip-up likely made the disappointment hit really hard. Did you ever get to hear exactly what your wife suggested as that "nudge"?

She just said she'd remind me that "one bad meal doesn't ruin everything." But in the moment, after I ate that cake, I couldn't believe that at all. It felt like I had already blown it for the whole week, so why even bother trying to eat right for the rest of the day? I ended up just grabbing a bag of chips later because I figured the day was already a loss.

It sounds like even though she offered the truth, your brain was too busy locking onto the "failure" story to listen to it at first. When we are caught in that all-or-nothing spiral, it often feels like any encouragement is just another reason to give up completely. Did you manage to grab a snack or do something small after realizing the chips wouldn't fix anything either?

No, I didn't. I just felt really gross and disappointed in myself, so I went to bed early to just shut the day out. I woke up this morning still feeling that weight, like I had to start all over again from zero. It's exhausting, you know? Trying so hard and then one thing just undoes all the progress I thought I made.

That exhaustion is completely understandable; when our minds convince us that we've failed entirely, the effort required to keep going feels impossibly heavy. It’s frustrating to spend weeks building momentum only to feel like you’ve lost it all overnight. Let’s explore whether looking at that cake eating as just one messy page in a book, rather than a destroyed novel, might help lighten that burden a little. Does viewing it as a single chapter make the task of eating healthy tomorrow feel less daunting, or does the feeling of "starting over" still dominate your thoughts?

It's hard to see it as just one page. I mean, I had been so good for almost two weeks straight, and then one slice of cake felt like it wiped out all that effort. But I guess... when you put it that way, it does sound a bit extreme. Like, I didn't suddenly gain all the weight back from one slice. But my brain just goes straight to "you ruined everything," and that feeling is so strong in the moment. I don't know how to stop that automatic thought.

That "automatic" nature is exactly why it feels so hard to catch—it's running the race before you even realize you've taken a wrong turn. Since you mentioned you have two weeks of solid history behind you, what if we treated that cake like a minor typo in your manuscript? It's noticeable, but it doesn't erase the beautiful pages written before it or dictate the story coming next. If we accept that tiny error as just a bump in the road, does the pressure to start over from absolute zero feel a fraction less crushing right now?

Maybe... a little bit. It's like, if I think of it as a typo, then yeah, the rest of the book is still there, right? I didn't throw out the whole two weeks. I guess I just get so focused on the mistake that I forget I even had those good days at all. So maybe I can try to remind myself of that next time. It's just hard to believe it in the moment.

That "typo" perspective is a huge shift, and recognizing that those two weeks of progress are still standing proves your brain needs help remembering its own success. It makes sense that in the heat of the moment, the mistake feels like the entire story. For now, let's just practice spotting that "ruined everything" thought when it pops up and gently reminding yourself: "This is just one typo, not the whole book." How does that simple reminder feel right now, or does it still feel like a hard sell?

It feels... like a good idea in theory, but also a little bit like I'm lying to myself. Like, if I say that to myself, will I actually believe it, or will I just be pretending? But I guess it's worth trying. I've been telling myself the opposite for so long, and that hasn't been working either. So maybe a little gentle reminder is better than just giving up completely.

That honesty about feeling like you're "pretending" is actually a sign of strength—you're catching the old habit before it takes root. It's not about believing it instantly, but just planting a seed so the old "failure" story doesn't get to run the whole race alone. Since we've built up that new angle, let's quickly confirm: what's the very next small step you'd like to take today to keep yourself honest?

I think... I'll try to have a normal, balanced breakfast without overthinking it. Maybe just eggs and some fruit, something simple. And if that "I already ruined everything" thought pops up, I'll try to tell myself it's just a typo and move on. That feels manageable, at least for today.

That is a perfect, grounded plan for today. Taking that simple breakfast without judgment gives you a fresh start for the day rather than a second chance at fixing the past. Just remember, if the "typos" thoughts come up during lunch, we'll gently remind ourselves that one meal doesn't rewrite the whole story. How does it feel to visualize yourself taking that calm, balanced breakfast?

It feels... relieving, actually. Like I can breathe a little easier knowing I don't have to be perfect. Just... eat some eggs, have some fruit, and not beat myself up over it. I think I can do that today. Thanks, that really helps put things in perspective.

That relief is exactly what we want to cultivate, and recognizing that you can choose a simple, kind approach over a cycle of self-criticism is a big victory. You've successfully identified a realistic strategy for today that honors your progress while allowing for mistakes. Before we wrap up, is there anything else weighing on your mind as you prepare for your breakfast, or are you ready to head out with this new perspective?

No, I think I'm okay for now. I feel a bit more ready to face the day than I did when I walked in here. I'll try that breakfast and see how it goes. Thanks for listening and for not making me feel like I'm crazy for getting so worked up over a slice of cake.

You are absolutely right to feel relieved that I validated your feelings rather than dismissing them; your reaction to the cake is completely human, not crazy, and it tells me you care deeply about your health. Please remember that tomorrow, once you're rested, you can revisit your plan with your wife to see if that gentle reminder lands differently now that we've practiced the "typo" perspective together. I look forward to hearing how your breakfast goes and checking in on you next time. Have a wonderful day ahead.

Hello, it is wonderful to see you again. Before we start, could you share how you've been feeling since we last spoke, particularly regarding your plan to say hello to your neighbor? Then, let's take a moment to decide together what feels most important to explore today.

Hi. Thanks for asking. Well, I did say hello to my neighbor the other day, but it felt so forced and awkward. I just ended up feeling stupid about it, like she probably thinks I'm weird now. I guess I want to talk about why I can't seem to make any real connection, no matter how hard I try.

I hear how difficult it feels to try reaching out and then immediately doubt yourself afterward. It sounds like the fear of being judged is so powerful that it overrides your initial success, leaving you stuck in that cycle of self-criticism. To understand this pattern better, could you walk me through a specific moment when you tried to connect recently and notice exactly what happened in your body right before you pulled away?

I remember just standing at my front door, holding the mail, and I saw her in her garden. My chest got really tight, and I started breathing shallow, like I was about to be in trouble. Before I even said anything, my stomach was in knots, and I almost just turned around and went back inside.

That intense physical sensation of your chest tightening and shallow breathing is your body's alarm system screaming that you are in immediate danger of being rejected. It makes complete sense that you froze because your mind interpreted those symptoms as proof that you were about to mess everything up, forcing you to retreat to safety. Could you identify the very first thought that flashed through your head when you saw her, before you had even a chance to act?

The first thing I thought was, "She's going to think I'm such a loser, standing here with nothing to say." It was like I could already see her pitying me or just being polite before walking away. That thought hit me so fast, it felt like the truth, not just a worry.

That certainty about being a "loser" in her eyes explains perfectly why your body chose to shut down instead of move forward. It seems like your brain has convinced itself that this interaction is a high-stakes judgment where failure is inevitable, which is why you feel such a heavy knot in your stomach. Have you noticed any evidence from past experiences or what you know about her personality that contradicts the idea that she will automatically see you as someone who doesn't belong there?

Well, I guess I don't really know her at all. She's just a lady in her fifties who waves sometimes, and she's never been rude or anything. I suppose I'm just assuming she's like my parents, always watching and finding fault, but she's never actually given me a reason to think that.

It makes perfect sense that you fill in that blank space with the familiar, critical voice of your parents, especially when you feel exposed. However, you are right to notice that there is no actual evidence she views you as a critic, yet your brain is treating a stranger like a personal examiner. If you were to look at the situation from a purely observational standpoint—ignoring your internal narrative entirely—what would happen if she simply smiled and waved back without offering any judgment? Would that scenario feel as terrifying as the one you've been imagining?

I guess... no, that actually sounds kind of nice, just a simple wave and a smile. It wouldn't be this big, scary thing, just two people being polite. I think I've been building it up in my head to be this huge test that I'm bound to fail.

That realization—that the reality is just a simple wave while your mind builds a battlefield—is a huge step toward seeing the truth. You've done excellent work identifying that the threat isn't real, and shifting from expecting humiliation to anticipating politeness changes everything about how you feel in that moment. Now that we've cleared up the fear of being judged, does moving forward feel slightly less daunting, or is there another specific worry holding you back?

It does feel a little less heavy, I suppose. But there's this other worry, too—that even if she is nice, I won't know what to say next. Like, I'll have a nice wave, and then I'll just stand there like a mute, and the awkwardness will ruin everything anyway.

It is completely understandable to feel stuck once the initial greeting passes; the fear of running out of words is often just as paralyzing as the fear of being judged. Many people struggle with this sudden silence because their brains jump straight to the worst outcome: that the interaction has failed because it wasn't perfect. To test whether you can handle a simple pause without catastrophe, could you imagine a script where you say a basic greeting, wait ten seconds for a response (or lack thereof), and then simply return to your own activity? How would that play out in your mind compared to the current scenario?

That actually sounds... manageable. Like, if I just say "hi" and then go back to watering my plant or whatever, it doesn't have to be this big conversation. I think I've been putting so much pressure on myself to be interesting that I forgot it's okay to just be ordinary. I might try that next time.

That insight about forgetting it's okay to be ordinary is incredibly powerful, and recognizing that you don't need to perform is a major relief. Since we've identified that the fear of judgment is largely unfounded and that the pressure to be interesting is unnecessary, I'd like us to solidify a very small, low-pressure plan for tomorrow morning. Would you be open to committing to saying just "Good morning" and then giving yourself permission to immediately turn back to your porch without waiting for a long response?

Yeah, I think I can do that. Just a simple "good morning" and then I'll just go back to checking my phone or picking up the newspaper. I won't wait around or try to force more words out. I'll try to just... let it be what it is.

That is a fantastic plan because it removes the pressure to sustain a conversation, allowing you to focus entirely on simply existing in that moment. Before we finalize this, I want to make sure we have a clear agreement: Tomorrow morning, you will greet her, allow yourself to feel whatever comes up, and then immediately return to your routine without trying to fix anything. Does that summary capture exactly how you intend to proceed, or is there anything else you'd like to add to this commitment?
That sounds right. I'll say "good morning," feel whatever I feel, and then just go back to what I was doing. No fixing, no forcing. I think I can handle that.

That sounds like a solid, achievable goal, and remembering to simply observe the interaction without trying to control its outcome is a very wise strategy. Before we conclude, I'd like to check in on how the session has gone so far. Did hearing about the "ordinary" interaction help reduce some of that heaviness you carried earlier, or is there something about our discussion you'd like to clarify?

It did help, actually. I came in feeling like a failure for even trying, and now I feel like maybe I was just making things way harder than they need to be. It's a relief to realize that I don't have to be perfect or interesting, just present. Thanks for listening and helping me see that.

It brings me so much joy to hear that our conversation helped lift that weight of expectation off your shoulders. Recognizing that you were simply making things harder than necessary is a powerful realization, and feeling relieved that you don't need to be perfect is a significant step forward. Please remember that even if tomorrow feels a bit shaky, the fact that you are choosing to show up and be ordinary is already a victory. Is there anything else you'd like to add before we close our session?
No, I think that covers everything for today. I'll try to remember that showing up is enough, and that I don't have to be perfect. Thank you again, really. I'll let you know how it goes next time.

It is truly wonderful to hear that you are carrying this new perspective with you. Remembering that showing up is enough, rather than needing perfection, is a gift you are giving yourself for tomorrow. I am very proud of how brave you've been to face that fear, and I can't wait to hear about how your "ordinary hello" goes when we meet again. Take care of yourself today, and know that I'm here whenever you need to talk.

Hello again, it is great to see you here today. First, could you briefly share how things have been since we last spoke, particularly regarding the anxiety level you mentioned was high after our last session? Then, let's look ahead together: what are the top two things you feel we should focus on to help you manage that pressure to be perfect?

Hi. Thanks for asking. Um, since last time, the anxiety hasn't really gone down. I keep trying to fix that one paragraph, but every time I look at it, my stomach just knots up. For today, I guess I'd like to figure out why one mistake makes me feel like the whole story is garbage. And maybe... how to stop lying awake at night re-running that same sentence over and over.

It sounds like that knotting in your stomach has been quite persistent, showing how deeply that fear of the "wrong" sentence has taken hold. Since we agreed earlier that the core issue seems to be the belief that one flaw ruins the entire story, I wonder if we can explore what happens in your mind right before you start ruminating on that sentence at night—is it a specific thought pattern that triggers the panic, or does it feel like a general sense of dread taking over?

It's more like a specific thought, I think. I'll be lying there, and I'll just remember typing that sentence, and my brain goes, "That's it. You've broken the whole thing. It's worthless now." Then I start picturing readers getting to that part and hating it, and I can't stop. It's like the one bad paragraph becomes the only thing that exists.

That image of the sentence becoming the "only thing that exists" sounds incredibly isolating, as if your brain has narrowed its view to just that one error. When you connect the internal thought—"you've broken the whole thing"—to the external fear of readers hating it, it creates a chain reaction that traps you in that rumination. To test how strong that link actually is, could you describe a situation where you noticed that first thought popping up, but then realized you were able to shift your attention away from the "worthless" conclusion? What happened instead of letting the panic take full control?

I... I'm not sure I've ever really shifted away from it, to be honest. Once that thought pops up, it's like my mind just locks onto it. There was one time last week, though, when I was making tea, and I started thinking about the paragraph. But then the kettle boiled, and I had to pour the water, and for maybe ten seconds I was just focused on the steam. It didn't last, but... I guess the panic didn't fully take over during those few seconds.

That moment with the kettle is a powerful clue that your brain can break free if you simply redirect your attention to something immediate, like watching the steam rise. Even though that break was only ten seconds, it proves that the "locked-on" state isn't permanent; you just need a small anchor to pull you out. Now that we've identified the specific trap of viewing one mistake as the end of the story, what is one tiny step we could try tomorrow morning to disrupt that pattern before you even lie down at night?

Maybe... I could try sitting in my backyard with my notebook but not opening it. Just sitting there for a few minutes, looking at the trees or something, before I even think about the story. So the space isn't only tied to that mistake anymore. I've been avoiding going out there at all, but maybe if I just sit and breathe, it won't feel so charged with failure.

That is a very wise observation; separating the physical space of the backyard from the mental weight of the story could indeed lower the stakes significantly. By sitting there first, you might train your brain to associate that peaceful environment with safety rather than impending failure. Before we finalize this plan, how does it feel knowing that you have a valid reason to stay in your chair for those first few minutes—namely, to reclaim a bit of peace before the work begins?

It feels... strange, honestly. Like I'm giving myself permission to not be productive, which I'm not used to. But it also feels a bit lighter, if that makes sense. Like maybe I don't have to dive straight into the panic every time I sit down. I think I could try it tomorrow morning, just to see if the backyard can feel normal again.

That shift in perspective—that sitting quietly gives you permission to just *be* rather than immediately perform—is a huge relief and shows how much flexibility you're starting to find. It sounds like tomorrow's plan is clear: go to the backyard, sit with your notebook open but untouched, and ride out whatever mild restlessness comes up without fighting it. As we wrap up today, is there anything else about that plan or our discussion that you feel ready to try or need to adjust before you go home?

No, I think I'm okay with this plan for now. I'm a little nervous about actually doing it, but I also kind of want to prove to myself that the backyard isn't cursed or anything. Thank you for helping me see that those ten seconds with the kettle meant something. I'll try to remember that tomorrow.

That is such a beautiful way to put it—the backyard isn't cursed; it just needs a fresh start to show you that it can be a place of calm again. Your willingness to face that nervousness and use the lesson from the kettle as a guide is exactly what will help you rebuild that connection. I hope tomorrow brings you a few quiet moments in nature that remind you of your resilience. I'll speak with you soon to hear how those first minutes went.

Hello again; thank you for coming in today. First, how are you feeling right now compared to where you were last time? Also, since we agreed to try talking to a coworker named Mike about your fatigue, would you like to check in on that first, or is there another topic you'd prefer to bring up?

Hey. I'm... okay, I guess. Still pretty tired, if I'm honest. As for Mike, I actually didn't bring it up with him. Every time I thought about starting that conversation, I kept telling myself I was just being weak, and that he probably has it worse than I do. So I just... didn't.

It takes courage to admit that you haven't followed through, especially when you know you had a great opportunity to try this new approach. That "weakness" voice you heard likely stepped in to protect you from the risk of rejection or looking foolish, even though it's blocking you from doing something brave. Can you remember what specific thought ran through your head the moment you realized you hadn't started the conversation yet?

I remember thinking, "I'm just complaining over nothing. Mike works just as hard as I do, and he doesn't seem to have any problems. I should just be grateful I even have a job." It felt so true in the moment that I just shut down and changed the subject when we were on break.

That comparison with Mike feels incredibly convincing because you are projecting your own fears onto him, assuming his resilience is fixed when he might be facing the same invisible struggles you are. It seems like that "complain over nothing" thought is acting as a shield, protecting you from the discomfort of realizing your fatigue is valid and shared, even if he doesn't show it. Did you catch yourself wondering if saying "nothing" meant your life was actually fine, or if you were just trying to convince yourself that you deserved to feel okay?

Honestly, it's both. Part of me thinks if I can just convince myself everything is fine, then I'll actually start feeling better. But then there's this other part that gets angry at myself for even thinking that way, because I know deep down I'm struggling. It feels like no matter what I do, I'm wrong.

That anger at yourself is actually a very important clue—it suggests you know deep down that your current "all is fine" narrative is keeping you stuck, yet your brain is still racing to protect you from facing the difficulty. It seems like you're trying to solve the problem by changing your story, but the story itself is becoming a barrier to feeling relief. When you say you feel "wrong" no matter what, is that feeling of being wrong mostly about how you *should* act, or is it about how you *are* feeling right now?

I think it's more about how I should act. Like, I should be tougher, I should be able to handle this without complaining, I should just push through like everyone else. When I actually notice how tired or frustrated I feel, it just makes me feel guilty, like I'm failing at being a decent employee or something.

That pressure to be "tougher" and "push through" is a classic survival instinct that trained you to hide your vulnerability, but it's now working against you by creating a gap between who you are and who you think you should be. It sounds like the core issue isn't that you lack toughness, but that you've tied your worth as an employee directly to suppressing your natural feelings of exhaustion. If we shifted the goal slightly—to allow yourself to feel tired without judging yourself as "failing"—how might that change the story you tell yourself when you notice those feelings again?

That's... a weird thought to wrap my head around, honestly. If I just let myself feel tired and didn't beat myself up for it, I guess I wouldn't have to waste energy trying to hide it or pretend. Maybe I'd even have a clearer head to actually figure out what I need, instead of just telling myself to shut up and work harder. But it feels risky, like I'm giving myself permission to be lazy or something.

Letting yourself feel tired isn't about being lazy; it's simply about removing the extra burden of pretending, which actually frees up the mental energy you need to function. The idea that you're "giving permission" comes from that same old voice that equates honesty with weakness, but consider this: admitting you're tired is just stating a fact, whereas forcing yourself to ignore it is actively fighting your body and draining you further. If we view "letting it be" as a strategic choice to conserve energy rather than a lack of effort, does that shift the risk into something more manageable for you?

I never thought of it like that—like it's a choice to save energy instead of just giving up. I guess when you put it that way, it doesn't sound so scary. Maybe I could try just noticing when I'm tired and not immediately adding a bunch of "should" thoughts on top of it. It feels weird, but maybe it's worth a shot.

That is a fantastic insight—shifting from "giving up" to "saving energy" changes the entire meaning of what you're doing. Before we finalize a plan, I want to make sure we are aligned: if we try this experiment of just observing your tiredness without the "should" judgments, does that sound like a safe and useful direction for us to take together today?

Yeah, I think it does. I'm not saying I'll be amazing at it right away, but I'm willing to try. It's better than staying stuck in that loop of feeling guilty and exhausted all the time. I guess I just need a little help catching myself when those "should" thoughts sneak in.

You are absolutely right, and I completely agree that catching those thoughts early is key. Since you mentioned you need help spotting them, let's agree to use a simple mental checkpoint: whenever you feel tired, pause for just three seconds before reacting and ask yourself, "Am I just feeling exhausted, or am I adding a 'should' story on top?" We will treat that pause as a break from the automatic loop. Does that simple three-second pause feel like something you can realistically commit to trying during your next shift?

Yeah, I think I can handle three seconds. It's not like I have to stop working or anything—just a quick pause to check in with myself. I'll give it a shot on my next shift and see how it feels. Thanks for giving me something so simple to try.

You are very welcome, and I'm glad that simple three-second pause feels doable for you. Please remember, the goal isn't perfection; even if you slip up and jump straight to the "should" thought, bringing yourself back to that pause is the win. Is there anything else you'd like to discuss before we head out, or shall we wrap up here knowing you have a tool to carry into your next shift?

Hello, I'm glad to see you again. How has your week been going since we last spoke, and were there any particular moments or events that stood out to you? Could we also take a moment to decide what topic feels most important for us to explore together today?

Hey, thanks for asking. The week's been pretty rough, to be honest. I keep seeing my dog's empty bed and it just hits me all over again. I think today I really need to talk about why I can't shake this feeling that it's all my fault.

It sounds like the sight of her empty bed is triggering that powerful feeling of responsibility again, and I completely understand why seeing that scene is so painful right now. Since your main focus seems to be untangling that specific knot of "why it's all my fault," shall we start by looking closely at the exact thoughts that come up when you see her bed?

Yeah, that makes sense. When I look at her bed, my mind just goes straight to, "If I'd been home more, she wouldn't have gotten out." I keep replaying that morning over and over in my head, thinking about how I could have done things differently.

That relentless replaying of the morning sounds incredibly exhausting, and it makes complete sense that your mind is trying to fix a past moment you can't change. When you hold onto the belief that you *could* have prevented this with more effort, does that feeling of "if only" create a heavier weight on your shoulders than simply accepting that it happened?

Yeah, it does feel heavier. Every time I do that "if only" thing, it's like I'm punishing myself all over again. But I don't know how to just accept it without feeling like I'm letting her down, you know? It feels like accepting it means I'm admitting I don't care enough.

That connection between accepting the situation and feeling like you aren't caring enough is heartbreaking to witness, and it shows how deeply you want to protect her memory by being perfect. Let's try a gentle experiment: if you imagine your best friend saw her dog run away and immediately blamed herself for not coming home, would you tell her she wasn't a good friend, or would you remind her that accidents happen even to the most attentive owners?

I mean... when you put it like that, I'd definitely tell her it wasn't her fault. I'd probably tell her that dogs are fast and sneaky and sometimes these things just happen, no matter how careful you are. But I guess it's harder to give myself that same kindness, isn't it?

That is such a profound realization—that you naturally extend this same logic of "accidents happen" to others while withholding it from yourself. It highlights how unfair your current standard of perfectionism has become. If we frame your self-talk not as a judgment of your character, but as an attempt to prove you were a good guardian despite the chaos, does that help separate the accident from your actual worth as a pet parent?

I never really thought about it like that before. I guess I've been treating this one mistake as proof that I'm a bad owner overall, even though I've taken great care of all my animals for years. Maybe I can start trying to see it more as just a really bad day rather than a reflection of who I am.

That is a huge shift in perspective, moving from defining yourself by one error to viewing it merely as a bad day. To help cement this, let's try rewriting that "if only" thought into a neutral observation. Instead of "If I'd been home, she wouldn't have escaped," how does it feel to say, "She slipped through a gap, and that was just unfortunate timing"? Does that slight change in wording make the event feel a bit less personal to you?

Huh... saying it that way does feel different. "She slipped through a gap, and that was just unfortunate timing" — that actually takes some of the weight off my chest. It's still sad, but it doesn't feel like I'm stabbing myself with guilt when I say it like that.

That relief you feel in your chest is exactly what we want to cultivate by separating the event from your identity. Since that phrase feels like a useful anchor right now, let's make a simple plan for tomorrow: whenever you catch yourself thinking "I should have known better," try replacing it with "she slipped through a gap, and that was just unfortunate timing." Would you feel comfortable testing that small swap with me first, perhaps by reading it aloud here, before you go back to your house?

Yeah, I think I can try that. So instead of beating myself up, I'll say, "She slipped through a gap, and that was just unfortunate timing." It still feels kind of weird on my tongue, but I can feel it's less harsh than what I usually tell myself. I'll give it a shot tomorrow and see how it goes.

That is a brave and wise decision to start with a conscious effort to soften your internal dialogue, even if the words feel awkward at first. Before we wrap up, could you share how it felt to work through this session together today, particularly regarding our exploration of separating the accident from your self-worth? And is there anything else you'd like to add or clarify before we part ways?

Honestly, I came in feeling pretty hopeless, but I think I'm leaving with a little bit of a different perspective today. It was hard to hear that I've been way harder on myself than I'd ever be on someone else, but I think I needed to hear it. Thank you for helping me see that I don't have to carry all this guilt around like it's proof of who I am. I think I'm ready to try that new phrase tomorrow.

It is truly wonderful to hear that you left with a renewed sense of perspective and a willingness to carry yourself with a little more kindness. Your commitment to trying the new phrasing tomorrow, even when it feels foreign on your tongue, speaks volumes about your dedication to healing. Thank you for trusting me with your story and for being so open to exploring these difficult feelings with me today. I hope you find some peace as you face that empty bed tomorrow.

Hello again. Welcome back. To start, I'd love to know how you've been feeling this week, perhaps on a scale of zero to ten, and how it compares to where we left off last time. Did you manage to try that game observation this past weekend, and how did it go?

Uh, hi. I guess I'm around a 5 or 6 this week. Not great, not terrible. Yeah, I did try the game observation thing. I watched a football match with my friends on Saturday, but instead of just enjoying it, I kept thinking about how they probably saw me as less smart for being so into it. It was hard to shake that feeling.

It sounds like the disappointment of the experiment—seeing the feeling persist despite the friendly environment—is quite frustrating, especially after doing the work to prepare for it. Since our goal is to break that loop, I'd like us to spend some time exploring exactly what happened in that moment when you spoke up. Can you walk me through your internal dialogue right after you said that analysis about the defense shift?

Well, right after I said it, there was this split second where I felt pretty good about noticing that play. But then almost immediately I thought, "Great, now they probably think I'm some dumb jock who can't talk about anything else." I remember looking around at their faces and just assuming they were bored or judging me. I didn't even ask them what they thought—I just went quiet and let that feeling sit.

It sounds like that initial surge of pride quickly got swallowed by the automatic assumption that they were bored, which made you withdraw. That pattern of "look, assume negative reaction, shut down" feels very familiar, but I'm curious: when you looked at their faces expecting boredom, what specific visual cue in their expression convinced your brain that judgment was happening? Was it their facial muscles, their eye contact, or something else entirely?

I think it was mostly the eye contact—or lack of it, I guess. One of my friends was looking down at his phone for a second, and I just latched onto that. I told myself, "See, he's not even paying attention. He thinks this is stupid." I didn't even notice that the others were still watching the game. It's like my brain just picked that one detail and ran with it.

That is such a powerful realization—that your brain seized on a tiny, isolated detail (one friend glancing at a phone) and spun it into a catastrophic story about your entire worth. It seems like that moment of silence afterwards wasn't necessarily a result of their reaction, but rather your own choice to retreat based on that distorted reading of the situation. Does recognizing that pattern as a habit of your mind, rather than proof of your failure, feel slightly lighter to carry?

I guess... yeah, it does feel a little lighter when you put it that way. Like, maybe it wasn't actually about them at all—it was just me doing that thing I always do, jumping to the worst conclusion. But it's still hard to fully believe that. Part of me still thinks, "Well, what if he really was bored?" I can't just erase that doubt.

That hesitation is completely understandable; even when we spot the pattern, our brains are wired to believe the original threat to our safety. Let's do a quick reality check on that doubt: if he was truly bored, would he have stayed silent, or would he have looked away and stopped engaging entirely? Also, given that you mentioned earlier they still joke with you and ask about your games, how does that history contradict the idea that one brief glance means they've lost interest in you?

When you ask it like that... I mean, if he was really bored, he probably would've just left or started a different conversation, right? He didn't do that. And yeah, they do ask me about games sometimes, and we still laugh together about stuff. So I guess that one glance doesn't really line up with all that. It's just... my brain makes it feel so real in the moment, you know?

That is a really important distinction you just made: the feeling of him being bored feels overwhelmingly real, yet the facts show a completely different picture. It seems like your brain creates a "movie" in your head that feels more intense than the actual event, which makes the doubt so sticky. Since we've explored the specific evidence against the "they're bored" story, how would you rate your confidence now that one glance didn't lead to disengagement, compared to before you looked at the evidence?

Maybe like a 6 or 7 out of 10? Before, I was probably at a 2, totally convinced I'd messed up. So it's definitely better. I can kind of see now that I might be blowing things out of proportion, but it's still not easy to just switch off that automatic feeling. I guess it takes practice.

That's a massive victory in itself, moving from a certainty of failure to acknowledging you might be exaggerating. It's not about instantly erasing the feeling, but realizing it's a habit that needs work rather than an absolute truth. Now that we've tested that specific doubt, I want to pivot to how you handled the aftermath of the conversation. Instead of letting that discomfort sit, what was one small thing you did or thought that helped you get through the rest of the evening without spiraling further?

Honestly, I just tried to focus on the game itself for a while. I stopped talking and let myself get into the plays, the scores, the energy of it. It wasn't like I felt amazing or anything, but by just paying attention to the match instead of my thoughts, I kind of distracted myself enough to stop the spiral. It's not a perfect fix, but it got me through the night.

That is a really useful skill to identify, and it's impressive that you noticed it working even if it didn't feel like a total cure. Focusing on the external world when the internal noise gets loud is a great grounding tool. Since we've covered the specific interpretation of that one glance and found a helpful distraction technique, what is the main takeaway or lesson you're most willing to carry into your next social interaction?

I think the main thing I want to remember is that my first reaction to someone's face or silence isn't always the truth—it's just my brain jumping to the worst case. And if I do start doubting myself, I can try to focus on what's actually happening around me instead of getting stuck in my head. It's not gonna be easy, but at least now I have a little bit of proof that it works sometimes.

That summary captures everything we've built together: separating the fleeting thought from the lasting reality, and using the present moment to anchor yourself. You've gained a reliable toolkit for navigating those tricky moments where your brain tries to tell you a story that isn't true. How does it feel to leave the session with this concrete understanding rather than just a vague sense of hope?

It feels... solid, I guess. Like, I'm not just hoping things will magically get better—I actually have something to try. It's still scary, but I don't feel as stuck as I did before. Thanks for helping me see that. I think I can actually work on this now.

That sense of solidity is wonderful to hear, and knowing you have tools to rely on instead of just waiting for magic makes a huge difference. You've turned a frightening spiral into a manageable challenge, and that shift in perspective is a major step forward. Before we wrap up, is there anything specific about today's work that feels particularly useful to you right now, or is there one small thing you wish you could have done differently?

I think the most useful part was actually walking through the moment in slow motion—when I saw my friend look at his phone. Just breaking it down like that made me realize how much I was filling in the blanks with my own fears. I wish I could have caught myself in that moment and asked him what he was doing instead of just assuming. Maybe next time I'll try that.

That is such a valuable insight—you realized that interrupting the automatic assumption with a direct question could have broken the cycle right then and there. Asking "What are you looking at?" turns a fearful guess into a simple curiosity, which shifts the dynamic entirely. Given that new strategy, would you like to practice formulating that exact question so it feels natural to say in the future?

Yeah, that actually sounds helpful. I think I'd say something like, "Hey, what's up? Everything good?" or maybe just, "You looked away—did you see something weird?" Something calm that doesn't sound accusing. I don't want to make it a big deal or put him on the spot. Just a casual check-in, I guess.

Those scripts strike a perfect balance—they're friendly and curious without putting anyone on the defensive. That "casual check-in" approach is exactly what you need to maintain the connection while stopping the spiral mid-stream. Before we finish, does practicing saying those lines out loud with me make them feel more natural and less risky to use in the heat of the moment?

Yeah, it does. Saying it out loud makes it feel less like a scary, risky move and more like just a normal thing you'd say to a friend. I think I could actually use that next time. It's still a little nerve-wracking, but at least I have a plan now instead of just going quiet.

That is a fantastic shift—from seeing it as a high-stakes gamble to viewing it as a simple, normal part of friendship. Having a concrete plan like that gives you the security to stand firm even when your nerves are racing. Before we officially close, how does it feel to end this session with a clear strategy in hand rather than just lingering in the uncertainty? Is there anything else you'd like to add before we say goodbye?

It feels way better than last time. I came in feeling kind of hopeless about this whole thing, and now I actually have a couple of things I can try. I think I'm ready to give that casual check-in a shot next time I'm with my friends. Thanks for helping me get to this point—I'll keep working on it.

Hearing you move from feeling hopeless to feeling equipped is such a testament to your resilience and the progress we've made together. You are absolutely ready to take that next step, armed with a plan that puts you in control rather than reacting to fear. I'm so proud of how far you've come today, and I look forward to hearing how those new strategies land for you in your upcoming conversations. Take a deep breath, trust in the preparation you've done, and see you next time.

Welcome back. First, I'd love to hear how you've been feeling since we last spoke and what mood you're carrying right now. Additionally, could you briefly outline what you'd like us to focus on together today?

Hi. Um, I guess I'm feeling pretty much the same as before—kind of flat and bored. I don't really know where to start, but I just feel stuck, like nothing I do is fun or interesting enough. I guess today I want to figure out why I feel like I'm not good enough to do the things I see other people doing.

Thank you for sharing that feeling of being flat and stuck; it takes courage to name it even when it feels so vague. To honor your request, let's spend some time exploring that deep-seated belief about not being "good enough" compared to others, and see if we can uncover the hidden thoughts driving it. When you catch yourself thinking you aren't good enough, what specific situation or memory tends to bring that thought to the surface?

It usually happens when I'm scrolling through social media or talking to my friends. Like, last weekend, one of my friends posted a video of her hiking trip with a group, and they all looked so excited and happy. I just sat there thinking, "I could never do that—I'm not adventurous or fun enough." I don't even know why I think that, but it feels so real in the moment.

That specific image of your friend's excited group really highlights how easily our minds jump to worst-case scenarios when we feel disconnected. It seems like that feeling of inadequacy isn't just about the hike itself, but perhaps a deeper worry that you're missing out on a version of life where everyone else is having the perfect time while you are left behind. When you noticed those thoughts popping up while scrolling, did you expect them to appear, or did they surprise you?

They surprised me, honestly. I wasn't even thinking about hiking or being adventurous before I saw the post. It was just a normal evening, I was watching a movie and relaxing, and then I saw it and suddenly felt so down. It's like my mood can change in a second just from seeing something like that.

That sudden shift from relaxation to feeling inadequate is such a sharp contrast, and it makes total sense that you found it surprising. It often feels like an external event controls our entire mood, but I wonder if your brain is actually interpreting that image through a very personal lens, expecting you to compare your current reality against someone else's highlight reel. Have you ever caught yourself wondering, "If I were just like them, wouldn't I be happier?" when that feeling first hits?

Yeah, I've definitely thought that. I'll think, "If I was more like them—if I was braver or more outgoing—then I'd be happy too." And then I just sit here watching movies alone, and it feels like proof that I'm boring. It's like I'm stuck in this loop where I feel bad about being bored, but then I also feel too scared or not good enough to try anything different.

That loop is exhausting—you're using your current boredom as evidence that you lack qualities you need to develop, which in turn paralyzes you from becoming who you want to be. It sounds like the fear of trying something new is stronger than the desire to enjoy it right now. Let's test that belief by asking: if you could imagine a version of yourself who was brave enough to try one new thing despite feeling scared, what would stop *you* from taking that small step today?

I think what stops me is the fear of failing or looking stupid. Like, if I tried hiking and I wasn't good at it, or I got tired and couldn't keep up, people would see that I don't belong there. I'd rather just stay home and not risk that embarrassment, even if it means feeling bored. It's like I'm protecting myself from being judged, but it just makes me feel worse in the end.

That is a very logical defense mechanism; it makes complete sense that avoiding the risk of judgment feels safer than facing the possibility of failure. It's hard not to appreciate how well that logic protects you from embarrassment, yet it also traps you in that cycle of boredom and self-doubt. Let's look closely at that "fear of looking stupid"—when you imagine hiking and getting tired, what specific thought runs through your head about how people will react to you?

I guess I imagine them whispering to each other or giving me that pitying look, like, "Oh, she's not really cut out for this." Or maybe they'd just be annoyed that I'm slowing them down. I'd feel so out of place, like everyone knows I don't belong there. I think that thought is so strong that it feels like it's already happened before I even try.

Those vivid images of whispers and pitying looks show how powerful your imagination can be, yet they seem to be based on assumptions rather than facts. If we strip away the assumption that everyone is judging you, what actually happens in the world when you join a group activity? Would they really stop to talk to you, or would they just continue whatever they were doing?

I guess... they'd probably just keep hiking and talking to each other, not even noticing me that much. Maybe someone would say hi or ask if I'm okay, but that's about it. When I slow down and think about it, people are usually just focused on themselves, not on me. It's hard to remember that in the moment, though.

That shift in perspective is really valuable; realizing that people are often absorbed in their own experiences can break the spell of constant scrutiny. It suggests your brain is projecting intense expectations onto strangers that simply aren't there. Now, let's bridge that insight to action: if we assume people won't judge you harshly, what is one tiny, low-stakes adventure you could try this week that involves stepping outside your usual routine?

Maybe I could try going for a walk in a park I've never been to before. It's not as big as hiking, but it's something new. I could just bring my headphones and walk around, no pressure to talk to anyone or perform. That feels manageable, like I'm not setting myself up to fail.

That sounds like a brilliant, realistic choice—a small step that respects your boundaries while still offering a fresh experience. Before we lock this in, I want to double-check your agreement on the core belief: if you walked into that unfamiliar park, would you still hold onto the thought that "everyone is judging me and I look foolish," or would you allow yourself the possibility that you might just enjoy the fresh air without an audience?

I think... I'd be nervous at first, but I'd try to remind myself that no one's really watching me. I mean, people in parks are just walking their dogs or jogging, they're not there to judge me. So maybe I could just let myself enjoy the fresh air and see what happens. It's worth a shot, right?

Exactly—that shift from "they are judging me" to "people are busy with their own lives" is the key to opening the door. It sounds like a perfect plan to test that belief safely. Before we finish, I want to hear your thoughts on this: does imagining walking in that new park with just your headphones feel like a comfortable challenge, or does the idea of being somewhere entirely new still trigger that old feeling of being exposed?

It feels a bit uncomfortable, but in a way that I think I can handle. I'm not dreading it like I would with a group hike. It's just me and the trees, you know? I think I can give it a try and see if I feel any different afterward.

That distinction makes a lot of sense; stepping out into nature feels less like performing for an audience and more like finding a quiet space for yourself. To seal in this plan, what would you like to call this small experiment, and is there one specific thing you hope to notice in yourself after the walk, whether it's a shift in mood or just a feeling of accomplishment?

I'll call it my "quiet adventure." And I hope that after the walk, I'll notice that I feel a little less bored and a little less hard on myself. Even if I just feel neutral, that's better than feeling stuck and down. I think just doing something different would be a win for me.

That is a wonderful definition of success, focusing on reducing the internal noise rather than seeking high-energy excitement. Your plan for the "quiet adventure" clearly outlines exactly what you'll do, where you'll do it, and what counts as a victory. Before we close, I want to check in: does this feel like something you can realistically commit to this week without feeling overwhelmed, and is there anything else you'd like to adjust in your plan before we finish?

I think I can commit to it. I'll plan to go this Saturday afternoon when the park is usually quiet. I don't think I need to change anything else—it's simple enough that I can't really make excuses. Thanks, this feels a bit more hopeful than when I walked in today.

That is a fantastic commitment, especially choosing a quiet Saturday afternoon to minimize distractions. It sounds like you've found a path forward that honors both your need for safety and your desire for a little bit of newness. Before I sign off, how are you feeling right now as we wrap up, and is there anything else you'd like to discuss about your "quiet adventure" or anything else on your mind?

I feel a little lighter, actually. I'm still nervous about it, but I'm also kind of curious to see what happens. I don't have anything else to add right now—I think I just need to follow through on this and see how it goes. Thanks for listening and helping me figure this out.

Please remember that regardless of the outcome, you have already done something important by choosing to act on your own terms. Take care of yourself this Saturday, and I look forward to hearing about your experience whenever you're ready to share.

Hello, thank you for being here. To start, how have you been feeling emotionally and physically since we last spoke? Is there anything specific from our previous discussion about feeling trapped that you'd like to revisit or add to our focus for today?

Hi. Well, I've been feeling kind of the same, honestly. I wake up most days just feeling heavy and restless at the same time, if that makes sense. My sleep is still pretty broken, and I've been picking at my food because my stomach just feels tight.

It sounds like that heaviness and restlessness are carrying a lot of weight across your whole body, especially when combined with the disrupted sleep and eating habits. Given that you mentioned feeling "trapped" last time, does waking up with that restless energy often lead you to immediately scroll through social media to escape the feeling, or do you tend to stay in bed trying to calm down first?

I usually grab my phone right away, honestly. It's like a habit—I just reach for it to distract myself from the heavy feeling. But then I see my friends posting pictures from their trips, and it makes everything worse, like I'm the only one stuck here. I tell myself not to look, but I can't stop.

It makes complete sense that your hand reaches for the phone as soon as you feel that heaviness, because your brain is trying desperately to numb the discomfort you're describing. Even though you know looking at those photos makes things worse, the urge to escape the silence seems so powerful that saying "no" feels impossible. Can we explore what happens in that exact moment when you reach for the phone versus what you might choose to do instead?

I think... when I reach for it, I'm just looking for something, anything, to fill the quiet. My mind starts racing about what I'm missing out on, and the phone feels like a lifeline, even though it's not. I guess I could try just lying there and breathing for a minute, but that silence feels so loud, you know?

That silence feeling so loud is exactly why the phone becomes such a lifeline, even though it traps us in more comparisons later on. Lying there while waiting for the noise to fade can feel incredibly lonely, but if we treat that quiet as a signal to ground ourselves rather than a void to fill, it might actually help. Would you be willing to try placing your phone face down on a distant surface and spending three minutes just noticing the weight of your feet on the floor before you reach for it again?

I could try that. It sounds a little weird, but also kind of... calming, maybe? I always thought I had to do something active to fix the feeling, not just sit with it. I'll give it a shot, though—what's three minutes, right?

Yes, three minutes is a very short window, just enough time to let your breathing slow down before the thoughts rush back in. Think of it as giving yourself a tiny gift to create a small space between the heaviness and the instinct to reach for the phone. Shall we try it right now, starting with just noticing your feet on the floor while you count slowly to ten?

Okay, I can do that. (pauses, looks down at her feet) I can feel the pressure of my heels on the ground... and the carpet feels a bit rough. I'm up to seven now... It's actually quieter in my head than I thought it would be.

That's a beautiful observation—the realization that the noise isn't gone but has softened enough to hear the quiet underneath. It sounds like this three-minute pause gave your brain a chance to step back from the race you were running, creating a tiny gap where you can choose differently. Now that we've practiced the breathing and grounding, would you like to share how you envision fitting this into your morning routine when you wake up, or should we discuss what might get in the way of sticking with it?

I think the biggest thing that might get in the way is just forgetting. In the moment, the urge to grab my phone is so strong that I don't even think about another option. Maybe I could put a sticky note on my phone case or on my nightstand that just says "feet first" or something to remind me.

That is a brilliant idea—turning a simple reminder into a physical cue can bridge the gap between your old habit and the new choice you want to make. A sticky note saying "feet first" serves as a gentle nudge just as your hand reaches for the screen, buying you that precious few seconds to choose your feet instead. Does placing that note seem like a realistic addition to your setup, or would you prefer a different word or image that feels even clearer to you?

"Feet first" feels really clear and kind of calming, actually. I think I'll write it in a bright color so I can't miss it. I can picture it now—my hand going for the phone, then seeing that note and stopping for just a second. That second could be all I need to make a different choice.

That visualization is powerful because it turns an abstract intention into a concrete visual trigger you can actually see. Seeing that bright note act as a roadblock gives your conscious mind just enough time to override the impulse to numb the silence. To wrap up our time today, would you like to try writing that note out right now, or is there anything else about the plan you feel ready to finalize before we finish?

I think I'm ready to actually write it out. (reaches into her bag and pulls out a sticky note and a marker) I'm going to use a bright orange marker—that should definitely catch my eye. "Feet first." (writes it down and holds it up) There. I'm going to put this on my phone case before I even go to bed tonight.

That is a fantastic commitment to the task, and choosing a bright orange marker adds a nice layer of visibility to ensure you don't miss the cue. Putting it on your phone case tonight means you'll have this safety net ready the moment you wake up and feel that familiar heaviness. Before we conclude, how does it feel to have taken this small, concrete step toward giving yourself control over those mornings?

Hello again. How are you feeling right now, and have things changed much since we last met? Let's quickly check in on your mood, then I'd love to know what feels most pressing for us to explore today—whether it's the lingering thoughts about the cats or something else entirely.

Oh, I'm... I'm managing, I suppose. My mood has been sort of up and down. The thoughts about the cats are still there, especially when I'm scrolling through social media and see those cute videos. But I think what's really been on my mind lately is how this connects to the new job—like, maybe I'm just not good enough for anyone or anything to like me. That's what feels most pressing today.

It takes courage to link those scary cat thoughts to a broader feeling that you aren't good enough for anyone or anything. That connection makes the fear feel much bigger, and I want to understand exactly how that general belief shows up when you see the videos or think about work. Does that thought sound like a hard fact about who you are, or does it feel more like a scary story you tell yourself whenever someone treats you neutrally?

It feels like a hard fact, honestly. When I'm at work, if a colleague doesn't say much to me during a meeting, I immediately think they must think I'm rude or unlikable. And then I come home, see a cat video, and think, "Even the cat wouldn't like me." It just seems so obvious that there's something fundamentally wrong with me.

Hearing that you interpret neutral actions from colleagues or animals as proof you are fundamentally flawed is incredibly painful, and it completely explains why the anxiety feels so constant. When a belief feels like an undeniable truth, it's very hard to step back and look at the evidence that might contradict it. Could we explore what happens in that split second when a coworker stays quiet? Is your mind jumping straight to "They hate me," or is there any physical sensation or internal voice that comes before that conclusion?

When a coworker stays quiet, there's this tightness in my chest right away, like my stomach drops. Then I start thinking, "I said something wrong again," or "They're annoyed with me." There's no real voice before that—just the feeling and then the thought. It's so quick that I don't even realize I'm doing it until I'm already feeling awful.

That tightness in your chest is your body warning you before your mind races to fill the silence with judgment, and it makes total sense that it feels unavoidable. Since the physical alarm happens almost instantly, it often overrides your ability to stop the negative story before it starts. Would you be open to slowing this process down slightly by noticing that initial tightness as a signal that a story is starting, rather than letting the story take over immediately?

I think I could try that, but I'm not sure I'd know how to stop the story once it starts. It just feels so automatic, like I'm on a roller coaster. But if I just focus on that tightness in my chest... maybe I could take a breath before the rest floods in? That sounds possible, at least in theory. I'd be willing to give it a shot.

That is a really smart observation about using the physical sensation as an anchor before the thoughts take full flight. Taking a conscious breath at that exact moment of tightness could create just enough space to interrupt the automatic rush of "I'm not likable." Before we practice this, does stopping the mental train to breathe feel like something you could realistically do when you're already caught in that cycle, or does it feel too difficult to pause at all?

Honestly, it feels a little difficult to pause in the moment—my mind just races ahead. But I think if I practice it enough, maybe it could become more natural. Like, I could remind myself that the tightness is just a signal, not a fact. I'm willing to give it a real try, even if I stumble at first.

That willingness to try, even knowing you might stumble, is the most important part of building a new habit. Reminding yourself that the tightness is just a signal rather than proof of failure gives you permission to breathe without fighting the feeling. Before we finalize this plan, does stopping to notice that physical cue and taking one breath seem like a realistic goal for us to practice together this week?

Yes, I think that's realistic. I can aim for that—just noticing the tightness and taking one breath before anything else. Maybe I'll even keep a little journal of when it happens, just to see the pattern. That sounds manageable, and I appreciate you breaking it down into such a small step.

That breakdown into a tiny, doable step makes the whole plan feel much safer and achievable. Keeping a quick note of those moments won't add pressure; it will just help you see exactly when the "tightness" shows up so you can catch it sooner. With that clear agreement on your breathing exercise and optional journaling, are there any other parts of the cat situation or your general self-worth that you'd like to talk about before we head out?

I think for now, this feels like enough. I'm a bit nervous about actually trying it, but I'm also curious to see what happens. Maybe if I can start noticing that pattern, the thoughts about the cats won't feel so overwhelming. Thank you for helping me see a way to start.

That mix of nervous excitement is completely normal when stepping into something new, and it speaks to your openness to growth. You've already done the hardest part: identifying that the tightness is a signal, not a verdict, and agreeing to test that new approach. Remember, even noticing the pattern without changing everything is a win. How does it feel to leave with that small, concrete plan in hand?

Hello again, and thank you for showing up. Before we dive into our agenda, let’s quickly check in on the last task we set: did you manage to spot that “cold, heavy knot” in your stomach when you received a grade back this past week? Once you share that, I’d love to know what you’re hoping to tackle together today.

Um, yeah, I did notice it actually. When my history test came back on Tuesday, I felt that same knot in my stomach, just like we talked about. It was pretty uncomfortable, but I guess it helped me realize I was doing that thing where I immediately tell myself I'm not smart enough.

Noticing that knot and recognizing the immediate self-criticism is a fantastic step forward, especially given how hard it is to catch those thoughts in real-time. Since you successfully practiced that awareness during our session, let's look at what we planned for this week: will you be using that five-second pause rule ("Okay, I'm feeling the knot") whenever you get a report card or quiz back? And beyond that, are there any other topics or worries you'd like to explore while we work on this?

I think I can try using the pause rule, but I'm honestly a bit scared it won't help much. When I see that grade, my mind just goes straight to "I'm so dumb" before I can even think about pausing. I guess I'd like to talk more about why I can't seem to stop comparing myself to the other kids in my class, even when I know it makes me feel worse.

That fear of failure is completely understandable, and it makes total sense that the comparison feels like an unstoppable force when your brain is already racing. Since we know the knot is a reliable early warning sign, maybe we can start by examining *why* the comparison feels so urgent—that sharp, "everyone else gets it but me" story keeps popping up automatically. Can you walk me through one recent instance where you compared yourself to another student and how quickly that thought arrived?

Okay, so last week in math class, Sarah got her test back and she was really happy with her B+. I saw her smiling and the first thing that popped into my head was "Of course she did well, she's actually smart." That thought came literally within seconds of seeing her face. Then I just sat there feeling small and stupid for the rest of the period, even though I hadn't even gotten my own grade back yet.

That instant jump from seeing her smile to immediately labeling her as "actually smart" while making yourself feel "small and stupid" highlights just how tightly woven that comparison pattern is. It sounds like your brain is trying to protect itself by casting you in a negative role before you've even finished your own work. When you feel that wave of shrinking right after watching her celebrate, does it feel like a prediction of what you'll be like once *you* get your grade?

Yeah, it does feel like a prediction. It's like I already know what's coming, so why even hope for anything different? My brain just skips straight to the worst outcome before I have any real evidence. And then when I actually do get my grade back, even if it's not terrible, I still feel like I was right to expect the worst because maybe it could have been better.

That sense of certainty about the "worst outcome" happening regardless of the actual result is a classic trap where we mistake our expectation for reality. It sounds like your brain has built a shortcut that predicts failure based on the comparison, skipping the actual data (like your own effort or the grade itself). Has it ever happened recently where you noticed your brain predicting a bad grade, but then the actual grade was fine, leaving you confused about why you felt so certain it would be terrible?

Actually... yeah, that happened just last week in English class. I was convinced I bombed my essay because I saw a few other people handing in theirs looking confident. When I got it back, I got a B, which is decent. But instead of feeling good, I just thought "Well, it should've been an A if I was actually smart." So even when the evidence is right there, I still find a way to twist it into proof that I'm not good enough.

That is such a powerful observation, and it points directly to a common pattern called "mindreading" or jumping to conclusions about what you deserve. It seems like your brain is filtering the "decent" B through a lens that expects perfection, turning solid evidence of success into proof of inadequacy. When you have that B sitting on your desk, what is the specific part of the comment or the grade that makes you feel justified in twisting it into a failure?

I think it's the fact that I know I could have done better. When I look at the B, I don't see the work I put in or the fact that I actually improved from my last essay. I just see the space between a B and an A, and that gap feels huge to me. It's like my brain ignores everything good and zooms right in on what I didn't achieve.

That is a very insightful description of your brain acting like a magnifying glass that only focuses on the missing pieces of the puzzle while ignoring the whole picture. It makes complete sense that focusing on the "gap" feels so threatening, even though you know you've made progress. When we look at that gap strictly as a measure of your worth, does it feel like the teacher's feedback on your improvements gets lost entirely? Or does the feeling of the gap override everything else in your mind?

Honestly, I barely even hear the teacher's feedback anymore. Like, she'll write comments saying my argument was strong or my thesis was clear, and I'll read them, but they don't really sink in. It's like my mind just skips over those parts and waits for the grade at the end. The gap between where I am and where I think I should be is so loud that everything else just gets drowned out.

That "drowning out" effect is incredibly exhausting, and it makes total sense that the loudest part of the feedback loop—the gap you perceive—overwrites the helpful information. It sounds like your brain is protecting itself from disappointment by refusing to process anything that suggests you're doing okay. If I were to suggest a small experiment where we intentionally listen to just *one* positive comment from the teacher before checking the number, would you be open to trying that next time you get a grade back?

I guess I could try that, but I'm not gonna lie, it sounds really hard. My instinct is always to look at the grade first because that's the number that matters, you know? But I can see how forcing myself to read the comment might change things a little. I'll give it a shot next time, even if it feels unnatural.

That willingness to try something that feels unnatural is exactly the kind of courage we need to break this cycle. Since you mentioned your instinct is to grab the grade first, let's refine our plan: next time you see a grade, will you commit to looking at just one positive comment from the teacher for ten seconds before checking the number, even if your hand wants to reach for the score immediately? What do you think might happen if you force yourself to hold onto that one encouraging remark for that brief moment?

I think... I might actually feel a little less crushed if I sit with the comment first. Like, maybe if I hear something good about my work before I see the grade, it won't hit me as hard when I notice the gap. It's worth trying, even if my brain is screaming at me to just look at the number already. I'll do it.

That is a fantastic insight, and it shows you're already seeing how changing the order of your attention can soften the blow. Since we've identified the specific thought patterns (the "gap" and the comparison) and tested the idea of reading a positive comment first, how does it feel to have a clearer path forward for the week? Are you ready to commit to trying the "comment first" rule alongside the five-second pause whenever a grade comes in?

Yeah, I think I'm ready. Having a plan makes it feel less overwhelming, like I have something to hold onto instead of just spiraling. I'll try the comment first rule and the pause, even if it feels weird at first. Thank you for helping me see that there might be another way to look at this.

It sounds like having a concrete plan gives you a much-needed sense of stability, even when the feelings are messy. To make sure you're set up for success, let's lock in exactly how you'll use these tools: Next time you receive a grade, will you commit to finding one positive comment first, holding it for ten seconds, then using your five-second pause before checking the number? And if that feels too big to start, what would be a smaller version of that step you could try tomorrow?

I think I'll start with a smaller version tomorrow. Since I have a quiz coming up in science, I could practice the five-second pause right after I hand it in, before I even get the grade back. Just take a breath and tell myself "Okay, I did what I could" instead of immediately predicting failure. That feels more manageable than waiting for a graded paper to come back.

That is a brilliant adjustment; shifting the focus to the act of submitting the work allows you to build confidence before the pressure of the grade hits. Taking a breath and acknowledging your effort as a distinct event from your intelligence is a great way to start that mental separation. Just to confirm, is doing the five-second pause and stating "I did what I could" after handing in the science quiz a realistic goal for tomorrow morning?

Yes, I can definitely do that. It feels realistic because it's just one moment, and it doesn't involve looking at any grades yet. I'll try to remember to take that breath and say that to myself right after I turn in the quiz.

That sounds like a perfect, low-pressure starting point for building that new habit. Remember, you don't need to get the breathing or the statement perfect; just giving yourself permission to pause for five seconds counts as a win. Is there anything else weighing on your mind, or would you like to close here with a sense of progress?

No, I think I'm good to close here. I feel like I have something small but real to work on, which is more than I had before. Thank you for listening and helping me find a way to step back from all those automatic thoughts.

Hearing that you feel you have something "real" to work on is such a meaningful way to end our session, and it speaks volumes about your growing agency. Please remember that tomorrow's goal isn't about perfection; it's simply about taking that one breath and offering yourself kindness right after handing in the quiz. I truly appreciate you bringing such honesty and courage to our conversations, and I'm excited to see how that small pause helps you navigate the science quiz. Take care of yourself!
