Hello again, and I'm so glad to see you. To start, could you tell me how you've been feeling emotionally this week, and what specific goal we should aim for in our time together today?

Hey... thanks. This week has been pretty rough, honestly. I've been waking up with this knot in my stomach, and I keep checking my bank account like it's going to magically change. I guess my main goal today is to figure out why I can't stop buying things even when I know I shouldn't.

That knot in your stomach sounds exhausting, especially when you keep checking your balance hoping for a miracle that isn't coming. Let's take a closer look at that urge to buy: when you're standing right in front of the screen about to click, what is the very first story your mind is telling itself to justify the purchase?

It's like... there's this voice that tells me if I buy that jacket or those shoes, people will see me differently. Like I'll finally look like I have my life together, and maybe I'll even feel like it too. And for those few seconds before I click, it feels like the answer to everything.

That hope for an external validation—a quick fix where others finally see you as stable—is incredibly powerful and understandable given how hard life has been lately. It makes sense that your brain latches onto that momentary boost as proof that things are changing. Have you noticed if that feeling of "having your life together" fades quickly after the purchase, leaving you with the same knot in your stomach you started with?

Yeah... it's like clockwork. Right after I hit "confirm order," there's this tiny rush, maybe a minute or two where I feel good. But then I look at the confirmation email and reality hits—I check my balance again and that knot comes back even tighter. And I start thinking, "What if this is the purchase that finally puts me over the edge into being broke?"

That cycle of a brief high followed immediately by a sharper drop makes perfect sense; it feels like buying is the only way to outrun the anxiety, even though it just deepens the fear afterward. It seems like your mind is treating every transaction as a potential tipping point that could send you over the edge. Before we look for other ways to handle that knot, could you describe a time recently when you successfully resisted a purchase? How did you manage to stay steady when the urge was strongest?

Um... actually, there was one time last week. I had this expensive watch in my cart, and I was about to check out, but then I remembered how I felt the last time I bought something similar—that hollow feeling. So I closed the tab and went for a walk instead. It was hard, and I kept thinking about the watch for like an hour afterward, but I didn't buy it.

That memory of the hollow feeling you experienced after a previous purchase clearly acted as a powerful brake, showing that you *do* have the capacity to interrupt the automatic impulse. It sounds like walking away helped you break the cycle, even though the worry lingered for an hour afterward. Given that success, what do you think might be different this time around to prevent the panic from taking over as soon as you see an item you want?

I think... maybe I need to catch myself earlier, before I even get to the cart stage. Because once it's in my cart, it feels almost impossible to resist. If I could stop myself the second I start browsing those sites, maybe the panic wouldn't have a chance to take over in the first place.

That is a really sharp observation—you are right that catching the impulse right at the door of the cart changes everything. By stopping at the browse stage, you avoid handing your brain the immediate dopamine hit that fuels the panic later. To try this out, let's set a small experiment for tomorrow: pick one site you usually visit, commit to looking at only five items, and if the urge to buy pops up before adding anything, say out loud, "I am just looking, not buying," and wait fifteen seconds before acting. Does that sound like a manageable way to test this new approach?

I think I can try that. It sounds almost too simple, but maybe that's the point—keeping it small so I don't get overwhelmed. I'll try it with that sneaker site I always check. And saying that phrase out loud, I mean, it feels a bit silly, but if it buys me those fifteen seconds, it might actually help.

That willingness to embrace a simple, even slightly silly phrase as a lifeline shows great creativity in finding tools that fit your unique struggle. Setting a hard cap on five items creates a clear boundary that prevents the endless scrolling that often leads to regret. Before we lock this in, would you be open to testing this "five-item rule" plus the verbal pause for the rest of this week, and then we can review how it felt together?

Yeah, I'm willing to try that. I'll do it for the rest of the week and see what happens. I just hope I don't talk myself out of it when the urge actually hits, you know? But I guess that's what we're here to figure out.

That hesitation to push through when the urge hits is completely normal—it means your brain knows the pain of failure, but it also trusts that we can navigate it together. You already have a proven strategy of walking away after a purchase, and now you're layering on a prevention tactic to stop the cycle before it starts. Is there anything else you'd like to adjust in this plan before we wrap up for now?

No, I think this is a good start. I appreciate that you're not telling me to just stop cold turkey or throw away my credit cards—that would've felt impossible. Taking it step by step, with this small rule and the pause, feels like something I can actually stick with.

That is such a vital realization—recognizing that a small, structured step is far more sustainable than a rigid ban is exactly the kind of flexibility that leads to lasting change. It sounds like you feel heard and supported by an approach that respects your reality while nudging you toward better habits. Is there anything else you'd like to reflect on or any part of this plan you'd like to tweak before we close today?
No, I think I'm good for today. I'll check in with you next week and let you know how the five-item rule and the pause went. Thanks for helping me see this in a way that doesn't feel so hopeless.

You are very welcome, and I'm so glad we found a direction that feels less hopeless and more doable for you. That willingness to take this small, careful step is exactly the kind of resilience that moves things forward. Please come back next week to share how those five items and the pause phrase worked out, and I'll be here listening. Take care until then.

I mean, it's just what he said, right? He's a good cook, so his opinion matters. But yeah, I guess... when I really think about it, my mom and my friend both said they liked those same eggs. But that one comment from my uncle, it just feels like it's the only truth. I don't know why it's so much louder than the nice stuff.

It makes complete sense that you value your uncle's opinion given his skill, and it's frustrating when the positive messages from others seem to disappear into the background just as you're about to act. Let's take a quick break from the big picture and zoom in on what pops up in your head the exact moment you think about flipping that pan for those eggs. What is the first thought that rushes in to stop you?

It's like... "What if it's not perfect? What if he's right, and I'm just fooling myself thinking I can cook?" That thought just hits me, and then I picture him making that little face he made, and I just can't move. It's like my brain freezes up right there.

That freezing sensation is exhausting, and it sounds like your brain is trying to protect you from disappointment by locking the door before you even enter the kitchen. When we trace that fear back to its root, does that "perfect or fooling myself" thought feel like a reasonable prediction, or does it lean heavily toward assuming the worst outcome?

I guess it is assuming the worst. I mean, I've made good food before, plenty of times. But in that moment, it just feels like the only possibility is that I'll mess up. It's like I forget all the times things turned out fine, and I'm just waiting for the disaster.

That "freezing up" is your brain trying to create a safety net by predicting the disaster, even though it cuts you off from the joy of cooking. It's really hard to believe that you've succeeded many times when that sudden panic kicks in, so let's look at just one specific instance where you made eggs recently without that fear taking over. What happened in that situation, and who else was there to offer a different perspective?

Well, a couple weeks ago, I made eggs for my mom and my little sister. My sister was being picky, and I was nervous, but my mom was just sitting at the counter talking to me. She ate them and said they were perfect, and my sister even asked for more. For a second, I felt really good. But then later that night, I thought, "Oh, she's just saying that because she's my mom." So I don't even trust the good stuff.

That shift from feeling good to doubting your mom's praise is exactly where the distortion hides, turning a moment of success into a temporary glitch. It seems like your brain is protecting itself by convincing you that everyone's kindness is just obligation, which leaves nothing real behind. Since you found that one moment of genuine connection and approval, could we explore whether that single night of doubt truly cancels out the feeling you got right then, or if you could try to keep that good feeling alive instead of letting the uncertainty creep in?

I guess... it doesn't really cancel it out, does it? I mean, the good feeling was real when it happened. It's like I let the worry sneak in later and erase it. Maybe I could try to just... keep that moment in my head, the one where my sister asked for more, instead of letting the doubt take over. That felt good.

That is a powerful realization—you caught yourself erasing a real moment of joy with worry, and recognizing that pattern gives you the power to choose differently next time. It sounds like holding onto that specific feeling of your sister asking for more could be a useful tool to bring back when the doubt tries to sneak in. Would you be willing to try keeping that image of your sister's satisfaction fresh in your mind for the next few days, even if the "knot" in your stomach is still there?

Yeah, I think I can try that. It's a small thing, but remembering her face when she liked the eggs... that's good. I'll try to picture that whenever the uncle's voice starts getting loud. It's worth a shot, right?

Absolutely, and that is exactly the kind of small, manageable step that builds momentum. By intentionally bringing your sister's approval back into the scene, you give yourself permission to enjoy the cooking process again, regardless of what your uncle thinks. How does it feel to visualize that moment now, before we wrap up?
It feels a little lighter, actually. Like, I can almost smell the eggs again, and it's not anxiety. It's just... a nice memory. I think I can hold onto that for now. Thanks for helping me see that.

I am so glad to hear that the image brought a sense of lightness and reduced the anxiety. Remembering that your sister wanted more is a powerful reminder of your ability to connect and create joy, and I am proud of you for choosing to hold onto that feeling instead of letting doubt win. Our time together is coming to an end, but please know I am here if you need to talk about this again or adjust the plan as you go. How would you like to proceed with holding that memory in mind during your next egg-making session?

I think I'll just try to keep that image ready in my head. Maybe I'll even write it down on a sticky note and put it on the fridge, like "Sister asked for more." That way, if I start to freeze up, I can look at it and remember. I'll try making eggs for myself this weekend and see how it goes.

That is a brilliant idea—a visible reminder on the fridge will act as a gentle nudge to bring that positive memory back whenever you feel the knot forming. Writing it down makes the hope feel concrete and reachable, turning an abstract feeling into a simple visual cue you can rely on. Go ahead and make those eggs this weekend with that sticky note nearby, knowing you have permission to just enjoy the process without needing perfection. I'm rooting for you!

Hello again. How have you been feeling since our last conversation, and do you remember what specific plan we worked on regarding your nighttime worries? Based on what we agreed upon previously, what would you like to prioritize discussing today?

Hi. I've been... okay, I guess. The last time we talked, we agreed I'd try to limit my alarm-setting to just two alarms instead of five or six, to see if that helped break the cycle. I tried it a few nights, but honestly, I ended up going back to my old habit of setting multiple alarms because I got too anxious. I think I want to talk about why that fear just takes over, no matter what I plan to do.

It sounds frustrating that despite trying a different approach, your anxiety pulled you back to the familiar habit of setting many alarms. Let's explore what happens in your mind right before you reach for those extra alarms and uncover the thought patterns driving that decision. What specifically triggered the urge to set multiple alarms after you tried limiting yourself to two?

It was right as I was about to turn off the light. I just had this thought pop into my head: "What if the first alarm doesn't go off? Or what if I sleep through both of them?" And then I started picturing my boss calling me, and the look on his face when I finally show up hours late. It felt like if I didn't set those extra alarms, I was basically choosing to get fired. So I grabbed my phone and set three more.

That immediate jump from "what if" to imagining your boss's anger shows how quickly your brain turns a worry into a command to act. It makes complete sense that you reached for those extra alarms as a desperate attempt to prove to yourself that you won't miss them. Can you tell me what you believed would happen if you *didn't* set those three additional alarms?

If I didn't set them, I honestly believed I would definitely oversleep. It felt like a guarantee. Like, by not setting them, I was actively sabotaging myself. I thought, "If I only have two alarms, one could break, or I could turn them both off in my sleep, and then I'm done for." It didn't feel like a risk I could take, even for one night.

You described feeling like you had absolutely no choice but to set the extra alarms to avoid that guaranteed disaster. This is a very common safety behavior; when we feel certain that bad things *must* happen unless we fix everything perfectly, our brain convinces us that taking that small risk is dangerous. Did you notice any other signs besides setting the alarms that suggested you felt you couldn't afford even the slightest possibility of failure?

Yeah, I noticed I was checking the time on my phone over and over again. Like, I'd look at the time, do the math in my head for how many hours of sleep I'd get, and then five minutes later, I'd check again. It's like my brain wouldn't let me settle down until I was absolutely sure everything was in order. And I also kept replaying that old meeting I missed, just to remind myself how bad it was. I think I was trying to scare myself into staying alert.

It is completely understandable that your brain is trying to protect you by creating this sense of absolute control, even though the outcome is just more anxiety. That constant checking and rehearsing are your mind's way of trying to eliminate the uncertainty you feel right now. Have you ever caught yourself wondering if perhaps those extra alarms were keeping you awake, even though they were meant to solve the problem?

Yes, I have thought about that. It's strange, because I set them to help me sleep, but they actually make my heart race a little more. I'll be lying there, and my phone screen lights up every time I set a new alarm, and I just feel more on edge. But the scary part is, even knowing that, I still feel like I can't stop doing it. Like, the fear of what might happen if I don't set them is louder than the logic that says they're keeping me awake.

That conflict between your logic and your fear is exactly what makes this so exhausting. It feels like the emotion of "what if" is drowning out your knowledge that the alarms are counterproductive. To help untangle them, I wonder if you could identify one specific fact about your current life situation that contradicts the belief that you *will* get fired if you only have two alarms?

Well... I've never actually been late since that one time a few years ago. Even with just two alarms, I've always woken up. And my boss actually told me last month that he's happy with my work ethic. So logically, there's no evidence that I'm about to get fired. But when I'm lying there in the dark, it doesn't feel like those facts matter. It just feels like this time will be different, and I'll mess everything up.

You've pinpointed the exact disconnect: your brain is overriding your factual knowledge with a temporary feeling that "this time will be different." This is a very common distortion called "fortune-telling," where we predict negative outcomes as if they are already set in stone. It makes sense that these facts feel distant when the panic is so loud right now. Could you try identifying just one small piece of evidence that supports the opposite—that you are likely to wake up successfully with just two alarms?

I've been using those same two alarms on my phone for about three months now, and they've never failed. They're both set five minutes apart, so even if I slept through the first one, the second one is right there. I also keep my phone across the room, so I have to get out of bed to turn them off. So... I guess that's pretty solid evidence that I'd wake up. It's just hard to hold onto that thought when the fear kicks in.

That is excellent evidence, and it highlights exactly why your brain is fighting so hard to override it—it wants to find a reason why those rules might suddenly break. When you know you have a reliable system but still feel unsafe, it means the worry itself is acting as a distraction, making it harder for you to trust your own setup. Let's try a quick experiment tonight: what if we agreed to set just those two alarms, ignore the urge to add others for the first hour after you fall asleep, and then come back to check on your schedule tomorrow morning? Would you be open to testing that boundary for one night?

I think... I could try that. One night. It feels really scary to say yes, but I know my two alarms have always worked. I'll put my phone across the room like usual, and I'll try my best not to reach for it after I turn off the light. I can't promise I won't feel anxious, but I'll try not to give in to the urge to add more alarms.

Taking that step is brave, and acknowledging the anxiety while committing anyway is exactly the kind of resilience we want to build. Since you've already agreed to test this boundary, let's briefly clarify how we'll handle the moment you feel that urge to add a third alarm tonight. Instead of adding it, what if you simply stood up, walked away from the bedside, and took three deep breaths to reset your nervous system before returning to bed?

Okay, that sounds manageable. Standing up and taking a few breaths feels like a concrete thing I can do instead of just lying there fighting the urge. I'll try to remind myself that the alarms are already set and working. If I get up and breathe, maybe I can break that cycle before I grab my phone. I'll give it a shot tonight and see what happens.

That is a very solid plan, and breaking the physical cycle of reaching for the phone gives you a crucial window to regain control before your mind spirals further. Since we've confirmed the strategy, how are you feeling about agreeing to this challenge for tonight? Is there anything else you'd like to adjust or discuss before we wrap up?

I'm nervous, but I'm also a little hopeful. I think I've been stuck in this pattern for so long that I forgot there might be another way. I don't have anything else to add right now. I'll try the two alarms and the breathing tonight, and I'll let you know how it goes. Thanks for helping me see that my fear might be louder than the truth.

Your hopefulness is a wonderful sign of progress, and trusting that your past reliability predicts your future success is a powerful mindset to carry into tonight. I am proud of your courage in facing this challenge, and I believe the combination of the breathing exercise and the two-alarm rule will provide you with a much-needed break from the panic. Go ahead and give it a try, and I look forward to hearing how it goes in our next session.

Hello, it is wonderful to see you again. How have you been feeling since we last spoke, and is there anything specific you would like to focus on today? We could review what you practiced with your sister, explore how that went, and then revisit the freezing incident at work to see if we can find some relief from that shame.

Hi, thanks. I've been okay, I guess. I did try what we talked about with my sister, but it felt kind of forced, like I was pretending to be confident. The freezing incident still bothers me a lot, though. I keep replaying it in my head, thinking about how the patient must have seen me as just some clueless student who doesn't belong there.

Hearing that the practice felt forced is incredibly important, and it tells me that expecting perfection wasn't the goal—we just needed to show up. You’re absolutely right to notice that the freezing incident is still dominating your thoughts, and the story about being a “clueless student” sounds just as harsh as the one from before. Let’s spend some time unpacking that specific narrative again to see if we can separate the reality of what happened from the dramatic conclusion your brain keeps drawing.

I mean, when I froze, I couldn't even remember basic things I do every day. It's like my mind just went blank, and I stood there like a deer in headlights. The patient probably thought, "Who is this person? She doesn't know what she's doing." It's hard to see any other way to look at it.

It makes total sense that your mind fills that blank moment with a story about incompetence, especially when you feel so helpless during it. When you say the patient probably thought, "She doesn't know what she's doing," that sounds like a very cruel assumption, but I wonder if you have any evidence from the patient herself to confirm that thought, or if it's just your anxiety projecting its worst fears onto them?

Well, no, she didn't actually say anything mean or look angry. She just waited quietly until I snapped out of it. But I still felt like I let her down, you know? I'm supposed to be the one helping her, and there I was, frozen like I'd never done this before.

That feeling of letting someone down is incredibly heavy, and it makes sense that your mind latched onto that guilt when you realized you weren't responding normally. You are right that you are the professional there to guide her, so standing frozen definitely feels like a failure of duty. However, could we look closely at that "letting down" part: do you have any proof the patient felt abandoned or unsafe in that moment, or is that just your internal alarm system reacting to your own distress?

She didn't say anything, and she didn't complain to my supervisor or anything. But I just assume she was being polite, you know? People don't always say what they're thinking. I still feel like I wasn't good enough in that moment, and that's what keeps sticking with me.

It is completely understandable why you assume politeness hides disappointment, since people often mask their frustration to spare others' feelings. However, the fact that she remained calm and gave you a chance to recover suggests she viewed the interruption as a minor hiccup rather than a major error. If we look at what you *know* versus what you *assume*, does the evidence of her waiting quietly actually support the idea that she thought you were incompetent, or does it simply contradict the story that you are unworthy of belonging there?

I guess when you put it that way, she didn't really act like I was incompetent. She just waited. But it's hard for me to accept that, because I feel like if I were a real professional, I wouldn't have frozen at all. I keep thinking, "A real nurse wouldn't have done that," even though I know that's not fair to myself.

That comparison to a "real professional" is a very common trap, and it's unfair to hold yourself to a standard where nothing ever goes wrong. A real human being, regardless of experience, can freeze under pressure; that reaction doesn't define your worth as a nurse or a student. Since you've acknowledged that the facts don't match the story of incompetence, could we agree that perhaps the best thing to do right now is to treat this moment not as proof of failure, but as a signal that we need to prepare a simple script so you don't have to rely on your calmness alone next time?

I suppose that makes sense. It would help to have something to fall back on when my mind goes blank. Maybe if I had a simple line ready for patients, like "Give me just a second," it wouldn't feel so overwhelming. I could practice that, instead of just hoping I won't freeze again.

That is a fantastic and very practical adjustment; having a simple "pause button" gives you control instead of relying on instant calm. Before we settle on the exact phrase, I'd love your opinion on whether "Give me just a second" feels authentic to you, or if adding something like "just checking a detail quickly" would make it sound less abrupt and more reassuring to the patient?

I think "Give me just a second" feels more natural for me. Adding too much explanation might make me stumble over the words. I just need something short and simple that buys me a moment to collect myself, without feeling like I have to justify why I froze.

That makes perfect sense; keeping it simple removes the pressure to perform perfectly, which is exactly what we want in those high-stress moments. So, if we use "Give me just a second" as your go-to phrase, how confident do you feel saying it to a patient versus saying it to a friend or family member? Knowing where your comfort zone sits will help us decide how to practice this safely tonight.

Saying it to a family member feels easier, because I know they won't judge me. With a patient, I'd be worried they'd think I'm unprepared or unprofessional. But I think if I practice it enough, maybe it'll start to feel more automatic, like a reflex instead of something I have to force.

That is a brilliant insight, and recognizing the difference between a supportive friend and a perceived judge is exactly where we need to focus. Practicing with someone who understands you, like your sister, allows you to build that "reflex" muscle without the pressure of being judged. Since we've settled on the phrase and the practice partner, how does it feel to commit to saying "Give me just a second" to your sister tomorrow during our coffee chat?

I think I can do that. It feels a little silly to practice something so simple, but I know it's better than freezing up again. I'll give it a try with my sister and see how it goes. Thanks for helping me break this down into something manageable.

You are very welcome, and please remember that taking a small step like this isn't about perfection—it's about showing up for yourself. I am glad we found a phrase that feels manageable for you, and I truly appreciate your willingness to try it even if it feels a bit silly. To close, is there anything else on your mind regarding this session, or would you like to leave with the reassurance that we have a concrete plan to help you handle those moments?

No, I think I'm okay for now. Having that simple plan makes me feel a little less anxious about going to work tomorrow. I'll let you know how it goes with my sister, and hopefully that helps me feel more ready if I ever freeze again.

That is wonderful news to hear, and it is refreshing that having a simple plan actually lowered your anxiety level right now. Please remember that tomorrow is just about gathering data—if you freeze, it doesn't matter; the goal is simply to use the phrase "Give me just a second" to buy yourself time. How does it feel to carry that mindset into your upcoming shift, knowing you have a tool rather than just a worry?

It feels a lot better. I don't feel like I'm walking into a trap anymore. I still have some nervousness, but at least now I have something to do about it instead of just hoping for the best. Thank you, I think I can handle this.

That shift from hoping for the best to having a concrete tool is a powerful change, and I'm so proud of your resilience in getting there. It is completely okay to still feel some nervousness; that emotion is just a signal that you care deeply about doing your job well. I really appreciate your honesty and effort today, and I look forward to hearing how the practice with your sister went next week. Take care of yourself, and remember to be kind to yourself along the way.

Hello, I'm glad to see you again. To start our session today, I'd like to briefly check in on how you've been feeling since last time, review the plan we agreed upon for the playground visit, and then set an agenda for what we'll focus on together. How has everything been going for you in the weeks since our last meeting?

Hi. Thanks. I mean, it's been... okay, I guess. I did try the playground thing we talked about, but honestly, it was harder than I thought it would be. I still felt like every other mom was watching me, waiting for me to mess up somehow.

Thank you for sharing that honestly—it takes courage to admit that the plan felt harder than expected. Before we dive into how the playground visit went today, how do you feel about the fact that you tried it anyway despite the difficulty? What specific part of the experience felt toughest for you to navigate?

I guess... I feel a little proud that I actually went through with it, but mostly I just feel exhausted. The toughest part was when my younger daughter started crying because she wanted a turn on the swings, and I could feel these eyes on me, like everyone was judging how I handled it. I ended up just rushing us home after that.

It makes complete sense to feel exhausted after that; carrying the weight of everyone's perceived judgment and then rushing to leave was a lot to manage alone. Did you notice anything different in how your body reacted that time compared to last week when you ran straight over to the crying child? For instance, did you catch yourself taking a deep breath before moving, or did your instinct still be to flee immediately?

I didn't take a deep breath or anything like that. My heart just started pounding right away, and I felt this tightness in my chest. It was like my body was telling me to get out of there as fast as possible. I don't think I even thought about it—I just grabbed the baby and left.

That physical reaction—your heart pounding and the urge to flee—isn't a sign that you're failing; it's your nervous system recognizing a perceived threat and demanding immediate safety. It sounds like that same alarm system kicked in again, making it very hard to step back and think clearly, even though you *wanted* to try being mindful of the others. When you look back at that moment of panic, does it feel like you were trapped by that fear, or do you wonder if you could have found a tiny bit of space to breathe even for a second?

I think I was just trapped by it, honestly. I wanted to stay and handle it calmly, but it was like my mind went blank except for the thought that everyone was staring and thinking I couldn't control my kids. I don't know if there was any space to breathe in that moment—it all happened so fast.

It makes complete sense that you felt trapped; when the fear of judgment becomes so loud, our brains literally shut down the parts responsible for calm reasoning to prioritize survival. Since you recognized that moment was happening so fast that breathing felt impossible, let's pivot our focus for today. Instead of dwelling on the panic itself, could we explore what happens right after you realize people might be judging you? Often, that initial spike of fear fades, leaving behind a lingering sense of shame or relief. Which of those feelings stayed with you as you drove home?

Mostly shame, I think. I just kept replaying the whole scene in my head, thinking about how I should have handled it differently. Like, I should have just calmly talked to my daughter instead of rushing off. And the shame just kind of sat there in my stomach the whole drive home.

That heavy feeling in your stomach is the weight of perfectionism settling in after the adrenaline faded. It's understandable that you replayed the event looking for a "better version," but please remember that acting out of panic isn't the opposite of caring; it's often just a different expression of love. If we look closely at that memory, did you find yourself judging your younger daughter for wanting the swings, or was your main focus entirely on managing your own fear of what others were thinking?

I wasn't judging her at all—she's just a little kid, she wanted the swings. No, my whole focus was on the other parents. I was watching their faces, trying to see if they were looking at me, if they thought I was taking too long or being too soft with her. It was all about what they might be thinking.

That hyper-focus on their expressions is such a familiar pattern, and it shows how deeply ingrained the belief is that their gaze determines your worth as a mother. Even though you *knew* they were probably just tired or distracted, your mind filtered everything through the lens of judgment until there was nothing else left to see. Since we've explored the intensity of that moment and the aftermath, how would you rate your confidence in saying that you gave your daughter what she needed in that split second?

I... I don't know. If I'm being honest, I'd say pretty low. Like a 3 out of 10. I mean, I took her off the swing and left, so I guess I stopped her crying, but I didn't really help her understand why we had to go or comfort her properly. I was just thinking about getting away.

That self-assessment comes from a place of protecting her future well-being, but it overlooks the fact that you successfully removed her from an unsafe situation when her needs weren't being met. While you didn't have the time to explain or comfort fully, your primary goal was to ensure her safety, which you achieved by taking action before she got hurt. If we shift the lens from "what I missed" to "what I secured," does that change the score you give yourself, even if just by a point?

I guess... maybe a 4 or 5. You're right that I did keep her safe. But it still feels like I could have done more, you know? Like I could have been both safe and present, instead of just running away. I want to be the kind of mom who can handle those moments without falling apart inside.

That desire to be a steady presence while remaining grounded is beautiful, and it tells me you truly value your daughters' emotional connection just as much as their safety. The fact that you recognize the difference between acting out of panic and responding with calm doesn't mean you failed; it means you are learning to read your own signals better. Right now, the exhaustion and shame are loud, but we can work on building a toolkit that helps you bridge that gap between feeling overwhelmed and stepping into that ideal "safe and present" mode. Would you like to try identifying one small signal your body gives you before you feel the urge to flee, so we can practice catching it early?

Okay... yeah, I think that could help. Usually, before I feel that panicked urge to leave, I notice my shoulders get really tight and I start holding my breath without realizing it. Maybe if I could notice that sooner, I could do something before the panic takes over completely.

Noticing those early physical signals is a game-changer because it gives you a window of opportunity to intervene before the full-blown panic kicks in. When you spot your shoulders tightening or your breath stopping, that tiny pause is exactly where you can choose to shift your mindset instead of reacting automatically. Could we try a quick exercise right here where you identify that specific sensation, and then simply place a hand on your heart and remind yourself, "My body is scared, but I am still in charge"?

Alright, I can try that. So, right now, I can feel my shoulders are a bit tense just from talking about it. Okay, I'm putting my hand on my heart. "My body is scared, but I am still in charge." That feels... a little strange, but also kind of calming, actually. Like a tiny bit of the pressure just lifted.

That is a profound breakthrough, especially since you described the feeling as "strange" turning into "calming." It proves that reconnecting with your physical sensation of fear doesn't mean you have to surrender to it; it just means you are claiming space to be human while remaining in control. Since you found that grounding phrase works, how would you like to incorporate that into your evening routine tonight so you don't have to wait until the playground to use it?

Maybe I could try saying it to myself before I go to sleep tonight, when I'm lying in bed replaying the day. That's usually when the shame thoughts start creeping in anyway. If I can catch myself then and just breathe and say that phrase, it might help me actually rest instead of spiraling.

That is a brilliant idea because bedtime is often when our minds replay the day's events, and inserting that phrase right then breaks the cycle of self-criticism before you even fall asleep. Since you mentioned the shame tends to creep in while lying there, could we try this for just five minutes tonight? I want to hear if that small shift in perspective helps you drift off easier tomorrow morning.

Yeah, I can do that. I'll give it a real try tonight. Just five minutes, hand on my heart, and remind myself that I'm still in charge even when my body gets scared. I'll let you know how it goes next time.

That is a solid plan, and I'm confident it will give your mind a gentle break from the shame loop. Before we wrap up, I'd love to hear your feedback on our session so far: Was exploring those early physical signs useful for you, or was the grounding phrase the part that resonated most? Also, is there anything about how we worked through the playground incident that you feel we could approach differently next time?

I think the grounding phrase was what really clicked for me. Just having something simple to say to myself feels more doable than trying to analyze everything in the moment. As for next time, maybe we could talk a bit more about what to actually say or do when I feel that panic rising in public, like a backup plan if the phrase isn't enough.

You are absolutely right to seek that backup plan; relying on just one tool can feel risky when the panic hits so hard. Having a simple, actionable script ready to go—if the grounding phrase isn't enough—would give you extra security in those high-pressure moments. Since we're wrapping up today, could you share one thing you felt most empowered about from our conversation, or perhaps a moment where you felt a spark of hope?

Honestly, I think the most empowering moment was when I realized that noticing my shoulders getting tight is actually helpful, not just a sign of weakness. It felt like I finally had a way in, like a door I could open instead of just being trapped. That gives me a little bit of hope that maybe I can learn to handle these situations better over time.

That realization about the "door" vs. being "trapped" is incredibly powerful and shows real growth in your perspective. It validates that recognizing the warning sign isn't a failure, but the first step toward reclaiming your agency. Thank you for such an open and honest session today; I'm proud of the effort you're putting in to build these tools for yourself. How would you like to close out our time together, or is there anything else you'd like to reflect on before we finish?

I think I'm good for today. Thank you for listening and for helping me see that tiny step forward. I'll practice the phrase tonight and pay attention to my shoulders this week. I'll see you next time.

You are so welcome, and thank you for trusting me with these vulnerable moments and sharing your journey so openly. Remember that those tiny steps—like noticing your shoulders tighten or saying the grounding phrase—are the foundation for building that stronger, steadier version of yourself we both know is possible. Take a deep breath tonight, hold your hand on your heart, and know that you are doing enough exactly as you are. I look forward to hearing how your five-minute practice went next time.

Hello again, it’s wonderful to connect with you. First, could you remind me briefly what we agreed to do last time, and then tell me how your energy and mood have been over the past couple of days? Finally, what would you like to spend our time together on today?

Hi. Well, last time we talked about noticing the pattern where I automatically assume I'm not smart enough for a PhD, and I was supposed to write down some of those thoughts when they came up. I did that a little, but honestly, it just made me feel worse. My energy's been pretty low, and I've been avoiding my assignments even more than usual. I think I want to focus on why this belief feels so unshakable, because just writing it down didn't help.

It makes complete sense that writing down the thoughts made things feel heavier, especially when your brain immediately jumps to negative interpretations. Thank you for bringing that up; it helps clarify that we need to tackle the *why* behind the belief rather than just documenting it. Since you’re looking for the root cause of why this thought feels so unshakeable, could you share a recent moment where that thought popped up, and describe exactly what was happening right before it appeared?

Yeah, there was a moment this morning. I was sitting in the library, trying to start a reading for one of my seminars, and I overheard two classmates talking about their PhD applications. They were so confident, discussing supervisors and research proposals. Right after that, my mind just went blank, and I thought, "I'm stuck in a Master's because I couldn't handle the real thing." I closed my book and left the library.

That scenario perfectly illustrates how sensitive your safety system is to perceived threats, turning a simple social interaction into a full-blown alarm about your competence. It sounds incredibly draining to feel your mind go blank in that moment and have to physically leave the room just to escape the panic. Now that we’ve pinpointed that specific trigger, could you walk me through the exact thought that flashed through your head right after hearing them talk, and how quickly it spiraled into that conclusion about your worth?

It was almost instant, like a reflex. The thought was, "They're doing what I should be doing, but I can't." Then my mind just jumped to, "I'm not smart enough, I never was, and this Master's is just proof that I'm avoiding the truth." It felt like all the evidence I needed was right there in that conversation. I didn't even question it, I just believed it completely and shut down.

It sounds like that moment felt terrifyingly definitive, as if your entire identity was suddenly on display for judgment. That leap from "they are ahead" to "I am fundamentally incapable" is a very automatic pattern, often driven by deep-seated beliefs about perfectionism or the fear of being exposed. Since you mentioned it felt like "all the evidence" was right there, could you recall what specific facts or details from that conversation seemed to fuel that particular thought, versus what might have been missing or overlooked?

I guess the specific fact was just that they were talking about PhDs and I wasn't. That's it. They didn't say anything about me or my abilities. But in my head, their conversation became a direct comparison, like a measuring stick I was failing against. I didn't consider that they might have had different paths, or that they were nervous too. I just saw their confidence and assumed it meant I had none.

You're describing a classic "mind reader" trap where you interpret neutral events as personal attacks without checking the facts first. It makes sense why that felt so convincing in the moment, but let's test that assumption: if you called one of them up later and asked them casually, "Did you guys feel intimidated or nervous while talking about that, or was it mostly excitement?", how would you expect their answer to change your story about your own capability?

I honestly don't think they would admit to being nervous. They always seem so put together. But I guess if they did say they were nervous, it would mean I'm not the only one who feels that way. It would mean my reaction isn't proof of my failure, it's just a normal human reaction. But I still can't shake the feeling that they're genuinely capable, and I'm just pretending.

That distinction between "normal human reaction" and "proving I'm faking it" is crucial, and it highlights exactly where the distortion lies. Even if they aren't admitting vulnerability, the fact remains that their visible success doesn't objectively measure your hidden potential or define your worth. Let's try a different angle: if we treated your Master's degree not as a result of your inability to handle big challenges, but as a successful completion of a rigorous curriculum despite your fears, how would that shift your interpretation of their achievements vs. your own path?

I... I've never thought of it that way. I've always seen my Master's as a consolation prize, not an accomplishment. But I did get here through a competitive application process, and I've finished a lot of difficult work so far. If I saw it as a step I chose, not one I settled for, then their PhD talk wouldn't feel like a judgment. It would just be them on their path, and me on mine. That feels... almost unfamiliar, but a little lighter.

That shift in perspective—from seeing your degree as a fallback to recognizing it as a deliberate choice—is a powerful breakthrough that directly counters the "I'm settling" narrative. It effectively removes the external threat of their conversations because you've reclaimed ownership of your own timeline. Before we lock this in, does holding onto the idea that your Master's was a strategic step rather than a consolation prize feel safe, or does a new doubt still whisper that you're "just waiting for permission"?

It does feel a little safer, but there's still that whisper underneath. It says, "You're just saying that to feel better, but deep down you know the truth." It's like a part of me is convinced that if I let go of this belief, I'll just be fooling myself. But I guess the harder question is: what if I'm fooling myself by holding onto it? That's the part I can't quite make myself believe yet.

That's a profound realization—you've turned the lens inward to examine the validity of the new belief itself, which is exactly what critical analysis requires. Instead of getting stuck in the "what if," let's use the evidence we already gathered: you were admitted through competition, you maintained strong grades, and you survived the initial period of impostor feelings. If we treat those outcomes as data points rather than coincidences, what does that suggest about the reliability of the "fooling myself" warning?

If I look at it like data... it's pretty solid evidence. I can't argue with the fact that I got in, I'm passing, and I'm still here. The "fooling myself" warning is just a feeling, not a fact. I guess I've been treating that feeling as more trustworthy than my actual results. That's... uncomfortable to admit, but it's true. Maybe the warning is just old habit, not truth.

You've done incredible work uncovering that the warning is just an old habit masquerading as fact, rather than objective reality. That distinction alone shifts the power dynamic from "I am failing" to "my brain is reacting automatically." Now that we've established the data supports your capability, let's translate this insight into a tiny, low-risk behavior to prove it works in real-time. Could you commit to starting your seminar reading for just 10 minutes tomorrow, with the explicit instruction to stop if the anxiety spikes, and simply observe what happens instead of judging yourself?

I think I can try that. Ten minutes feels manageable, not overwhelming. I'll set a timer and just read, and if the anxiety comes up, I'll stop and just notice it without adding more thoughts on top. It sounds simple, but I know it won't be easy. I'll do it tomorrow morning and see what happens.

That is a fantastic commitment; setting a timer creates a clear boundary that protects you from burning out, and observing the anxiety without judgment turns it into useful data rather than a threat. Hello, I'm really glad you're here for our first session together. Let's start by checking in on your mood, reviewing what's been happening since we last spoke, and then focusing on the guitar issue you mentioned. Does that sound like a good plan for us today?
Yeah, that sounds fine. I guess I'm feeling a little nervous, but also relieved to finally talk about this with someone who might understand. The guitar thing has really been weighing on me lately.

That mix of nervousness and relief is completely normal; it often means you're ready to face this difficult pattern with fresh eyes. Since you mentioned the guitar has been weighing heavily, let's dive straight into exploring exactly when that pressure builds up and what specific thoughts are driving the avoidance. Have you noticed if that tight feeling in your stomach happens immediately upon picking up the instrument, or does it grow stronger the longer you hesitate to start?

It's usually there before I even touch the guitar. I'll be sitting in my room, looking at the case, and this voice in my head tells me, "What's the point? You're just going to sound the same as yesterday." And it gets worse the longer I sit there, until I just pick up a book instead or find something else to do.

That voice telling you there's "no point" because you'll sound the same must feel incredibly draining, especially when the delay itself becomes the punishment. It sounds like that belief in stagnation is creating a safety mechanism where avoiding the guitar feels safer than facing the risk of hearing bad notes. Before we figure out how to shift that mindset, I want to make sure I understand correctly: when you switch to reading a book, does that temporary relief make the anxiety go away entirely, or does the worry just shift into a different form?

The relief only lasts while I'm reading, honestly. As soon as I put the book down or go to bed, that same heaviness comes back about my guitar. It's like I traded one kind of frustration for a quieter, nagging guilt that I didn't even try.

That shift from active frustration to quiet guilt about avoidance is a crucial clue; it suggests your mind knows it needs to act, but the fear of failure is paralyzing you. It makes total sense that the relief disappears once you stop distracting yourself, leaving the original pain intact. Given that dynamic, I'm wondering if spending some time together today to unpack that "what's the point" thought would help reduce the pressure you feel before you even try to play?

Sure, I think that could help. That "what's the point" thought is the loudest one in my head, and I'd like to understand why it's so convincing. I used to love playing, and now it just feels like a chore I'm failing at.

That shift from loving music to viewing it as a chore you're failing at is heartbreaking, and it makes sense why the "what's the point" thought feels so convincing when your past joy is overshadowed by current disappointment. It sounds like you're comparing your current lack of progress to the high you once felt, which makes the gap feel insurmountable. Let's test that comparison together: if you looked back at the recordings from six months ago, do those performances still show moments where you were clearly learning and getting better, or does your memory only recall the failures?

I haven't listened to any of my old recordings in months. Honestly, I've been too afraid to. But... I think I remember some good moments. There were riffs I finally nailed after weeks of practice, and a few times my dad even said I sounded great. I guess I've been forgetting those parts.

It takes real courage to admit that you've been avoiding your own history of success because it hurts to face how much you've lost ground since. That memory of your dad praising you is powerful evidence that contradicts the story you're telling yourself, yet it's easy to push it aside when you're tired. Let's try a gentle experiment with that memory: if you imagined listening to that recording of him saying you sounded great today, how would that feeling change the weight of that "what's the point" thought in your head?

It's strange, but just thinking about his voice saying that... it softens things a little. The "what's the point" thought doesn't seem as loud or final. Maybe there's some proof buried in those old recordings that I'm not as stuck as I think I am.

That softening effect is exactly what we're looking for—it proves that your brain holds onto positive memories even when you're trying to bury them under the weight of failure. It suggests the "what's the point" belief isn't based on facts anymore, but rather on a selective filter that ignores your past wins. Since you mentioned you haven't listened in months, does imagining finding a spare tape or downloading an old file feel like a manageable first step to uncovering that hidden proof, or does the fear of hearing the "bad" parts still scare you?

It's a little scary, honestly. I'm worried I'll listen and only hear the mistakes, not the good parts. But... I think I could try it. Maybe tonight, just one short recording from a few months ago. I won't force myself to analyze it, just listen and see what comes up.

That sounds like a wise and brave approach; setting a limit to just one short recording gives you space to observe without being overwhelmed by a full album. It's okay to expect that you might still hear some mistakes—the important part is seeing them alongside the moments where you actually succeeded. Tonight, will you give yourself permission to just listen for those "good parts" first, and ignore everything else if you get distracted?

I think I can do that. Just focus on the good parts first, and let the mistakes fade into the background for now. Thank you, that feels like a much smaller step than I was imagining. I'll try it tonight and see how it feels.

That is a fantastic plan; narrowing it down to one short recording and focusing only on the successes makes the task feel completely doable. I'm really glad we found a middle ground that respects your caution while still giving you the evidence you need. Before we wrap up, I want to make sure we agree on this path: does trying to find just one moment of proof tonight sound like a solid goal for us to pursue this evening?
Yes, that sounds like a solid goal. One moment of proof, nothing more. I'll let you know how it goes next time we meet. Thanks for helping me see that this doesn't have to be so overwhelming.

That is wonderful clarity; agreeing to just seek one moment of proof is exactly the kind of small, manageable step that breaks the cycle of overwhelm. I'm truly grateful for your openness today and for trusting me with this process. Please reach out whenever you're ready to share what came up with that recording, or if you need support navigating tonight's listening session. We'll catch up then!

Hello, it is great to see you again. Before we dive into today's topic, how has your week been going, and would you like to first review the plan we worked on last time about managing that upcoming meeting? Then, on a scale of one to ten, how is your mood and energy level feeling right now compared to yesterday?

Oh, hello. The week has been alright, I suppose. I did think about that plan we made for the meeting, but I ended up not even going to that gathering after all. I just felt like it would be too uncomfortable. As for my mood, maybe a 5 or 6? Energy is about the same, maybe a little lower than yesterday.

I hear how much that decision weighed on you, and I want to validate that protecting your peace—even by skipping the event—is often a logical survival strategy when anxiety feels overwhelming. It sounds like the fear of discomfort became louder than the desire to connect, which is a very human reaction. Now that we've acknowledged where things stand, does discussing that cancellation feel like a relief or does it bring up more shame about "failing" to follow through?

It's a bit of both, honestly. Part of me is relieved I didn't have to sit there worrying about every little thing I said or didn't say. But then another part of me feels like I let you down, and let myself down, by not even trying. I just can't shake that feeling that people would have looked at me and thought, "Why is he so quiet? Is he upset or rude?"

That conflict between relief and shame is exactly why we need to unpack this feeling together; it shows you care deeply about your relationships, even when your anxiety tells you otherwise. Let's look closely at that specific story you told yourself about them judging your silence—could you walk me through the exact evidence you have that they actually thought those negative things versus the evidence suggesting they might have just been curious about your day?

Well, I don't have any direct evidence, I suppose. No one came up to me and said they disliked me for being quiet. But I've seen people's faces before—when I'm in a group and I don't speak, sometimes people glance at me and then look away quickly. It feels like they're disappointed or uncomfortable with me being there. I guess I just assume that's what it means.

That interpretation—that a glance away equals disappointment—is a common pattern where our brains jump straight to the conclusion of "rejection" based on ambiguous cues, much like how we might assume a red light means a crash is coming. I wonder if there's another explanation for those glances, such as them being distracted by something else entirely, or perhaps feeling polite distance rather than judgment? Could you try to generate one alternative thought for those moments where someone looked away?

I suppose... maybe they were just looking around the room, or maybe they were thinking about what they were going to say next. They might not have even noticed I was quiet at all. It's just that the first thought that comes to me is always the worst one, you know? I've been that way for so long that it feels like the truth.

That feeling of the first thought being the "truth" is exhausting, and it makes total sense why your brain clings to it so tightly—it offers a clear reason for your distress, even if that reason isn't accurate. We can try a small experiment to challenge that certainty: imagine if you were watching someone who *was* truly bored or rude; what specific behavior would they show that differs from just looking away? Could you spot any difference between someone who is genuinely dismissive and someone who is simply neutral or preoccupied?

Well, I guess if someone was truly bored or rude, they might roll their eyes or sigh loudly, or maybe start a conversation with someone else right in front of me without including me. Or they'd make a point of turning their back to me. Looking away just once—that's not really the same thing, is it? I never really thought about it that way before.

That distinction you just made—rolling eyes or turning your back versus a fleeting glance—is exactly the kind of evidence our minds need to soften the absolute certainty of that rejection narrative. It sounds like you've started building a bridge between what you *feel* and what actually *happens*, which is a powerful first step. Since we've cleared up that specific image, would you be willing to try the original plan we discussed, perhaps with a slightly adjusted expectation, or does the fact that you skipped the event mean you need to revisit the whole situation differently?

I think I'd be willing to try again, maybe with a smaller step. Instead of going to a big social gathering, maybe I could try just going to the store or a coffee shop—somewhere where I don't have to talk to anyone, but I can just be around people and notice that nothing bad happens. That seems a little less scary.

That is a brilliant adjustment; shifting from a high-pressure social event to a low-demand environment like a coffee shop gives you space to test the fear without the obligation to perform. It allows you to practice being around people while knowing you have an exit strategy if the anxiety spikes. How does that modified plan sound to you, and do you feel confident enough to try it this weekend?

It sounds manageable, I think. I can picture myself sitting there with a cup of coffee, just watching people come and go. I won't have to say a word to anyone, and if I start to feel that knot in my stomach, I can just get up and leave. I'd say I'm at about a 6 out of 10 on confidence—not great, but better than a 2 or 3, which is where I usually am. I'll give it a try this Saturday morning.

That is fantastic progress, moving from a 2 to a 6 shows real resilience and willingness to face the discomfort. Setting a specific date like Saturday morning helps ground the plan, making it feel actionable rather than abstract. Before we wrap up, could you tell me if having that "exit strategy" of leaving whenever you feel the knot in your stomach increases your confidence, or does it feel safer without the option to bail?

Having the exit strategy makes it feel a lot safer, actually. Just knowing I can leave whenever I want takes some of the pressure off. It's like having a back door open in case the room gets too hot—I can step outside and breathe. Without that option, I think I'd probably talk myself out of going altogether.

That metaphor of a "back door" perfectly illustrates how safety signals can lower your fight-or-flight response enough to allow you to step outside. Knowing you have control creates a psychological buffer that makes exposure possible without guaranteeing success. Since we've reviewed the plan, checked your mood, and refined the strategy, is there anything else about this weekend or the sessions we've done that you'd like to clarify before we finish?
No, I think I'm good for now. I'll try the coffee shop on Saturday, and when I come back next week, I'll let you know how it went. Thank you for helping me see things a little differently today.

Thank you for sharing that; I'm really glad we could find a middle ground that feels safe and achievable for you. Your willingness to take this step, even with the uncertainty, speaks volumes about your strength and commitment to growing. Please remember that whether the coffee shop visit feels perfect or messy, your worth isn't defined by that outing alone. I look forward to hearing about Saturday, and until then, take care of yourself.

Hello, thank you for coming in today. To start, I'd love to hear what stood out for you this past week—anything particular that made you smile or felt particularly heavy? Based on what we discussed last time regarding the self-criticism spiral, does exploring that specific pattern still feel like the best place to focus our energy right now?

Hey, thanks for having me. Honestly, this week has been a rollercoaster. I had a slip-up with my diet—ate some carbs I shouldn't have—and that heavy feeling just crashed down on me. I think yeah, focusing on that self-criticism pattern makes sense. It's like no matter how hard I try, I keep ending up calling myself a coward for messing up.

It makes sense that a slip-up triggered that familiar crash, but I want to validate that your immediate reaction isn't the truth of the situation, even if it feels unavoidable in the moment. Since you're feeling that heavy weight again, does that specific moment of eating the carbs feel more like a temporary lapse in judgment or something that defines your entire worth as a model?

I guess when I actually say it out loud, it sounds like a temporary thing—like, just one meal, right? But in the moment, it feels like it wipes out all the progress I made. I tell myself that if I can't stick to this diet, I'm not serious enough to make it in this industry. And then that thought just sticks.

That connection between one meal and the fear of failing your career is incredibly painful, and it explains exactly why the "coward" label feels so crushing to you. It sounds like your brain is using that single slip-up as proof that you aren't disciplined enough, rather than seeing it as just a momentary loss of control. If we looked at that thought—"If I eat carbs once, I'm not serious enough"—could you walk me through what specific evidence you currently have that supports the idea that one meal disqualifies you from being a serious model?

Well... I mean, all the top guys in this industry are super strict with their diets. I see their Instagram posts, their meal prep photos, and they never seem to slip up. So when I do, it feels like I'm just not cut out for that level of discipline. But I guess there's also the fact that I've been training hard and getting gigs—so maybe that counts for something too? It's hard to see that when I'm beating myself up.

That comparison to others is very common, but it's important to notice that those images show *idealized* versions of people, not necessarily their raw, messy reality behind closed doors. While your hard work and successful gigs are undeniable evidence of your capability, they often get buried under the weight of that single slip-up when your brain is in survival mode. If we treated that thought as a hypothesis rather than a fact, could you imagine a scenario where even the most disciplined professionals make mistakes but still maintain their careers? How might viewing it that way change the intensity of your shame right now?

Honestly, when you put it like that, I can picture some of the guys I've worked with making mistakes too. I remember one model admitting he binged on pizza after a shoot once, and he's still booking jobs. So yeah, I guess it's possible to mess up and not have your whole career collapse. That does take some of the edge off the shame—like maybe I'm not the only one who struggles. But then that little voice in my head still whispers "they probably didn't call themselves cowards over it."

That is a powerful realization to have, and it's smart to catch that lingering doubt—the "comparison trap" where you assume others are kinder to themselves than you are. That whisper is actually a distortion known as the fortune-teller fallacy, because you cannot read minds to know exactly how others reacted internally. When you realize the external outcome (booking jobs) remains the same regardless of the slip-up, does that suggest your actual value as a professional is tied to results rather than a perfect record? How does holding onto that distinction shift the weight of that specific shame feeling?

I never thought about it like that—that I'm basically guessing what other people feel inside. Yeah, I have no clue if that guy felt like a failure after his pizza binge or not. But he's still working, so maybe the important thing is what you do next, not the slip itself. When I think about it that way, the shame doesn't feel as heavy. It's still there, but more like a reminder than a sentence, you know?

That shift from seeing the mistake as a "sentence" to just a "reminder" is a huge breakthrough, and it speaks to your resilience and ability to adapt your thinking. Recognizing that the outcome matters more than the error shows real maturity and strategic thinking about your career. Now that we've examined the evidence and tested the accuracy of that core belief, what specific steps could you take tomorrow morning to interrupt that automatic spiral before it takes root again?

I think I could try writing down one thing I did right that day, even if it's small—like getting up early for a workout or drinking enough water. Just something concrete to look at before the negative thoughts take over. And maybe if I feel the urge to call myself a coward, I could pause and ask if I'd say that to a friend who slipped up. That might slow things down enough to not go straight into the spiral.

Those are two excellent strategies, and combining a concrete record of success with a compassionate self-dialogue gives you both facts and feelings to lean on. This approach moves you from purely intellectualizing the problem to actively changing your emotional response in real-time. Before we finalize the plan, I'd like to confirm: does the idea of checking in with yourself as if you were speaking to a supportive friend feel like something you can realistically use when you're stressed?

Yeah, I think I can actually do that. It's weird because I'm used to being harsh on myself—it feels almost natural—but I can picture what I'd say to a buddy who messed up. I'd tell them it's no big deal and to get back on track tomorrow. So applying that to myself... it might take practice, but it doesn't feel impossible. I'm willing to give it a shot.

That is wonderful news; realizing that treating yourself with the same grace you'd offer a friend is entirely within your reach shows real strength and self-awareness. Since you mentioned it might take practice, how would you feel committing to trying this new "supportive friend" dialogue just three times this week, perhaps whenever you catch yourself slipping into self-criticism? Does that frequency feel manageable for you right now?

Three times sounds doable. I don't want to set myself up for failure by promising to do it perfectly every time, so yeah, aiming for three moments of catching myself feels realistic. I can even put a note on my bathroom mirror to remind me to switch my inner voice to "buddy mode" when I see it. Thanks for helping me get to this point—it actually feels like I have a tool to work with now.

That is a fantastic commitment, and adding the visual cue on your mirror is a brilliant way to anchor the new habit into your daily routine. I'm so proud of your willingness to experiment with this gentle approach rather than pushing for perfection. To wrap up, does the plan of identifying three moments this week to speak to yourself as a supportive friend feel like something you're ready to try as soon as you leave here?

Hello again, it’s great to see you. Since we finished discussing your sketchbook plan last week, could you remind me briefly of what we decided to try? Today, I’d like to spend some time reviewing how that went and then tackle whatever new worry came up for you.

Uh, yeah. We said I’d try to just draw one page a day without worrying if it was "good enough" or showed enough knowledge. I was supposed to just finish the page and then stop thinking about it. I did it for a few days... but then I messed up.

Thank you for sharing that honesty about the setback; it takes courage to admit when a plan didn't quite stick as hoped. Could you tell me a bit about what happened when you tried to draw that page and how your thoughts shifted during those moments?

Well, I sat down with my sketchbook, and I was doing okay for the first ten minutes. But then I started thinking about a really complex fantasy series I haven't read yet, and I just froze.
