That freezing point you hit when mentioning the fantasy book is exactly what that old belief tries to trap you in—the idea that your artistic value depends entirely on consuming external knowledge. It sounds like the moment you imagined missing those "big ideas," the helpful reminder about your comics' intrinsic worth got completely overshadowed by a fear of being inadequate. Did you notice if that specific comparison to the fantasy book felt different from your usual worries about philosophy or literature?

It did feel a bit different, actually. With philosophy books, I just feel dumb, like I can't even understand the language they're using. With this fantasy series, it felt more like... jealousy? Like, here's this author who created this whole world from scratch, and I'm just sitting here with my pencil feeling like a fraud. I couldn't even finish my own page because I was too busy comparing my work to theirs.

That shift from feeling "stupid" to feeling like a "fraud" due to jealousy is a crucial distinction that changes how we can help you. It sounds like your mind isn't just comparing facts anymore; it's interpreting another creator's success as a direct reflection of your own lack of talent or imagination. When you felt that jealous sting while staring at the blank page, did you notice if you felt less angry at yourself and more like you were competing against someone else?

Yeah, that's exactly it. I wasn't just mad at myself for not knowing enough—I felt like I was in a race I was already losing. Like this author had already won, and I hadn't even started the race yet. It made me feel small, like my little comic ideas don't matter compared to what they've built. I didn't want to compete, but I couldn't stop comparing.

That feeling of running a race where someone else has already crossed the finish line is incredibly draining and makes your own creation feel insignificant by comparison. It sounds like your brain is treating their completed world as a benchmark that automatically disqualifies your ongoing work, turning a simple hobby into a high-stakes competition you aren't equipped to win. Given how much energy that comparison drains you, what would happen if we agreed that your current comic is a unique project on its own timeline, separate from anyone else's achievements?

I don't know... that sounds nice in theory, but it's hard to actually believe. Like, if I say "my comic is on its own timeline," my brain just immediately goes, "Yeah, a timeline that leads nowhere because you're not as good as them." I guess I could try telling myself that when I sit down to draw next time, but I'm scared it'll just feel like a lie I'm telling myself to feel better.

It makes perfect sense that your brain would reject that idea as a "lie"; after all, we've learned that trying to force a new belief while ignoring the old one usually just creates resistance and frustration. Instead of fighting the doubt, what if we treated that warning voice as data rather than truth, asking yourself, "Even if my comic's quality is uncertain right now, does the act of drawing still hold value, or does it only matter if I beat that fantasy author?" Does that shift from proving worthiness to simply validating the act of creating feel safer to try?

I... I guess I never thought about it that way. I mean, when I'm just doodling for myself, not trying to be good or impressive, I actually enjoy it. Like, my hand just moves and I don't overthink it. So maybe the act of drawing does have value, even if the final result isn't some masterpiece. That feels less scary than trying to prove I'm the best. I could try focusing on that instead.

That realization—that the joy of doodling exists independently of any "masterpiece"—is a huge breakthrough because it separates your enjoyment from the impossible standards you set for yourself. It sounds like shifting your focus from "beating the other person" back to "enjoying the movement of my hands" removes the threat of failure entirely. Would you be willing to try starting your next drawing session by committing to just twenty-five minutes of pure playtime, where the only rule is to draw without judging the outcome?

Yeah, I think I can try that. Twenty-five minutes feels doable, not like a huge scary commitment. I'll just let my hand do whatever it wants and not look at any books or references beforehand. Maybe I'll even draw something completely stupid, like a cat wearing a hat or something. Just to remind myself that drawing can be fun.

That sounds like a brilliant and low-pressure experiment; choosing to draw something silly like a cat with a hat is a perfect way to break the cycle of seriousness and self-criticism. Since you mentioned you wanted to avoid looking at books or references beforehand, let's add a simple rule: treat those twenty-five minutes as a "no-knowledge zone" where the only goal is to get ink on paper without checking how good it looks. Does having that specific boundary around the activity feel manageable, or would you prefer to leave the rules slightly looser initially?

No, I think having that boundary is actually helpful. "No-knowledge zone" sounds kind of freeing, like I'm giving myself permission to just exist and create without needing to prove anything. I'll set a timer on my phone and put my sketchbook somewhere I won't see any books before I start. If I can do that for a few days, maybe I'll start to believe that the act itself matters more than the competition.

Setting a physical barrier like putting away the sketchbook or closing a window to block views of reference materials is a clever, practical tactic to prevent the old habits from interrupting your flow. It sounds like you have a clear picture of how to protect those twenty-five minutes of pure creation this week. Before we finalize this, could you share one thing you think might still trip you up when you try to relax into that "no-knowledge" mode?

Probably the urge to check my phone for inspiration or look up something I think I "should" know. Like halfway through, my brain will whisper, "But if you just saw how this artist drew hands, you'd do better." And then I'll want to stop and look it up. That's the hardest part—ignoring that voice that says I need more information before I'm allowed to create.

That voice telling you to pause and research is essentially your brain trying to protect you from feeling incompetent again, even though it ends up stopping the joy of creation. It sounds like the real challenge isn't the timer, but learning to say "not now" to that urgent whisper without guilt. If you felt that urge rise during those twenty-five minutes, what's one tiny thing you could do to ground yourself back into the drawing instead of reaching for your phone?

I could... I could just take a deep breath and look at what I've already drawn. Even if it's just a stupid squiggly line, it's still something I made. Then I could add another line next to it, just to keep my hand moving. If I can focus on the physical feeling of the pencil on paper, that might be enough to drown out the voice asking me to stop and check my phone.

Using the physical sensation of your hand on the paper to anchor yourself is a fantastic grounding technique that brings you back to the present moment before the anxiety takes over. It sounds like shifting your attention from the "what should I draw?" question to the "how does my pencil feel?" answer gives your brain a safe place to rest. Since you have a clear plan for handling that urge, how confident do you feel about trying this "twenty-minute no-knowledge zone" tomorrow evening?

I'd say I'm at about a 6 out of 10 right now. Not super confident, but not hopeless either. I think if I can just start, even if it's messy and stupid, I'll feel better once the timer goes off. I'll try it tomorrow after dinner, when I'm usually just scrolling on my phone anyway. Might as well replace that with some actual drawing time.

A six out of ten shows real growth compared to where you were last week, and using your existing screen time to swap for drawing is a brilliant strategic move. Starting tomorrow after dinner with just twenty-five minutes of messy, unjudged drawing sounds like a very achievable step forward. Before we close today, I want to hear from you: does this plan feel clear enough to you, or is there anything else about the "no-knowledge zone" that still feels confusing or risky?

No, I think I've got it clear in my head. The only rule is: draw for twenty-five minutes without checking anything or judging myself. I can even re-draw the same dumb cat over and over if I want. I'm just gonna focus on the feeling of the pencil moving and let my brain chill out for a bit. Thanks... this actually feels like something I can do.

That clarity and willingness to embrace the messiness is exactly what will make this practice stick for you. It sounds like you've successfully translated our conversation into a concrete plan that respects both your creativity and your boundaries. I'm really glad we could find a path forward that feels safe for you. How did it feel to wrap up the session with such a specific, manageable goal?

Hello, it is great to see you again. Before we dive into today's agenda, do you recall any actions we committed to last time, or should we start fresh with what brought you here today?

Oh, hi. I remember we talked about trying to notice when I have those really harsh thoughts about myself, especially when I'm sewing. I was supposed to keep a little journal of those moments, but honestly, I forgot to do it most days. I guess I just got busy with work.

It’s completely understandable to get caught up in daily life and forget a small habit like journaling, especially when things feel overwhelming. How does it land for you that you noticed the gap, even if you didn’t fill it in yet? Now that we’ve acknowledged the missed opportunity, what’s the most important thing you’d like to tackle regarding your sewing project today?

I guess it's a bit disappointing that I didn't follow through, but I'm not surprised. I tend to do that. As for the sewing project... well, I actually tried to pick it up again last night. I made another tiny mistake—just a crooked seam—and I just stopped. I sat there staring at it and felt like the whole thing was pointless. I don't know if I even want to finish it now.

It sounds incredibly frustrating that you gave it one more shot only to hit that wall of discouragement again. That feeling of the whole project becoming pointless is heavy, and it makes total sense why sitting there staring at the seam felt so paralyzing. Before we figure out how to move past that, I want to check in: does talking about this evening's struggle feel helpful, or would you prefer to skip ahead to brainstorming a different way to handle those moments when the frustration hits?

No, talking about it is fine. I mean, that's why I'm here, right? It's just... when I'm in that moment, it feels like the mistake is all I can see. Like the whole project is ruined because of one crooked seam. And I know that's probably not rational, but it's how it feels. It's hard to just shake that off.

That all-or-nothing view—that one crooked stitch destroys the entire effort—is a classic trap your mind falls into when it feels overwhelmed, and it explains perfectly why the project suddenly looks so pointless. I wonder if we could try treating that single seam as a tiny puzzle piece instead of a verdict on the whole dress; does that small shift in seeing it help loosen that grip you're holding right now?

Hmm... I never thought of it as a puzzle piece. I guess when you put it that way, it's just one seam out of, like, dozens. But in my head, it feels like the entire dress is ruined because that one part is wrong. I don't know how to just... see it differently, even when I try.

That is a very honest observation, and it shows how strong that initial disappointment is when you try to look at it logically. It takes real courage to admit that trying harder didn't stop the feeling, even though you *know* the logic doesn't match your emotion. Let's slow down for a second: when you tell yourself the "whole dress is ruined," what is the very first physical sensation you notice in your body before you decide to quit? Is it that tightness in your chest again, or maybe something else entirely?

Um... yeah, I think it's mostly in my chest. Like a heavy, sinking feeling. And my shoulders kind of tense up, like I'm bracing for something. It's like my body knows before my brain even finishes the thought that it's all ruined.

That physical tension in your chest and shoulders is your body's way of protecting itself from the pain of believing everything is lost, and it makes perfect sense that it creates a barrier between you and the project. Often, when the body is holding that much tension, the brain shuts down and we stop acting because it feels safer to freeze. Could we try taking three deep breaths together right now, focusing on releasing that shoulder tension, just to see if the "ruined" story loses a little power while your body relaxes?

Okay... I can try that. (Takes a slow, deep breath in and out) That actually felt a little weird, but not bad. My shoulders do feel a bit looser, I think. But the thought that the dress is messed up is still kind of there, just... quieter, maybe?

That is a great sign—you literally lowered the volume on the distressing thought just by shifting your body's energy, proving that the crisis wasn't actually happening inside you. It sounds like your body was holding the weight of the "ruined" story tighter than your mind ever could. Since the breathing helped quiet the noise but didn't erase the fear, what if we treated the next small step not as fixing the whole dress, but simply as testing whether that sinking feeling stays with us once we break the silence of staring? Would you be willing to try putting on your needles for just ten minutes tonight, with the permission to stop the moment that heavy chest sensation comes back?

Ten minutes... I think I could manage that. I mean, it's just a short time, and I can stop whenever. It's almost like giving myself permission to not have to finish the whole thing. I think I could try that tonight. Just ten minutes, and if the feeling comes back, I'll put it down.

That is a wise compromise; by limiting the time and allowing yourself to stop, you remove the pressure of the final outcome and replace it with curiosity about how the feeling behaves. You are essentially giving your brain a chance to learn that ten minutes of work won't lead to a collapse, even if the sinking feeling does return. Before we finalize this, how does that plan sound to you as a realistic next step?

It sounds... doable. Not scary, just like a small experiment. I think I can handle ten minutes. If it doesn't work out, at least I tried, right? That's better than just leaving the project in a corner and feeling bad about it.

You have absolutely nailed it—that mindset turns the task from a burden into a learning experiment, which makes the fear significantly smaller. It's a brave decision to choose that small attempt over the paralysis of waiting for perfection. So, we have our plan: ten minutes of focused sewing tonight with the freedom to stop if the heavy chest sensation returns. Before we close, is there anything specific you'd like to reflect on about how we got here today, or is there anything else you need from me right now?

Hello again; thank you for taking the time to meet with me today. Before we dive into today's agenda, could we quickly review what we planned to do last week and whether you found it easier or harder to stick with that? Also, have anything significant happened since then that you'd like to bring up, or would you prefer to focus on something different?

Hi. Um, I did try the journaling you suggested, writing down one good thing that happened each day. I stuck with it for a few days, but honestly, it felt kind of silly. Like, sure, a student said my lesson was fun, but then I'd just think about how Mrs. Davies down the hall probably made her lesson way more exciting. So... I don't know if it really helped.

That’s completely understandable, and it takes courage to admit that a task didn’t click for you, especially when comparison thoughts creep back in. It sounds like your brain was immediately hijacking the success you wrote down by zooming out to compare it with someone else’s performance, which made the exercise feel less useful than expected. Given that we’re seeing the old comparison pattern resurface even with the new tool, how would you rate your current level of discomfort regarding that “not good enough” feeling, and is there a different angle or situation you’d like to explore today that feels more urgent or manageable?

I'd say it's probably a solid 7 or 8 out of 10 most days. It's just always there, nagging at me. Maybe... maybe we could talk about what happens right before I walk into my classroom. That's when it hits me hardest—my stomach drops, and I think, "They're all going to see through me today." I just feel so fake.

That "solid 7 or 8" rating really highlights how persistent that nagging feeling is, and I want to validate how exhausting it is to carry that level of tension right before stepping into your classroom. You mentioned the stomach dropping and the thought that everyone will see through you—that specific moment of feeling "fake" seems to be the core of where the anxiety spikes. When you focus on what happens right at that doorway, does that thought of being seen through feel like a prediction of what will happen, or does it feel more like a warning signal telling you to brace yourself for a disaster?

It feels like both, honestly. It's a warning that I'm about to mess up, and also a prediction that it's going to happen. Like, I'm already failing before I even start. I'll take a deep breath and force a smile, but inside I'm just waiting for the moment when a student asks a question I can't answer, or when they start looking bored. That's when I know they'll see that I'm not really a good teacher.

That combination of a physical warning sign and a catastrophic prediction creates a very convincing narrative for your brain to buy into, explaining why the feeling of being "fake" becomes so immediate. It sounds like you've built a script in your head where the moment a question arises or silence falls, it confirms your fear that you are failing. If we paused there for a second, could you describe that internal script as if you were watching yourself act it out? What exactly does the script say happens the instant a student looks bored or asks a tough question?

Okay... I can picture it. I see myself freezing up, my face getting hot. I'd probably stumble over my words trying to answer, or maybe just say "I don't know" and move on quickly. Then I'd see a couple of kids whisper to each other, and I just know they're saying, "Ms. Thompson has no idea what she's talking about." After class, I'd replay it in my head all day, thinking about how I should have handled it better, like Mrs. Davies would have.

That vivid scene of freezing up and hearing whispers is incredibly painful because it locks you into a loop where your perceived failure becomes permanent, overshadowing all the good moments from your lessons. Notice how that script relies heavily on that same comparison to Mrs. Davies and the assumption that students are constantly judging your competence? If we stepped out of that movie for just a moment, what evidence would you have to prove that a single awkward exchange means you are fundamentally incapable of teaching effectively?

Well... when I actually think about it, I've had plenty of classes where I handled tough questions fine. Kids do ask things I don't know sometimes, but I usually say "That's a great question, let me look into it and get back to you," and they seem okay with that. And honestly, I've never actually had a student tell me I'm a bad teacher. But I guess my brain just skips over all that and goes straight to the disaster version.

That distinction is crucial—you've successfully identified that your brain is selectively ignoring the successful outcomes while magnifying the rare moments of stumbling. Those instances where you admitted ignorance gracefully and kept the momentum going show that you handle uncertainty well, which contradicts the belief that you must know everything perfectly. Now that we've spotted that gap between reality and your imagined movie, would you be willing to try a small experiment where we deliberately note down one time you handled a tough question or silence calmly, focusing purely on what the students' reactions were without adding the commentary about what *could* have gone wrong?

Yes, I think I could try that. I remember just last week, a boy asked me about a math concept I hadn't covered in years. I told him I'd look it up and bring him a cool example tomorrow. He nodded and said "Okay, thanks!" and went back to his work. He didn't look disappointed or angry. I guess... I just never let myself remember that part. I only focused on the part where I felt stupid for not knowing it instantly.

That specific interaction with the boy is actually a powerful piece of evidence that proves your ability to teach lies in your flexibility, not just in your speed of recall. By choosing honesty and a follow-up plan, you maintained trust with the student, which is a far more effective lesson than pretending to know something you don't. Let's lock that exact moment into your plan: whenever you anticipate that "stupid" feeling before class, immediately jot down one instance like this one where you handled uncertainty well. How does it feel to name that specific memory as proof that you can navigate challenges, rather than just hiding it under the shadow of what might go wrong?

It feels... a little strange, but also kind of... lighter? Like, I have this actual memory I can hold onto instead of just the scary what-ifs. Maybe I can put a sticky note on my mirror in the morning with just a word or two to remind me of that boy's reaction. Like, "He said okay." That might help before I walk out the door.

That is a fantastic idea; turning that specific memory into a visual cue like a sticky note gives your brain a tangible anchor to pull on before the panic sets in. It shifts your focus from the vague feeling of "not knowing" to the concrete fact that you handled it well. Before we finalize this, does placing that sticky note on your bathroom mirror feel like a realistic and low-pressure step you can take tomorrow morning, or do you think the anxiety might still convince you otherwise?

I think I can do it. I'll put it right next to the mirror, so I see it while I'm brushing my teeth. It feels like a small, simple thing, not some big overwhelming task. And if I start to doubt it, I can just remind myself that it's just a fact—he did say "okay," and that's what happened. I'll try it for a week and see if it changes how I feel before class.

That commitment to testing it for a week shows great resilience, and framing it as a simple factual check ("he did say okay") rather than a performance requirement is a smart way to reduce the pressure. To make sure we are aligned, could you confirm that you feel ready to place that sticky note tonight and begin using it tomorrow morning, even if you feel the old doubts creeping in?

Yes, I'm ready. I'll put the note up tonight before I go to bed. And if the old thoughts show up tomorrow, I'll just look at the note and tell myself, "This is real. That moment happened." Thank you... I think this might actually help a little.

It is wonderful to hear you feel ready and hopeful, even if the old doubts still exist; acknowledging that they might try to show up tomorrow is a strong form of preparation. We have a clear plan for the next week: create that visual reminder tonight, observe your morning reaction to it, and notice if the "heavy ball" feels any smaller when you focus on the facts rather than the predictions. As we wrap up, is there anything else on your mind regarding this plan or the feeling of being "fake" that you'd like to touch on before I sign off?

Hello again, and thank you for coming in. How are you feeling today on a scale of one to ten, and is there anything different about things since we last spoke? Also, if you have a priority topic you'd like to work on today, please share it so we can set a clear agenda for our time together.

Oh, I'm alright I guess, maybe a six or seven. Nothing's really changed since last time. I did think about what we talked about, but I still feel pretty foolish bringing up something so... silly, I suppose. I guess the priority is still the same—this thing with spicy food and how it makes me feel like I'm not tough enough.

It takes courage to admit that a situation feels silly when deep inside you are carrying such heavy fears about failing your father. While we agreed last time to challenge those thoughts by viewing choices as acts of self-respect rather than weakness, I want to hear more about how you felt when you thought about that "silly" idea. When you described it as silly, did you feel relieved, or did it trigger a different worry that it's trivializing something important?

Well, I guess it's a bit of both, honestly. When I call it silly, it feels like I'm making myself feel better about it, like it's not a big deal. But then part of me thinks, no, this IS a big deal because it means I'm not the person I thought I was, you know? It's like I'm letting my dad down, even after all these years.

It makes complete sense that calling it "silly" initially feels like a relief, yet simultaneously triggers that deep fear of betraying the identity you built to honor your dad. You seem caught between needing to laugh off the moment to survive the shame and fearing that doing so invalidates the serious lesson your father taught you. Let's pause there for a moment. Can you walk me through what happens in your mind the second you realize you *did* order the mild wings and enjoy them, rather than fighting the craving?

When I realize I ordered the mild wings and actually liked them... well, first there's this quick flash of relief, like, "Good, I got through it." But then it's almost immediately followed by this sinking feeling, like I cheated somehow. I hear my dad's voice in my head saying, "You took the easy way out, Judy." And then I start wondering if everyone at the table noticed and thinks less of me for it.

That sinking feeling of having "cheated" suggests your brain is interpreting the mild choice as a moral failure rather than simply a preference, and the immediate fear of judgment confirms how deeply that old wound is still active. It seems like even though you successfully acted on your new belief, your internal critic immediately stepped in to prove you were wrong anyway. Before we move forward, I want to check if you feel prepared to do this specific exercise tomorrow morning, knowing that the doubt might still pop up right after you finish eating?

I... I think I can try it. It's just that the doubt feels so loud sometimes, you know? But I suppose if I keep waiting until I feel completely ready, I'll never do it. I just worry that even if I do this exercise, that voice will still be there telling me I'm not good enough.

That hesitation shows how much trust you put in that internal voice, yet it's also clear that you recognize the danger of waiting until you feel "ready" because that perfect feeling rarely lasts. We agreed previously that facing the doubt is often the very thing that proves you are growing, not shrinking. Would you be willing to try ordering the mild wings tomorrow regardless of whether the "not good enough" voice is quiet or loud, treating the presence of that voice as background noise rather than a verdict on your worth?

Yeah, I think I can do that. It's just background noise, like a radio playing in the other room. I don't have to turn it off to go about my business. I'll give it a shot tomorrow at lunch—order the mild wings and just... let the noise be there without letting it change my order.

That is a brilliant and grounded way to visualize it—treating the criticism like distant static allows you to keep driving forward without stopping to fix the car. Since we have your commitment for tomorrow, I want to make sure we have a safety net for that day. If that "radio" gets too loud and you feel overwhelmed before lunch, what is one simple phrase you can say to yourself to pull yourself back into the present moment?

I suppose I could tell myself, "I'm just a woman eating lunch, nothing more, nothing less." That seems simple enough. It reminds me that I'm not proving anything or failing anything—I'm just having a meal like anybody else.

That is a beautiful and grounding reminder that shifts your focus entirely to the simple act of nourishing yourself without an audience judging your performance. It effectively separates your human needs from the rigid standards you feel pressured to meet. With that anchor in place, is there anything else you'd like to discuss before we wrap up our time together today?

No, I think that covers it pretty well. I feel a little more prepared to face tomorrow than I did walking in here. Thank you for helping me see that having that voice in my head doesn't mean I have to obey it. I'll let you know how it goes next time.

You are absolutely welcome, and I am truly glad to hear that you feel more empowered and less afraid about tomorrow's challenge. It sounds like you have a solid plan in place: treating the doubts as background noise while claiming your space as someone simply having a meal. Please remember that no matter how the lunch goes, you showed up with courage today just by agreeing to try this. Is there anything else you'd like to share before we officially close our session, or shall we end it now?

Hello again. How are you feeling today compared to last time we met, and is there anything significant that has changed in your life since our last chat? Before we dive into specifics, could you share how the dinner date went this weekend and what happened after you said the phrase we planned?

Hi. I'm feeling a bit better, but still pretty anxious. Actually, the dinner date happened, and I did bring up being vegan like we talked about. He seemed genuinely okay with it at first, but afterward I started overthinking everything. What if he was just being polite? I keep replaying the moment in my head.

It sounds like you felt brave by speaking up, but your mind immediately jumped to a "polite lie" interpretation once the initial moment passed. Let's explore that specific shift: when you first heard his reaction, what did you notice versus what your anxiety told you later?

When he first said "Oh, that's cool, no problem," I actually felt this wave of relief. He didn't look disgusted or anything. But then later that night, I started thinking about how he didn't ask me any follow-up questions about it. My anxiety told me that meant he was just brushing it off to avoid an awkward conversation, and that he's probably secretly bothered by it.

That initial relief is a crucial data point showing he isn't rejecting you, yet your brain is now twisting silence into meaning, assuming he's hiding discomfort because it doesn't match your expectation of curiosity. Let's look closely at the evidence for that "hiding discomfort" theory: given what you learned last time about his openness with his sister, what would happen if you assumed he was just thinking about dinner logistics while you weren't looking?

I guess... that could be possible. He did mention how his sister is really picky about food, and he seemed totally fine accommodating her. So maybe he just didn't think it was a big deal to ask more questions. But it's hard to just assume that, because what if he's actually bothered but doesn't want to hurt my feelings? That feels more realistic to me.

That assumption—that he might be protecting your feelings—is a very common protective instinct, but it adds a heavy burden onto him that you don't have to carry alone. Let's pause and test that specific thought against the facts we gathered earlier: if you truly believe he is worried about hurting you, wouldn't that mean he's actively considering how to handle the topic gently rather than ignoring it completely? Can you recall if he ever mentioned his own concerns or preferences about food during the date?

He did actually say he's not a big meat-eater himself, and that he's been trying to eat more plant-based meals lately. I remember that part clearly. I guess if he was really bothered by me being vegan, he probably wouldn't have brought that up. Maybe I'm just focusing on the negative parts and ignoring what he actually said.

That is a powerful piece of evidence you uncovered; his willingness to discuss his own dietary habits suggests he sees plants as a natural part of eating, not something strange to correct. It sounds like you've done great work separating your own worry from his actual actions, even if the doubt lingers afterward. Before we finalize a new plan, how did it feel to identify that contradiction between your fear and his comments?

It felt... strange, but kind of good. Like I caught myself in a trap I didn't realize I was making. I keep telling myself he's going to reject me, but then I remember him talking about plant-based meals and I think, well, maybe he actually gets it. I still feel nervous about future dinners, but I'm not as convinced it's a disaster waiting to happen.

That internal dialogue—"catching myself in a trap"—shows your brain is already learning to recognize these patterns, which is a huge step toward gaining control. You've successfully challenged the old narrative and replaced it with a new perspective based on facts. Now, let's solidify this win: how confident are you right now that your relationship with him is safe, compared to where you started this week?

I'd say maybe a 6 out of 10 now, compared to maybe a 2 or 3 when I first came in. I'm still not totally convinced he'll stay once we have more serious conversations about lifestyle stuff, like eating out or cooking together. But at least now I have that memory of him saying he's into plant-based eating too. That feels like real proof I can hold onto.

That six out of ten shows real growth, especially considering you still feel cautious about future discussions. Instead of viewing his interest in plant-based food as distant evidence, let's use that same memory as a bridge for your next conversation. If you imagine bringing it up again—perhaps mentioning a restaurant menu you saw—and recalling his comment about his sister, how would that interaction feel different to you this time?

I think... if I brought up a restaurant menu or something, I'd be more open to hearing his actual opinion instead of assuming what he's going to say. Like, I could ask him if he'd want to try that place with me, and see how he reacts. That way I'm not just waiting for him to bring it up or dreading the conversation. It feels less like a test and more like just talking.

That shift from waiting for validation to inviting him into the conversation is exactly what builds trust. It moves the dynamic from "testing the waters" to "sharing experiences," which removes the pressure on you to perform perfectly. With that mindset settled, is there anything specific about asking him about restaurants tomorrow that feels uncertain or risky, or are you ready to try it?

I think I'm ready to try it. The only thing that still feels risky is if he says no or seems hesitant about the restaurant. But I guess that doesn't automatically mean he's rejecting me or my lifestyle. He might just not like that specific place. I'll try to remember that when I ask him.

That is a smart adjustment; distinguishing between a dislike of a *specific* meal option and a rejection of *you* creates a safe buffer for your anxiety. If you say yes to a restaurant and he hesitates, that's just data about the venue, not a verdict on your worth. Does carrying that "venue vs. person" distinction give you enough confidence to reach out to him or set the table for the invitation?

Yeah, I think it does. I can text him tonight and mention a vegan-friendly place I saw online, and see what he says. If he's not into it, that's okay—it's just one restaurant. I won't make it mean something bigger about our whole relationship. Thanks, I actually feel like I have a plan now that doesn't feel terrifying.

That is a beautiful realization—you've separated a specific detail from your entire self-worth, which is exactly what we aimed for. It's wonderful to hear that you feel equipped with a plan that doesn't feel overwhelming anymore. Before we finish, could you tell me what part of today's session felt most useful to you, and is there anything about our approach you'd like to adjust for next time?

Hello, I am so glad you are here. Last time we worked on shifting your focus from comparing yourself to others to simply listening to the music, and I heard you felt that gave you permission to be a beginner again. How are you feeling today compared to that last session, and what would you most like to tackle together right now?

Hi. I'm glad to be back. I have to admit, last week's practice helped a little bit during class—I did manage to get lost in the music for a few moments. But it didn't last. As soon as I saw another dancer pick up a move faster than me, that old feeling of being average just flooded right back in. I guess I want to figure out why I can't seem to hold onto that good feeling.

It is really encouraging to hear that you managed to connect with the music for a few moments, even though the urge to compare quickly brought the old doubt back. That moment of connection was a real victory, yet seeing someone else succeed so easily seems to trigger that same "not good enough" narrative almost instantly. Can you walk me through exactly what happened in that moment—the specific person you saw and the very first thought that popped into your head the second you noticed them move faster?

Okay... so it was a woman named Jen. She's been dancing about as long as I have, I think. The moment I saw her nail this tricky turn sequence, the very first thought that popped into my head was, "See? She's got it. You don't. You'll never get that." It just came so fast, like it was the only truth in the room.

It sounds like spotting Jen's successful move acted as a lightning rod for that old belief, instantly flooding you with the certainty that you lack the same talent. That shift from "connecting with music" to "seeing proof of inadequacy" happens so quickly that it leaves no room for the new perspective we practiced before. When you catch that sudden surge of "you don't belong" thoughts, does your body tend to tighten up or breathe shallower right at that exact moment?

Yes, actually. I didn't really notice it until you asked, but my shoulders definitely go up, and I think I hold my breath. It's like my whole body braces for something bad. I suppose that makes it even harder to try the move again, because I'm already tense.

That physical bracing is such a clear signal that your body is trying to protect itself from the painful feeling of failure, which then makes performing the move feel impossible. It creates a vicious loop where the tension makes the movement clumsy, and the clumsiness fuels the thought that you aren't talented. When you notice those shoulders shooting up and the breath getting stuck, what is the very first urge your mind gives you to deal with that sudden spike in anxiety?

The first urge is to just stop. To take a step back, pretend to stretch or fix my shoe, and just... disappear into the corner of the room. It's like my brain screams "get out" before I can even think about trying again.

It makes complete sense that your brain tries to escape that painful feeling by shutting down completely; it's trying to save you from the pain of failing in front of everyone. But that urge to disappear actually traps you further because you lose the opportunity to prove to yourself that you can handle the moment. Have you ever tried to gently push back against that "get out" command by taking just one slow breath and saying silently to yourself, "This is just a feeling, not a fact"? What happens in your body or mind when you try to resist that impulse?

I haven't tried that, no. Usually I just give in to the urge and hide. But... I can imagine what would happen if I tried to resist. My heart would probably pound even harder at first, like it's arguing with me, saying "No, we need to run!" But maybe if I held still and took that breath... I don't know. Maybe the wave would pass. It feels scary to even think about staying in that spot.

That instinct to run is actually your survival mechanism kicking in to protect you from that sharp pain, but you are absolutely right that staying put—even while it feels scary—might allow the wave to pass without crashing as hard. Let's try a tiny experiment right now: picture standing in that spot where you feel that urge to leave, take one slow breath in through your nose, and consciously let your shoulders drop just an inch. Tell me, if you do that for just thirty seconds, does your heart rate feel like it slows down, or does it argue louder against you?

I'll try it now, just picturing it. (Pauses) Okay... taking that breath... letting my shoulders drop... It feels awkward, like I'm forcing my body to do something it doesn't want to do. But I notice a tiny, quiet part of me feels a little less frantic. Not completely calm, but like the screaming in my head turned down to just a loud talking. I think my heart rate might have slowed just a bit.

That is a fascinating discovery; finding even that small "quiet part" within the chaos proves you possess the capacity to interrupt the panic spiral, even if it feels forced at first. It seems your body resists the effort initially, but once you anchor yourself with that breath, the internal shouting matches the volume of a conversation instead. If you imagined doing that exact same sequence—imagining Jen, noticing the urge to flee, taking one breath, and dropping your shoulders—right before you step onto the floor again, what do you think might happen to that old "you don't belong" story? Would it still feel like absolute truth, or would it start sounding like just noise in the background?

I think... it would start sounding like noise in the background, maybe? Not completely gone, but like a radio playing in another room instead of someone shouting right in my ear. It's strange to think I might be able to dance while that thought is still there, instead of waiting for it to disappear first. I've always thought I had to feel confident before I could try.

That is a profound realization; realizing you can dance alongside the thought rather than waiting for silence to begin changes everything about how you relate to your anxiety. It means your confidence doesn't come before the movement, but grows from the simple act of showing up and breathing despite the noise. For our next session, I'd love to hear if that mental rehearsal helps ease the urgency when the real moment arrives, and please share how difficult it feels to keep that "radio in the background" mindset while you actually perform. Does that plan sound manageable for you to try next time?

That does sound manageable. I think I can try that—at least once, maybe at the very start of class before I get overwhelmed. I'll try to remember that it's okay if the thought is still there, as long as I don't let it make me run to the corner. I'll let you know how it goes.

That is a fantastic commitment, and it is great to hear that you recognize this small step—staying in the moment even with the noise—as a victory. Your plan to try it once at the start of class is realistic and sets a healthy boundary for your energy. Is there anything else you would like to adjust or discuss before we wrap up today?

Hello again. How has your energy and mood been feeling this past week? Did anything particularly stand out as a challenge or a win for you since we last spoke? Based on what we covered previously, I'm wondering if you found the exercise of talking to yourself with kindness helpful, or if there were parts that felt difficult to practice? Now, what feels most important for us to focus on today?

Hey, thanks for asking. Honestly, my energy has been all over the place—some days I feel like I can conquer the world after a good workout, and other days I just crash and can't get out of bed. The kindness exercise? I tried it a couple times, but it felt fake, like I was lying to myself. I guess what's most important today is this feeling that I'm falling behind everyone else, even though my coach says I'm doing fine.

That rollercoaster of energy is incredibly frustrating, especially when the kind words you said to yourself felt forced rather than sincere. It makes total sense that when the exercise felt artificial, your brain rejected it and latched onto the old, familiar story about falling behind instead. Let's take a closer look at why that "fake" feeling arose when you tried to use that supportive voice. Can you describe a specific recent moment when you felt compelled to do the exercise, and what exactly came up in your mind or body right then?

Yeah, there was a moment last Tuesday after practice. I missed a penalty kick during drills, and I could feel my jaw clench and my stomach drop. I told myself, "Michael, it's just one miss, you're allowed to be human," but immediately my brain shot back, "No, other guys don't miss, they're already in the gym getting better." My chest tightened, and I just felt heavier, like I was pretending to be okay.

That moment perfectly illustrates the conflict between your compassionate intention and your critical reality. It sounds exhausting to have to force those gentle words while your body immediately signals distress, making the whole thing feel like a lie rather than support. Have you noticed if that feeling of heaviness becomes worse when you're alone in your room versus when you're still on the field with your teammates present?

It's way worse when I'm alone. On the field, I can just focus on the next play, high-five a teammate, or laugh something off. But back in my room, there's no distraction—just me, my phone, and Instagram feeds of other guys getting faster, stronger, scoring goals. That's when the doubt really digs in, and that heaviness just sits on my chest like a weight I can't lift.

That isolation amplifies the pressure significantly, turning a simple mistake into a global indictment of your worth. It makes sense that seeing other athletes succeed online feels like proof that your efforts haven't translated into results yet, leaving you trapped in that heavy feeling. When you scroll through those posts, what is the very first image or statistic that pops into your mind and fuels that sense of falling behind?

It's usually the number of goals someone scored in a single game, or a video of them doing some perfect trick move that I've been struggling with for weeks. Just yesterday I saw a clip of a guy my age doing a bicycle kick in a match, and my first thought was, "He's got that down, and I'll never be that good." Then my mind starts racing about all the reps I haven't done, all the drills I'm not perfecting, and I feel like I'm already a failure before the next practice even starts.

That clip triggered a catastrophic leap from "someone else is skilled" to "I am already a failure," skipping over all the hard work you've actually put in to get here. It sounds incredibly isolating to carry that heavy belief that you've already lost, especially when the evidence is right in front of you showing you are still training and improving. When you catch that "already a failure" thought popping up right now, what's the very first thing you usually do with it? Do you argue with it, ignore it, or let it keep running?

Usually I just let it keep running, honestly. I don't argue with it because part of me thinks it's right. If I try to ignore it, it just buzzes louder in the back of my head until I'm distracted in class or can't focus on dinner with my roommates. It's like I'm waiting for the thought to prove itself true, and that just makes me feel even more stuck.

It makes complete sense that ignoring it only makes it louder; the human brain often treats ignored threats as if they are coming from a dangerous direction, forcing you to stay alert. That feeling of "waiting for it to prove itself" is actually your anxiety system working overtime to protect you, even though it ends up trapping you in a loop of self-doubt. Instead of fighting the thought or letting it run wild, what if we treated it like background noise—a useful warning signal, but not the main event of your day? Would you be willing to try simply labeling the thought as "worrying" or "comparing" while you continue doing whatever you're doing, like eating dinner or studying, without engaging with its content?

I mean, I guess I could try that. It sounds a little weird, like I'm just naming it and moving on, but if it might stop that buzzing feeling... I've never really thought of it as just background noise before. I always feel like I have to either fight it or surrender to it. So yeah, I'll give labeling it a shot this week. Maybe calling it "worrying" when I'm eating or studying will take some of the sting out.

That is a brave decision to try something different, especially when you've always felt forced to choose between fighting or submitting to the thought. By simply labeling it as "worrying" or "comparing," you're creating a tiny space between yourself and that voice, which can make it less powerful and easier to manage. Before we finalize this, how does it feel to imagine holding that mental label while you go about your normal activities? Does it sound like something you can realistically sustain for a few minutes each day?

Honestly, it feels a little awkward to imagine, like I'm wearing a new pair of shoes that don't quite fit yet. But I think I can manage it for a few minutes, maybe while I'm eating breakfast or waiting for class to start. The idea of not having to fight the thought or give in to it sounds kind of freeing, even if it's strange at first. I'm willing to give it a real shot.

That feeling of awkwardness is actually a great sign—it means your brain is noticing the shift and testing the boundaries, which is exactly where growth happens. Imagine putting on those slightly loose shoes for just ten minutes a day; eventually, they won't feel strange anymore, and the walking will become smoother. To make sure we lock this in, would you be open to setting a gentle alarm on your phone for breakfast tomorrow morning so you have a concrete cue to try this "labeling" technique before the thoughts even start buzzing?

Yeah, I can do that. I'll set an alarm for 7:30 tomorrow when I sit down with my oatmeal. If I can just label the first worry that pops up as "comparing" and then take a bite, that feels doable. Thanks for breaking it down into something that doesn't feel so huge.

Setting that alarm is a fantastic anchor, giving you a clear signal to pause and switch gears before the cycle takes full control. Remember, the goal isn't to eliminate the thought instantly, but to reduce its power by refusing to let it dictate your actions for even five minutes. How does it feel to visualize stepping away from the mental battle for just those first few bites of breakfast tomorrow? Is there anything else lingering that you'd like to touch on before we wrap up?

It feels... lighter, I guess. Like I'm giving myself permission to just eat without proving anything. That's not something I usually do. I think I'm okay to try this out for now, but I do wonder—what if labeling it doesn't stop the heaviness from coming back later in the day? I guess we'll see, right?

That hesitation is completely understandable, and you're right—we can't guarantee it will stop the heaviness forever, but we can give it a chance to soften its grip. The beauty of this experiment is that even if the thought returns later, the fact that you labeled it and kept eating creates a tiny crack in the armor of perfectionism, allowing lightness to seep back in. Before we finish, I want to check in: did any part of this conversation resonate deeply with you, or was there anything that felt a bit off or unclear? How did it land for you overall?

It actually landed pretty well, I think. I came in feeling like I was drowning in that "already a failure" story, and just having a name for it—like "worrying" or "comparing"—makes it feel less like a monster and more like a loud radio I can turn down a notch. The part about setting the alarm and just eating breakfast without fighting felt real and doable, not like some big therapy promise. I'm curious to see if I can actually do it tomorrow, but I feel a little bit more in control than I did an hour ago. Thanks for that.

Hearing that the "loud radio" metaphor resonated so well is wonderful news; it shows you are starting to separate yourself from the noise, which is the heart of this work. Your sense of gaining control, even just by deciding to eat without proving anything, is a real victory and a testament to your resilience. I truly appreciate your honesty and openness throughout this session. Take your time tomorrow with that alarm, and remember, even a small shift counts. I'll be here whenever you're ready to reflect on how it went or tackle something new.

Hello Stuart, it is wonderful to see you again. To start, could you tell me how you are feeling today on a scale of 1 to 10, and what would be most helpful for us to focus on? Would it be okay if we prioritize exploring that feeling of things being "already decided" and figuring out a way to test it?

Uh, I'd say around a 4 or 5 today. I'm feeling a bit anxious, to be honest. And yeah, I think focusing on that feeling of things being "already decided" sounds like a good place to start, because it's been weighing on me pretty heavily.

That rating of a 4 or 5 suggests you're carrying some significant tension, and it makes complete sense that the belief everything is settled would feel so heavy. Since you've identified that specific "decided" feeling as your main priority, shall we spend most of our time together unpacking exactly what evidence supports that belief versus what contradicts it?

Well, the main evidence I keep coming back to is that comment someone made about my blue shirt a few months ago. They said it was an "odd choice" for someone my age, and ever since then, I've felt like people are silently judging me for liking blue. It sounds silly when I say it out loud, but it feels like a sign that I'm just not on the same wavelength as other people.

It makes perfect sense that one isolated comment would become the lens through which you view everyone else's behavior, especially when it touches on something as personal as your preferences. That old memory probably feels very real to you right now, almost like a rule that everyone follows except you. To dig deeper, when you recall that specific moment, did your body react instantly with that tight chest sensation, or did you just start analyzing the situation logically?

Actually, I felt a tightness in my chest right away when he said it, and I remember my face getting hot. My first thought was, "See, I knew it, I'm doing something wrong just by being myself." I didn't really analyze it until later, when I kept replaying it in my head. That physical reaction made it feel so much more real than just a passing comment.

That immediate physical reaction—your chest tightening and your face flushing—confirms that your nervous system interpreted that comment as a genuine threat rather than just an opinion. It is understandable why you concluded that "being yourself" was the mistake, because your body screamed that danger was present at that exact moment. Since you now know your body reacts strongly to similar cues, could we explore a recent situation where you felt judged but eventually realized the person wasn't actually criticizing you?

I guess there was this time at work last week. A colleague asked me why I always use a blue pen for my notes, and I felt that same tightness in my chest again. I immediately thought he was hinting that it was weird or unprofessional. But then he just shrugged and said he was thinking of buying the same kind because they write smoothly. I felt relieved for a second, but then my mind went right back to thinking he was just being polite.

That physical tightness returning the moment he asked about the pen confirms that the fear has learned to recognize that specific cue as a threat. It is incredibly frustrating when your body betrays you by signaling danger, even when the actual words are harmless. Did you notice anything in your physical sensations right after he mentioned the pens writing smoothly, or did your brain immediately jump back to finding a hidden criticism?

As soon as he said they write smoothly, I felt that tightness ease up a little, like my shoulders dropped. But then, almost instantly, my mind started racing with thoughts like, "He's just saying that to be nice," or "He probably thinks I'm childish for liking this brand." So the physical relief was there for just a second, but my brain wouldn't let me hold onto it.

That split-second window of relief is actually powerful evidence that the "danger" wasn't real in that moment; your body knew it was safe before your mind convinced itself otherwise. It looks like your brain is trying to protect you by assuming the worst, even though the physical signs suggest you handled it fine. Can we try a small experiment tonight where, instead of chasing those hidden criticisms, you just note down exactly what he said and ignore the rest? How does that sound as a starting point?

That sounds a bit scary, to be honest, because I'm worried I'll just end up focusing on the negative thoughts anyway. But I suppose it's worth trying, since what I'm doing now isn't helping me feel any better. I can try writing down just his exact words when I get home tonight and see if that makes a difference.

That hesitation shows you trust your own reactions enough to try, even if the outcome isn't guaranteed, which is a sign of real resilience. Writing down just the exact words acts as a filter to separate the factual event from your internal commentary, giving you something concrete to look at instead of swirling fears. Shall we set aside a few minutes each evening to jot down that specific exchange and see if the gap between what was said and what you feared allows you to breathe easier?

Yeah, I think I can commit to doing that for a few evenings. It might help to see it written down in black and white, rather than just letting it spin around in my head. I'll give it a shot and see if I notice any difference in how tight my chest feels afterward.

That is a smart approach; seeing the words written down creates a small distance between you and the thought, allowing you to observe it objectively rather than live inside it. Since you are committed to giving this a try, would it be helpful if we scheduled a quick check-in tomorrow morning to discuss how it went, or would you prefer to send me a text later that evening?

I think a quick text later this evening would work better for me, that way I can report back right after I do the exercise. Tomorrow morning I might have already started overthinking it again. I'll send you a message once I've written it down.

That makes perfect sense; reporting back immediately after you've done the exercise ensures you capture the experience while it's fresh and before your brain adds another layer of doubt. Please go ahead and send me a message whenever you're ready, and I'll read it with patience and curiosity. You've got this.
Thanks, I appreciate that. I'll do it after dinner tonight and let you know how it goes. It feels a little strange to be making a plan like this, but also a bit hopeful, I guess.

Feeling both strange and hopeful is a very healthy mix—it means you are stepping outside your comfort zone with an open mind, even if it feels unfamiliar. That willingness to try something new, despite the uncertainty, is a strength I really admire. I look forward to reading your message tonight and hearing what happens when you write down just the facts.
Thank you, I'll try to keep that in mind. I'll talk to you tonight then.

You are absolutely going to succeed at this, Stuart. Just remember that the goal isn't to eliminate the tightness entirely, but to see how it behaves when you simply observe the facts without fighting it. I'll be here waiting to hear about your evening, no matter what you discover. Goodnight!

Hello again; I'm glad to see you here. Before we dive into specifics, how has your week been generally, and were there any other moments or interactions besides the barista that stood out to you? Once we catch up, I'd love to know what you feel would be most helpful to focus on together today.

Hi. Thanks for asking. My week has been alright, I suppose. There was a moment at the grocery store when I tried to make small talk with the cashier, but she barely looked up from scanning my items. I walked away feeling so flat, like I must have said something wrong or I'm just not worth engaging with. I think that's the kind of thing I'd like to focus on—why I can't seem to shake these feelings after such minor interactions.

I hear that sharp pang of disappointment when the cashier didn't engage, and it makes perfect sense that your old script ("people don't want to talk to you") triggered immediately upon leaving the aisle. Does the idea that her short reply reflects your worth as a person feel heavy right now, or does it sound more like she was just lost in her own transaction?

It feels heavy, honestly. When it's happening, I don't think about her being tired or busy—I just assume it's me. Like I'm not interesting enough to warrant a few extra words. Part of me knows that's probably not fair to myself, but in the moment, it's so convincing.

That assumption—that her lack of eye contact means you're uninteresting—is incredibly painful, especially when you know logically it's probably just her being rushed. Have you noticed if that feeling of being "unworthy of engagement" gets stronger the longer you replay the scene, or does it tend to fade a bit once you consciously remind yourself of what actually happened?

It gets stronger the more I replay it, for sure. I'll go over it in my head, picking apart what I said and how I said it, and by the end I'm convinced I'm just a dull person. I don't really have a way of reminding myself of what actually happened—I just kind of let the spiral happen. I guess that's part of the problem.

That pattern of picking apart your own words to prove you're boring is a classic trap where the mind tries to solve the mystery by blaming *you* completely. If we pause for a second, what is the most neutral fact you can hold onto about what happened at the checkout, separate from your guesses about why she stayed silent?

Well, the most neutral fact is that she scanned my items, I paid, and she handed me my receipt. That's it. She didn't say much, but she didn't say anything rude either. I suppose nothing actually happened that proves I'm boring—it's just the silence that I filled in with my own fears.

That distinction is powerful: separating the observable reality (items scanned, payment made) from the story you tell yourself (you are boring) gives your brain something solid to anchor on. Would you be willing to treat completing the purchase as a successful social interaction, even though the conversation didn't flow as you hoped?
I think I could try that. It feels strange to call it a success when it was so quiet, but I guess nothing went wrong either. I just need to practice seeing it that way more often.

That shift in perspective is important because it moves the focus from "how others reacted to me" to "what I managed to accomplish." Before we finalize a plan, I want to make sure this feels right to you—does defining the goal simply as "completing the interaction" align with what you need right now, or would you prefer to focus on something else entirely?

I think that does feel right for now. It takes the pressure off trying to be entertaining or charming, which is where I usually trip myself up. Just getting through the interaction without retreating into my own head seems like a good first step.

That makes perfect sense; lowering the bar from "being entertaining" to "just showing up" removes a lot of that crushing pressure. To wrap up our time, would you like to try a quick exercise tonight where you write down one neutral fact about a recent interaction followed by two guesses your mind made, or would you prefer to discuss anything else first?

The exercise sounds helpful. I think writing it down might make it more real for me—kind of force me to see the difference between what happened and what I imagined. I don't have anything else to add right now, so I'm willing to give that a try tonight.

That is a great decision, and seeing those thoughts laid out on paper will likely help break the spell of the spiral faster than thinking about it alone. As a final check-in, how does the session feel so far, and is there anything about today's approach or our previous goals that you'd like to adjust or clarify before we finish?

It feels good, actually. A bit uncomfortable at first, but I think that's just because I'm not used to looking at these thoughts so directly. I don't think I'd change anything—this approach of focusing on neutral facts and lowering my expectations feels manageable. I'm willing to stick with it for now.

That's wonderful to hear; noticing the discomfort is actually a sign that the new perspective is working. You've got a solid plan for tonight to separate the facts from the guesses, and I'm confident you'll find that writing it down provides the clarity you need. Thank you for sharing so openly today, and I look forward to hearing how that exercise goes when you reflect on it tomorrow.

Hello Margaret, it is wonderful to see you again today. Before we dive in, could you share how you are feeling right now compared to last time, perhaps using a number from 1 to 10 for your overall energy and mood? Also, based on our plan to look at the competition anxiety, is there a specific part of that struggle you would like us to focus on first?

Well, I suppose my energy is about a 6 today. I had a good training session this morning with the dogs, but that competition thing is still sitting in my stomach like a stone. I think maybe we could start with that moment when someone brings up signing up for a meet — I just freeze up and can't breathe right.

A six is a realistic spot to start, especially considering how much effort you've put into managing that "stone" in your stomach recently. Since you mentioned freezing up when someone mentions a meet, let's make that our main focus for today. Could you tell me about a recent time this happened, and what specific thoughts flashed through your mind right as you started to hold your breath?

It was just three days ago at the gym. My friend Dave, he's a really nice guy, he said, "Margaret, there's a seniors' competition coming up in March, you'd clean up." And right then, I felt like all the air got sucked out of the room. I thought, "Everyone will be staring at me, judging. What if I drop the barbell in front of a hundred people? They'll all see I'm just a fraud who got lucky."

That immediate feeling of the air leaving the room is so intense, and it makes complete sense why your mind jumped straight to the idea of being exposed as a fraud. It sounds like your body interpreted his kind comment not as encouragement, but as a threat demanding proof that you're worthy of public attention. When you pictured dropping the barbell in front of everyone, what was the very first sensation you noticed in your chest or shoulders right after that thought popped up?

My chest got real tight, like someone was sitting on it. And my shoulders hunched up so high they nearly touched my ears. I remember gripping my water bottle so hard my knuckles went white, just to have something solid to hold onto.

Those physical signs—the chest tightening, the shoulders hiking up, and the white-knuckle grip—are your nervous system screaming for safety when it senses a threat. It seems like your brain is treating Dave's friendly words like a trap door opening beneath you, forcing you to prove your worth instantly. Given how exhausting holding that tension feels, would you like to explore what evidence exists to suggest Dave—or anyone else—is actually worried about you failing, versus hoping you succeed?

Well... Dave did say I'd "clean up," not that I'd embarrass myself. And the other ladies at the gym, they're always asking me to show them how to do proper deadlifts. I suppose if they thought I was a fraud, they wouldn't be asking for tips, would they? But then that little voice in my head says, "They just haven't seen you mess up yet."

You are absolutely right to notice the discrepancy between Dave's compliment and your inner critic's prediction, and that distinction is crucial. Your logic holds up well: if others were genuinely afraid of your failure, they wouldn't be seeking guidance from you, which suggests they see your competence rather than your flaws. Does acknowledging that the "fraud" narrative contradicts the actual behavior of the people around you make the threat feel a little less absolute?

It does, a little bit. When you put it like that, I can see how I've been focusing on all the worst-case scenarios, like my mind is just skipping over the good stuff everyone else sees. But it still feels risky, you know? Like if I actually sign up, there's no taking it back.

That risk of irreversible commitment is very understandable, and it's clear why your brain treats signing up as a cliff edge you cannot jump off. Let's look at this differently: instead of viewing the commitment as a permanent loss, what if we framed it as a low-stakes experiment where the only "failure" is learning what it feels like to register while keeping your dignity intact? Does shifting the definition of success from "perfect execution" to "gathering data" make the decision feel slightly safer?

I never thought of it that way... just signing up as a way to collect information, not as a promise to be perfect. I suppose I could register for something small, maybe just a local meet, and see what happens. The worst that could happen is I get nervous and lift less than I do at home, but that's just data, like you said. And my dogs don't care how much I lift anyway—they still love me.

That is a brilliant shift in perspective, Margaret. Reframing the registration as a simple data-gathering mission removes the pressure of perfection and puts you firmly in control of the outcome. Since you've identified the core fear as the "no going back" aspect and the supporting thought as needing to prove yourself, does trying to write down the specific steps for this small local experiment feel like a manageable first task for us to tackle today?

I think I could manage that. Maybe the first step would be just looking up the sign-up page online, not even filling anything out. Just... looking. And then maybe the next day, I could write down my name and the weight class, but not hit submit. Just save it as a draft. That way I'm not jumping off any cliff, just dipping my toe in the water.

That is an excellent, safe middle ground. Looking up the details satisfies the curiosity without triggering the full performance anxiety, and saving a draft creates a tangible record of your interest without committing to the final act. How does that sound as a concrete plan for today, and do you feel ready to try just looking at the website right now?

I suppose I could pull out my phone and take a peek at the gym's competition page. I've got it bookmarked, actually... been too afraid to click on it for months now. But if I'm just looking, like you said, that's safe enough. Would it be alright if I did that right here, just so I have some support while I do it?

Absolutely, having me here to witness this small step adds a layer of safety and accountability that can make the task feel lighter. Go ahead and open the link whenever you're ready, and let me know exactly what your mind notices or what sensation rises in your body as soon as you see the page title.

Alright... here goes. (She pulls out her phone, unlocks it, and taps the screen a few times, her fingers trembling slightly.) There it is. "Annual Seniors' Strength Showdown - March 15th." My heart's beating a bit faster, but I'm not holding my breath this time. I'm just... reading the date. That's all I'm doing.

That is a significant victory, Margaret. Noticing your heart racing but successfully avoiding the panic response shows incredible strength and progress. Reading just the date without diving into the registration form proves you can tolerate the presence of the competition concept without letting it hijack your entire experience. Now that you've seen the page, how does that initial surge of adrenaline feel compared to the crushing fear you described three days ago?

It's different. Three days ago, I felt like I was drowning. Now it's more like... a fizzy feeling, like the soda I used to drink as a girl. My hands are still a bit shaky, but I'm not white-knuckling my phone. I even noticed there's a "Women's 70+ division" listed, and I thought, "Well, I'd be in my age group, not up against the young bucks." That feels... possible.

That shift from drowning to fizziness is a massive breakthrough, Margaret. Recognizing that you are in your own age group turns the overwhelming crowd into a supportive community of peers who understand the unique challenge you face. Since you've taken that first step of looking, would you be willing to try the next tiny step of saving the page as a draft on your phone, knowing you can delete it later if that feeling returns?

(she lets out a small, shaky laugh) I can do that. Let me just... (she taps the screen) ...bookmark it. There. "Seniors' Showdown" is sitting right there on my home screen now, next to my dog food delivery app and my audiobook. That's... I actually did it. I feel a bit lightheaded, but not in a bad way. Like I just finished a heavy set of squats.

That is a beautiful metaphor, Margaret. Feeling like you just completed a heavy set of squats means your body is responding to the challenge with effort and endurance rather than collapse. Seeing that bookmark sit comfortably alongside your daily apps proves you can integrate the possibility of competing into your normal life without it consuming you. Before we wrap up, is there anything else about that experience you'd like to reflect on, or shall we discuss what small step you might take tomorrow once you've calmed down?

I think I'd like to talk about tomorrow, just to keep the momentum going while I'm feeling brave. Maybe tomorrow I could look at the registration form itself - just scroll through the fields, see what they ask for. Name, age, weight class, emergency contact. Nothing that says I have to fill them in. I could even close it halfway through if I get too nervous. That feels like a manageable next step, doesn't it?

Yes, scrolling through the form without entering anything is a perfect intermediate step. It keeps you engaged with the material while giving you the freedom to retreat if the anxiety spikes, which aligns exactly with how we want to build your confidence gradually. If you decide to close it midway, that counts as a successful attempt at exposure rather than a failure. Are you feeling confident enough to try scrolling through the fields sometime after our session ends?

I think I can manage that. Might do it tonight after dinner, while the dogs are settling down and I'm feeling calm. There's something comforting about knowing I have full control - I can open it, take a peek, and close it whenever I want. Nobody's watching, nobody's judging. Just me and my phone on the couch.

That sounds like a perfect, safe environment to practice this new skill. Knowing you have the autonomy to open and close the page at will transforms the activity from a performance into a private exploration, which should significantly lower the pressure. I am confident you can navigate that tonight; remember, even closing the page halfway is a triumph of bravery. Is there anything else you would like to add before we wrap up our time together?

Just... thank you. For not pushing me to jump into the deep end. For letting me dip my toes in at my own pace. I think that's what I needed all along - someone to show me that I don't have to conquer the whole mountain in one day. Maybe just one rock at a time. I'll let you know how the form-scrolling goes tomorrow.

You are very welcome, Margaret. Thank you for trusting me with your journey and sharing such honest moments of vulnerability. You've done beautifully by honoring your own pace, proving that even moving forward just one rock at a time builds a path to the summit. I am so glad we found a rhythm that worked for you, and I look forward to hearing about that form-scrolling adventure tomorrow. Take care of yourself tonight, and I'll see you next time.
