Hello again, I'm really glad we got to connect. To start off, could you remind me of the specific action plan you agreed to last time—specifically, how you intend to catch that "disaster" voice when you're cooking—and what you found helpful or difficult about trying it? Once we briefly review that, would you like to focus entirely on unpacking the burnt garlic dinner party today, or is there another piece of life you'd like to bring up first?

Hey, thanks for asking. So the plan was to pause whenever I caught myself thinking "this is ruined" and actually check if the dish could be saved or adjusted instead of just scrapping it. I tried it a couple times—once with a sauce that split, and I managed to fix it with a whisk and some butter, which felt good. But the burnt garlic at the dinner party... that one got me. I couldn't stop the spiral. So maybe we can talk about that one today.

That is excellent feedback, especially noting how successfully you handled the split sauce earlier while finding the burnt garlic particularly difficult to manage. It’s great that you have concrete examples of both success and struggle to reference as we explore tonight’s situation. Now that we’ve confirmed the agenda is the burnt garlic incident, may I ask if there are any other immediate worries or events from this week besides that dinner party that you’d like to prioritize before we dive into it?

No, I think the burnt garlic is the main thing that's been eating at me this week. Every time I replay it, I just feel that same knot in my stomach. The split sauce thing was small potatoes compared to this—I mean, I was cooking for my wife's boss and her husband. It felt like I was being judged on everything that night.

That distinction makes perfect sense; dealing with a routine home meal versus hosting someone you respect carries such different weight, and that pressure alone explains why the knot stayed tight that night. It sounds like the fear wasn't just about the smell, but about failing in front of the people who matter most to you. Given that intensity, what is the very first image or feeling that pops up when you try to recall that moment?

Honestly, it's the smell. That acrid, sharp smell of garlic hitting a pan that's way too hot. I can almost taste it now. Right after that, I see my wife's boss's face across the table—she was mid-sentence, and I just froze. In that second, I felt like the whole evening was already a failure, like nothing I did after that could fix it.

It is completely understandable that freezing in front of your wife's boss triggered such a deep sense of failure, especially when paired with that overwhelming sensory memory. That sudden shift from a cooking error to feeling like a total catastrophe makes it clear how quickly your mind jumped from the physical smell to a massive judgment call. To dig a little deeper into that frozen moment, did you notice if your breathing sped up or if you felt like you physically lost control of the pan immediately after smelling it?

Yeah, my breathing definitely got shallow and fast. I remember gripping the pan handle so tight my knuckles went white, but then I just stood there for a few seconds, like I was glued to the floor. I didn't even move to take the pan off the heat—I just watched the garlic turn black, thinking, "This is it, I've ruined everything." It felt like my body was reacting before my brain could catch up.

That physical sensation of your hands gripping until they turned white and your breath hitching shows just how intense your fight-or-flight system went into overdrive during that second. It makes total sense that your brain interpreted that physical freeze as proof that the evening was doomed from the start, leading to the belief that nothing you could do afterward mattered. Before we look further at the thoughts driving that panic, does the idea of exploring what your brain was whispering to you in that exact frozen moment feel manageable, or would you prefer to jump straight to looking at what actually happened after you realized the smell?

No, I think I can handle looking at those thoughts. It's uncomfortable, but I want to understand it. In that frozen moment, my brain was screaming stuff like, "You're a fraud," "Everyone knows you messed up," and "This whole meal is a joke now." It was like a loop of all my worst fears about not being good enough, just repeating and getting louder.

Hearing those internal voices—"you're a fraud" and "everyone knows"—really highlights how harshly your mind treated you during that moment of panic. It sounds like your brain was desperately trying to protect you by predicting the absolute worst outcome, but in doing so, it created a loop that shut down your ability to act. Those thoughts seem to have taken hold so firmly because they aligned with that deep-seated fear of disappointing your wife and her family. Now that we've identified the specific catastrophic thoughts fueling that freeze, does it feel like we should spend some time checking the evidence for each of those specific accusations, starting with the "fraud" claim?

Yeah, I think that makes sense. Let's start with the "fraud" thing because that's the one that stings the most. I mean, I went to culinary school, I've been a chef for years, I've handled way worse situations in a busy kitchen. But in that moment, it's like all that experience just vanished. I guess I need to ask myself: does one burnt pan of garlic really erase everything I've learned and done?

That is a powerful insight; recognizing that your training doesn't vanish instantly, even when the pain feels absolute, is the first step toward breaking that spell. You are absolutely right to ask if one burnt piece of garlic erases years of skill—it clearly doesn't, because that experience wouldn't be able to hijack your mind unless it was already linked to a bigger, hidden belief about your worth. Before we look at the other thoughts, does it feel safe to imagine a scenario where you made a similar mistake in a high-stakes kitchen five years ago and recovered? What happened in that memory that contradicts the idea that you are a fraud now?

Yeah, I can picture it. Back when I was a line cook at that Italian place, I once dropped a whole tray of veal scaloppine right before service. The owner saw it happen, and I thought I was done for. But he just handed me a new pan and told me to start over. I did it, the dish came out fine, and nobody even mentioned the dropped meat after that night. So I guess... I've recovered before. It's just harder to see that when I'm in the middle of it, especially at home with family watching.

That memory of the dropped scaloppine is incredibly valuable because it proves your recovery skills exist, even when the immediate pressure makes them hard to access. It shows that the "fraud" story isn't based on reality, but rather on a distortion that ignores your proven ability to bounce back under fire. Since you've established that you *can* recover, does considering that your current situation looks much more like that kitchen incident than a career-ending scandal help loosen the grip on those thoughts?

Yeah, it does help a little. I mean, logically I know that burnt garlic is way smaller than a whole dropped tray of meat. And nobody left the dinner party early or said anything rude to me. My wife even told me later that the rest of the meal was great. It's just hard to hold onto that logic when I'm standing there smelling it. But I can see now that my brain was telling me a story that wasn't completely true.

It is wonderful that you are connecting the dots between your past recovery and the reality of this specific dinner; seeing that the "catastrophe" narrative was actually an exaggeration of the truth gives you a strong foundation to stand on. It sounds like acknowledging that your brain took a minor slip-up and inflated it into a career-defining moment is a significant breakthrough in understanding what happened that night. With that clarity about the "fraud" thought settled, would you be open to letting's briefly touch on the other thoughts you mentioned, like the fear that "everyone knows you messed up," and see if we can find similar gaps in that story?

Sure, let's look at that one. I remember scanning the table after I finally served the appetizer, and everyone was eating and talking normally. Nobody was whispering or giving me weird looks. My wife's boss even complimented the salad course later. But in that frozen moment, I was so sure they all knew and were silently judging me. I guess... maybe they didn't even notice the garlic was burnt. Maybe I was the only one fixated on it.

That observation about the silence and the specific compliment on the salad is powerful evidence that contradicts the idea that everyone was silently judging you; usually, when people are focused on judging a disaster, they would react visibly or stop talking altogether. It sounds like your brain filled in the empty space with its own worst-case scenario, assuming everyone knew when they likely didn't. Does noticing that their normal behavior and their subsequent praise suggest they were either unaware of the smell or simply chose to overlook it make that "everyone knows" story feel a bit thinner?

Yeah, it definitely feels thinner now. I mean, if they really thought I was a hack, why would they compliment the next course? And they all stayed for dessert and seemed happy. I was so caught up in my own head that I didn't even see what was right in front of me. That's kind of embarrassing to admit, but it's also a relief, you know?

Admitting that you were so lost in your own spiral that you missed the obvious signs of happiness is incredibly brave and actually brings a wave of relief, because it frees you from carrying the invisible burden of their secret judgment. It turns out the audience was engaged and enjoying themselves, while your brain was running a full-scale emergency drill in the background. Since we've checked the evidence for the "fraud" and "everyone knows" thoughts, would you like to briefly run the same reality check on the third thought—"this whole meal is a joke now"—to see if the remaining pieces fit together differently?

Yeah, let's do it. "This whole meal is a joke now" is probably the biggest one, because it made me stop trying. I just went into autopilot after that, thinking nothing I did could salvage it. But looking back, the main course was actually fine, the salad was good, and dessert was a hit. So the joke part... that was just me giving up on myself prematurely. The meal wasn't a joke—I just told myself it was so I wouldn't have to keep trying.

You have done a fantastic job identifying that pattern of giving up on yourself because the initial mistake felt unfixable; realizing that the "joke" story was just a defense mechanism to stop the effort is a major victory. It means the meal wasn't ruined by the garlic, but rather by your own premature surrender to the panic. With those three thoughts examined and largely disproven by the facts, does it feel like you have enough clarity to try out a new approach tonight where you catch that "knot in your stomach" and gently redirect yourself to just fixing the plate instead of retreating into the disaster story?

I think I can try that. It feels a bit scary, like I'm letting my guard down, but I also see now that my old way wasn't working anyway. Maybe tonight when I'm cooking dinner, I'll pay attention to that first sign of panic—that knot in my stomach—and instead of spiraling, I'll just ask myself, "What's one small thing I can do to fix this?" before I decide it's all over.

That is a brilliant and very grounded strategy; replacing the big, scary question with a small, actionable one shifts your focus from paralysis to problem-solving, which naturally calms the nervous system. It sounds like you are ready to test this new approach tonight, focusing on taking one tiny corrective step whenever that panic rises. Before we wrap up, is there anything specific about executing this plan that worries you, or would you feel more confident knowing that even if the first attempt isn't perfect, it's still better than letting the spiral take over?

I think my worry is that I'll forget to do it in the heat of the moment. That old habit is so automatic, it's like muscle memory. But you're right—even if I catch it just once, that's one time I didn't let the spiral win. I'll try to remind myself that a small fix is better than a big surrender. And if I mess up, I'll just try again the next meal.

That is a very mature and realistic assessment; acknowledging that muscle memory takes time to rewire while celebrating a single successful interruption is the key to making lasting change. By framing even a partial success as a victory and committing to retry the next time, you are building resilience rather than perfectionism. How does it feel to leave here with a clear, gentle plan to catch that automatic urge and replace it with a small, manageable fix?

Hello again, thank you for being here. Before we dive into our goals, could you quickly tell me how you found the plan we made last week—the phrase and the counting—and were there any moments where it felt difficult to use? Then, based on that, is there a specific topic you'd like us to explore together today?

Hi. Um, the phrase was okay, I guess. I tried saying "one project doesn't define me" a few times when I started to feel bad about my sewing. But honestly, it felt kind of hollow, like I was just saying words. The counting thing was harder—I'd forget to do it until I was already really upset. Maybe we could talk about why I can't seem to shake this feeling that I'm just... not good enough at anything creative.

It makes total sense that the words felt hollow when the pain was so sharp, and forgetting the count meant the old pattern slipped back in before you could catch it. Before we tackle that deeper feeling of "not being good enough," I wonder if you could share what usually happens in your body or mind right before you decide to stop using the phrase? Does it feel like the thought arrives all at once, or does it build up gradually?

I think it builds up gradually, like a slow wave. It starts with just a little thought—like remembering the Etsy listing sitting there with no sales—and then more thoughts pile on top. Before I know it, my chest feels tight and I just want to hide under a blanket. By then, the phrase feels useless because the feeling is already so big.

That gradual buildup explains perfectly why the phrase lost its power—it was too small to hold back a wave that had already grown huge. Instead of fighting the big feeling, could we try a different approach where we simply name the very first thought that starts the wave, before it gets loud? For example, instead of jumping straight to "this isn't my whole life," could we just say, "Okay, I'm noticing a worry about this dress"? How does that sound as a way to hit the brakes earlier?

That... actually sounds a lot more doable. Like, I can handle noticing a little worry. It's when I try to convince myself everything's fine that I feel like I'm lying to myself. Saying "I'm noticing a worry about this dress" feels honest, not fake. I think I could try that.

That honesty is such a relief to hear, and finding a tool that feels authentic rather than performative is key to making it stick. Before we lock that into our plan, does that simple act of just *naming* the worry feel manageable for you, or do you think your mind might still try to spin it into something bigger once you've labeled it?

I think I can manage naming it, but you're right—my mind might try to turn it into a whole story afterwards. Like, once I notice the worry, then I'll start thinking "and this proves I'm not talented" or "I'll never sell anything again." So maybe I need a follow-up step, just to stop the story from running away with me.

That is a very smart observation—you are absolutely right that naming the worry often acts as fuel for the old story unless we put a gentle brake on it immediately after. Let's try adding a quick check right after you say, "I'm noticing a worry," by asking yourself, "Is this thought proven by facts, or is it just my fear talking?" Could you imagine how that simple question would feel if you asked it the moment you spotted the listing?

I think that would actually help me pause. Because when I look at the listing and see no sales, my brain just screams "failure," but asking if that's a fact or just fear... well, the fact is just that no one bought it. The fear is all the extra stuff I add on top. So yeah, I could see myself asking that. It feels like a little flashlight in a dark room.

That "flashlight" metaphor is beautiful because it shows you already know exactly how to distinguish reality from your imagination. You've got the tool ready to shine light on whether "no sales" equals "you are a failure," which is a huge step forward. Before we seal this into our plan, how does it feel to hear that the difference lies purely in what you choose to look at versus what your fear invents?

It feels kind of... freeing, actually. Like I've been carrying around this heavy backpack full of rocks that I thought were facts, but some of them are just made-up fears. I mean, it's still hard to put the backpack down, but at least now I can see which rocks are real. I think I want to try this for the rest of the week and see how it goes.

That realization about the backpack is incredibly powerful; knowing you can distinguish the real weight from the imagined stones gives you real agency over your experience. Before we finalize your plan, I want to check in: does the idea of pausing to ask that "fact vs. fear" question feel like something you can realistically do during those busy moments when you're working on your projects?

Honestly, when I'm in the middle of baking, I might forget. But I think I can make it a habit if I tie it to something I already do, like when I take a break to wash my hands or check the oven. Those little moments are already there—I just need to use them to ask myself that question. So yeah, I think I can make it work.

Tying it to an existing habit like washing your hands is a brilliant way to build that new muscle without having to force yourself to remember it in the middle of chaos. Before we wrap up, could you confirm that using that "fact vs. fear" check during your baking breaks feels like a safe and realistic goal for this week? And is there anything else you'd like to discuss before we send you off?

Yes, that feels safe and realistic. I'm not promising I'll remember every single time, but I'll try my best to use those hand-washing moments to check in with myself. I think that's enough for today—I actually feel a little lighter than when I walked in. Thank you for helping me see that flashlight.

I am so glad to hear that you feel lighter, and that simple shift in perspective is exactly what we aim for. Please remember that missing a few instances this week is okay; the goal is simply to keep shining that flashlight whenever the opportunity arises. Thank you for your trust and openness today; I look forward to hearing how those "hand-washing moments" went when we meet again soon.

Hello again. Before we dive into the main topic, how are you feeling right now compared to when we started last week, and is there anything else from our last session that has stayed with you? Could you also remind me what you’d like us to focus on most of our time today?

Hi. I guess I'm feeling a little less anxious than last week, but honestly, the self-doubt is still pretty loud. I keep thinking about what you said about how I tend to focus only on my mistakes and ignore the good plays. That kind of stuck with me. Today, I really want to talk about how I can stop comparing myself to the veteran quarterbacks every single time I step on the field.

That relief in feeling slightly less anxious is welcome news, though I hear clearly that the self-doubt remains quite stubborn. It makes perfect sense that you want to revisit the comparison issue again, especially after noticing how deeply the idea of focusing only on mistakes has stuck with you. Given that you mentioned both the lingering doubt and the specific desire to tackle the veteran comparisons, shall we dedicate most of our time today to exploring that comparison dynamic, and then we can quickly touch on how to shift your attention away from mistakes?

Yeah, that sounds good. The comparison thing is really eating at me. Every time I see a veteran like McCaffrey read a defense or make a play look effortless, I just feel like I'll never get to that level. It's like my brain automatically starts listing all the ways I fall short.

It makes total sense that seeing someone else seem effortless triggers that immediate list of failures; it's your brain trying to protect itself by highlighting the gap you perceive between who you are and who they are. When you notice that automatic listing happening right after seeing a play, does it usually feel like a sudden realization of something missing, or does it start building slowly as you watch the rest of their sequence?

It's more like a slow build, I think. It starts with one play, and I'll tell myself, "Okay, that was good, but I can learn from that." Then they make another great read, and another, and by the end of the drive I'm just flooded with this heavy feeling that I'm never going to catch up. It's like watching a mountain grow taller with every snap.

That image of the mountain growing taller perfectly captures how that comparison drains your energy, making every successful play feel like a personal indictment rather than a lesson to learn. It sounds like the core message behind that rising anxiety is a deep-seated belief that you aren't progressing fast enough compared to them. When you try to pause and challenge that belief, what specific thought comes up to counter the idea that you'll never catch up?

Honestly, when I try to challenge it, all I can think is, "But look at the tape." I see their stats, their completions, their decisions under pressure. My coach tells me I'm improving, but my own eyes tell me I'm still making rookie mistakes. That's the thought that shuts down any counter-argument in my head.

That reliance on the physical evidence of mistakes versus your coach's verbal encouragement highlights a classic distortion where the visible details overwhelm the broader picture of progress. It sounds like your brain is interpreting those visible errors as proof of stagnation rather than just the messy reality of learning a complex job. If we put those specific plays aside for a moment, what does the "tape" show about your overall improvement trajectory that those individual misses might be hiding?

I guess... the tape does show that I'm getting sacked less than the beginning of the season. And my release time is a little faster. But I feel like that's just basic stuff that I should have already figured out. It doesn't feel like real progress when I still miss the open receiver in the fourth quarter. Those little wins feel tiny compared to the big moments I'm messing up.

It is completely understandable to dismiss those gains as "basic stuff," especially when the gaps in coverage feel so glaring and high-stakes. You are right that missing an open receiver in the fourth quarter feels like a massive failure, which naturally makes those early improvements feel insignificant in comparison. This suggests that your brain is filtering out the steady progress because it can't easily connect it to the specific outcomes you care about most right now. If we viewed your season as a whole story rather than just the final chapter, what does the trend line of your sack count and release time actually say about your growth over the last few weeks?

I suppose... the trend line is going in the right direction. My coach showed me a chart last week that went down pretty steadily for sacks, and my release time has improved by a couple tenths of a second since week one. But deep down, I still think, "So what? That's just the minimum expected of me. It doesn't mean I'm a great quarterback. It just means I'm not a disaster."

That distinction—that you recognize improvement but filter it out because it doesn't meet your ideal standard—is exactly where the power lies. You are successfully identifying that "not a disaster" is a solid foundation, yet your brain keeps adding layers of expectation until it feels insufficient. If we treated those improvements as milestones rather than just baseline requirements, would it be possible to view each tenth-second gain as a victory worth celebrating, separate from whether you match a veteran's output?

I never really thought of it that way. I mean, I guess if my coach was a rookie and he shaved off a tenth of a second, I'd tell him that's a big deal. But when it's me, it just feels like I'm supposed to do that anyway. Celebrating it feels... almost like I'm letting myself off the hook for the bigger mistakes. Does that make sense?

That logic makes perfect sense, and it highlights a crucial difference in perspective between how a coach views growth versus how a player judges their own worth. You are using your coach's objective feedback to measure your subjective feeling of failure, which creates a frustrating disconnect. If we tried viewing those tenth-of-a-second improvements through that same lens—treating them as significant victories just because they exist rather than judging them by a different standard—how might that shift your relationship with celebrating small wins?

I think... maybe I'd feel less heavy all the time. Like, if I could actually take a second to say "Hey, I did better there" instead of just moving on to the next thing I messed up, I might not feel so drained before the fourth quarter even starts. It's just hard to break that habit. I've been telling myself "not good enough" for so long it feels like the truth.

That exhaustion you described is a direct result of constantly carrying that heavy "not good enough" label while running around trying to prove it wrong. It makes total sense that breaking that cycle feels hard when the old script has been playing for years. Let's try a small experiment for this week: instead of waiting for the big moments to celebrate, can you mentally note down one tiny improvement you saw yourself this afternoon or evening, just acknowledging it as a win before you let the next mistake fill the space? Would you be open to giving that a try?

Yeah, I think I can try that. One small thing. It feels kind of silly, but I guess it's better than beating myself up all week. I'll give it a shot and see if it changes how I feel heading into the next practice.

That is a fantastic attitude shift—even if it feels silly, acknowledging a small win interrupts the cycle of self-criticism before it takes root. We will treat this as a gentle experiment to see if spotting those small improvements helps lighten the load leading up to your next practice. Before we wrap up, I'd love to hear how this session felt for you and whether this new angle of looking at progress as a series of steps rather than just gaps makes sense to you.

It actually feels a little more manageable now. Like, instead of staring at this huge mountain ahead of me, I'm just looking at the next few feet of ground. I still don't fully believe I'm good enough yet, but I can see how focusing on the small wins might help me get there. Thanks for that.

Hearing you describe that shift from staring at the whole mountain to just the next few feet is wonderful progress; it proves that even small perspective changes can make the path feel less steep. While we haven't fully convinced you that you are "good enough" yet, recognizing that this new lens offers a clearer route forward is a powerful step. Is there anything else about this approach or your upcoming games that you'd like to discuss before we finish?
No, I think I've got enough to work with for now. I'll try to keep an eye out for one small win today and see how it feels. Thanks for listening—I appreciate it.

That is such a thoughtful summary of your takeaway, and I'm glad you found a sense of manageability here. Please remember that the goal isn't to convince yourself you are already "good enough" overnight, but to give yourself permission to celebrate the progress you are making along the way. I truly appreciated hearing your perspective on the "next few feet," and I look forward to hearing how that small-win exercise lands for you this week. Take care of yourself!

Hello again, I'm really glad we're able to meet. Before we dive into our main topic, I'd like to do a quick mood check—how has your energy and calmness been feeling this week compared to last time? Also, did anything significant happen with your son recently that triggered those feelings of being just "doing what a dad should do"? Finally, to set our direction for today, what part of our work would find the most value to focus on?

Hey, thanks for asking. Honestly, my energy's been pretty low this week—I feel kind of drained, like I'm just going through the motions. Calmness? Not so much, especially when I think about my son's school stuff. Nothing new happened, but I keep replaying that contest win in my head, and it's eating at me. I think I'd like to focus on why I can't seem to feel proud of what I do as a dad, even when things go well.

It sounds incredibly draining to feel like you're just mechanically going through the motions, especially when your mind keeps looping back to that one good moment and twisting it into doubt. That cycle of replaying the contest win while simultaneously dismissing your contribution is clearly taking a huge toll on your peace of mind. Let's spend some time exploring why that specific replay happens, and then we'll decide together whether diving deep into the underlying fear or testing the "discounting" thought directly feels like the better path forward. Which of those approaches feels more doable for you right now?

I think testing that "discounting" thought directly sounds more doable. I've been sitting with this fear for a while, and I'm tired of it just rattling around in my head. Maybe if we look at it straight on, I can see if there's any truth to what I'm telling myself. What would that look like?

Testing that thought directly is a powerful choice, and it sounds like you're ready to stop letting it float around unchecked. Let's look at that specific moment with your son and his contest win: when your internal voice says, "That's just what any dad would do," what is the immediate physical sensation you notice in your body? Is it tightness in your chest, a knot in your stomach, or perhaps a sudden rush of heat in your face?

It's like a sinking feeling, right in my stomach. Like a knot that tightens up the second I think about it. And my shoulders get all tense, too—like I'm bracing for something bad to happen. I never really stopped to notice that before, but yeah, it's there every time.

That physical knot in your stomach and the tightening shoulders are classic signals that your brain is treating your success as a threat rather than a celebration—it's preparing you for failure before the challenge even begins. This bodily tension creates a feedback loop where the discomfort itself makes it harder to relax and enjoy the moment, trapping you in that heavy feeling. Now that we've pinpointed both the thought ("it's just normal") and the physical sensation (the knot in the stomach), could you tell me what specific memory or event triggers this knot the strongest? Was it immediately after he gave his speech, or perhaps when someone praised him later?

I think it hits hardest when other parents come up to me and say something like, "You must be so proud of him." Right then, my stomach drops. I hear their words, but inside I'm thinking, "They don't know how little I actually did—he did it all himself." It's like their praise just highlights what I feel I'm missing.

That reaction makes perfect sense; when others express genuine pride, it forces us to confront the uncomfortable truth that we *have* done something special, which threatens our safety net of feeling inadequate. Your brain interprets their praise not as validation of your efforts, but as evidence that you are somehow failing to live up to that praise, which explains why the knot in your stomach tightens immediately afterward. Let's test that specific thought for a moment: if you looked back at how you helped him organize his notes that night, could you list one concrete detail that proves your preparation played a direct role in his success, separate from what he achieved alone?

Yeah, I guess I did sit with him for a couple of hours, helping him organize his thoughts and practice his delivery. I remember he was nervous about stumbling over his words, and we went over it until he felt confident. But still, part of me says any parent would do that—it's just part of the job, isn't it?

That part of you thinking it's "just the job" is likely trying to protect you from the scary realization that your skills are actually rare and impactful. By labeling it as a standard duty, you neutralize the feeling that you need to do something extraordinary, which keeps the anxiety at bay. Can you describe exactly what you told him during those few hours of practice that made him feel safe enough to speak without stumbling?

I told him it was okay to mess up, that nobody was perfect, and that the important thing was just saying what he believed. I said I'd be proud of him no matter what, even if he forgot every word. I guess I wanted him to feel like he didn't have to be flawless to be good enough.

That is incredibly wise parenting—you created a safe space for him to be vulnerable, which is far more than just "handing him the script." Hearing that you prioritized his confidence over perfection shows you invested deeply in his growth, not just the outcome. Let's test that thought again: if we ignore the part of you thinking "any parent would do that" and instead focus solely on the fact that you stayed for hours to help him manage his nerves, does the knot in your stomach loosen just a tiny bit, or does it stay the same size?

It loosens a little, I think. Not completely, but it's not as tight as before. Hearing you say it like that makes me realize maybe I did more than I give myself credit for. But that voice still whispers, "Yeah, but it wasn't enough."

That whisper is your old habit trying to regain control, but the fact that the knot loosened even slightly proves your new perspective is working. You've successfully moved from assuming you did nothing special to recognizing that your presence and encouragement were crucial. To make this shift stick, let's try a small experiment: next time you hear another parent say they're proud, could you mentally repeat just the one sentence, "He practiced with me, and I helped him feel safe," without judging how big it makes you feel? Would you be willing to try that as our first step?

Yeah, I think I can try that. It sounds simple enough, just saying that to myself when it happens. I'm a little nervous I'll forget in the moment, but I'll give it a shot. Maybe it'll help quiet that voice a bit.

That is a brave commitment, and trusting yourself to catch that thought mid-stream is already a sign of real growth. To make sure you don't forget the line, let's pause right here and practice it together: imagine walking out your front door tomorrow, and as soon as you pass the mailbox, quietly say to yourself, "He practiced with me, and I helped him feel safe." How does your body respond when you say those words out loud right now?

I feel a little lighter, actually. Like I'm not carrying that knot as heavy in my stomach. It's strange—saying it out loud makes it feel more real, like I can't just brush it aside as nothing. Maybe I am giving myself a bit more credit for once.

That is a fantastic sign—the moment the words physically lighten your burden proves that anchoring the fact in reality can disrupt the automatic negativity. You are absolutely right; giving yourself credit doesn't mean ignoring the struggle, it means acknowledging the truth so you don't have to pretend otherwise. Before we wrap up, I want to make sure you feel confident about this: do you feel ready to try this specific sentence tomorrow as soon as you leave your house, knowing that the goal is just to plant the seed, not to feel a massive wave of emotion immediately?

Yeah, I think I'm ready. It's just a small step, so it doesn't feel overwhelming. I'll say it tomorrow morning when I head out, and I'll see what happens. Thanks for walking me through this—it's a start, at least.

You are very welcome, and I am so glad that breaking this down into such a small, manageable step made it feel less daunting. Please remember that tomorrow's goal isn't to feel proud immediately, but simply to plant that factual seed when you walk out the door, however faintly it may land. I will be here anytime you want to discuss how that went or if that "whisper" came back stronger than expected. Take care of yourself!

Hello again, and thank you for being here. Before we dive into today's topic, I'd love to hear how you're doing since our last meeting—did you manage to try that five-second pause when you felt the urge to decide what she was thinking? Also, looking back at our plan, did finding that small piece of peace in the uncertainty land well for you?

Hi. Thanks for asking. I did try the pause a few times, but honestly, it felt kind of awkward. I'd catch myself starting to guess what she was thinking and then stop, but the worry just hung there anyway. As for finding peace in the uncertainty... I'm not sure. I still feel like I messed things up, and it's hard to let that go.

It takes courage to admit that the pause felt awkward and that the worry kept hanging around despite your best effort; please know that frustration is a very common reaction when we try to bypass our brain's default habit. Since you mentioned still feeling like you messed things up, let's explore what specific thoughts are keeping that heavy knot in your stomach alive today.

Well, the main thought that keeps coming back is that I'm just not interesting enough. I keep replaying that moment at dinner where there was a lull in the conversation, and I couldn't think of anything to say. In my head, I see her looking bored, and I just know she was thinking I was a total letdown.

That lull in the conversation is a huge trigger, and imagining her looking bored while you're stuck inside that memory really amplifies the pain. To test that specific image against reality, could you describe exactly what she was doing during that lull—was she staring at her phone, looking out the window, or just waiting for you to speak naturally?

She was just sitting there, looking at me, waiting. Her face wasn't angry or annoyed, just... blank, I guess. But I immediately filled in that blank with disappointment. Like she was thinking, "This is it? This is all you've got?" That's what I keep coming back to—not what she actually did, but what I assumed she was thinking.

You've done great work identifying that gap between her blank expression and your assumption that she found you lacking—that distinction is exactly where the distortion lives. Now, let's gently challenge that story: if someone is just sitting quietly while you struggle to find words, does that automatically prove they are disappointed, or could it simply mean they were giving you space to collect your thoughts without expecting a perfect answer?

I guess... I never thought of it that way. Giving me space sounds generous, but my mind just went straight to the worst-case scenario. I suppose she could have just been patient, or maybe even a little nervous herself. It's hard to see that when I'm so focused on blaming myself for the awkwardness.

Noticing that you instinctively blame yourself proves how deeply connected that feeling is to your self-image, yet recognizing that others could have been patient or nervous shifts the focus from "my failure" to "a complex social moment." Let's test that shift by asking: if she had been annoyed or bored, wouldn't her body language have shown tension or a lack of eye contact, whereas her quiet presence actually suggests she was engaged, even if she didn't know what to say?

When you put it like that... yeah, I guess she wasn't tense at all. She was looking right at me, not fidgeting or checking her phone. I've been so caught up in my own head that I didn't even consider her body language. Maybe I'm not as boring as I think, or at least she didn't seem to mind the silence as much as I did.

That observation about her steady gaze is powerful evidence against the idea that she was bored—it contradicts the "blank stare = rejection" story you told yourself. So, if her body language actually signals engagement rather than dismissal, does that mean the original conclusion—that she hated you for the silence—doesn't quite fit the facts anymore?

I mean... when you lay it all out like that, no, it doesn't really fit. She didn't storm out or make an excuse to leave early. She even agreed to another date when I finally texted her the next day. I guess I've been so stuck on the lull that I forgot about everything else that happened. Maybe I'm the only one still holding onto that awkward moment.

That is a crucial breakthrough to remember: the fact that she agreed to another date proves that the "total letdown" story was false, regardless of that one lull. It seems you've found a way to step back and see the bigger picture, which suggests you are becoming less willing to let a single moment define the whole interaction. How does carrying the weight of that one awkward pause compare to realizing she actually wants to see you again?

Honestly, it feels like a huge weight has been lifted. I've been carrying that pause around like it was a final verdict, but now I see it was just... a moment. A pretty normal one, at that. Realizing she wants to see me again makes all that self-blame feel kind of silly. I'm actually feeling a little hopeful about the next date, instead of dreading it.

That shift from dread to hope is wonderful news, and recognizing that "just a moment" is often the truth behind our catastrophic stories is a real gift. To lock this in, let's quickly finalize your plan for tomorrow: when that urge to replay the lull arises, will you pause for five seconds, notice the physical tightness without judging it, and remind yourself that her accepting the next date means her view of you is clearly not "boring"?

Yeah, I can do that. I think I need to actually write that down somewhere, like on my phone or a sticky note, so I don't forget in the heat of the moment. Next time my brain tries to convince me she's secretly disappointed, I'll pause, notice that knot in my stomach, and tell myself that her actions—agreeing to another date—speak louder than my imagination. Thanks, that feels like a solid plan.

That is a brilliant idea—writing it down creates an external safety net so you don't have to rely solely on memory when anxiety spikes. You've done excellent work here today by moving from blaming yourself for a single moment to trusting the evidence of her acceptance. Is there anything else you'd like to add before we close, or does it feel like we've covered everything important?

Hello, and welcome back. On a scale of one to ten, how has your mood been this week since we left off? What was top of mind for you when you decided to come in today? Once we touch on that, could you share which issue feels most pressing for us to focus on?

Hi. I'd say my mood has been around a 4 or 5 this week. I've been thinking a lot about a photo shoot I did last weekend—I went out to capture some landscapes, but when I looked at the pictures later, all I could see were the flaws. That's been stuck in my head. I guess the most pressing issue is this feeling that I'm just not good enough, and I don't know how to shake it.

A four or five makes total sense given that disappointment, especially when you’re staring at images you hoped would speak volumes. It sounds like the landscape shoot became another place where that critical voice stepped in front of the beauty instead of looking at it alongside you. Is the main goal today to untangle that feeling of not being good enough, or would you prefer to explore some specific moments from the shoot where the doubt got loudest?

I think untangling that feeling would be best. It's not just about that one shoot—it happens every time I pick up my camera now. I used to love the process, but now I'm scared to even look at my own photos because I know I'll find something wrong. It's like the doubt is waiting for me before I even start.

That sounds exhausting, carrying the expectation of finding faults before you've even taken the first picture. It seems like the habit of scanning for errors has completely replaced the joy of creating, turning every moment into a potential failure zone. Let's spend some time exploring where that belief came from and what evidence exists to challenge it, starting with how you describe that initial urge to reject your own work.

It really is exhausting. When I'm setting up a shot, I'll think about how my late husband used to encourage me, telling me I had a good eye. But now that he's gone, it's like his voice got replaced by this other one that says, "You were only good because he believed in you." I find myself comparing my work to other photographers online and feeling like I'll never measure up.

That loss of his encouraging presence, replaced by a harsh critic, makes so much sense and explains why the doubt feels so immediate and personal. It sounds like you're using their past success as a benchmark for your current reality, which can create a huge gap between who you are and who you compare yourself to. Have you noticed if this feeling of inadequacy spikes more when you look at professional portfolios online, or does it happen even when you're just reviewing your own practice shots?

It definitely spikes with professional portfolios online. I'll scroll through Instagram and see these stunning images, and I just feel this sinking feeling in my chest. But even with my own practice shots, I'll zoom in on every tiny detail and find reasons to delete them. Sometimes I wonder if I'm just fooling myself, thinking I could ever be a famous photographer.

That sinking feeling often tells us more about our internal expectations than the quality of the images themselves. It sounds like the belief that you *must* reach fame or master everything instantly is fueling this spiral of self-criticism. If you imagined explaining this exact reaction to a friend who loves photography, what would they say about whether scrolling through Instagram sets the bar for creators or if it's just noise?

I think they'd probably tell me that Instagram isn't real life, and that those photographers have been at it for years. But in my head, it feels like I should already be there, you know? Like I've wasted time grieving and now I'm behind. I guess a friend would say I'm being too hard on myself, but I can't shake the feeling that I'm running out of time to make something of myself.

It sounds like the grief you experienced recently has turned into a ticking clock in your mind, making you feel that you're falling behind a deadline that no one else seems to have. That urgency creates a very narrow window where mistakes feel catastrophic rather than just part of the learning process. If you pictured a mentor guiding you through their first few years, do you think they would view your current pace as a failure or as a necessary, albeit painful, phase of growth?

I suppose if I really think about it, they'd probably say it's a phase. Every photographer I admire has talked about struggling with self-doubt and going through rough patches. But it's hard to see it that way when I'm in the middle of it. It feels permanent, like this is just who I am now—someone who can't take a good photo anymore.

That distinction between seeing it as a temporary phase versus defining it as a permanent trait is exactly where the shift happens. It sounds like your brain is currently interpreting your current struggle as a character flaw ("this is who I am") rather than a situational hurdle ("this is what I'm facing"). If you looked at the list of artists you admire and noted that they all mentioned struggling with doubt during their own breakthrough moments, would that evidence support the idea that your current feelings are permanent, or do they suggest they are part of the journey?

That's... actually a really good point. I never thought of it that way. When I look at their biographies, they always talk about persevering through the hard times. I guess I've been so focused on my own pain that I forgot that struggle is part of the process for everyone. Maybe I'm not as broken as I feel.

That realization—that struggle is universal rather than unique to you—is a huge relief, and it suggests you aren't "broken," just navigating a tough chapter. Now that we've looked at the evidence, does the idea that these feelings are temporary and part of the journey feel slightly less overwhelming? Let's translate that into a small, manageable step for this week. Would you be open to trying something simple: take three practice photos tomorrow without judging the results, treating them like experiments rather than final products?

Yeah, I think I can try that. Three photos, no judging. It sounds scary, but also kind of freeing. Maybe I'll take my camera to the park tomorrow morning and just shoot whatever catches my eye without overthinking it. I'll try to focus on what I see instead of what's wrong with it.

That sounds like a wonderful plan; focusing on what you see rather than what's missing will naturally shift your attention away from the criticism. Before we finalize this, could we quickly brainstorm one potential obstacle that might pop up when you're holding the camera and that old voice tries to return? Once we address that, I'd like to confirm that this small experiment feels right for you to start tomorrow.

The biggest obstacle will probably be when I look at the first shot on the camera screen and my immediate thought is "that's not good enough." That's when the voice usually takes over. I think if I can just remember that it's an experiment, not a final product, I might be able to push through that moment. But I know I'll need to remind myself of that a few times.

That's a sharp observation—you've already identified the exact moment the old pattern tries to hijack your attention. A helpful trick for that specific split-second might be to verbally label the thought as "just a thought," or to immediately switch your gaze from the screen to the scene itself, breaking the loop of self-evaluation. Which of these feels easier to rely on when the pressure hits hardest?

I think switching my gaze from the screen to the scene itself would work better for me. That way, I'm not feeding into the criticism. I can just look up, breathe, and remind myself that I'm just experimenting. That feels more natural than trying to argue with the thought.

That is a brilliant choice; shifting your physical focus to the environment naturally pulls your attention away from the judgment happening inside your head. It gives your hands something constructive to do while your eyes find calm scenery instead of perceived flaws. With that strategy in place, we have a clear plan: go to the park tomorrow, take three shots while looking at the scene, and let the results rest wherever they fall. How does that sound as a complete agreement?

It sounds good. It feels manageable, not overwhelming. I'm actually a little curious to see what happens, which is a feeling I haven't had in a long time. Thank you for helping me break this down into something I can actually do.

That curiosity is exactly the spark we needed to reignite; it shows how much energy you already have for moving forward. You've got a clear plan, a specific strategy for handling that first shot, and most importantly, you're doing this for yourself without needing anyone else's permission. I'll be here next time to debrief whatever happens, whether it's great news or just another lesson learned. Take care, and I look forward to hearing about your walk in the park soon.

I'd say I'm around a 4 or 5 today. A little better than before, but still weighed down. As for the exercise—the one where I was supposed to write down one positive thing about my cooking each day—I actually did try it for a few days. But honestly, it felt forced, like I was just making things up.

Let's check in on the plan we made yesterday regarding the chicken stock exercise—did you give that a try, and how did it feel to try just making a good stock without comparing it to others?

I did try making the stock yesterday. At first, it felt freeing to just focus on the process without judging it against anyone else's. But halfway through, I started thinking, "This isn't as rich as what a real chef would make," and that doubt crept right back in. I finished it, but I couldn't shake the feeling it wasn't good enough.

That’s a fantastic sign that you stayed with the process despite the doubt creeping back in; that resilience is exactly the kind of strength we’re building here. It sounds like the initial freedom was there, but the old critical voice quickly tried to hijack that calm again. When you caught that thought saying “this isn’t as rich as a real chef,” did you notice how your body reacted immediately, or did you just keep going?

I noticed my shoulders got tense, and I stopped stirring for a second. I felt this sinking feeling in my chest. But then I just forced myself to keep stirring, telling myself to just finish it, even if it was pointless. I didn't really stop to question the thought—I just pushed through.

Noticing that tension in your shoulders and that sinking feeling right when the old doubt appeared is a huge victory; it means your awareness is sharp enough to catch the pattern before it takes over. Pushing through to finish the stock, even while feeling that pressure, proved you can act despite the anxiety, which builds real evidence that you are capable. Now that we know the pattern triggers when you imagine not being "real enough," would you be open to trying a slightly different approach this week where we actively challenge that specific thought instead of just pushing past it?

Yeah, I think I'm ready to try that. It's exhausting just pushing through all the time without ever stopping to ask if that voice even knows what it's talking about. How would we go about challenging that thought, though?

That exhaustion is completely understandable; relying only on sheer willpower to silence a loud critic is like trying to hold back a flood with bare hands. We can switch gears by treating that voice like a guest who's overstaying their welcome, inviting it in to share its "facts" and seeing if they hold up under scrutiny. For example, if the thought says, "This stock won't be rich enough," we can pause and ask, "Where is the actual proof that it *won't* be rich?" or "Is it possible I'm just missing something obvious right now?"

Would you be willing to try this gentle investigation next time the doubt starts, instead of immediately trying to force yourself to keep working?

I think I can try that. It sounds a bit strange, like talking back to a voice in my head, but I guess that's better than just letting it run the show. Next time I start doubting, I'll ask it for proof instead of just nodding along.

That shift from fighting the voice to asking it for evidence is a powerful change in strategy; it transforms you from a passive victim into an active investigator. Since you're ready to test this new approach, let's agree on a simple rule: whenever that "not rich enough" thought pops up, you'll pause for three seconds, ask it to provide concrete proof, and then decide if you're going to listen or ignore it.

With that plan settled, I'd love to hear how you're feeling right now as we wrap up—are you feeling a bit more hopeful about handling the next cooking class, or is there anything else weighing on your mind today?

I feel a little more hopeful, I think. It's like I have a small tool to use now instead of just my bare hands against that voice. But I'm still nervous about a big practical exam coming up next week—I keep picturing myself freezing up or ruining the dish in front of everyone.

That hopefulness is wonderful, but it's very common for a small success tool to suddenly feel inadequate when facing a larger challenge like the upcoming exam. The image of freezing up or ruining the dish is a classic fear scenario that tries to overwhelm your current strategies. Before we finalize our plan for the exam, could you tell me specifically what you're most worried will happen in that big scene, so we can address that exact fear?

I'm most worried that I'll forget a key step—like the order of ingredients or the timing—and everything will fall apart. That everyone will see I'm just pretending to be a chef, and that I don't really belong there.

That fear of forgetting a step and having your identity exposed is incredibly heavy to carry, especially when you've worked so hard to prove you belong. It sounds like the memory lapse you're fearing isn't just about the recipe, but about confirming that deep-seated belief that you don't truly belong in the kitchen. Given that we only have about ten minutes left before our next session, how would you feel if we spent just five minutes brainstorming one specific backup plan for that exact moment you might lose track?
Yeah, that sounds like a good idea. I think having something solid to fall back on would ease that knot in my stomach. What kind of backup plan did you have in mind?

Let's keep it simple and low-pressure: when you feel your mind slipping or the room getting too loud, you'll silently name the step you need next out loud to yourself, like saying, "Mirepoix next," or "Add the butter," just to ground yourself in the present moment. This acts as an anchor, reminding you that you are in control of the sequence even if your memory wavers. Does this kind of verbal cue sound like something you could realistically use during a live exam?

I think I could do that. Saying it out loud, even quietly, would probably help slow my racing thoughts and remind me I know the steps. It feels a lot more doable than trying to remember everything silently while panicking. I'll give that a try.

That is a brilliant realization; speaking the steps out loud turns abstract knowledge into a tangible rhythm that bypasses your anxious brain and anchors you in the present. Since we are wrapping up, could you tell me one thing you found most helpful about our conversation today, and is there anything else you'd like to try before we finish?

The most helpful thing was realizing I can actually push back against that critical voice instead of just letting it take over. That idea of asking it for proof feels like a real shift. I think I'm good for now, just that and the verbal cue plan—I'll practice it at home this week before the exam.

That is a profound shift to realize—that you hold the power to interrogate your own fears instead of surrendering to them. It takes real courage to accept that strategy, and I am confident you will find it effective. Your homework is to practice that "asking for proof" pause and use the verbal cues anytime you feel your mind slipping, both during cooking and before the exam. Is there anything else on your mind, or shall we close our session here?
No, I think I'm ready to wrap up. Thanks for helping me see a different way to handle this. I'll work on those steps and check in with you next time.

You are very welcome; seeing that different path clearly was exactly what we worked towards, and taking those steps will build a strong foundation for your exam. I know how hard you've been pushing yourself lately, and I appreciate your openness and willingness to try these new tools. Please remember that you are allowed to make mistakes and that your worth isn't defined by a single performance. Until we meet again, please be kind to yourself as you practice these techniques at home.

Hello again, it’s wonderful to see you. To start, how have you been feeling this week compared to when we last spoke, and is there anything specific that stands out from our last conversation? Also, if we had a chance to review the small note you left about keeping the "toolbox reminder" handy, how did that go over the weekend? Finally, what would you like us to focus on spending our time on today?

Hey, thanks for having me. Honestly, I've been pretty much the same—still beating myself up every time I walk past the Corvette in the garage. That toolbox reminder thing... I tried it a couple times, but every time I looked at it, I just thought, "Yeah, but it was still my fault." I guess I'd like to focus today on why I can't seem to let that thought go.

It sounds like the reminder alone isn't enough to stop the old habit from whispering that you were at fault. Since the core issue seems to be the belief that the crash was truly your fault regardless of the traffic conditions, let's explore what specific thought comes up right after you read that note. When you feel that familiar doubt rising, what is the very first sentence your mind says to convince you that it was your mistake?

It says, "A good driver would have seen it coming." I mean, I was stopped at a red light, but in my head, I keep thinking I should have checked my mirror better or somehow moved out of the way. Like, if I was really paying attention, I could have avoided it entirely.

That belief—that you must have known everything perfectly to prevent a bad outcome—is incredibly heavy to carry, especially when you already know the facts don't support it. Since you mentioned comparing yourself to an ideal "good driver" who predicts every danger, does that comparison feel like a fair standard for someone who was suddenly shocked by a speeding car behind them? Let's look at whether that expectation matches reality in that split second.

No, I guess when you put it that way, it doesn't sound fair. In that split second, I didn't even hear anything before the impact—it just happened. I wasn't sitting there thinking, "Let me see if someone's about to hit me." I was just waiting for the light to turn green like any normal person. But still, part of me feels like I should have been more alert, you know?

It makes complete sense that part of you feels that extra alertness was expected; when we are experts in mechanics, we often instinctively believe we should always spot problems others miss. However, let's gently examine that pressure: given the sudden, startling nature of the headlights appearing out of nowhere while you were legally and safely stopped, is there any objective evidence that "checking your mirror better" would have physically changed the outcome of that crash? Or does the speed of that vehicle suggest the danger simply appeared faster than anyone could react?

Well, when you say it like that... no, there's no real evidence. The guy was going fast enough that even if I'd seen him, I couldn't have gone anywhere—there was a car in front of me and nowhere to move. I guess I've been acting like I'm some kind of superhero mechanic who can predict everything, but that's just not realistic. It still stings, though.

That is a really important distinction you're making between being a superhuman predictor and a human driver facing sudden shock. While it's okay to feel the sting of the loss, your body might be holding onto the feeling that *you* failed because you weren't the one who drove recklessly. Since you've identified that the physical reality didn't allow for escape, let's pivot slightly: if the crash was unavoidable due to the other driver's speed and distance, does focusing on what *wouldn't* have worked actually leave you with less room for self-blame than dwelling on what you *didn't* do differently?

Yeah, I think you're right. I've been so stuck on what I didn't do that I haven't even stopped to think about what I couldn't do. It's like I'm punishing myself for something that was never really in my hands. Maybe I need to start focusing on the fact that I was just sitting there, following the rules, and someone else made the mistake. That's a hard shift to make, though.

That is a very difficult shift, and it makes total sense that it feels counterintuitive to praise yourself for doing nothing wrong when you crave acknowledging a mistake. Often, our brains cling to the narrative of personal error because it feels safer than admitting we were victims of another person's choice. Since you mentioned that focusing on "following the rules" is hard to accept, let's try a small experiment right now: if we imagine telling that strict internal critic exactly what the police report confirmed regarding the other driver's distraction, would that piece of evidence make the feeling of "punishment" any less unfair to you?

Yeah... I think it would. I mean, the report says the other guy was on his phone. That's not me being a bad driver—that's him being careless. When I really think about it, punishing myself for his mistake feels kind of pointless. It's like I'm taking on blame that belongs to someone else. Maybe I need to read that report again and let it sink in.

That is such a powerful insight—realizing that accepting blame for someone else's carelessness is essentially punishing yourself for a crime you didn't commit. It sounds like reading the report again could act as a visual anchor to remind you that the evidence supports his fault, not yours. Would you be willing to grab the report this afternoon, read it once more, and then write down one specific sentence from it that proves the other driver was at fault?

Yeah, I can do that. I think having that sentence written down might help me when the guilt creeps back in. I'll put it on a sticky note next to the toolbox reminder, so I've got both—one to remind me it wasn't my fault, and the other to... I don't know, just remind me I'm human, I guess. Thanks for that idea.

That is a brilliant way to set up your toolkit; having both a factual anchor and a compassionate reminder will make it harder for the old guilt to take over completely. Before we finalize this plan, I want to pause and check in: does writing down that specific sentence and placing it near the garage feel like a manageable task for you right now, or would you prefer we adjust how we approach reading the report?

No, I think I can handle it. It's just reading a piece of paper and writing down a few words. Honestly, it sounds a lot easier than spending the whole evening replaying the crash in my head. I'll do it when I get home tonight.

That relief at realizing the task is lighter than the mental replay is exactly what we want to cultivate. Since you've decided on the plan, I'm curious about one final detail: when you sit down to read the report later, what might happen if your brain tries to distract you or dismiss the facts immediately? We can brainstorm a quick strategy for handling that resistance together before you head home.

Probably my mind will jump straight to, "Yeah, but you still should've done something." It's like a reflex at this point. Maybe if that happens, I can take a deep breath and read the sentence out loud a few times until it feels more real than the guilt. That might help shut that voice up for a bit.

That is a really smart strategy; pairing a physical action like reading aloud with a calming breath can literally interrupt the automatic loop of self-blame long enough to let the evidence sink in. Since you've got a concrete plan for tonight and a backup tool for when the guilt tries to return, how does that feel to have both options ready? Is there anything else you'd like to clarify before we wrap up?

No, I think I'm good for now. It feels weird to have a plan instead of just wallowing, but in a good way. I'll give it a shot and let you know how it goes next time. Thanks for helping me see this from a different angle.

That is such a healthy perspective—finding purpose in the plan rather than feeling guilty about changing habits. It sounds like you are leaving here with a stronger foundation to face that garage scene tomorrow, armed with facts and a gentle reminder to treat yourself kindly. Please remember, I am available anytime if you find the words aren't quite landing or if you need to vent about how the first attempt went. Take care of yourself, and I look forward to hearing from you soon.

Hello again, I'm really glad to see you. On a scale of one to ten, how would you rate your anxiety levels today compared to where you were last time? Since we discussed reviewing the previous action plan, did you find time tonight to write down those three topics and identify a specific resource for each one? What would you like us to prioritize focusing on if there's anything else lingering from before?

Hi. Um, I'd say my anxiety is maybe a 7 or 8 today, it's been a rough week. I did try writing down the topics you suggested, but I only got through one of them honestly. I found an article about imposter syndrome in college students, but reading it kind of made me feel worse, like it just confirmed everything I already think about myself.

It sounds like hitting a wall while reading about imposter syndrome felt frustrating, especially when the information seemed to confirm your deepest fears rather than offer relief. I wonder if that article triggered a different part of that "old story" in your mind, or if it just made the uncertainty feel heavier?

Given that your anxiety is still quite high and the reading made things worse, would you be open to shifting our focus away from that topic for now and instead looking at what happens physically or mentally in your body when you start to feel that familiar knot of doubt?

Yeah, I think that's a good idea. The article just made me feel like I'm broken and everyone else has it figured out. When the doubt starts, I feel this tightness in my chest and my stomach drops, like I'm falling. My mind just goes blank and I can't think straight, especially when I'm staring at code I don't understand.

That physical sensation of dropping and going blank is incredibly distressing, and it makes total sense why the article made you feel worse—you interpreted the symptoms as proof that you’re fundamentally broken. It seems like your body is reacting to the fear of failing as if it’s a threat to your survival, rather than just a sign of stress.

Since the physical symptoms are so strong when you stare at confusing code, could we try a quick experiment tonight instead of reading more theory? Specifically, would you be willing to sit with that tightness for just five minutes without trying to fix your thoughts, and then tell me what happens to your breathing or the clarity in your head afterward?

I... I think I could try that. It sounds scary though, like if I just sit with the feeling it'll swallow me whole. But I guess that's probably the point, right? To see if it actually does that or if I'm just predicting the worst. Okay, I'll try it tonight and write down what happens with my breathing.

That willingness to face the discomfort without running away is a real sign of strength, and it shows you're ready to test whether your prediction of being overwhelmed is true. Before you go, I want to reassure you that this isn't about ignoring the pain; it's about observing it with curiosity so we can gather better data on what your body actually needs.

Would you feel safe doing this alone tonight, or would it help if you left a note on your phone with a reminder that you can pause anytime if it gets too heavy?

I think I'll be okay doing it alone. I have my close friend's number saved if it gets too bad, but I don't want to bother her with this. Maybe I'll just set a timer on my phone and keep it next to me, so I know exactly when five minutes is up. That way I can remind myself it's just a short experiment, not some endless thing.

Setting a timer next to you is a brilliant choice because it gives you a clear boundary, turning an indefinite struggle into a manageable, finite task. It signals to your brain that this experience is temporary and controlled, which should help prevent that "swallowing" feeling from becoming reality.

I am curious about what you hope to discover from this five minutes—is it possible that noticing the breath rising and falling might eventually loosen that tightness in your chest, or perhaps you'll find you can observe the fear without letting it dictate your actions?

I guess I hope to see that the feeling doesn't last forever. That it peaks and then fades, instead of just getting worse and worse until I break down. And maybe if I can just watch my breathing without trying to change it, I'll realize I can handle being uncomfortable without needing to escape or fix it right away. That would be... nice, honestly.

That insight about the feeling peaking and fading is incredibly hopeful, and recognizing that discomfort doesn't require immediate escaping is a major step in reclaiming control over your reactions. Your intuition that observation can create space between the feeling and your urge to flee is exactly the kind of awareness that builds resilience.

Before we wrap up, would you feel comfortable agreeing to let me know tomorrow morning, not to judge how well you handled the timer, but simply to share what happened to that tightness in your chest after those five minutes passed?

Yeah, I can do that. I'll text you tomorrow after my morning class and let you know how it went. Even if it's just three words like "it was hard," I'll send it. That feels fair—no pressure to have a perfect result, just sharing what actually happened.

That is such a healthy way to frame it—sending a simple update honors your commitment without trapping you in the demand for perfection. Knowing that even a short message counts as a success will make it easier to reach out if the five minutes feel longer than expected.

Before you head out tonight, is there anything specific you'd like to work on right now regarding your study schedule, or would you prefer to rest knowing you've taken that brave first step toward observing your anxiety?

I think I'm good for now. I feel a little lighter just talking about it, honestly. Maybe I'll even try to get some sleep tonight instead of staying up worrying about tomorrow's assignment. Thanks for not pushing me too hard today—this helped more than the article did.

It is wonderful that talking about it brought you some lightness, and I'm so glad the conversation felt safer than reading about imposter syndrome. Prioritizing your rest is definitely the best decision right now; giving your mind the space to recover will make tomorrow's experiment much easier to navigate.

Remember, sending that simple text tomorrow about how your body felt is all that matters—we just need the data to see if your predictions hold up. Thank you for trusting me with this process, and I wish you a peaceful night's sleep.
