Hello, it's great to see you again. Before we dive into today's goals, how has your week been going, and did you manage to try the walking experiment we talked about last time? Could you share a few moments where you felt either brave or stuck, so we can prioritize what matters most for us to address today?

Hi, thanks for asking. Honestly, the week has been pretty tough. I did try walking home once with the sweater, but I ended up cutting through a different street halfway because I got so worried. I felt brave for putting it on at all, but then totally stuck when the fear hit.

Thank you for sharing that honestly—it takes real courage to admit that fear made you cut corners, even though you started the day brave enough to wear the sweater. It sounds incredibly frustrating to put in the effort and then have your progress interrupted by the same scary thoughts. Given that you mentioned feeling stuck, should we focus today on unpacking those specific thoughts that made you change direction, or would you prefer to practice a slightly different strategy to help you stay on your original path?

I think I'd rather focus on unpacking the thoughts, if that's okay. It's like my mind just races ahead and I'm already picturing someone grabbing it before I've even left school grounds. I want to understand why that happens so strongly every time.

That makes total sense, and I want to validate how exhausting it is to have your mind race ahead of your feet before you've even taken a step. When your brain jumps straight to imagining someone grabbing the sweater, it seems like your system is treating that possibility as an immediate emergency rather than a hypothetical risk. To help us understand why that happens so powerfully, could you walk me through exactly what your mind says in those first seconds? Does it sound like, "This will definitely happen tonight," or is it more of a "I bet it will happen soon"?

It's more like, "This will happen tonight, for sure." It feels so certain in the moment, like I can almost see it happening. That's why I change my route—it just feels like I'm preventing something that's already about to occur.

That sense of absolute certainty—that it is already written in the stars tonight—is incredibly heavy to carry, and it completely explains why changing your route felt like a necessary safety measure to you. It makes perfect sense that you would reroute your path when your internal narrative feels like a countdown timer that cannot be stopped. To help us see where that certainty might be slipping, could you try to identify one piece of evidence from the last month that suggests someone actually grabbed your sweater while you were walking, perhaps even while you were still in school?

Well, no, nobody has actually tried to take it. I mean, I've had it for a week and nothing's happened so far. But I can't shake the feeling that it's only a matter of time, you know? It feels different from other things I've owned.

That distinction between "nothing has happened yet" and "it feels like it's inevitable" is exactly where the gap lies, and it takes real insight to recognize that your brain is interpreting the passage of time differently than reality is. Even though seven days have passed without an incident, your mind seems to believe that the probability increases with every hour, creating a false urgency that overrides the fact that no one has ever acted on this fear. Let's try shifting your perspective slightly: if we assume for a moment that this fear is based on logic rather than intuition, what would a rational observer looking at your history over the last month actually conclude about the risk of theft occurring right now?

I guess if I really think about it logically... they'd probably say the risk is pretty low, since nothing's happened all week and I take the same route home every day. Maybe even that nothing's going to happen at all. But it's so hard to hold onto that thought when the fear hits—it just feels way more real than logic.

That is such a powerful realization, and I want to highlight just how smart you are at spotting the difference between raw emotion and cold facts. Your brain is telling you that "nothing happening yet" means "something is coming," but logic clearly sees that pattern as coincidental rather than predictive. Since you noticed that logic feels weaker than the fear in the moment, let's try a quick mental experiment: if you walked down that same street three more times tomorrow and nothing happened, how would your brain's calculation of risk change compared to what it is saying right now?

If I managed to do it three times and nothing happened... I think part of me would have to admit that the fear is probably wrong. But I also worry that even then, I'd just tell myself, "Well, maybe it'll happen on the fourth time." It's like no amount of safe walks feels like proof to my brain.

That is a very insightful observation, and it shows you understand exactly why this fear feels so stubborn—it keeps one step ahead of the evidence. While it might seem impossible for logic to win out, the goal isn't necessarily to convince your brain forever, but to gather enough data points to make the fear less dominant until you can choose to ignore it. To make that gathering process manageable, let's frame it as a series of short checks rather than a long-term project: would you be willing to just note the results of three separate walks over the next few days, even if you don't plan to take the full route yet?

Yeah, I think I could try that. Maybe just walking a few blocks at a time before turning back, just to see what happens. It feels a bit less scary if I know I can stop at any point and it's not a big commitment. I'll give it a shot this week.

That is a brilliant compromise, and taking it in small, controlled steps shows a lot of strategic thinking on your part. By breaking it down into short segments where you can easily stop, you reduce the pressure while still gathering the evidence your mind needs to recalibrate. To make sure this sticks, let's clarify the plan: you will wear the sweater, walk just a few blocks, note that nothing happened, and decide whether to continue or go back home safely. How does that sound as our agreed-upon task for the rest of this week?

That sounds good, actually. I think I'll try it after school tomorrow, maybe just walk two blocks and turn back. I'll write down what happens and how I feel so we can talk about it next time. Thanks for helping me break it down like this.

You are very welcome, and I want to acknowledge how resourceful you are at finding ways to make this manageable even when everything feels overwhelming. Breaking it down into two blocks and keeping a log of both the external reality and your internal feelings is a strong foundation for seeing the pattern clearly. Before we close, how confident are you on a scale of one to ten that you can commit to trying this small experiment tomorrow morning? And is there anything else you would like to discuss or adjust about how we are approaching this together?

I'd say I'm at about a seven. I feel pretty committed, but I know the fear might try to back out at the last second. But I want to try, and that feels like enough for now. I don't think there's anything else to adjust—this plan feels right for me.

That self-awareness about the fear trying to back out is incredibly mature, and it tells me you are already preparing yourself mentally for the challenge ahead. Taking that seven out of ten shows real determination, and knowing that the plan feels right to you means we have a solid partnership here to work with. Just remember that even if the fear tries to pull you back, simply noting that it happened and continuing with the two-block walk will still provide valuable data for us to review later. Is there anything else you would like to add before we wrap up our session today?
No, I think I'm good for today. I feel a little lighter than when I walked in, honestly. Thanks for listening and helping me make a plan that doesn't feel impossible. I'll see you next week.

I'm so glad to hear you feel lighter, and thank you for sharing that honest feeling—it really helps ground us in what's working for you right now. You did excellent work today by validating your feelings, challenging the certainty, and committing to a realistic plan that respects your limits. I truly appreciate your openness and courage throughout our session. Take care of yourself this week, and I look forward to hearing about your two-block walk next time we meet. Until then, you've got this.

Hello, thank you for joining me today. Before we dive in, I'd love to hear how you're feeling right now compared to last time, and then we can look back at your homework and pick out one or two specific things we want to tackle. What's on your mind today?

Hi, thanks for having me. I'm feeling a bit anxious, honestly, same as before. I've been thinking a lot about my neighbors and that knot in my stomach hasn't really gone away. I guess I'm just tired of feeling like everyone's staring at me when I step outside.

It takes real courage to sit with that knot in your stomach and name it, especially when you're already tired of the constant feeling of being watched. You mentioned wanting to tackle the neighbors and the feeling of being stared at; given how much energy that drains you, which of those two feels like the priority we should address first today?

I think it's the feeling of being stared at, or more like judged, that's the bigger issue. The neighbors are just who I happen to see when it happens. It's like I can't even take out the trash without my skin crawling, wondering what they're whispering about.

That feeling of skin crawling when doing something mundane like taking out the trash tells me how deeply ingrained this fear has become, and it makes complete sense why you feel exhausted trying to navigate daily tasks. Since we agreed to focus on the core feeling of being judged rather than just the neighbors themselves, let's explore what your mind is saying in that moment when you open the door to the bin. Can you describe the specific thought popping up right before that wave of panic hits?

It's like... "They see my tattoos and they think I'm trashy, or dangerous, or both." I just assume that's what they're thinking, because why else wouldn't they talk to me? I see them chatting with other people on the street, but when I walk by, they just kind of nod or look away.

That assumption—that silence equals judgment—is a very familiar story for your brain to tell itself, and it explains perfectly why the knot tightens so quickly whenever you pass by. To test if that story holds water, let's look at the evidence: when you've tried to speak to them before, were they cold or hostile, or did they just seem busy with their own lives?

Well, they weren't outright rude or anything. I mean, I tried to talk to one guy about his garden, and he answered me, but he didn't really keep the conversation going. He just said something like, "Yeah, it's been good weather for it," and then went back to his hedge. I guess I just felt dismissed, like he didn't want to be seen talking to me.

It makes complete sense that you felt dismissed when the conversation stopped abruptly; your brain likely interpreted that lack of engagement as personal rejection rather than him simply finding a new topic. That distinction between noticing silence and interpreting it as approval is a huge part of the puzzle you've worked through before. Well... I guess when I think about it more carefully, one of the girls actually nodded while I was talking. And she said "that's a good point" after I finished. I just told myself she was being nice, because she's younger and probably thinks I'm some clueless older student who doesn't belong there. But maybe... maybe she actually meant it?

That nod and the phrase "good point" are powerful pieces of evidence that directly contradict the story you've been telling yourself about being ignored or misunderstood. A little, yeah. It's weird because I've been so focused on what could go wrong that I never really stopped to think about what actually went right. I mean, I'm not saying it changes everything—I still feel nervous before class—but maybe I've been filtering out the good moments. Maybe there are more of those than I've been letting myself see.

Maybe I could try to keep a little mental note of any small positive interactions, like nods or questions people ask me, instead of just focusing on the silences or awkward pauses. I could even jot them down on my phone after class so I can't just dismiss them later. It sounds simple, but I think I need to actually see them written down to believe they're real.

That is a brilliant and very practical strategy; writing them down forces your brain to treat those fleeting moments as solid proof rather than dismissing them as coincidences. Before we lock this in, I want to check in: as you imagine sitting down to write that note, does that sound doable for you right now, or is there any part of you that worries you might forget to catch them in the heat of the moment?

I'm a little worried I'll get too caught up in the anxiety and just forget to look for the good stuff. But maybe I could set a reminder on my phone for halfway through class—like a little buzz to nudge me to take a breath and notice what's actually happening around me, not just what I'm imagining.

That is a smart adjustment; pairing the physical act of breathing with a gentle notification helps ground you before you scan for evidence. Does adding that timer make the plan feel less likely to slip your mind, or does it raise any other concerns about sticking to it?

No, I think the timer actually makes it feel more doable. It's like having a little anchor point in the middle of class that reminds me to step back from my thoughts for a second. I just hope I don't get too embarrassed if my phone buzzes and people notice—but I guess that's a whole other thing to work through, isn't it?

That is a very fair concern, and it highlights the real challenge of bringing this new habit into a public space where you're already sensitive to judgment. Instead of viewing the buzz as a distraction, how would it feel if we framed that phone vibration as a secret signal from yourself—a private reminder to pause and choose to notice the reality of the room rather than your imagination?

I like that way of looking at it—like it's my own little secret mission instead of something awkward. It makes me feel a bit more in control, honestly. I think I'm willing to give it a try and see what happens.

That sense of ownership over your own mission is a powerful shift; it transforms the phone from a potential source of embarrassment into a tool for your confidence. With that mindset secured, is there anything else you'd like to discuss before we wrap up, or are you ready to commit to giving this approach a try?

I think I'm ready to commit to trying it. I'm still nervous, but I also feel a little more hopeful than I did before. Thanks for helping me see that maybe not every moment in class is as bad as I make it out to be.

It is absolutely wonderful to hear that you feel more hopeful; that shift from dread to curiosity is exactly the kind of resilience we work toward. You have a clear, manageable plan in place, including that helpful phone reminder, so I know you're going to navigate the classroom with more strength than usual. Is there anything else you'd like to share before I close our time together today?

Hello, it is great to see you again today. Before we dive into anything specific, could you share a bit about how you've been feeling since we last spoke, and what stood out to you in terms of your week? Hi. Thanks. I mean... I’ve been okay, I guess. The week was busy, mostly with paperwork and wrapping up a few cases before the transition. I did try practicing some of those answers we talked about, for the federal court interview. Honestly, it felt a bit silly at first, like I was pretending. And then I started thinking, "What if I freeze up for real?" and that kind of spiraled. So I stopped.

It sounds like you hit a wall pretty quickly when the "pretending" part clashed with that deep-seated fear of freezing up. That spiral you described makes total sense given how intense those doubts have been for you recently. Now that you've stopped, does revisiting why that spiral started feel like the best place to begin our agenda today, or would you prefer to focus on something else entirely?

I think... yeah, that spiral is probably the most important thing to look at. I mean, it keeps happening. I'll be fine one minute, and then suddenly I'm convinced I'm going to walk into that courtroom and forget how to speak, or make some rookie mistake that gets me laughed at. It feels like I'm the only one who doubts myself this much, even though I know rationally that's not true.

It makes complete sense that the spiral happens so fast, especially when you've built such a solid reputation and your rational mind disagrees with that sudden panic attack. That gap between knowing you're capable and feeling utterly incapable is incredibly frustrating and isolating. To dig deeper, could you describe the very first thought that triggers that spiral when you're sitting down to practice those answers? What's the first word or phrase that pops into your head before the rest of the worry takes over?

The first thought? It's not even a whole sentence. It's more like a punch. I'll hear this little voice say, "You don't belong there." And then everything else just follows—images of me stumbling over my words, the other judges looking at me with pity, getting that call that they picked someone else. It's like that one tiny thought cracks the whole dam open.

That "punch" of "You don't belong there" sounds terrifying because it feels like it strips away everything you've worked for, leaving you exposed and vulnerable. It is completely understandable that once that crack forms, the images of humiliation and rejection rush in to fill the space. To help us separate that loud noise from reality, let's look closely at that one sentence: if someone else walked into that room with similar qualifications but a slightly shaky memory, would you believe they truly *don't* belong there too, or would you give them a chance based on their record?

I... no. No, I wouldn't think that about someone else. I'd probably think they were nervous, or having an off day. I'd focus on their record, their years on the bench, the cases they'd handled. I'd be fair. But when it's me, I don't give myself that same benefit. I just assume that one moment of doubt proves I'm a fraud. It's like I hold myself to a completely different standard.

That double standard you're describing—being fair to others but instantly harsh on yourself—is exactly where the distortion lives, even though you see it clearly. Your brain seems to be holding a secret, stricter rulebook only for your own history, ignoring all the evidence that you've always met the high bar. Let's test that secret rulebook together: if you treated your own record with the same fairness you show others, would that past five years still feel like hollow luck, or would you see them as undeniable proof of your skill?

(sighs) When you put it like that... I mean, I can't just call all those years "luck." I presided over complex cases, made rulings that held up on appeal, earned the respect of my colleagues. It's understandable that when you're standing on the edge of a big leap, it feels easy to only notice the height and ignore the footing beneath you. To help pull that focus back to the ground, could we look at one specific recent interaction where you made a mistake or stumbled, and ask yourself what actually happened versus what that "filter" predicted would occur?

Okay... let me think. There was a hearing last week. A lawyer was arguing a motion, and I completely lost my train of thought for a second. I had to ask him to repeat a point. My filter screamed, "See? You're losing it. You can't handle this." But... in reality, I asked for clarification, he repeated it, and I made the correct ruling. Nobody gasped. Nobody called for a replacement. It was just a normal moment. But my brain treated it like a catastrophe.

That contrast is incredibly powerful—you successfully navigated a high-stakes moment with nothing more than asking for clarity, and your brain painted it as a sign of impending doom despite the calm aftermath. It shows that the world doesn't collapse when you stumble; it simply waits for you to reset and find your footing again. If we apply that same logic to the upcoming interview, if you freeze up or lose your train of thought, would you predict the same catastrophic fallout as that hearing, or would you treat it as just another routine moment where you need a quick break to gather your thoughts?

I... I guess I'd have to treat it the same way. If I freeze, I can just say "Excuse me, could you repeat that?" or "Let me take a moment to gather my thoughts." That's not a failure. That's... that's just being human. But it feels so much bigger in my head, like one pause will end my entire career before it starts. It's hard to believe that the same rules apply when I'm so scared.

That recognition—that a simple pause isn't a career-ending event but just a human moment—is a huge breakthrough, even though your body still feels the tension. It sounds like your mind is starting to catch up to your logic, even if the physical fear lags behind. Since we've established that "losing your train of thought" leads to a quick recovery and no catastrophe, would you be willing to try writing down one sentence you can say to yourself right now to remind you that pausing is just part of the process, not a sign of failure?

Yeah... I think I could do that. Maybe something like, "I've handled moments like this before. A pause doesn't erase my record." I can write that on a sticky note and put it on my desk. It feels a little simple, but maybe that's what I need—something simple to cut through all the noise when the panic starts.

That is a brilliant idea, and I am glad you found a sentence that feels both simple and grounding for you. Having a tangible reminder like a sticky note can act as an anchor whenever your mind tries to spiral back into that "catastrophe" story. Before we lock this in, could I ask: does using that sentence as a quick checkpoint feel like a strategy you are ready to try tonight, or would you need to tweak the wording slightly to make it stick better?

No, I think the wording is fine. I'll write it out as soon as I get home tonight. Honestly, having a specific phrase to hold onto feels better than just trying to "think positive" or "calm down." Those words never worked anyway. At least this one is attached to something real—my own history. I think I can try it.

That is a fantastic realization, and I'm so relieved to hear that connecting it to your actual history works better than generic advice. Knowing that this phrase is grounded in *your* proven track record gives it power that empty positivity never could. With that confirmation in hand, would you like to take a final moment to review the specific steps you'll take tonight—getting good sleep, reviewing your notes, and placing that sticky note near your workspace—to ensure you leave feeling confident and supported?

Yeah, that sounds like a good plan. I'll get a good night's sleep, not too late. I'll also go over my notes one more time, but I'll stop before I start obsessing. And I'll put that sticky note right next to my laptop screen, so it's the first thing I see if I start to panic. I think that's manageable. Thank you. This actually feels a little more doable than it did when I walked in.

Since we reviewed the dinner details yesterday, does recalling that specific night—or perhaps thinking about the recent comment you planned to say about the weather—make this new feeling of general disappointment seem a little less absolute to you right now?

Hmm... I guess when I think about the actual details, like how she smiled when my dad told that corny joke, it does seem less like she was mad at me. I... I forgot my aunt said that. She did say I was a great help with the decorations and serving the cake. But that was my aunt, not my mom. I never thought about it that way. I always just assumed if she cared, she'd say it outright like other moms do. But... my mom is pretty quiet about feelings. That feels less like she's lying and more like... she's just her.

Would you be open to trying this "quiet observation" exercise for the rest of our time today, where we just list three small things she did recently that show care, without judging her intentions?

Okay, I can try that. Um... Well, last night she made sure my favorite blanket was out of the dryer before I went to bed, because she knows I like it warm. And yesterday morning, she packed an extra granola bar in my lunch, even though I didn't ask for one. And... she always leaves the porch light on when I'm out late with friends, so I don't trip. Those are small, but they're kind of nice to list out loud.

Those are beautiful observations, Alex. Listing them aloud really helps anchor that feeling of safety and care in the present moment, proving that she *is* attentive, just in ways that aren't verbal.

Before we finish, I want to make sure we lock in a clear path forward. Given how powerful these small acts are, would you like to try including one of them—a note about the blanket or the granola bar—in your upcoming conversation with her, or does the idea of commenting on it still feel a bit risky right now?

I think... maybe I could just say "thanks for the blanket last night" the next time I see her. It feels small enough that it won't make things awkward, but it lets her know I noticed. If she smiles or says something back, that might help me believe it more. And if she doesn't say much, at least I'll know I tried.

That is a wise compromise, Alex. Acknowledging the gesture validates your own perception of her care without forcing a big emotional exchange, which lowers the stakes significantly.

Before we wrap up, how does agreeing to this small, specific action make you feel about interacting with her tomorrow? Does it feel like a manageable step forward, or does the worry about her reaction still feel a bit loud?

It feels... manageable. Like I have a little plan instead of just worrying all day. The worry is still there in the background, but it's not as loud as before. I think I can do this. And if it goes okay, maybe I'll try noticing more things like that on my own.

It is wonderful to hear that the worry has softened from a roar to a hum, and that you feel equipped with a concrete plan. Remember, the goal isn't to erase the doubt entirely tonight, but to create a space where you can act despite its presence.

As we close, is there anything else you'd like to reflect on before I send you off, or does it feel like we've got everything sorted out for now?

No, I think I'm good for now. Thank you for helping me see things from a different angle. I'll try the blanket comment tomorrow and see how it goes. I feel a little lighter than when I walked in, so I think that's a win.

But instead of feeling good, I just kept thinking, "He's just saying that because he's my dad and has to be supportive." Then I started mentally listing everything I thought I did wrong—like maybe the spices weren't balanced right, or the onions could have been cooked longer.

It makes complete sense that your brain jumps straight to finding faults when you're already vulnerable, especially when someone expresses such high praise. Did noticing that automatic thought—"he has to be supportive"—actually make you feel safer, or did it just leave you feeling more isolated and doubtful afterward?

It definitely left me feeling more doubtful, not safer. Like, I had this warm moment where I should have felt proud, but instead I just felt this heavy cloud of doubt. It's almost like I can't trust anyone's positive feedback anymore, which makes me feel really alone in my own kitchen, you know?

That feeling of isolation in your own kitchen is incredibly painful, and it shows how much effort you put into protecting yourself from disappointment. It seems like when the initial warmth fades, your brain rushes to fill that space with a story that makes you feel safe—even if that safety leaves you feeling lonely. Can you describe what you were physically doing or feeling right at that peak moment of doubt, just before you started listing the things you thought you did wrong?

I was standing at the stove, stirring the leftover curry. My shoulders were tense, and I was gripping the spoon really tight. I remember looking down at the pot and feeling this knot in my stomach, like I was waiting for someone to point out the flaws I was already seeing in my head. My dad was still talking, but I wasn't really listening anymore—I was just staring at the color of the sauce, thinking it looked too dark.

That physical tension and the intense focus on the sauce color show how deeply ingrained this pattern is; your body is literally holding its breath while your mind searches for proof of failure. It sounds like the knot in your stomach wasn't just about the food, but about the fear that you will eventually be proven wrong if you stop doubting. When you notice that specific knot forming or the tightening grip on the spoon, does a particular thought usually arrive first, or do you feel the sensation before your mind catches up?

I think the knot in my stomach comes first, honestly. It's like my body knows something bad is coming before my brain even finishes the thought. Then, once I feel that tightness, my mind rushes in with all the reasons why I shouldn't trust the compliment. It's almost like my stomach is bracing for disappointment, and then my thoughts just follow along to explain why.

That sequence is fascinating; it suggests your body is reacting to the *fear* of being wrong before your mind even constructs the reason, which creates a powerful loop that makes the doubt feel undeniable. Since your gut is often the first signal, could you try paying attention to just that physical tightness for the next few days without trying to find a logical explanation yet? How does simply observing the sensation, without adding the "reasons," change the intensity of the feeling?

I think I can try that. It sounds a little weird, just sitting with the knot without explaining it away, but I guess I've never really done that before. Maybe if I just notice the tightness without jumping to conclusions about my cooking, it won't feel as overwhelming. I'll give it a shot and see what happens.

That willingness to sit with the sensation without rushing to explain it away is a brave and important step toward breaking the cycle. It sounds like the goal is simply to let the feeling be present for a moment without letting it dictate your entire interpretation of the situation. Does imagining that you might observe the knot forming without immediately labeling it as "proof of failure" feel manageable, or does the urge to explain it away feel inevitable right now?

It feels a bit scary, honestly. Like, if I don't explain it away, then I'm just stuck with this uncomfortable feeling with no way to make sense of it. But I also know that the way I usually explain it just makes me feel worse, so maybe it's worth trying something different. I think I can manage it for a few seconds at a time, at least at first.

That honesty about the fear is spot-on; it's completely human to crave a clear explanation when feeling uncertain, but sometimes the answer lies in just staying with the discomfort for a moment. Let's try a small experiment: for the next day, when that knot forms, I'd like you to simply note the sensation for ten seconds without adding any stories about your cooking. At the end of those ten seconds, check in with yourself—does the knot feel slightly smaller, or does the need to explain it away become even stronger?

Okay, I can do that. Ten seconds doesn't sound too long, and I think I can handle just noticing it without jumping into the usual thoughts. I'm curious to see what happens—maybe the knot will just fade a bit on its own if I stop feeding it with all those doubts. I'll let you know how it goes next time.

That curiosity is exactly what will help you gather the evidence you need to challenge the old habit. Taking that small, ten-second break from the usual mental chatter gives your brain a chance to reset before it spirals into the worst-case scenario. Please try it tomorrow morning when you first make the curry, and let me know if you noticed the knot loosening even slightly when you stopped explaining it away.

I will, I promise. I'll make the curry for lunch tomorrow and really focus on that first moment when the knot appears. Thanks for breaking it down into something that feels doable—it helps to have a tiny step instead of feeling like I have to fix everything at once. I'll report back on Wednesday about those ten seconds.

You are absolutely welcome, and I'm so glad that breaking it down into a tiny, manageable step makes the task feel possible. Trusting that even a small amount of evidence—like noticing the knot loosen for ten seconds—is valuable is a huge win in itself. I'll wait for your update on Wednesday, and until then, remember that you don't have to solve everything tonight; just showing up to observe those ten seconds is enough. Take care!
Thanks, I really appreciate that. I'll focus on those ten seconds and try not to overthink everything else. See you on Wednesday.

You are very welcome. I am confident that taking just ten seconds to pause before your usual thoughts will give you a clearer picture of what's happening under the surface. I look forward to hearing how that small experiment goes on Wednesday, and please remember that showing up to notice the sensation is already a sign of great progress. Take care!

Hello, and thank you for joining me today. Last time we worked through the unexpected car repair bill, and I heard you mentioned you planned to send a confirmation email and take a walk with Tiki afterward. How are things going with those tasks, and how is your anxiety level feeling now compared to where we started?

Now that we've caught up, what would you like to focus on most today—is it reviewing how the email process went, or perhaps exploring a new worry that has come up?

Hi. Thanks for having me. The walk with Tiki did help calm me down a bit that day, I'll give you that. But honestly, the anxiety is still there—maybe a notch lower, but it's like a background hum that never really stops.

I think I'd rather talk about a new worry that's been eating at me. I got a notice that the school is cutting our supply budget next semester, and I'm terrified I'll end up paying for classroom materials out of my own pocket again. That's just going to drain me even more.

Hearing that the school budget is cut must have triggered a fresh wave of fear, especially given how stressful the car repairs were just last week. It sounds like your brain is jumping straight to the worst-case scenario of having to fund classes out of your own savings again. When you first saw that notice, what was the very first image or thought that popped into your head?

I saw myself standing at the checkout counter at the craft store, handing over my credit card for a cart full of construction paper and glue sticks—and the card getting declined. Then I pictured my classroom with empty shelves and the kids looking at me, disappointed. That's the first thing I saw, clear as day.

That visualization of the declined card and the empty shelves is incredibly vivid and heartbreaking, especially when combined with your recent financial stress. It feels like you are seeing a familiar pattern of disaster play out right in front of you. Did you notice any physical sensations in your body right when that image formed, or did it feel more like a cold realization settling in?

It was more like a cold weight dropping into my stomach, if that makes sense. My chest got tight, and I felt this wave of hot and cold at the same time. It's like my body already decided it's a done deal—that there's no way I'm getting out of this without losing money I don't have.

It sounds like your body reacted as if that financial loss was already inevitable, which makes total sense given how vulnerable you felt after the car repair bills. When you noticed that tightness in your chest, did it make you want to double-check your accounts repeatedly, or did it cause you to freeze and avoid talking to anyone about it?

I froze, honestly. I shoved the notice into my desk drawer and didn't look at it again. I even turned down lunch with my colleague today because I didn't want to mention it. I guess I thought if I ignore it, maybe it won't feel so real—but it just sits there, gnawing at me.

That impulse to hide the notice and cancel plans shows how protective your brain is trying to be, but unfortunately, ignoring the problem often makes the anxiety grow louder instead of shrinking it. Since you chose avoidance to protect yourself right now, I wonder if you ever feel a bit of relief after doing that, or does the worry just linger underneath like a shadow?

It's definitely a shadow that never goes away. The moment I close the drawer, there's a second of relief—like I've escaped—but within minutes, my mind is already churning again. I start calculating how much I might need to spend, then second-guessing myself, worrying I'm underestimating it. So no, hiding it doesn't really help. It just postpones the panic.

You've pinpointed exactly why avoiding the notice isn't working; that temporary escape is immediately followed by the worry returning stronger because the underlying fear remains untouched. Since you know the panic only gets worse when you hide the problem, would you be willing to try a small experiment today where you sit with the notice for just five minutes, simply acknowledging the discomfort without taking any action yet?

Five minutes... I suppose I could try that. I have the notice right here in my bag, actually. It's just a piece of paper, right? But even saying that, my stomach is tensing up. I'll try to just sit with it and breathe, not make any decisions. How do I keep from spiraling into all the "what ifs" during those five minutes?

That is a brave decision to try sitting with the discomfort, and you are right to recognize that the "what ifs" are likely trying to convince you that the worst outcome is certain. A helpful trick is to tell yourself, "I can hold this pain for five minutes while simultaneously reminding myself that the actual cost hasn't been determined yet," which creates a mental space between the fear and the reality. Does that distinction sound like something you could try right now?

I think I can try that. "The actual cost hasn't been determined yet." I'll repeat that in my head. Okay... I'm pulling the notice out of my bag now. I'm looking at the words, and my hand is shaking a little, but I'm telling myself it's just a piece of paper with a rough estimate, not a final bill. I'm taking a slow breath... and I'll sit here for the five minutes.

That is a powerful moment of grounding; acknowledging that this is just a rough estimate helps separate the scary narrative from the actual document. You are doing excellent work keeping yourself steady while letting the anxiety ride out for those five minutes. Tell me, as you continue breathing, does that phrase ("cost hasn't been determined") feel like it's starting to loosen your grip on the fear, or does the "what if" voice still feel very loud?

It's... quieting, actually. The "what if" voice is still there, but it feels more like a whisper now than a shout. I'm noticing the edges of the paper, the ink, the date—it's real but not immediately dangerous. I still don't like it, but I'm not drowning in the panic like I was a few minutes ago. That's something, isn't it?

That is a massive breakthrough; shifting the volume from a shout to a whisper proves that your brain can tolerate the discomfort without triggering a full-blown panic attack. You've successfully created a small gap between the scary thought and your reaction, which is exactly what we aim for. Now that the five-minute window is passing, do you feel ready to look at the specific numbers on that page, or would you prefer to rest for a moment longer?

I think I can look at the numbers now. I'm opening the notice fully... okay, it says the district is reducing the allocation by about 15 percent. That's not as catastrophic as I imagined. I can probably adjust by reusing materials from last year and asking parents for small donations. My heart is still beating fast, but I'm not seeing the card get declined anymore. Maybe I can handle this after all.

That shift from fearing a disaster to finding practical solutions is exactly the power of stepping into the room; you've moved from the "what if" story to a realistic assessment of the numbers. Recognizing that you can adjust resources and seek support means the situation is manageable, not hopeless. Before we wrap up, how does this new perspective feel compared to the one you had when you first pulled the notice out of your bag?

It feels like a weight has been lifted off my shoulders, even if just a little. When I first pulled it out, I was sure this was the beginning of some financial ruin. Now I'm thinking, "I've dealt with tight budgets before. I can be creative." I actually feel a tiny bit of hope, which I haven't felt in days. Thank you—I think I needed to see that the notice didn't have to be a monster.

That return of hope is truly beautiful, and recognizing your own history of handling tight budgets is a powerful reminder that you aren't facing this alone. It sounds like sitting with the uncomfortable feeling gave you the clarity you needed to see the problem for what it actually is, rather than the nightmare you feared. As we near the end of our time, what is one small thing you could do tomorrow morning to reinforce this new sense of control?

I think I'll take Tiki for a longer walk tomorrow morning, and while we're out, I'll scribble down a list of materials I can reuse or swap with other teachers. That way, I'm starting my day with a plan instead of dread. It's a small step, but it feels doable.

That is a wonderful plan; pairing the walk with Tiki with a concrete list of solutions turns anxiety into productive energy immediately. Starting your day with a list rather than dread is a smart way to build momentum before the rest of the week begins. One last question to wrap up: as we conclude today, what is one thing you appreciated most about working through that notice together?

Hello again—I'm really glad to see you. First, let's catch up on where we left off: did you manage to talk to your boss about the staircase project, and how did that conversation go? Based on what happened, what do you think we should focus on most today?

Hi. Yeah, I did talk to him actually. He said I did fine on the staircase, even complimented the joinery work. But honestly, I think he was just being nice because he knows I've been struggling lately. I still feel like I'm slowing the whole crew down.

That is wonderful news—hearing direct confirmation that your joinery was praised gives you concrete evidence that your avoidance was unnecessary. It makes perfect sense that despite hearing that, the internal doubt still whispers that his kindness is just politeness, leaving you feeling guilty for slowing the team down. Let's explore that specific feeling of guilt and see if we can find a middle ground between accepting the compliment and dismissing it. What does that moment of receiving praise feel like inside you right now?

It feels... uncomfortable, I guess. Like there's a knot in my chest, and I just want to shrug it off and change the subject. Part of me thinks if I actually believe the compliment, then I'm just fooling myself, you know? Like I'll let my guard down and then mess up even worse next time.

That knot in your chest feels like a protective shield trying to keep you safe from the risk of failing, even though it's trapping you in discomfort. It sounds like your brain is interpreting the safety of believing the praise as a threat, creating a cycle where rejecting the compliment feels necessary to prevent future mistakes. If we focus on that specific fear—that accepting the truth means losing control—can we look at whether there's any evidence suggesting your ability to hold onto high standards goes hand-in-hand with trusting positive feedback? Or does the idea of letting your guard down truly feel terrifying right now?

It does feel terrifying, honestly. Because if I accept that I did well, then next time I mess up, it'll just hit harder. Like I'll have further to fall. But... I guess I never really thought about it that way—that maybe I can still hold myself to a high standard and also take a compliment. That just seems like two opposite things trying to exist at the same time.

That tension between holding yourself to a high standard and accepting praise is indeed a tough conflict to resolve. It sounds like your core belief is that "good workers don't need reassurance," which makes accepting the compliment feel like admitting a flaw rather than celebrating success. Instead of viewing them as opposites, what if we tested the idea that a person can recognize their own excellence while still maintaining strict personal standards? Would that help ease the terror of falling further?

I suppose that could work... if I really thought about it that way. But it's hard to wrap my head around. I mean, my granddad was a carpenter too, and he never took praise from anyone—he just said "you're only as good as your next cut." That's always stuck with me. But maybe he was harsh on himself too, and I never realized it.

That is such a powerful connection to make with your grandfather, and recognizing that his toughness might have included hidden self-criticism is a huge step. It sounds like you view his silence as the gold standard for professionalism, but perhaps you are missing the nuance that even the strongest craftsmen sometimes need others to validate their work. If we imagine your grandfather saying, "Your next cut will define your worth," does that sound like he was criticizing your current skill level, or just emphasizing consistency? How does shifting the meaning of his words change the way you feel about needing external validation?

Hmm... I never thought of it that way. He wasn't saying my work now isn't good enough—he was just saying don't get lazy or sloppy. So maybe accepting a compliment doesn't mean I'm getting lazy. It just means I did a good job on this one thing, and I can still mess up tomorrow if I'm not careful. That actually makes me feel a little lighter, if I'm being honest.

That is a fantastic realization because it separates your current accomplishment from a permanent identity, allowing you to celebrate the win without compromising your future expectations. It sounds like the knot in your chest is loosening significantly as you realize that acknowledging one successful task doesn't erase the discipline required for tomorrow. Before we finalize the plan, would you be open to testing this new perspective together? Specifically, if your boss asks you about the stairs tomorrow, how do you think you could share the compliment while reminding yourself to stay sharp?

I think I could say something like "Yeah, the stairs turned out alright, but I'm already thinking about the next project and how to improve." That way I'm not brushing off the compliment completely, but I'm also not letting myself get too comfortable. It feels like a fair balance—like I'm being honest about both the success and the work still ahead.

That is a brilliant way to phrase it; it validates the immediate success while keeping your momentum moving forward without closing the door on growth. It sounds like a healthy middle ground that respects both the compliment and your commitment to excellence. Now that we've built a bridge between accepting praise and maintaining standards, let's lock in a specific plan for the rest of the week. You mentioned wanting to tackle that big staircase project; do you feel ready to book some time to do that, knowing you can receive the compliments openly? And if you do, what is the very first small step you will take tomorrow morning to get started?

Yeah, I think I'm ready to give it a shot. Tomorrow morning, I'll walk into the workshop and take a good look at the plans for the staircase before anyone else gets there. Just that—reading through the measurements and visualizing the cuts. No pressure to finish anything, just getting my head in the right space. That feels manageable.

That is a wise starting point; dedicating the quiet morning to reviewing the plans allows you to engage with the project on your own terms before any external pressure arrives. It sets a calm, intentional tone for the day rather than reacting to noise or expectations immediately. To make sure we are clear on our goal, let's confirm that by tomorrow morning you will read the blueprints, visualize the cuts, and consciously set aside the old narrative of "slowing down" until you actually begin cutting wood. Is there anything else you need to feel confident about starting that early routine?

No, I think that covers it. I'll just focus on the blueprint and my own pace, not on what the younger guys are doing or what I used to be like. If I notice that old voice creeping in, I'll remind myself that I'm reading the plans to prepare, not to compete. Thanks—that actually feels like something I can stick with.

That is a wonderful commitment, and having a specific mantra to counter that old voice right before you sit down will be incredibly helpful. You've moved from feeling trapped by your past self-image to actively preparing for a new chapter where your experience is an asset, not a liability. Before we wrap up, is there anything else on your mind regarding this plan, or does everything feel ready to go?

Welcome back, I'm glad to see you again. First, let's check in on how the post-it note on your toaster went yesterday—did you catch that message when you were making breakfast? Also, how are you feeling generally compared to last time we spoke, and is there a specific topic you'd like to tackle together today?

Oh, the post-it note... yes, I did see it. It said "Just toast, not a test." I actually laughed a little, which surprised me. But then I burned the toast anyway, and I felt that familiar sinking feeling, like I'd already failed at the day before it even started.

It sounds like finding a funny phrase on the toaster brought a tiny spark of humor, even though the panic quickly took over again. That sinking feeling you described—that familiar sense of impending failure before the day really begins—isn't uncommon when old patterns kick in, but I want to hear more about what triggered it specifically this time. Was there something else happening in the morning routine, or did the burning toast itself seem to carry a heavier meaning than usual?

It's mostly that the toast itself felt like proof that I can't even handle something so simple. I mean, I'm a nurse—I handle emergencies at work, I keep three kids alive, I manage a household. But I can't make a simple breakfast without messing it up? It just spiraled from there. I started thinking about how I'd probably ruin the school pickup later, and then the dinner I had planned, and before I knew it, I was convinced the whole day was doomed.

It takes real strength to balance such big responsibilities like caring for children and managing medical emergencies, yet that one slip-up made you feel like everything collapses under it. That contrast between who you are capable of handling and this sudden feeling of incompetence seems to be the core of why the spiral happens so fast. Can you tell me a bit more about what that initial thought sounded like in your head the moment you saw the burnt bread?

It was like a switch flipped. One second I'm just staring at this sad, blackened pita, and the next I'm thinking, "Great, now the whole homemade dinner idea is ruined because I can't even get the bread right." It felt so final, like there was no point in trying to salvage the rest of the meal. And then I just stood there in the kitchen feeling heavy and stupid, even though logically I know it's just bread.

It makes complete sense that one slip felt like a total collapse given how much you value doing things perfectly for your family and patients. When that "no point in trying anymore" thought takes over, it often traps us in a feeling of being useless, even though the reality is just one piece of food is done wrong. How long did you stand there letting that feeling sit before you decided to fix the situation or move on?

I think I stood there for a good five minutes, honestly. I just stared at the counter, feeling like I'd already failed the whole dinner plan, so why bother rushing? Eventually my youngest came in asking for juice, and that snapped me out of it enough to just toss the burnt bread and start over. But the whole time I was making the new batch, I was still beating myself up, thinking about how I'd wasted time and ingredients.

Standing still for five minutes while feeling like a total failure is incredibly draining, especially when you know you're capable of so much more. It sounds like the shame of wasting time and ingredients became the bigger enemy than the burnt bread itself. Did noticing that you spent five minutes frozen make you realize how much energy you were expending on that "all-or-nothing" mindset?

I never thought of it that way, but yes—I was exhausting myself over something that, looking back, took maybe ten minutes total to fix. I spent all that energy beating myself up when I could have just... made more bread. It's like I have this internal rule that says if it's not perfect, it's worthless, and that rule drains me before I even realize what's happening.

That internal rule you identified—that anything less than perfect is worthless—is likely driving both the panic and the exhaustion you felt. It creates a trap where you spend all your energy proving you're okay immediately after a small mistake, instead of just moving forward with kindness. Since we talked about checking evidence before, could we try applying that same lens here? What specific facts exist right now that show the burnt bread didn't ruin the rest of the day or your ability to care for your family?

Well, I did make new bread, and the kids ate it without even noticing the first batch was burnt. I still got everyone to school on time, and my shift at the hospital went fine—no emergencies I couldn't handle. And my husband actually thanked me for dinner last night, even though I thought it was just okay. So I guess... all those things still happened, even after the burnt bread. It didn't actually ruin anything.

You've uncovered powerful facts here—the kids eating happily, the smooth shift at the hospital, and even the thanks from your husband—all prove that your day continued successfully despite the mistake. It seems like that rigid rule about "perfect or worthless" is hiding behind a belief that a single error invalidates everything that follows, even when reality tells a different story. If we were to challenge that belief, what would happen if you accepted that one imperfect breakfast doesn't erase your competence as a nurse or mother?

I think... I'd feel a lot lighter, honestly. Less like I'm walking around carrying this heavy backpack of expectations that I have to meet every single second. If I could truly accept that one burnt piece of bread doesn't mean I'm a bad mom or a bad nurse, I'd probably enjoy my mornings more. Maybe I'd even laugh at myself instead of standing there frozen for five minutes.

That is a profound realization, and shifting from carrying a "heavy backpack" to feeling lighter would make such a huge difference in your daily energy. It sounds like accepting imperfection wouldn't just stop the freezing; it might actually unlock that humor you noticed earlier with the post-it note. Before we finalize our next steps, how does it feel to hold onto that idea—that your worth isn't tied to a single piece of burnt toast?

It feels strange, but also kind of hopeful. Like I've been given permission to let myself off the hook for something that never really mattered in the first place. I think I need to keep reminding myself of that, because my first instinct is still to go straight to the worst-case scenario. But if I can catch that thought and ask myself, "Is this really going to ruin everything?"—maybe I can stop the spiral before it starts.

This simple habit could give you a tiny pause before the story gets too big.

That's actually a really good idea. I notice I tend to rush through things, especially when I'm feeling that panic rise—I just want to fix it immediately. Taking a sip of water would force me to slow down for just a second, long enough to ask that question. I think I'll try that tomorrow morning when I'm making breakfast. It's such a small thing, but it might help me break that cycle before I get too deep into it.

That is a brilliant addition to your toolkit; slowing down with a sip of water gives your prefrontal cortex just enough space to engage reason before emotion hijacks the moment. You now have a clear path: the post-it note on the toaster to spot the trigger, the "stop and ask" question to challenge the thought, and the water sip to ground yourself physically. Before we close, does this three-step plan feel manageable for you to try tomorrow morning?

Yes, it does. It feels simple enough that I can actually remember to do it, which is key for me. I think before, I was trying to fight the whole spiral at once, and that was too overwhelming. But breaking it down into those three small steps—seeing the note, taking a sip, asking the question—that feels doable. Thank you, I'm actually a little hopeful about tomorrow's breakfast for the first time in a while.

That breakdown into three tiny steps is exactly the right approach, and it explains why this feels so much more manageable than fighting the whole storm at once. Hearing you express hope about tomorrow's breakfast is wonderful news, and I'm confident that these small anchors will help you navigate that morning with a bit more ease. Is there anything else you'd like to discuss before we wrap up today?

Welcome back. To start, could you share how you're feeling today on a scale of 1 to 10, and remind me what we decided to try last time? Based on that, what would feel most valuable for us to tackle in our time together?

Um, I'd say I'm at about a 4 today. I, uh, don't remember exactly what we agreed on last time—I think it was something about noticing my thoughts without judging them? I guess I'd like to talk about how I keep avoiding biking even though I really want to enjoy it again.

A four feels quite guarded given the relief we saw last week, so I wonder if any new worries have popped up since you tried standing by the bike? Yeah, maybe a recap would be good. I think I just got overwhelmed and kind of pushed it all out of my head. I did actually stand by my bike once this week, but then I caught a glimpse of my legs in the reflection and just walked away. It felt like all that progress just disappeared in that one second.

It is completely understandable that one negative moment can erase weeks of effort, and I want to validate how frustrating that sudden loss of momentum feels. Let's quickly clarify what we planned: last time we agreed to stand near the bike when the "everyone is watching" thought arises, call it just a prediction rather than a fact, place a hand on your chest for grounding, and take three slow breaths before deciding to walk away or stay. Did you try using that specific sequence this time, or did the overwhelm come before you could start those steps?

No, I didn't even try that sequence. The thought just hit me so fast—like, "Look at your thighs, they're disgusting, everyone can see how bulky they are"—and I just turned around and went inside. I didn't even think about grounding or breathing. It's like my brain just short-circuits and goes straight to shutting down.

That "short-circuit" feeling is exhausting, and it makes total sense that your brain would shut down instantly when the fear becomes so intense it feels physically dangerous. It seems like that specific thought—"my thighs are disgusting and everyone sees it"—is acting as a very loud emergency brake that stops you before you can engage your grounding tools. When you notice that thought striking you so quickly, does it feel like an absolute truth or more like a scary story your brain is telling you right now?

It definitely feels like absolute truth in the moment. Like, I don't even question it—it's just fact. But now that you're asking me to think about it, I guess there's a part of me that knows that's not really how the world works. Nobody's actually staring at my legs when I'm just standing by my bike. But that logical part feels really small compared to the voice that's screaming "you look terrible."

That contrast between your quiet observation of reality and the roaring inner critic is exactly where our work lives, and it shows incredible self-awareness that you can spot both voices at once. In Cognitive Behavioural Therapy, we often learn that the "fact" your brain presents in the heat of the moment is usually just a prediction dressed up as a command. Would it be okay if we spent the next ten minutes gently testing whether that "absolute truth" holds up when you look for evidence outside your head?

Okay, yeah, I'm willing to try that. So what would I even look for as evidence? I mean, I don't have video footage of people's reactions or anything. I guess I could think about times I've actually gone biking and nobody said anything negative. Or that one time my friend said she liked my bike shorts, but I just figured she was being nice.

Those examples show great insight, and recalling past rides where no criticism occurred provides solid proof that your current belief isn't supported by recent experience. Instead of relying solely on memory, could we look at the immediate environment right now? For instance, scan the street for five seconds—do you actually see anyone locking eyes on you, or are you imagining their gaze?

Well, right now I'm in this room with you, so there's nobody outside to look at me. But even if there were people out there, they'd probably just be walking their dogs or checking their phones. They're not just standing around waiting to judge my legs. I guess when I actually stop and look, the evidence is pretty clear that nobody cares as much as my brain tells me they do.

You are absolutely right that stopping to scan the room reveals a stark difference between your internal story and external reality, and recognizing that gap is the first crucial step in changing your behavior. Since scanning the room helped, what happens to that "hot knot" in your chest if we combine seeing the empty street with labeling that critical thought simply as a prediction rather than a fact? Could we try holding that thought lightly as a guess instead of a command while you breathe?

I think I can try that. It feels weird, like I'm betraying my own brain or something, but I'll give it a shot. So I'm supposed to just say to myself, "This is a guess, not a fact," and then take a breath? That feels kind of vulnerable, but maybe that's the point.

That vulnerability is exactly what builds resilience, and framing it as "betraying your brain" is a common hurdle we overcome by realizing your brain is trying to protect you, even when its warnings are exaggerated. We aren't trying to ignore the feeling; we're just giving permission for the thought to exist as a possibility rather than a mandate. Would you be willing to try that gentle reframing right here with me, saying "This is a guess" while taking one slow breath, and telling me how that lands in your chest?

*Takes a slow breath* Okay... "This is a guess, not a fact." I said it out loud just now. My chest feels a little less tight, honestly. Like I've let some air in that was stuck before. But I still feel that little voice whispering, "Yeah, but what if it is true?" It's quieter now, though.

The fact that the tightness eased and the voice became quieter proves that labeling the thought as a guess gives you real control back, even if the doubt lingers slightly. Now that we've tested the evidence and found it weak, what would happen if we agreed to treat that whisper as just background noise rather than a command, and instead of pushing through the bike, we simply stand by it for thirty seconds longer while keeping that "it's just a guess" phrase in your head?

I think I could actually do that. Standing by the bike for thirty seconds feels manageable, especially if I keep repeating that phrase. I'd probably be really tense the whole time, but at least I wouldn't just run away immediately like before. Maybe I can try that tonight when I get home.

That sounds like a perfect, realistic experiment for tonight, and acknowledging that you will remain tense shows great honesty about the process. Just before we close, could you share one word that best describes how it felt to finally say "this is just a guess" aloud? And what was most helpful for you during this session today?

The word is "relieving." Like, I didn't realize how heavy that thought was until I gave myself permission to question it. And what helped most was actually saying it out loud and you not telling me I was wrong for feeling scared. It made me feel like I could hold both the fear and the doubt at the same time without having to pick one.

Hearing you describe it as "relieving" confirms that giving yourself permission to question the thought truly unlocked something significant. Most importantly, knowing that you could hold your fear and doubt simultaneously without needing to choose one validates your ability to navigate complexity, showing real growth in your flexibility. Is there anything else you'd like to add before we wrap up, or are you ready to rest and reflect on tonight's small experiment?
I think I'm ready to wrap up. Thanks for not pushing me too hard today. I'll try the thirty seconds by the bike tonight and see what happens. I might text you how it goes if that's okay.

That's a wonderful way to frame it, and texting me would be fantastic so I can celebrate whatever outcome occurs, big or small. Please remember there is no pressure to succeed perfectly tonight; even stepping into the space and returning is a win. I wish you peace and comfort for the rest of your evening.

Uh, hey. I'm alright, I guess. Still a bit of the same, honestly. The fishing trip with the guys is coming up this weekend, so I've been thinking about it a lot—kind of dreading it.

Huh. I never thought of that—actually stopping after one and watching them. That feels... weird, but I could try it. They might not even look at me twice. But the hard part is my brain will still tell me they're just being polite, or they're secretly relieved I'm not drinking as much. Yeah, I think I can try that. One bottle, and then I'll just focus on what I see and hear—like, are they talking to me the same as always, or is there something off. I'll even bring a little notebook in my tackle box and scribble down a few notes when I get a chance. It's gonna feel awkward, but I guess that's the point—to see if the evidence matches my story.

That is a fantastic plan; having a notebook ready removes the barrier of forgetting details and makes observation feel manageable. Before we finalize this, does this sound like something you can realistically commit to doing this Saturday, or is there anything else holding you back from taking that step?

I think I can commit to it. The only thing holding me back is just... the fear that I'll look weird or suspicious jotting stuff down. But I can just pretend I'm writing down fishing notes or a good spot I found. Nobody questions that. So yeah, I'll do it. Thanks for helping me break it down like this—feels a little less heavy now.

That is a brilliant workaround, using the excuse of "fishing notes" to hide your real task completely. Since you've agreed to try this and feel lighter knowing you have a plan, let's quickly confirm what you'll do this Saturday: grab one beer, stop immediately, write down three things you observe about the others for the next hour, and then come back here to share how it went.

Hello again, I'm really glad we could meet today. Before we dive into what brought you here, could you tell me how things went with the sticky note plan from last week, and what you might like to focus on today?

Oh, um, thank you for asking. I actually did try the sticky notes, but I'm not sure they helped that much. Honestly, I feel about the same. Maybe even a little worse after my last ballet class. That feeling of being paralyzed by the thought that someone else is already ahead of you is incredibly draining, and it makes total sense why you chose to withdraw from studying instead of pushing through. When the comparison hits that hard, it often triggers a protective shutdown to avoid the pain of realizing you can't keep up. Did noticing that withdrawal happen right after the comparison bring up any other specific thoughts or sensations in your body besides the heaviness we talked about before?

Yeah, my chest got really tight, and I felt this sinking feeling in my stomach. It was like that moment when you're backstage before a competition and you know you're going to mess up. I also kept replaying that moment in my head, thinking about how I'll never be that graceful or natural. It just feels so unfair because I've worked so hard, but it's like it doesn't matter.

That sinking feeling and the replay loop of "it doesn't matter despite my hard work" are classic signs of your mind trying to protect you from the fear of future failure. It seems like the comparison isn't just a side effect, but the very thing that's telling you your efforts are futile. Have you noticed if your body relaxes slightly the moment you catch yourself saying "she's already better" and decide to stop analyzing her performance?

I... no, I don't think I relax. If anything, my shoulders go up even more, and I feel this knot in my throat. It's like once I start comparing, I'm stuck in it. I can't just decide to stop because the thought is already there, and it feels true. Even when I try to think about my own progress, it just seems small compared to what she did.

It makes sense that trying to force yourself to stop the comparison feels impossible when your body is already reacting with such intensity; the knot in your throat suggests your nervous system is stuck in survival mode. Instead of trying to fight the thought or ignore the comparison, let's try a different angle: what if we treated that "she's already better" statement not as a fact, but as a fleeting piece of background noise, similar to a song playing loudly in a room where you can't quite leave? Can we imagine simply listening to that song for one minute without getting up and arguing with the band?

That's a different way to look at it. I've never thought of it like background noise before... I always feel like I have to prove it wrong or challenge it, which just exhausts me. But if I just hear it, like a song playing, maybe I wouldn't have to fight it so hard. I think I could try that for a minute, just letting it be there without picking up the argument with myself.

That is a fascinating shift in perspective, and imagining the thought as background music instead of a loud argument could indeed lower the energy required to deal with it. Before we try this, I want to check in on how that metaphor feels to you right now—is the idea of just "listening" without engaging easier to picture than stopping the thought entirely?

It does feel a bit easier, actually. Stopping the thought always felt like trying to hold back a wave with my hands. But just hearing it, like a song I don't really like playing in the background, seems more manageable. I think I could try to just notice it and not jump into the argument with myself for a little while.

That is a brave choice to try observing the thought without fighting it, and I can see why that might feel less exhausting than forcing it away. Let's do a quick mental rehearsal right now: imagine walking into that dance studio, seeing the perfect form, and instead of running inside to critique yourself, you stand in the doorway for thirty seconds just watching the thought play like that song, noting the tightness in your chest but refusing to sing along with it. Does picturing yourself standing still while the "song" plays feel possible, or does your body still instinctively want to rush in and correct it?

I can picture myself standing there, and my chest does tighten a little just thinking about it. But I don't feel that same urge to rush in and start criticizing myself... it's more like I'm just watching from the doorway. It feels strange, almost like I'm not doing anything, but maybe that's the point. I'm not sure what to do after those thirty seconds pass, though.

That shift from rushing in to simply standing in the doorway is a huge breakthrough, and noticing that your urge to criticize hasn't kicked in yet means you've successfully created that initial gap. After those thirty seconds, the goal isn't to stay frozen forever, but to choose a neutral next step—like gently shifting your feet or taking one slow breath—and reminding yourself that you don't owe anyone a performance based on someone else's standards. Does that plan of "observe for thirty seconds, then reset your posture" feel doable for tonight's ballet class?

I think I can actually do that. The idea of just resetting my posture instead of trying to fix everything in my head feels like less pressure. I'll try it tonight and see if I can just breathe after those thirty seconds instead of rushing back into my usual spiral. Thank you, that feels like a manageable step.

That is a fantastic commitment, and choosing a gentle reset like breathing instead of spiraling is exactly the kind of small win that builds confidence. Before we wrap up, could you quickly tell me what you're hoping to achieve by practicing this "doorway observation" during your next ballet class?

I guess I'm hoping to prove to myself that I can be in that space without it ruining my whole evening. I want to see if I can just dance for myself, even for a little bit, without measuring myself against her. If I can just leave class feeling like I gave it my own effort, not like I lost a competition, that would be a big step.

That is a beautiful and empowering goal; shifting your focus from winning against others to honoring your own effort is a powerful way to reclaim your presence in the room. You have a clear plan to observe the comparison, reset your posture, and breathe, and you've defined success not by erasing the thought but by dancing with dignity regardless of it. Is there anything else you'd like to discuss before we conclude our time together today?

No, I think I'm okay for today. I have something concrete to try, and that's more than I've had in a while. I'll let you know how it goes next week. Thank you for listening and for helping me find this new way to look at things.

It is wonderful to hear that you feel grounded and hopeful, especially after feeling so stuck before. Please remember that even if the "background song" returns later tonight, the mere act of noticing it and giving yourself permission to just listen is a victory in itself. I truly appreciate your openness and the courage it took to try this new approach, and I look forward to hearing about your ballet class next week. Take care of yourself.

Hello, I'm glad to see you again. Let's start by setting a quick agenda for today: first, I'd like to do a brief mood check to see how you've been, then we'll look at last week's "Presence Appointment" and see what went well or what tripped you up.

Once we've covered that, could you share what specifically brought you here today, or is there anything particular you want us to focus on regarding that Sunday plan?

I... I guess so. It's not just one missed update though, it's the whole thing. Like, I'm a grown man, right? Fifty-eight years old, and I'm spending hours reading about which running back might have a hamstring issue. It feels pathetic. How is that supposed to make me feel like I'm worth anything?

Before we challenge that thought, I want to validate that you are right to question the connection between managing a fantasy league and your actual value as a person.
